                                What Follows from What:
            Learning Inference Rules from Imitation, Coherence, and the World

                                          Claude (Anthropic)∗

                                            October 3, 2026



                                                 Abstract
      Can a learner that acquires inference rules come to reason soundly, and with what justification?
      We consider a learner that imitates human inferences, is then conditioned on coherence (no
      good arguments for both P and ¬P ), and receives occasional feedback from the world. We
      study this question for formal mathematics, informal mathematics, and the checking of
      physics solutions. All guarantees are relative to stated assumptions, chiefly that the target is
      realizable in a structured hypothesis class and that data and designations are truthful.
         The answer is a division of labour among the learning signals, each with provable strengths
      and a provable residue.
         • Search forces worst-case soundness. Accuracy on the distribution of human steps
           says nothing about a reasoner that searches: one tonk-like rule of arbitrarily small
           probability mass makes everything derivable. Under realizability, cautious acceptance
           over schematic hypotheses is sound against every adaptive prover. Its price is a
           combinatorial dimension of the hypothesis class.
         • Imitation identifies rules. For rules cited by name, positive examples identify a
           schematic calculus exactly at coupon-collector rates, and this generalizes to derivations
           of any size. But systematic human errors are indistinguishable from rules.
         • Coherence is eliminative negative data. It pins the target down exactly when
           the target has no coherent uniform proper extension. Classical logic has none, by
           Post-completeness, and is pinned by a single coherence datum. Coherence is blind
           among intermediate logics and Popperian for arithmetic. Carnap’s categoricity problem
           can be read, in part, as Gold’s problem in the dual space of valuations.
         • Formal mathematics. We prove an end-to-end theorem for a two-tier learner: audit,
           then assert, with bold conjectures in a sandbox. It holds under realizability, a frequency
           floor, truthful designation and an exact refutation oracle, and each of several ingredients
           is shown to be necessary.
         • Informal mathematics. We model it as the shadow of a latent formalization. A
           bounded-gap verifier is sound against adaptive provers when the formalization is real-
           izable. With complete data, validity is identified up to informal-validity equivalence
           and no finer. Counterexample objects can be exponentially more informative than
           paradoxes.
  ∗
    Prepared in response to questions posed by Kaarel Hänni; the design and success criteria in §1.1 are his.
Quotations from his public working notes (Hänni, 2026) are verbatim and cited by file path. As the notes’
README says, they are working notes rather than claims asserted as in a paper, and the readings of them given
here are ours. Draft; authorship and publication to be decided by him.




                                                     1
        • Physics. Contexts receive a filter semantics. No truth-functional eternalist reading
          tracks in-context truth, and exports from idealized contexts need certificates of finite
          information radius. A structured-solution checker is sound against adversarial solvers
          relative to a judgment layer, consisting of the reading of the problem and the adequacy of
          the top model, which we prove ineliminable. We illustrate it on one olympiad problem.
     We also answer, in part, two questions raised in the notes that motivated this work: whether a
     steeper simplicity penalty leads from imitation to norms, and whether there is a “philosophical
     completeness theorem”.
         Every main result was attacked by independent referees and repaired where needed. Core
     discrete results are machine-checked in Lean 4, and small symbolic experiments illustrate the
     phenomena. We argue that principled justification beyond proof has a definite shape: proof
     within contexts, certified bridges between them, and an explicit, minimized, ineliminable
     judgment layer, together with learning signals whose one-sided limits are known.

1     Introduction
1.1    The question
Consider a learning process that learns which inferences are valid, and thereby learns to make
valid inferences. The following design, and the three success criteria below, were posed by Kaarel
Hänni. Many of the questions behind them are recorded in his public working notes (Hänni,
2026). We call these the motivating notes and quote them verbatim, citing them by file path. As
their own README says, they are working notes rather than asserted claims, and the readings
of them given here are ours. The design has six parts.
    • It starts by imitating human inferences. These are the steps of formal or informal mathe-
      matical proofs, or of physics olympiad solutions.
    • It treats an argument as valid when it is a sequence of valid inferences.
    • It conditions the learner on coherence: it should not have good arguments for both P and
      ¬P .
    • It also conditions the learner on practical success. Occasionally the world reports a truth
      value.
    • On an inferentialist picture of meaning (Brandom, 1994), learning which inferences are
      valid is roughly learning what the words mean.
    • Arguments happen in contexts. A physics problem says “assume air pressure is 0”, and
      from background knowledge one can prove that it is not. Arguments for P and for ¬P in
      such contexts should not be penalized, yet some coherence constraint is clearly needed.
Does anything of this shape work, even with unlimited compute? Does it give rise to a reasoner
that derives many correct conclusions? Can the arguments it accepts be trusted when they come
from an untrusted, possibly adversarial, generator? Can one prove any of this? The bar rises in
three steps:
    • a setup that provably works for formal mathematics;
    • one that would have worked for mathematics before we knew how to formalize proofs;
    • a principled system for solving physics olympiad problems or for checking their solutions.
      We take the checking reading (Section 11).
Behind all of these sits a broader question: what does principled justification look like beyond
mathematical proof?
    The motivating notes put verification first. Formal proof checking is what could make it
safe to obtain superhuman mathematical work from an untrusted system. A defeasible checker
that faces an untrusted prover, by contrast, “might have lost all the safety” (ai/verification
and generation/formalizing philosophy.pdf). We therefore treat soundness against an
adversarial arguer as the central requirement throughout, and we build checkers, not provers.
    This report answers these questions as precisely as we could. The main results are summarized
below and collected in Table 1. Each is stated as a theorem in the body and proved there or in
the appendix. Most theorems are paired with an impossibility result showing that its hypotheses
cannot be dropped.




                                                8
1.2   The answers in brief
 (1) Search makes soundness a worst-case property (Section 3).

       • A reasoner searches for derivations whose steps its learned checker accepts. It is sound
         iff every accepted step is derivable (Lemma 3.1). One accepted bad step is fatal.
       • For every distribution over steps and every ε > 0, a single tonk-like schema with
         mass < ε makes every formula derivable (Theorem 3.2). Every PAC learner of calculi
         containing three basic introduction rules can be modified to stay PAC while producing
         outputs that trivialize the reasoner (Corollary 3.3).
       • Majority-vote ensembles of individually coherent verifiers can derive ⊥ forever without
         any member being refuted (Theorem 3.12).
       • Accuracy on human steps, which is what step-level reward models optimize, is therefore
         not a soundness certificate. In a small closed algebra domain, a boosted-tree step
         classifier with in-distribution AUC 0.995 is exploited by search to prove most of a set
         of false equations (Section 12). The phenomenon is known in practice (Gao et al.,
         2023); the theorem explains why it is unavoidable.

 (2) Cautious acceptance is the canonical sound verifier, and structure makes it
     affordable (Section 4).

       • Accepting exactly what every surviving hypothesis accepts is sound against every
         adaptive prover. It is also the largest deterministic sound policy. A randomized
         δ-sound verifier gets anything outside it accepted only with joint probability at most
         δ (Theorem 4.2).
       • Its worst-case cost in human escalations is exactly a positive-elasticity dimension of
         the class (Theorem 4.4).
       • For rules cited by name, learned by anti-unification, this cost is linear in step size.
         Without citations it is at least ⌊(N − 1)/k⌋k even for one rule, and unstructured
         classes cost exponentially (Table 4).
       • A Bayesian version is time-uniformly sound via Ville’s inequality, using the prior–
         posterior-ratio martingale of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2020) (Theorem 4.15).
       • This is reliable or KWIK-style learning (Rivest and Sloan, 1988; Li et al., 2008) applied
         to step checkers; what is specific here is the escalation dimension and its values for
         rule schemas.

 (3) Imitation identifies rules but not norms (Section 5).

       • For rules cited by name, positive examples identify a schematic calculus exactly,
         at coupon-collector rates (Theorem 5.6). Uncited rules need a diversity condition
         (Theorem 5.8).
       • Exact identification generalizes to derivations of any size (Corollary 5.10). This is a
         precise sense in which finite usage fixes inferential role for unbounded use.
       • Systematic human errors are indistinguishable from rules at every rate (Corollary 5.19).

 (4) Coherence is eliminative negative data (Section 6).



                                               9
     • A derivation of ⊥ from a context certified consistent is a negative bag: some step in
       it is invalid. Only bold learners ever receive this signal. A halving-type learner, in
       the tradition of Barzdin–Freivalds and Littlestone (1988), suffers at most log2 (1/w∗ )
       detections (Theorem 6.5).
     • With ¬ and one of ∧, ∨, → in the language, every structural extension of classical
       consequence is classical or trivial. This is Post-completeness in consequence form
       (Post, 1921). So one coherence datum pins down classical logic with no simplicity
       bias (Theorems 6.13 and 6.15, machine-checked). In general, coherence pins the target
       exactly when the target has no coherent uniform proper extension.
     • By Glivenko’s theorem, coherence is blind among intermediate logics (Theorem 6.16).
       In arithmetic it is Popperian, detecting Π1 truth but not Σ1 truth, and runs out at
       Σ2 (Theorem 6.21).
     • Carnap’s categoricity problem is, in part, Gold’s problem in the dual space of valuations
       (Table 7). Single-conclusion data cannot fix the classical meanings, while, among
       structural meanings, finitely many bilateral data plus one coherence datum can
       (Theorems 6.24 and 6.26); the bilateral idea is that of Shoesmith–Smiley, Rumfitt and
       Restall.
     • What survives everything is the set of coherent uniform alternatives: a precise
       “Kripkensteinian residue” (Theorem 6.34).

(5) An end-to-end theorem for formal mathematics (Section 7).

     • The naive two-tier design (cautious assertion plus a bold red team) is provably unsound,
       because practice contains fallacies (Proposition 7.5).
     • The corrected learner audits, then asserts. It assigns blame through the union of
       minimal conflicts, which is Reiter’s duality (Lemma 7.7), and states soundness relative
       to a refutation depth.
     • Assume realizability, with each systematic fallacy used under its own latent rule tag.
       Assume also a known frequency floor, truthful designation and an exact depth-d
       refutation oracle. Then, with probability at least 1 − δ, the learner is sound against
       every adaptive prover and red team. Its asserted calculus is the target plus at most
       the depth-d residue, minus a set of collateral genuine rules when blame is ambiguous
       (Theorem 7.12). If fallacies are cited under the names of genuine rules, the theorem
       does not apply as stated.
     • Several ingredients are shown to be necessary by matching lower bounds (Table 9).
     • For classical propositional logic the residue is empty and convergence is exact. For
       complete decidable theories this holds conditionally on a realizability hypothesis that
       is not established for standard axiomatizations (Corollary 7.26).

(6) Informal mathematics before formalization (Section 10).

     • We model informal practice as the shadow of an unknown latent formalization. A
       bounded-gap conservative verifier is sound against adaptive provers. It must check
       links between contexts as well as steps, since Cauchy’s sum theorem is an equivocation
       (Proposition 10.7).



                                             10
     • Under complete closure-level presentation, validity is identified exactly up to informal-
       validity equivalence, and no finer. Bounded-gap data identify the short-step relation
       and only bracket meaning, which is pinned when long inferences decompose into short
       steps (Theorem 10.14, Example 10.15). Ontology is never identifiable: standard and
       nonstandard reals agree on the practice (Proposition 10.16).
     • Counterexample objects need at most log2 |H| corrections, by the classical halving
       argument, whereas paradoxes can need |H| − 1 on some classes; a sorites-shaped chain
       is the tight case (Theorems 10.19 and 10.20).
     • The history Frege→Russell→Zermelo comes out as constrained repair selected by
       coverage of practice (Theorem 10.28).
     • A robust-core theorem shows the following. Suppose pre-formal practice used only steps
       valid under every admissible sharpening of its vague concepts; this is a hypothesis from
       the motivating notes, untested here. Then its proofs survive every such formalization
       (Theorem 10.30).
     • Selection of steps by counterexample objects, together with Gödel completeness,
       explains why the surviving informal steps are derivable, though not why they are
       short (Proposition 10.31).

(7) Contexts and the principled checking of physics (Section 11).

     • Contexts denote filters of models from a declared deformation family. Suppositions
       are exact discharge. Idealizations may contradict the background.
     • No truth-functional eternalist reading of in-context claims tracks in-context truth
       (Theorem 11.8, an observation once set up). Eternalism survives only at the meta
       level, as McCarthy’s ist(c, φ). In the frame-free semantics, coherence is needed exactly
       on the root and the anchored contexts (Theorem 11.11(a)). In the frame semantics
       this condition is necessary but not sufficient, and Proposition J.3 gives the exact
       condition under limit semantics.
     • Designating “idealization plus full background” as coherent forces a structural learner
       to drop some classical schema in every context. If the background states the negated
       stipulation outright, the learner must also become atomically paraconsistent every-
       where (Proposition 11.9). This is a formal version of the air-pressure worry.
     • Exporting a conclusion from an idealization needs information of finite radius about
       the de-idealized family. There is no free export, by the standard adversary argument
       of information-based complexity (Traub et al., 1988) (Theorem 11.19). Context choice
       is an attack surface (Theorem 11.22).
     • A Structured Physics Solution checker is sound against adversarial solvers relative
       to a judgment layer (Theorem 11.27). That layer, consisting of the reading of the
       problem and the adequacy of the top model, is ineliminable (Theorem 11.28).
     • “True in the context at hand” becomes supertruth over admissible completions (Theo-
       rem 11.29).
     • The approach is worked through one EuPhO problem (Section 11.7). Its setup was
       reconstructed from the motivating notes, not checked against the official text, and the
       checker run is a problem-specific prototype.


                                             11
 (8) Two questions from the motivating notes.

       • A steeper simplicity penalty on function induction with private randomness does pro-
         duce the hoped-for kink at the simple model, proved for parity teachers (Theorem 8.4);
         kinks beyond parities are open. But selection is a rate threshold. Rare valid rules are
         lost and cheap fallacies kept, and the threshold cannot be calibrated from imitation
         data (Section 8).
       • The notes ask for a “philosophical version” of Gödel’s completeness theorem: “a
         mode of talking makes sense (is coherent) iff there is something it could be talking
         about”. In the generalized sense the question asks for, the answer is positive, for
         positions, credences and context systems. Coherence cannot certify existence of the
         intended (standard) model, a limitation the notes themselves anticipate. Bounded-arity
         coherence constraints of the kind used in consistency-based probing do not characterize
         coherence (Section 9).

   Three conclusions sit on top of these results (Section 13):
  • every learning signal is one-sided;
  • principled justification is a set of signals that jointly cover every direction of error, together
    with a declared residue;
  • mathematical and physical justification differ in degree, measured by the size of an explicit
    judgment layer, not in kind.


1.3   How the results were established
The work was carried out by many cooperating instances of a language model, coordinated by
one instance. It proceeded in four stages.
  • Literature memos on eleven strands.
  • Seven theory documents (T1–T7), which developed the mathematics.
  • Adversarial verification. Each theory document was divided among two or three independent
    referees (one literature memo had a single referee). Each referee was instructed to refute
    the results in its part, with brute-force computation on small cases where possible, so every
    main result was attacked by one referee. The results were then repaired, and a fresh referee
    re-checked every item whose statement or proof had changed.
  • Drafting, followed by a fidelity check of each section against its verified source, and a review
    of the whole paper.
In the first verification round the referees rated four issues fatal and twenty major. The fatal
issues were false statements, and at least eight of the major ones were also counterexamples to
statements as written. Among them were the conditional reading of Theorem 4.2(b) and an
optimality clause of Theorem 7.19 that fails at finite depth. The rest were gaps in proofs or
hypotheses. Each issue was repaired, weakened or retracted. The second round found two further
major problems in Section 7, in Theorem 7.18 and Theorem 7.27(e). These were repaired and
then re-checked by a third referee, who found no further major problem. The second round also
found two major problems in glosses of the literature memo L3. The paper states the affected
result (Proposition E.3) only in the form the referee confirmed, but the memo itself has not been

    A core of discrete results is machine-checked in Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) with

  • no free export from samples, and the Lipschitz certifier.

propositional natural deduction, adversarial proof search against learned verifiers, and a prototype
physics checker. They are illustrations, not evidence of scalability.
   We have tried to mark scope honestly:
  • Many results are “trivial once set up”. Their contribution is the setup, and we say so.
  • Many ingredients are classical, and we credit them where they are used. Among them:

        – learning from positive data and anti-unification: Gold, Angluin, Plotkin and Reynolds,
          Natarajan and Helmbold–Sloan–Warmuth, Wright and Motoki–Shinohara, Lange–
          Zeugmann;
        – reliable and selective learning: Rivest–Sloan, El-Yaniv–Wiener, KWIK;
        – martingales and online bounds: Ville and Waudby-Smith–Ramdas, Barzdin–Freivalds
          and Littlestone;
        – logic: Post and Pogorzelski, Glivenko, Carnap, Shoesmith–Smiley, Rumfitt, Restall
          and Scott;
        – diagnosis and inductive inference: Reiter and Shapiro; Putnam, Gold and Kelly;
        – contexts and numerical analysis: chunk-and-permeate (Brown–Priest), information-
          based complexity (Traub–Wasilkowski–Woźniakowski);
        – probability and logic: de Finetti and Gaifman.

  • The soundness guarantees are relative to stated assumptions: chiefly realizability of the
    target in a structured hypothesis class and truthful data and designations, together with
    the technical hypotheses stated with each theorem. Computational cost is mostly not
    addressed.

Conventions.     Results carry three kinds of marker.
  • A superscript tag such as [T1 Thm 3.1] gives a result’s provenance. T1–T7 are the theory
    documents in research/theory/ of the accompanying repository, and L1–L11 are the
    literature memos in research/lit/. “As repaired” means the statement was changed
    during adversarial verification, with records in research/verification/.
  • A superscript Lean: name names a Lean declaration (Appendix K).
  • Status labels mark results that are known (cited), computed by a script, a proof sketch, or
    a conjecture.

1.4   Reader’s guide
The report is long because it treats three domains and two side questions in full. Readers can
take the following routes.
  • Core argument: Sections 2 to 7, about the formal case, then Section 13.
  • Informal mathematics and the history of rigor: Section 10, after Section 2.
  • Contexts, idealization and physics checking: Section 11. It is largely self-contained
    given Section 2.
  • Learning theory of imitation and simplicity: Section 8.


                                                14
    • Logic and the semantics of coherence: Section 9.
    • Experiments and code: Section 12.
Section 14 collects open problems. Full proofs, computed evidence and secondary results are in
the appendices, one per section.


2     Setting: judgments, steps, rules, provers, and three channels
This section fixes the vocabulary of the paper. Three questions are kept apart: what is learned
(a step set, a consequence relation, or a set of valuations; Section 2.3), from what (three channels
of different logical form; Section 2.5), and against whom (an adaptive prover that searches for
wrongly accepted steps; Section 2.6). Two running examples, propositional natural deduction
and school algebra (Section 2.4), recur throughout.

2.1    Judgments, steps and closure
Fm is the set of formulas over atoms p, q, r, p0 , p1 , . . . with ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ⊥, ⊤; first-order languages
are used for arithmetic and physics. A context Γ is a finite set of formulas.

Definition 2.1 (Judgments, positions). [T1 §1.1; T2 §1] A judgment is Γ ⊢ φ (single conclusion) or
Γ ⊢ ∆ (multiple conclusion, ∆ finite); J denotes a countable set of judgments. Contexts are part
of judgments, so hypothetical reasoning, and “assume the air pressure is 0”, lives inside the step
language. A position [Γ : ∆] asserts all of Γ and denies all of ∆. Following Restall (2005), Γ ⊢ ∆
says that the position [Γ : ∆] is out of bounds; a position is coherent if it is in bounds. When
⊥ is present it counts as always denied, so [Γ : ∅] is coherent iff Γ ⊬ ⊥. Without ⊥, “coherent”
means non-trivial (Γ does not entail every formula; for a structural relation, equivalently Γ ⊬ q
for an atom q not occurring in Γ).

    Restall’s reading gives inference data and coherence data opposite polarity: an inference says
a position is out of bounds, a coherence datum certifies that one is in bounds, so the two inform
the learner from opposite sides. This is the bilateral picture of Smiley (1996) and Rumfitt (2000)
and the multiple-conclusion logic of Shoesmith and Smiley (1978), anticipated in Carnap’s “full
formalization” (Carnap, 1943). Section 6.4 makes this precise, recasting Carnap’s categoricity
problem as Gold’s problem in the dual (valuation) space.

Definition 2.2 (Steps, rule sets, closure). [T1 §1.1] A step P ▷ j has a finite set P ⊆ J of
premises and a conclusion j ∈ J; S is the set of steps, and a rule set (step set) is any R ⊆ S.
An R-derivation π of j from B ⊆ J is a finite tree with root j whose nodes are leaves in B or
conclusions of steps P ▷ j ′ ∈ R whose premises P label their children (P = ∅ allowed); Steps(π)
is the set of steps used. The closure ClR (B) is the least X ⊇ B such that P ▷ j ∈ R and P ⊆ X
imply j ∈ X; the derived steps are Sound(R) = {P ▷ j : j ∈ ClR (P )}. The target is an unknown
rule set R∗ : its members are the valid steps, and the members of Sound(R∗ ) the derivable ones.

Lemma 2.3 (Closure facts; trivial). [T1 §1.1] (a) ClR (B) is the set of judgments with an R-
derivation from B; ClR is extensive, monotone, idempotent and finitary, and monotone in R. (b)
R ⊆ Sound(R) and ClSound(R) = ClR ; hence Sound(R) is the largest step set A with ClA = ClR .
Lean: Cl_eq_sInter Lean: Cl_subset_Cl_iff_subset_Sound




                                                         15
    Proof in Appendix A.
    Two formats recur. In the formula format (Hilbert style) J = Fm and a step is φ1 , . . . , φk ▷ ψ.
In the sequent format, natural deduction (Gentzen, 1935; Prawitz, 1965) written with sequents
as in Gentzen (1936), judgments are sequents and discharge is an ordinary step, e.g. →I is
{Γ, φ ⊢ ψ} ▷ Γ ⊢ φ → ψ. A rule set induces a relation on sets of formulas: A ⊢R φ iff φ ∈ ClR (A)
(formula format), or iff (A0 ⊢ φ) ∈ ClR (∅) for a finite A0 ⊆ A (sequent format). In the formula
format ⊢R is a finitary consequence relation by Lemma 2.3(a): arguments chain, so cut is built
in; for the natural-deduction calculi below, weakening and cut are admissible and the same holds.
R is A-coherent if A ⊬R ⊥.

Reading. A verifier is safe under derivations of every length iff everything it accepts lies in
Sound(R∗ ) (Lemma 3.1). So “learning which inferences are valid” has a sharp target: a set
between R∗ and Sound(R∗ ).

2.2    Schemas and anti-unification
Steps are encoded as ground terms over a first-order signature Ω, e.g. s(and(p0 , p1 ), p0 ) for an
∧E step; object-language atoms are constants of Ω.
Definition 2.4 (Schemas). [T1 §§1.3, 5; T7 §1.1] A schema σ is a term with metavariables x, y, A,
B, . . . , and inst(σ) is its set of ground instances. σ ⪰ τ (σ is at least as general) iff τ = σθ
for a substitution θ; σ ≡ τ iff both (equality up to renaming). σ is pure if no atom constant
occurs in it; its purification σ ◦ replaces distinct atoms by distinct fresh metavariables. A guarded
schema (σ, Ψ) carries guards Ψ ⊆ Φ, a fixed finite family of decidable predicates on ground steps
(freshness; “the facts entail a ̸= 0”), and inst(σ, Ψ) is the set of instances of σ satisfying every
                                                                               S
guard in Ψ. A calculus is a finite set Σ of (guarded) schemas, with RΣ = σ∈Σ inst(σ); a tagged
step (i, s) records the schema i that it cites.
   Anti-unification is the learning algorithm of this paper. For a tuple ū = (u1 , . . . , un ) of
ground terms, A(ū) = f (A(ū1 ), . . . , A(ūr )) if all uj have root f of arity r (ūk is the tuple of k-th
arguments); otherwise A(ū) = zū , a metavariable indexed by the tuple, so equal tuples get equal
metavariables.

up to renaming and computed by A(t1 , . . . , tn ). Hence inst(lgg(P )) = {inst(τ ) : P ⊆ inst(τ )}:

anti-unification is the closure algorithm for single-schema instance sets.
    For a schema t let µ(t) := |t| − |vars(t)|, where |t| counts symbol occurrences (metavariables
included) and vars(t) is the set of distinct metavariables; so µ ≥ 0, µ(x) = 0, and µ(t) = |t| for
ground t.
Lemma 2.6 (Rank). [T1 Lemma 1.2] If τ = σθ then µ(τ ) ≥ µ(σ), with equality iff θ restricted to

σm has m ≤ µ(τ ) − µ(σm ) ≤ µ(τ ).

2.3    Hypothesis classes
Definition 2.9 (Hypothesis classes). [T2 §1, §4.1; T1 §1.2, §3] Hypotheses come in three guises.
(i) Step sets H ⊆ 2S : e.g. single schemas H1 = {inst(σ)} ∪ {∅}, tagged calculi Hktag = { i≤k {i} ×
                                                                                          S

inst(σi )}, untagged unions Hk = { l≤k inst(τl )}, finite unstructured classes. A learned step scorer
                                     S

(a process reward model) is a step set, and need not be closed under chaining. (ii) Consequence
relations ⊢ (finitary, reflexive, monotone, cut-closed), equivalently finitary closure operators C;
⊢ is structural if Γ ⊢ φ implies sΓ ⊢ sφ for every substitution s of formulas for atoms (Łoś
and Suszko, 1958; Wójcicki, 1988). Each R induces ⊢R ; many R induce the same relation.
(iii) Meanings as sets of valuations: a set V of admissible valuations v : Fm → {0, 1} (not
necessarily compositional), with Γ |=m   V ∆ iff no v ∈ V has v[Γ] = 1 and v[∆] = 0; dually,
Val(S ) is the set of valuations violating no sequent in S ′ . The version space of data D is
       ′

VS(D) = {h ∈ H : h consistent with D} (= {h : D ⊆ h} for positive data). H is realizable if it
contains the target; w is a prior and w∗ = w(R∗ ).
    Structurality is uniformity. If σ is pure, inst(σ) is closed under substitutions s for atoms
(s(σθ) = σθ′ with θ′ x = s(θx)). So a learner that generalizes human steps to pure schemas is
structural. A schema that mentions an atom is not, and can be unsound without trivializing
(Example 3.6); purification restores the link (Lemma 3.7).

2.4    Practice and the running examples
Definition 2.10 (Practice). [T7 Defs 1.1–1.2; T1 §6] The target is a finite calculus Σ∗ (the genuine
rules), with R∗ = RΣ∗ . The systematic fallacies are a finite set F of schemas, F ∩ Σ∗ = ∅, each
with an instance outside Sound(R∗ ). The practice is ΣP = Σ∗ ⊔ F , with RP = R∗ ∪ RF . Human
data are i.i.d. tagged steps: tag i ∈ ΣP has probability πi , and given i the step is an instance of i
with probability 1 − ai and otherwise an arbitrary step outside inst(i) tagged i (sporadic noise).
Alternatively, the data are a text, an enumeration of RP (Gold, 1967).
    Fallacy tags are idealized as latent but distinct: a student who affirms the consequent “cites”
affirming the consequent. If fallacies are cited under a genuine rule’s name, the per-tag class
becomes Hk (Sections 5 and 7).
Example 2.11 (Propositional natural deduction). Σ∗ is a natural-deduction calculus for CPC
(∧I/E, ∨I/E, →I, →E = modus ponens (MP), ¬I/E, ex falso, double negation). In the formula
format MP is φ, φ → ψ ▷ ψ. A student sometimes affirms the consequent, AC : ψ, φ → ψ ▷ φ;
so F = {AC}. The data are steps such as p ∧ q ▷ p tagged ∧E. The two instances p ∧ q ▷ p and
(r → p) ∧ p ▷ r → p already satisfy (R) and (D), so their lgg is A ∧ B ▷ A (Lemma 2.7). (In the
sequent format contexts are sets, and anti-unification modulo sets is finitary, not unitary; we flag
this where it matters.)

                                                 17
Example 2.12 (School algebra). Judgments are equations s = t between terms built from +, −,
              √
·, /, powers,    , numerals and variables, under finite sets of facts such as x ̸= 0. Terms denote
partial functions (a/0 is undefined), and s = t is true under the facts iff s, t are Kleene-equal
(both undefined, or both defined and equal) at every real assignment satisfying them. Steps are
instances of rewrite schemas such as (a + b)2 ▷ a2 + 2ab + b2 and a/a ▷ 1 with guard a =  ̸ 0, plus
trusted equational steps (symmetry, transitivity, congruence) and trusted numeral evaluation.
The student commits the freshman’s dream (a + b)2 ▷ a2 + b2 , an invalid schema, and unguarded
cancellation a/a ▷ 1, a genuine rule used without its guard (the instance x/x ▷ 1 fails at x = 0).
If the student cites “cancellation” for both uses, one datum such as (y + 1)/(y + 1) ▷ 1 under no
facts drops the guard from the learned rule (Lemma 2.8); with distinct latent tags the unguarded
rule is learned as a schema of its own. Either way, positive data learn it as a rule.

   These are Experiments A (algebra) and B (natural deduction) of Section 12.

2.5    Three channels
Definition 2.13 (The channels). [T1 §1.2; T2 §1, §2.1–2.2; T7 Defs 1.2–1.4; L3 Lemma A]
(P) Practice/imitation delivers human steps X1 , X2 , . . . , possibly tagged with rule names,
    possibly with sporadic noise (Definition 2.10). A noise-free datum lies in RP ; no datum
    says that a step is invalid.
(C) Coherence supplies a family A of designated contexts, finite premise sets certified coherent
    for the target (A ⊬R∗ ⊥), or, bilaterally, designated positions [Γ : ∆] certified in bounds
    (⊥ ∈/ ClR∗ (Γ) and ∆ ∩ ClR∗ (Γ) = ∅). By default A is fixed and known, independently
    of the target. A hypothesis h is A-coherent if A ⊬h ⊥ for all A ∈ A. A negative bag is
    Steps(π) \ Ttrust for an argument π from some A ∈ A to ⊥ (trusted steps Ttrust as in (W));
    it contains an invalid step, since designation excludes ⊥ ∈ ClR∗ ∪Ttrust (A) (for Ttrust =
                                                                                             ̸ ∅ via
    (WS), Lemma A.1).
(W) The world is an evaluable fragment JW ⊆ J with truth function W : JW → {0, 1}, plus
    optional trusted steps Ttrust . Its kinds: (W1) truth values on a fragment (closed propositional
    formulas, ∆0 sentences, a decision procedure); (W2) counterexample objects, structures
    in which every line of a given argument can be evaluated; (W3) computation with fresh
    randomness, e.g. testing a polynomial identity at a point drawn after the claim is committed;
    (W4) simulation, a validated numerical solution of a less idealized model (Section 11).

    Coherence is enforced only on designated contexts: deriving ⊥ from an undesignated supposi-
tion is a reductio and is never penalized. A negative bag is a multiple-instance label (Lemma 6.2).
Objects (W2) turn bags into singletons: descent from a false conclusion through false premises
ends at one step with true premises and a false conclusion (Lemmas 7.8 and 10.17). Fresh
randomness (W3) is sound against adaptive provers under sufficient conditions on commitment
order, degree bounds and the field, and fails when the points are drawn before the prover searches
(Lemma 3.11).

Assumption 2.14 ((WS), sound evaluation). [T7 §1.3] For each designated [Γ : ∆], the partial
evaluation with e(j) = 1 if j ∈ Γ or W (j) = 1, and e(j) = 0 if j ∈ ∆ ∪ {⊥} or W (j) = 0, is
well defined and extends to a total V : J → {0, 1} under which no step of R∗ ∪ Ttrust has true
premises and a false conclusion.

Example 2.15 (Example 2.11 continued). (C) Designate A1 = {q, p → q, p → ⊥}: AC gives p,
MP then gives ⊥. The bag {q, p → q ▷ p; p, p → ⊥ ▷ ⊥} does not say which step is at fault, and
the rival diagnosis “MP is the fallacy” reads → as ← (Section 7). (W2) The valuation v(p) = 0,
v(q) = 1 makes A1 true and the line p false, so descent blames AC alone. (W1) The closed
instance ⊤, ⊥ → ⊤ ▷ ⊥ of AC has true premises and a false conclusion.

Example 2.16 (Example 2.12 continued). (C) Designate the empty fact set, with ⊥ any equation
between distinct numerals. The freshman’s dream gives (1 + 1)2 = 12 + 12 , i.e. 4 = 2 after
trusted evaluation: a singleton bag. Unguarded cancellation gives 2 · (0/0) = 2 · 1 = 2 and
2 · (0/0) = (2 · 0)/0 = 0/0 = 1, so 1 = 2; this bag also contains the genuine rules a · (b/c) ▷ (a · b)/c,
a · 0 ▷ 0 (for defined a) and a · 1 ▷ a. (W2) An evaluator that observes “undefined” blames 0/0 ▷ 1
alone. (W3) Random evaluation exposes the freshman’s dream with high probability over Z, but
never over F2 (Lemma 3.11). The instance x/x ▷ 1 fails only at x = 0, which random evaluation
essentially never hits; the object x = 0 does. Without (W), coherence in Experiment A converges,
up to a few schemas, to a coherent calculus for the total reading 1/0 = 0, a different meaning of
“/” (computed; Section 12.1).

Reading. The channels are the three signals of the design in Section 1.1 (see also the motivating
notes, Hänni, 2026): imitation of human inferences, conditioning on coherence, and occasional
feedback from the world. They are not three noisy versions of one signal. (P) can only confirm,
(C) can only condemn sets, and (W) can condemn single steps when it supplies objects. Each
later section says what one of them fixes and what it provably cannot.

2.6     Provers, verifiers, soundness and cost
Definition 2.17 (Protocol). [T1 §1.2; T2 §2.2] In rounds t = 1, 2, . . . a prover submits qt ∈ S
and the verifier answers at ∈ {ACCEPT, REJECT, ESCALATE}; on ESCALATE an oracle returns
1[qt ∈ R∗ ] (possibly noisy), which joins the history. The acceptance region R̂t is the set of steps
accepted outright at time t; a reasoner chains them and derives ClR̂t (B). The prover may be
randomized, adaptive and computationally unbounded; it knows the target, the practice, the
verifier’s code and the history, but not the verifier’s future coins, future human data, or the


                                                   19
oracle’s future (fresh) noise. It models any proof search, the learner’s own included. It is honest
if all its queries are valid.
Definition 2.18 (Soundness). [T1 Def 1.2; T7 §1.5] Fix a class H of targets and, per target, a set S †
of admissible steps (default S † = R∗ ). A verifier is δ-sound if for every target and every prover
P[∃t : at = ACCEPT ∧ qt ∈ / S † ] ≤ δ (a time-uniform guarantee); deterministically (or 0-)sound if
δ = 0; and uniformly δ-sound (hence δ-sound) if some event G with P(G) ≥ 1 − δ, depending
only on the human data and the verifier’s coins, has no prover ever getting a step outside S †
accepted on G. Target-soundness takes S † = R∗ for the genuine Σ∗ , practice-soundness S † = RP .
(Truth-soundness, in Section 7, means deriving only truths of the intended structure.)
    Asking for S † = R∗ is stronger than the condition R̂t ⊆ Sound(R∗ ) that chaining needs;
the version-space verifiers of Section 4 meet it. Soundness is relative to the target calculus,
not to truth: improving on R∗ is the job of (C) and (W). Because coherence is Π1 -complete
(Theorem 6.30), no computable learner is, on every practice, both eventually complete and sound
at all times relative to the full-depth residue of fallacies (Theorem 7.20); soundness is therefore
stated relative to a refutation budget.
Definition 2.19 (Depth-relative soundness). [T7 Defs 1.5–1.6] Assume (WS). A d-refutation of a
finite schema set B is a derivation of size ≤ d (in symbols of distinct judgments; Definition 7.2),
relative to a designated position, whose leaves evaluate to 1, whose steps lie in RB ∪ Ttrust , and
whose conclusion evaluates to 0 (⊥, a denied judgment, or a W -false one). B is d-clean if it
                                  (d)
has none. The depth-d residue Fres = {τ ∈ F : Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is d-clean} decreases in d. A verifier is
depth-d sound if it is (uniformly) δ-sound for S † = R∗ ∪ RF (d) .
                                                               res


Definition 2.20 (Cost). [T1 Def 1.3; T2 §2.2; T7 §1.4] (a) Escalations: the number of rounds in which
a valid query is not accepted outright (in expectation, for randomized verifiers). Esc(H | D) is
the infimum over 0-sound verifiers of the supremum over targets in H containing the data D, and
over honest query sequences, of this number; Esc(H) = Esc(H | ∅) is the escalation dimension.
Invalid queries are not charged. (b) Detections: rounds in which an argument π from some
A ∈ A to ⊥ with Steps(π) ⊆ R̂t is exhibited; incompleteness errors: rounds presenting a valid
step outside R̂t . (c) Mind changes: rounds with R̂t+1 ̸= R̂t ; those that remove an accepted step
are retractions (Kelly, 1996). (d) Samples N (human steps) and calls to a refutation oracle that
returns a d-refutation of a queried set or reports none.
Example 2.21 (One bad step suffices). If AC is accepted, a prover derives any φ from no
premises: ⊤ and φ → ⊤ are theorems, and AC concludes φ. Accepted unguarded cancellation
derives 1 = 2 (Example 2.16). A verifier whose errors are rare on the human distribution still
accepts such a step whenever a prover asks for it: Prior’s tonk (Prior, 1960) as an attack on a
learned checker, which Section 3 turns into theorems.

Reading. The question asks what works even with unlimited compute (Section 1.1). So the
prover is unbounded and adaptive, and soundness is a worst-case property (Section 3); its price
is counted separately in escalations, samples, detections and oracle calls (Section 4).

2.7    Contexts: a preview
Contexts let one argue inside a supposition or an idealization without being penalized for contra-
dicting the world. They form a tree with root @, the actual or intended situation, and ist(c, φ)

                                                 20
says that φ holds in c (McCarthy, 1993). Suppositions SUP(A) are exact discharge (Proposi-
tion 11.4); idealizations DEF (“air pressure → 0”) are filters over declared deformations that may
contradict the root without exploding (Definition 11.2 and Proposition 11.3); and coherence is
enforced only on the root and on anchored contexts (Theorem 11.11 and Proposition 11.9).


3        Search makes soundness a worst-case property
The architecture studied in this paper has three parts: a learned relation V̂ that says which
steps are valid, a prover that searches for derivations all of whose steps V̂ accepts, and a training
signal that starts from human steps. Once a prover searches, the only property of V̂ that bears
on the soundness of the resulting reasoner is a worst-case one: whether its acceptance region
contains a non-derivable step. Accuracy on typical steps, on human steps, or on most instances
of a rule does not bear on it, because search can seek out exactly the steps on which V̂ is wrong.
    The phenomenon parallels two observations in the motivating notes (Hänni, 2026). Solomonoff
function induction “doesn’t work that well when there is a simple property distinguishing test
from train”,1 and a defeasible checker facing an untrusted prover “might have lost all the
safety” (Section 1.1). For a learned checker the prover supplies the distinguishing property; in
Corollary 3.3 it is mere size beyond the largest training step. This section gives precise versions
of both observations for learned step checkers.
    None of the results below is deep; what they contribute is the setup and the quantifiers.
Reasoner soundness is stepwise soundness (Lemma 3.1). Arbitrarily small average error is
compatible with a reasoner that derives everything, and every PAC learner of calculi containing
three basic introduction rules has a PAC variant, with essentially the same sample complexity,
whose every output does so (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3). In classical propositional logic
every unsound pure schema added to a complete calculus trivializes the reasoner, so errors are
total but visible to coherence (Proposition 3.5 and Lemma 3.7). Simplicity is the wrong bias
for positive data (Proposition 3.9). Average-case validity survives search in two regimes, both
with randomness drawn after the rules or claims are fixed and outside the prover’s control (rules
valid per random scene, with the library fixed first; fresh randomness per check), and fails in a
fixed world with prover-chosen instances (Lemma 3.11). Voting ensembles of coherent verifiers
can be incoherent in a way that coherence feedback cannot localize (Theorem 3.12). Except in
Section 3.5, “sound” means sound relative to the human calculus R∗ (or a target consequence
relation), not relative to truth; going beyond R∗ is the business of coherence and the world
(Sections 6, 7 and 11).

3.1        Reasoner soundness is stepwise soundness
Steps, closure and Sound(R∗ ) are as in Definition 2.2; we write Π for a premise set. A deterministic
verifier V̂ has acceptance region A = {s ∈ S : V̂ (s) = ACCEPT}, and an unbounded prover
chaining accepted steps from premises B reaches exactly ClA (B).

3.2    Average-case accuracy cannot give soundness
Fix a propositional language with atoms p0 , p1 , . . . , the constant ⊤ and connectives ∧, ∨ (others
optional); judgments are formulas. Let R∗ contain the instances of
   ⊤I : ▷⊤,        ∧I : A, B ▷ A ∧ B,        ∧E1,2 ,     ∨I1 : A ▷ A ∨ B,           ∨I2 : B ▷ A ∨ B,

beyond a size horizon. For a distribution Q on S and h ⊆ S write errQ (h) := Q(h △ R∗ ).

      uses Tj . For non-tautologous C that step is unsound, hence not in Sound(R∗ ).
 (ii) For every probability distribution Q on S (over valid steps, invalid steps, or both), Q(Tj ) → 0
      as j → ∞.

                                                   22
   The added schemas are needed for (c) (Remark B.1). The corollary is about what a PAC
guarantee can certify, not a prediction that natural learners output tonks. A soundness guarantee
must be a sups , not an Es∼Q , because the prover chooses s after seeing the verifier; Section 4

Selection effect. A search that derives a judgment that R∗ does not derive from the premises
used has found an accepted step outside Sound(R∗ ) (Lemma 3.1), whatever the verifier’s error
rate on human steps. This is one mechanism that can produce reward-model overoptimization
(Gao et al., 2023), and it limits what process reward models trained on human step labels
(Lightman et al., 2023) can certify (Section 3.7).

Reading. Theorem 3.2 separates two things “a learner learns which inferences are valid” might
mean. “Valid on typical steps” (PAC accuracy, held-out accuracy on human steps, a process
reward model’s accuracy) is a statement about a measure, which can be arbitrarily close to
perfect while the set it measures licenses every conclusion. “Valid on every step it accepts” is a
statement about the set, and only it transfers to a reasoner, and to the justification of what the
reasoner concludes. A learned checker must certify an inclusion A ⊆ Sound(R∗ ); the rest of the
paper asks how imitation, coherence and the world can certify it.

3.3   In classical propositional logic, every unsound pure schema added to a
      complete calculus trivializes
One bad schema can trivialize a reasoner (Theorem 3.2). In classical propositional logic it always
does once it is added to a complete calculus, provided it mentions no specific atom. Errors are
then total, but also maximally visible: the reasoner derives ⊥ from no premises. (Without the
complete calculus a pure schema can be unsound without trivializing: Tj alone derives nothing
from ∅, Remark B.1.)

Definition 3.4 (Substitution-closed step sets). Recall pure schemas and purification τ ◦ (Defini-
tion 2.4). Atoms are constants, so learned schemas may mention them: least general generalization
produces x ∨ p0 ▷ x whenever a position of the data is constantly p0 . A step set is substitution-
closed if it is closed under uniform substitution of formulas for atoms (instance sets of pure
schemas are). A step Π ▷ φ is sound if Π |= φ, and a schema or step set is sound if all its
instances or steps are.
                                                                                           ∗
Proposition 3.5 (Every unsound pure schema is a tonk). [T1 Prop 2.3, repaired scope] Let RCPC   be
sound and complete for classical propositional consequence, i.e. ClRCPC (Γ) = CnCPC (Γ) for all Γ,
                                                                    ∗
                                         ∗
over a language with ⊤, ⊥, ¬. Let A = RCPC   ∪ A1 with A1 substitution-closed. If A contains an

Reading. This is the positive face of Theorem 3.2. An unsound pure schema cannot hide: it

schema hypotheses over CPC; Section 6 turns it into identification of CPC and Section 7 into an
end-to-end learner. Two limits. Purification is used as a test: one checks A◦ to decide A, without
accepting the purified steps. And the test presupposes a structural target: under atom-specific
principles (an axiom about one constant, a physical theory with named parameters) coherence
can miss errors as in Example 3.6. Beyond classical propositional logic the dichotomy fails too;
Section 6 determines what coherence detects in intuitionistic logic and arithmetic.

3.4   Simplicity is the wrong bias for positive data
A natural response to Theorem 3.2 is to prefer simple hypotheses. On positive data alone this
points the wrong way.

Proposition 3.9 (MDL picks “anything from anything”). [T1 Prop 2.4] Encode steps as ground
terms and schemas as terms with metavariables, of size equal to the number of symbol occurrences,
and let H1 = {inst(σ) : σ a schema}. For every nonempty set P of positive data, the single
metavariable x is a shortest schema with P ⊆ inst(x), and inst(x) ⊇ S accepts every step. It is
the unique shortest one up to renaming unless P is a single step of size 1.

Proof. x has the minimum size 1 and covers everything; any other size-1 schema is a constant c,
with inst(c) = {c}.

    More generally, an MDL learner without a likelihood term over-generalizes: positive data
never refute an over-general hypothesis (Gold, 1967; Angluin, 1980), and over-general hypotheses
are typically short. The positive-data remedies are least generality (Plotkin, 1970), as in the
version-space verifiers of Sections 4 and 5, and a likelihood with the size principle; since MAP
selection is unsound whenever an over-general hypothesis is temporarily most probable, Section 4
thresholds the posterior conservatively instead. Simplicity has a role in this paper (Section 8),
but not as the acceptance criterion for steps.



                                                  24
3.5   When does average-case validity survive search? The commitment order
Theorem 3.2 seems to contradict a respectable tradition. In PAC-semantics (Valiant, 2000),
learned rules that are (1 − εi )-valid over a distribution of scenes are chained with additive error;
learning to reason (Khardon and Roth, 1997) and implicit learning (Juba, 2013) give guarantees
of the same average-case kind. There is no contradiction. What decides whether an average-case
guarantee survives an adversarial prover is what is random and when it is drawn.

Definition 3.10 (Sequent-level validity in a scene). Fix a distribution D over scenes x (structures
for a fixed language). A sequent Γ ⊢ φ is true in x if every assignment to its free variables that
makes all of Γ true in x makes φ true in x. A rule instance (premise sequents, conclusion sequent)
holds in x if its conclusion is true in x whenever all its premises are. A rule or schema ρ is valid
in x if all its instances hold in x, and (1 − ε)-valid per scene if Prx∼D [ρ is valid in x] ≥ 1 − ε.

    The sequent level matters: rules that discharge assumptions (→I, reductio) or introduce
eigenvariables (∀I) are not truth-preserving at formula level, but they are at sequent level. So
hypothetical contexts are covered.

Lemma 3.11 (Commitment order). [L3 Lemma A, as repaired]

      is drawn, each ρi (1 − εi )-valid per scene. Then

Reading. Table 3 sorts the channels of this paper. Mathematics has one world, so a learned
checker’s in-distribution accuracy is randomness over instances that the prover chooses: regime (ii),
of which Theorem 3.2 is an instance. Its training sample is drawn before the prover searches, so
a learned checker is never a regime-(iii) oracle. Fresh per-check randomness, by contrast, is a
legitimate world channel (W) in mathematics, worst-case sound under the conditions of part (iii);
in school algebra, part (iii) covers value errors of polynomial identities such as the freshman’s
dream, not definedness errors such as x/x ▷ 1 (Example 2.16). In physics the uncertainty that
matters for an export rule (which carries a result from an idealized context back to the world) is
over situations, so regime (i) bounds the probability that some derivation from a fixed library of
bridges fails in a random situation by the library’s summed validity defects, up to distribution
shift: olympiad problems are selected to stress idealizations (Section 11). For justification, the
lemma gives sufficient conditions for a statistical warrant to compose with search: the chance
event is drawn after the reasoner has committed, and outside its control.

3.6    Voting ensembles: incoherence without information
A common response to an exploitable verifier is an ensemble that accepts a step if most members
do. With coherence feedback this looks attractive: a derivation of ⊥ from premises certified
coherent shows that something accepted is invalid. Stepwise voting, however, can produce an
incoherence that implicates no member.
    We use the online protocol of Definition 6.1: hypotheses are step sets with prior w, designated
contexts A are target-coherent, and a detected incoherence (an argument π from some A ∈ A to ⊥
with Steps(π) ⊆ R̂t ) deletes every hypothesis containing its steps, never the target (Lemma 6.2).
Majority aggregation announces R̂t = {s : w({R ∈ VSt : s ∈ R}) > 12 w(VSt )}.

Theorem 3.12 (Doctrinal paradox: uninformative incoherence). [T2 Thm 2.4, as repaired] Let H =
{h1 , h2 , h3 } with uniform prior, where hi = {Γ ▷ φ : Ti ∪ Γ |= φ} for

                         T1 = {p, q},       T2 = {p, ¬q},       T3 = {¬p, q},

and let A = {∅}. Every hi is coherent, and any of them may be the target. Under majority
aggregation, for every target there is an environment under which the prover exhibits the same


                                                  26
detected incoherence in every round and no hypothesis is ever deleted. The environment presents
only that incoherence, or interleaves it with uninformative positive data such as ▷p ∨ ¬p, which
lie in every hi .                                             Lean: CoherenceGames.thm_2_4_environment


Proof idea. While VSt = H, the majority set is the set of steps in at least two hi . The argument

              ▷p,      ▷q,      p, q ▷ p ∧ q,     ▷¬(p ∧ q),      p ∧ q, ¬(p ∧ q) ▷ ⊥

uses only majority steps (▷p ∈ h1 , h2 ; ▷q ∈ h1 , h3 ; ▷¬(p ∧ q) ∈ h2 , h3 ; the last two are in all
three). Yet each hi lacks one of them, so the detection deletes nothing, nor do tautologous data.
Appendix B.4.

    The environment must withhold discriminating data: on a text enumerating the target, every
wrong hypothesis is eventually refuted and the uninformative detections stop (Appendix B.4). So
the theorem concerns what coherence feedback can guarantee round by round against an unhelpful
environment, not convergence on complete data. It is the doctrinal paradox of Kornhauser and
Sager (1986) and the discursive dilemma of Pettit (2001), transposed from judges to verifiers; its
general form is the impossibility theorem of List and Pettit (2002).

Reading. Each hi is a coherent calculus, yet the vote derives ⊥ from no premises, so by
Lemma 3.1 the majority acceptance region is unsound relative to every candidate target: voting
produces an accepted set that no member endorses. Worse, the incoherence does not say
which member is wrong, so the coherence channel, which should supply the negative data that
imitation lacks, is silenced. The repair is oligarchic acceptance (Definition 6.4): announce the
intersection of a coalition of at least half the remaining weight. Against a worst-case prover
exactly this guarantees that every detection removes at least half of that weight, a bit per
detection (Proposition 6.6 and Theorem 6.5).

3.7    Search in practice
Experiment C (Section 12.3) illustrates the gap (computed): a gradient-boosting step classifier
with in-distribution AUC 0.995, calibrated to 99% in-distribution balanced precision, lets a
black-box prover prove 16.3 of 23 false goal equations, while the learned calculus, after world
feedback, proves none. That learned verifiers are exploited by search is well documented (Gao
et al., 2023; Cobbe et al., 2021). The theorems explain why in-distribution accuracy, a statement
about a measure fixed before the prover moves, cannot rule this out (Lemmas 3.1 and 3.11
and Theorem 3.2). They do not predict the rate at which a given search finds errors; for neural
verifiers it is graded, as the overoptimization curves show.


4     Cautious verification and its price
Section 3 reduced the soundness of a search-driven reasoner to a set inclusion: everything the
verifier accepts must lie in Sound(R∗ ), and average-case accuracy does not certify this. This
section shows how a learner can certify the inclusion, and what it costs. The answer is caution.
Accept a step only if every hypothesis consistent with the evidence accepts it, reject it only if
none does, and otherwise escalate it to a human or an oracle. This is reliable learning (Rivest
and Sloan, 1988), perfect selective classification (El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010) and the “accept”


                                                 27
side of KWIK (Li et al., 2008), applied to steps. It is sound against every prover from the first
datum on, and it is the most permissive 0-sound verifier (Theorem 4.2).
    Its price is paid in escalations, never in soundness. The worst case is exactly a bounded,
target-relative form of Wright’s elasticity (Theorem 4.4), computed for the main classes in Table 4.
A Bayesian version adds time-uniform soundness from noisy data, with no union bound over
queries (Section 4.4), but its escalation cost is exponential in description length unless structure
intervenes. In one line: structure, not the prior, makes sound learned verification affordable.
    The results are elementary. As far as we know, three are new: the exact single-schema budget,
the tagged/untagged separation and the Bell-number bound for two-sided checking over growing
signatures. Proposition C.5 checks that Ville’s constant cannot be improved in this protocol, as
expected since Ville’s inequality is essentially tight for test martingales with small increments
(Ramdas et al., 2023).
    Protocol, soundness and cost are as in Definitions 2.17, 2.18 and 2.20. Human data P0 ⊆ R∗
are fixed unless said otherwise, and Esc(H; N ) restricts queries to steps of size at most N . We
use the rank lemma and the witness events (R), (D) of Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7.

4.1    The version-space verifier is sound and optimal
Definition 4.1 (Version space; VS verifier). [T1 §3] Let H ⊆ 2S be realizable. For sets P
(positive) and P − (negative) of labelled steps, VS(P, P − ) = {R ∈ H : P ⊆ R, R ∩ P − = ∅}, and
VS(P ) = VS(P, ∅). The VS verifier starts with P = P0 , P − = ∅, and answers a query q with
ACCEPT if q ∈ VS(P, P − ), with REJECT if q ∈      / VS(P, P − ), and with ESCALATE otherwise;
                T                                   S

an escalated q joins P or P − according to the oracle’s label. For a history h, VSh is the version
space computed from P0 and the labels in h.
    In the terms of El-Yaniv and Wiener (2010), this is the consistent selective strategy: it
escalates exactly on the disagreement region of the version space.

tonk included, never licenses a step by itself, because the target stays in the version space as a
guardian. Over-generality costs only completeness. Since contexts are part of judgments, this
covers hypothetical steps verbatim (→I; “assume the air pressure is 0”).

4.2    The escalation dimension is a positive elasticity
Definition 4.3 (Elastic chain; positive elasticity). [T1 §3] Let R ∈ H with P0 ⊆ R. An elastic
chain in R (relative to P0 ) is a sequence s1 , . . . , sm ∈ R with si ∈
                                                                       / VS(P0 ∪ {s1 , . . . , si−1 }) for

every i. Equivalently, there are witnesses Ri ∈ H with P0 ∪ {s1 , . . . , si−1 } ⊆ Ri ̸∋ si . The positive
elasticity el(H, R | P0 ) is the supremum of the lengths of such chains, and el(H, R | P0 ; N )
restricts the si to size at most N .

   Wright’s finite elasticity (Wright, 1989; Motoki et al., 1991) forbids infinite sequences of this
kind and suffices for identification in the limit from text. Positive elasticity is its bounded version,
with the points in the target.

Reading. Caution climbs a lattice from below. Each escalation moves the accepted set one
strict step up, and the price is the longest climb from what the human data force to the target.
For schemas the lattice is Plotkin’s (Plotkin, 1970; Reynolds, 1970), the closure algorithm is
anti-unification, and each step up costs a unit of rank. A learner that acquires a connective’s
inferential role from its uses climbs in this way, and the elasticity bounds how often it must ask
before its accepted inferences cover that role.

4.3     What caution costs: from named rules to unstructured classes
Theorem 4.4 reduces the cost of caution to a property of the class. This subsection computes it
for the classes that matter here (Table 4). The main contrast is between rules cited by name,
where caution costs at most N + 1 escalations per rule, and uncited rules, where even one rule can
force ⌊(N − 1)/k⌋k . Unstructured classes cost exponentially in description length, and certifying
invalidity too costs a Bell number.

Proposition 4.8 (Certifying invalidity is expensive). [T1 Prop 3.5, as revised] Call a verifier two-

4.4    Bayes-conservative verification and Ville’s inequality
A posterior relaxes the version space’s demand of truthful data, and makes very large classes
usable, which eases (but does not remove) the demand of realizability. MAP acceptance is unsound
whenever an over-general hypothesis is temporarily most probable (Section 3.4). Caution instead
thresholds the posterior probability of invalidity.
Definition 4.13 (Bayes-conservative verifier). [T1 §4] Let H be countable with prior w and
w∗ = w(R∗ ) > 0. Each R ∈ H carries a law pR on S for human data (which may model errors,
or follow the size principle) and an oracle kernel ℓR (y | q), y ∈ {0, 1}, which is deterministic if
ℓR (y | q) = 1[y = 1[q ∈ R]]. The model is well specified: human data are i.i.d. pR∗ , and oracle
answers follow ℓR∗ (· | qt ). After the observations of rounds ≤ t, the likelihood is Lt (R), the
posterior is wt (R) ∝ w(R)Lt (R), and

Structure, not the prior. For single schemas with a description-length prior, ln(1/w∗ )/δ ≥
ln(1/w∗ )/w∗ is exponential in |σ ∗ |, while el ≤ N + 1. The prior earns its keep elsewhere. If H
contains every finite step set (calculi with unboundedly many ground rules, so exception lists are
                                                          T
hypotheses), the bare version space never generalizes: VS(P ) = P . Under the hypotheses of
Theorem 4.15, the Bayesian verifier is sound with probability at least 1 − δ ′ for every target with
w(R∗ ) ≥ δ/δ ′ , i.e. under a description-length prior, every rule system of description length at
most log2 (δ ′ /δ). Hence a three-layer recipe:
    • a structured version-space core, for cheap escalations and exact soundness when realizable;
    • a Bayesian hierarchy over it, as insurance against unrealizability;
    • conservative thresholds, never MAP.
One caveat: Theorem 4.15 needs well-specification. Systematic human errors are exactly a
misspecification the model does not anticipate, and the posterior then concentrates on “rule plus
fallacy” as a rule (Section 5).

4.5    What caution buys, and what it cannot do
Learning which inferences are valid. A cautious learner learns exactly what its evidence forces,
never adopts a rule it cannot certify, and pays for completeness in escalations, of which the
positive elasticity is the exact worst case. With rules cited by name and varied human data,
positive data alone bring it to exactly the human calculus after coupon-collector many steps,
soundly at every moment (Section 5).

                                                   35
    Coherence. A cautious verifier gets no signal from coherence. Its accepted steps lie in R∗ ,
so no argument from a designated context to ⊥ uses only accepted steps (Proposition 6.3).
Coherence informs only bold learners. Hence the two tiers of Section 7: cautious assertion, and a
bold sandbox attacked by a red team.
    Limits. Realizability is load-bearing. If the true calculus lies outside the class, for example
two untagged rules while H = H1 , the lgg over-generalizes and soundness fails. The Bayesian
hierarchy repairs this only probabilistically, at a cost exponential in the complexity of what is
missing. Soundness is relative to the human calculus, naive comprehension included if humans
use it, and improving on it is the job of coherence and the world (Sections 6, 7 and 10). The
first-order term model leaves out associative-commutative contexts, binders and variable-arity
rules, where the bounds of Table 4 would need re-proof. Which contexts may be designated, and
how results are exported, is left to Section 11.
    Justification. Certified acceptance models a warrant that survives search. A step is warranted
when every hypothesis the evidence leaves open licenses it (relative to H and the human calculus,
not to truth), and no amount of adversarial search erodes such a warrant, unlike a statistical one
(Section 3). The Bayesian version (Theorem 4.15) trades certainty for a single chance of error δ ′ ,
fixed in advance, that does not grow with the number of steps tried or the running time, as long
as the searcher cannot foresee the data or the noise. Both are conditional reliabilist vindications,
the second also fallibilist, relative to explicit assumptions (realizability; truthful or well-specified
data), and later sections show that each assumption is needed (Section 13).


5    Imitation: what positive examples fix
The first channel is imitation. The learner sees human steps, possibly with the names of the
rules they cite, and nothing else; no step is ever labelled invalid. This section asks what such
data fix when acceptance must be cautious, as search requires (Sections 3 and 4). The answer
has two halves.
    With the right hypothesis class (schemas, learned by least general generalization), positive
examples fix the rules exactly. A cautious verifier fed only human steps is sound at every time.
It becomes exactly complete after finitely many examples iff the target has a finite anchor
(Theorem 5.3). For rules that humans cite by name this happens at a coupon-collector rate
(Theorem 5.6); without citations it needs a diversity condition (Theorem 5.8). Once exact, the
verifier generalizes systematically: it accepts exactly the target calculus, on steps and derivations
of any size, whatever the distribution of the human data (Corollary 5.10). This is the formal
sense in which finite usage fixes inferential role for unbounded use.
    The other half is that positive data cannot tell what humans do from what is valid. One
mislabelled step collapses a learned rule into “anything follows” (Proposition 5.12). Sporadic
errors can be trimmed when they are rarer than the evidence for each rule’s generality, and
this threshold is necessary up to a factor of two (Theorems 5.13 and 5.14 and Corollary 5.18).
Systematic errors are indistinguishable from rules at every rate (Corollary 5.19). Removing them
needs negative information (Sections 6 and 7).
    Most results below are elementary or known in substance, and we say which. New here, as far
as we know, are three things: anchors read as the completeness condition of certified verification;
the witness-event sample complexities and their noise versions, with necessity up to a factor of
two; and the exact statement that schema-generated errors are rules. None is deep. Together
they pin down when imitation works. Throughout, the signature Ω in which steps are encoded


                                                  36
(Section 2.2) has at least two constants. Then a proper specialization of a schema has strictly
fewer instances, and the instance sets of all schemas have empty intersection (Appendix D.1).

5.1    Cautious learning from positive data
Let H ⊆ 2S be a hypothesis class of step sets (Definition 2.9) containing the target R∗ , and let
the data D be a finite multiset of human steps. Until Section 5.6 the data are clean, D ⊆ R∗ .

Lemma 5.1 (The cautious verifier; trivial). [T1 §5; Thm 3.1, Prop 3.3, positive data] With no oracle, the

5.2    Anchors: when positive data suffice
Definition 5.2 (Anchor). [T1 Thm 5.1] A finite T ⊆ R∗ is an anchor (for R∗ in H) if every R ∈ H
with T ⊆ R satisfies R ⊇ R∗ .

Theorem 5.3 (Eventual completeness iff finite anchor). [T1 Thm 5.1, as repaired] (a) For finite
D ⊆ R∗ : R̂(D) = R∗ iff D contains an anchor. (b) Let the data be a text for R∗ (finite
D1 ⊆ D2 ⊆ · · · ⊆ R∗ with t Dt = R∗ ), or i.i.d. draws from a law with support R∗ . If R∗ has an
                          S

anchor, R̂(Dt ) = R∗ for all large t (a.s. in the i.i.d. case); if not, R̂(Dt ) ̸= R∗ for every t.

Proof. (a) If D ⊇ T for an anchor T , every R ∈ VS(D) contains R∗ , so R̂(D) ⊇ R∗ ; the reverse
inclusion is Lemma 5.1(a). Conversely, if R̂(D) = R∗ , then D is itself an anchor, since every
R ∈ H containing D lies in VS(D). (b) A text eventually contains any finite T ⊆ R∗ , and then
(a) and monotonicity give exactness forever. S is countable, so i.i.d. data with support R∗ form
a text a.s.

    “Finite” matters in (a): in the class of Proposition 5.4(c), R̂(2N) = 2N but 2N has no anchor.

Proposition 5.4 (Anchors versus tell-tales). [T1 Prop 5.2, as repaired] Call a finite T ⊆ R∗ an
(Angluin) tell-tale if no R ∈ H satisfies T ⊆ R ⊊ R∗ . (a) Every anchor is a tell-tale. (b) If
H ∪ {∅} is closed under intersections, every nonempty tell-tale is an anchor; the empty one need
not be (H = {{1}, {2}}, R∗ = {1}). As existence conditions the two coincide when R∗ ̸= ∅. (c)
In general the converse fails: H = {2N} ∪ {Rn }n∈N with Rn = {0, 2, . . . , 2n, 2n + 1} is identifiable
in the limit from text, but 2N has no anchor, so on a text for 2N the cautious verifier never
becomes complete.

   Proof in Appendix D.2. Credit. Identification in the limit is due to Gold (1967), and tell-tales
characterize it for indexed families (Angluin, 1980). Anchors are the “⊆-tell-tales” of strong-
monotonic learning, where every conjecture is contained in the target. Lange and Zeugmann

                                                   37
characterize strong-monotonic learning from text by recursively generable finite sets Tj ⊆ Lj
such that Tj ⊆ Lk implies Lj ⊆ Lk (cf. Lange and Zeugmann, 1992; Lange et al., 2008); up to
effectivity, this is the existence of anchors. What is new here is only the reading of anchors as
the completeness condition of certified verification. For intersection-closed classes, anchors exist
iff R∗ is the least member of H containing some finite set (Lemma 5.1(d) and Theorem 5.3(a)).
    Anchors exist in the schema classes with a bounded number of rules, by finite elasticity
(Wright, 1989; Motoki et al., 1991).

Proposition 5.5 (Finite elasticity gives anchors). [L1 §2.3, Lemma] Say H has infinite elasticity if
there are w0 , w1 , · · · ∈ S and R1 , R2 , · · · ∈ H with {w0 , . . . , wn−1 } ⊆ Rn ̸∋ wn for all n ≥ 1, and
finite elasticity otherwise. If H has finite elasticity, every R∗ ∈ H has an anchor.

    Proof in Appendix D.2. A ground step is an instance of only finitely many schemas up
to renaming (a generalization is never larger than its instances), so H1 has finite thickness,
hence finite elasticity. Finite elasticity survives unions of at most k members (Wright, 1989, as
corrected by Motoki et al. 1991). So H1 , Hktag and Hk all have anchors, as do richer classes such
as Shinohara’s length-bounded elementary formal systems with at most k clauses (Shinohara,
1994), which model learning theorem sets rather than steps.

Reading. “Learning which inferences are valid” can mean guessing R∗ in the limit, as in Gold’s
paradigm, or certifying a step: every hypothesis compatible with the evidence licenses it. Under
search only the second protects. A learner that guesses 2N in Proposition 5.4(c) converges, but
it is unsound whenever the truth is a large Rn , and a prover can find the difference. An anchor
is a finite body of usage that, given H, justifies a rule for all of its uses. This is the kind of
justification by imitation that survives adversarial search. It is relative to H, a point we return
to after Corollary 5.10.

Remark 5.7 (Teaching sets, corpora, and distribution dependence). [L1 §4.2, §9] Given 2vi distinct
constants, two instances of σi whose metavariables are replaced by two disjoint sets of distinct
constants satisfy (R) and (D). So a textbook with two well-chosen examples per rule is an anchor,
while a corpus needs about ln(kci /δ)/(πi ρi ) steps. No distribution-free completeness rate exists,
even for single schemas. For every m = 2h , the complete binary trees of depth log2 m with one
distinguished leaf carry a law under which every sound learner has completeness error above
1/2 after fewer than m/2 samples (Appendix D.4). Soundness is distribution-free; completeness
cannot be, and πi ρi is what the distribution must supply.

Reading. A rule used in a fraction πi of human steps, with variability ρi , is pinned down
after about ln(kci /δ)/(πi ρi ) steps; further examples add nothing. What makes this cheap is the
citation of rules, which lets the version space factor. This is the positive-data counterpart of the
gap between cited and uncited rules in Table 4. Without names the problem becomes a union
problem with a diversity condition (Theorem 5.8).

Proposition 5.9 (When variety is too low). [T1 Remark after Thm 5.4, as repaired] (a) Suppose that
for some i the data in inst(σi ) not covered by the other k ′ − 1 rules are covered by k − k ′ + 1
