of σi lies outside these specializations and the other rules. Then R̂Hk (D) ̸= R∗ . (b) For k ′ ≥ 2,
low variety need not block identification: for k = k ′ = 2, R∗ = inst(p(x)) ∪ inst(q(y)) and
D = {p(a), p(b), q(a), q(b)}, R̂H2 (D) = R∗ , although x takes only 2 = k roots.

    For k ′ = 1, (a) says that identification fails while a metavariable is instantiated with at most
k root symbols (and others are possible). Proofs are in Appendix D.6. For k ′ ≥ 2 the exact
threshold, between “no cover by k failure sets” and “a cover by k − k ′ + 1 plus an uncovered
instance”, is open. So “allow up to k rules” is a real assumption about the diversity of usage:
without rule names, imitation must see each rule used in more ways than the k − k ′ + 1 spare
schemas of the class can absorb. This is the positive-data face of the escalation lower bound for
untagged unions (Theorem 4.10).

5.5    Systematic generalization: finite usage fixes inferential role
Corollary 5.10 (Systematic out-of-distribution generalization; trivial). [T1 Cor 5.5] If R̂(D) = R∗ ,
the verifier accepts exactly R∗ and the reasoner derives exactly ClR∗ (B) for every B, including
conclusions that need derivations far longer, and judgments far larger, than any in the data,
independently of the distribution that produced the data.

Proof. R̂(D) = R∗ gives ClR̂(D) = ClR∗ .

   Theorems 5.6 and 5.8 supply its hypothesis, and Lemma 5.1 keeps the verifier sound before
that. The result is a learner of inference rules from imitation that is sound at all times against
adaptive search, exact after about maxi ln(kci /δ)/(πi ρi ) cited steps, and systematic: correctness
on terms of size 40 is the same event as on terms of size 10. A learned step scorer comes with
none of these guarantees (Sections 3 and 5.8).

Reading. Under an inferentialist picture of meaning (Brandom, 1994), the meaning of a
connective is its inferential role, the steps in which it may figure. Corollary 5.10 says that a finite
set of uses (an anchor; for cited natural-deduction rules, two generic instances per rule) fixes
that role for unbounded use. Three qualifications make this precise. (i) The role is fixed relative
to H. An anchor leaves open, within H, only hypotheses that contain R∗ , so the cautious verifier


                                                  40
accepts exactly R∗ ; it says nothing about hypotheses outside H. Quus-like alternatives (Kripke,
1982) are excluded by the choice of hypothesis class, not by the data. Which of simplicity,
coherence and convention does that work is the subject of Sections 6, 8 and 13. (ii) On clean data,
overgeneralizations such as tonk are never adopted, because the lgg is the least generalization
covering usage. The learner adds to a connective’s role only what usage forces. This is a
learning-theoretic analogue of Belnap’s conservativeness requirement (Belnap, 1962), and it is
why simplicity is the wrong bias here (Proposition 3.9). (iii) The role fixed is that of practice:
a fallacy used systematically becomes part of it (Section 5.6). Contexts. Contexts are part of
judgments (Definition 2.1), so steps inside suppositions are data like any other, and the theorems
apply to them unchanged as long as contexts are encoded as first-order terms (Remark 5.11). But
they must be in the data. Theorems determine a structural consequence relation only up to the
interval between derivable and admissible rules, which is non-degenerate for intuitionistic logic
(the Kreisel–Putnam rule is admissible but not derivable). So, unless the hypothesis class enforces
a deduction theorem, assertions alone cannot in general teach reasoning under hypotheses.
Remark 5.11 (Side conditions). [T1 §5, extensions] With guards from a finite family Φ (Definition 2.4),
the guarded single-schema class stays intersection-closed. Its closure is the lgg with the strongest
guard true on all data (Lemma 2.8), anchors exist, and the escalation budget of Section 4 grows
by at most |Φ| (Appendix D.7). But a positive example shows that a guard held, never that it
was needed. A guard is learned only from the absence of violating uses. It is lost as soon as
one human use omits it (Example 2.12), and it cannot be learned at all if Φ cannot express it.
Set-valued contexts and binders lie outside first-order anti-unification; modulo AC it is finitary
rather than unitary, and the bounds above would need re-proof.

5.6    Noise: sporadic and systematic errors
Human data contain errors, and the two kinds behave completely differently.

Proposition 5.12 (One error collapses the lgg). [T1 Prop 6.1] Let D consist of ∧E1 instances
s(and(Aj , Bj ), Aj ) whose Aj do not all have the same root, plus one invalid step s(φ, ψ) tagged
∧E1 , with φ not a conjunction. Then lgg(D) = s(z, w) with z ̸= w: the learned rule accepts every
one-premise step, and from any derivable formula it derives everything.

Proof. The premise column mixes the root and with the root of φ; the conclusion column has
mixed roots because the Aj do. Both become metavariables, distinct because the columns differ
(and(A1 , B1 ) ̸= A1 ).

(computed) A mis-tagged “p0 ∨ p1 ▷ p0 ” does exactly this. A 15% rate of affirming the consequent,
cited as MP, turns MP’s lgg into s2 (imp(v0 , v1 ), v2 , v3 ): from A → B and anything, infer anything.
This is the tonk of Theorem 3.2, produced by learning: the lgg is least among generalizations of
all the data, errors included.
    The remedy for sporadic errors is to let hypotheses miss a few data. Counting with multiplicity,
let VSe (D) = {R ∈ H : |D \ R| ≤ e}, and with per-tag budgets VS(ei ) (D) = {R ∈ H :

Definition 5.15 (Robust soundness). [T1 Thm 6.4] A positive-data verifier maps the data so far
(and private coins) to an acceptance set Acct . It is (δ, α)-robustly sound for H if for every R∗ ∈ H
and every law Q on S with Q(S \ R∗ ) ≤ α, i.i.d. data from Q give P[∃t : Acct ̸⊆ R∗ ] ≤ δ.

data from Q, every q ∈ R′ \ R∗ has P[∃t : q ∈ Acct ] ≤ δ. So if δ < 1, the verifier is not complete
for the target R′ under its clean law Q.

Proof. Q is an admissible noisy law for the target R∗ , and q ∈ Acct implies Acct ̸⊆ R∗ ; the data
law is the same in both scenarios.

Proof idea. If a witness frequency is at most α, then Q is an α-noisy law for the target in
which σi is replaced by σi [x 7→ f (z̄)] (resp. σi [y 7→ x]), and Theorem 5.16 applies. Proofs in

    So Theorem 5.14 asks for ρi,x βi > αi and ri,xy βi > αi (plus margins), while necessity asks
for (1 − mi,x )βi > αi and ri,xy βi > αi . By Lemma 5.17 the two differ by at most a factor of two
in the root frequencies and agree on the equality frequencies; the factor two in the lemma is
attained. The trade-off is unavoidable. A positive-data verifier that tolerates error rate α must
refuse every generalization supported by less than a fraction α of the data. With human error
rates around 1%, the generality of a rule used in less than about 1% of steps needs negative
information.

Corollary 5.19 (Systematic errors are rules). [T1 Cor 6.5] Let human errors be schema-generated:
the data law is Q = (1 − α)Q0 + αQerr , with Q0 supported on R∗ and Qerr on inst(τ ) for a
schema τ with inst(τ ) ̸⊆ R∗ . Suppose R′ := R∗ ∪ inst(τ ) ∈ H, as holds whenever H is closed
under adding a schema (tagged calculi with a fresh tag for τ ; untagged unions with room for one
more schema). Then Q is a clean law for R′ at every error rate α. Hence a (δ, α)-robustly sound
verifier with δ < 1 accepts each q ∈ inst(τ ) \ R∗ with probability at most δ under Q. So with
probability at least 1 − δ it never accepts all of R′ , a calculus in which τ is a genuine rule used at
the same rate.

Proof. Q(S \ R′ ) = 0; apply Theorem 5.16 to R∗ ⊊ R′ .

    So no positive-data method, with any amount of data, can both tolerate schema-generated
errors at rate α and learn genuine rules used at rate α. This also removes the protection of
the Bayes-conservative verifier (Section 4). Its time-uniform guarantee assumes a well-specified
likelihood. A model of errors as sporadic is misspecified for Q, and the clean hypothesis R′ fits
Q exactly.
Remark 5.20 (Imitation identifies practice). [T7 Prop 2.2; T1 §6] With latent but distinct fallacy
tags (Definition 2.10), the theorems above apply to the practice ΣP = Σ∗ ⊔ F tag by tag. On the
event of Theorem 5.14 the trimmed verifier accepts exactly RP = R∗ ∪ RF , including an instance
of every fallacy outside Sound(R∗ ), which a prover will query. In classical logic with a complete
Σ∗ and a pure fallacy schema, one closed instance with true premises and a false conclusion
trivializes the reasoner (Proposition 7.5; cf. Proposition 3.5). If fallacies are cited under genuine
rules’ names, a learner with one schema per tag collapses the rule instead (Proposition 5.12).

Reading. The line between sporadic and systematic errors is exact. Positive data remove an
error only if it is rarer than the witness frequencies of the genuine rules. Rule-like errors, at
any rate, need negative information: escalation (Section 4), coherence (Section 6), or the world
(Sections 7 and 11). For the program of the motivating notes (Hänni, 2026), imitation learns
which inferences are used, and which are valid only insofar as use is valid. Getting from the
first to the second is what the coherence and world channels are for, and positive data provably


                                                  43
cannot do it. In the language of justification, imitation can certify a step as licensed by the
practice, never as licensed by anything beyond it. This is why the cautious tier of Section 7 is
sound only relative to practice, and why coherence must act on a separate, bold tier.

5.7    An exactly solvable case: dimensions as inferential roles
The dimension of a physical quantity is its inferential role: which sums and equations it may
enter. For dimensions, learning meaning from positive examples is solvable in closed form
(Remark D.2; proof sketch in Appendix D.12): the finest grading that makes the observed
equations homogeneous is computed by Smith normal form, every target has a finite anchor,
positive data never refute “everything dimensionless” but the cautious learner never adopts it,
and the choice of base dimensions is a convention that no inference can see.

5.8    Imitation in practice
Experiment A (Section 12.1) illustrates each limit on school algebra: rule shapes are recovered
once a rule has a few instances and generalize out of distribution, but no guard is ever displayed,
all five systematic fallacies reach support, and spurious schemas from sporadic noise grow with
N under a fixed support threshold. Appendix D.13 gives the positive-data numbers.
     In short, what positive data fix is: rule shapes, given an anchor (at coupon-collector cost for
cited rules, under a diversity condition for uncited ones); their extension to unbounded use; side
conditions only as “strongest guard true on all data”; and sporadic errors rarer than every witness
frequency. What they cannot fix is: the choice of H, the necessity of a guard, generalizations
rarer than the error rate, and any schema-generated error. Sections 6 and 7 show what coherence
and world feedback do about the latter.


6     Coherence: what contradictions fix
Imitation cannot tell a systematic human error from a rule (Corollary 5.19). The second ingredient
of the motivating design (Section 1.1) is a coherence loss: penalize having good arguments for
both P and ¬P (Hänni, 2026). In our setting this is channel (C) of Definition 2.13: a family A of
designated contexts is certified coherent, and a derivation of ⊥ from one of them shows that one of
its steps is invalid. In brief: coherence is negative data, but only for bold learners, and it controls
only one of two error types (Section 6.1); it pins the target exactly when the target sits at the top
of its coherent version space, as classical propositional logic does by Post-completeness, and it is
blind for intuitionistic logic (Section 6.2); in arithmetic it is Popperian (Section 6.3); Carnap’s
categoricity problem is, in part, Gold’s problem in the dual space; among structural meanings it
is solved by data with two denials plus one coherence datum (Section 6.4); coherence catches
tonk but not non-conservativity (Section 6.5); what survives is the Kripkensteinian residue of
coherent uniform alternatives (Section 6.6); and this use of coherence is eliminative, untouched
by the coherentist impossibility theorems (Section 6.7).
     Most results are known in substance. Post-completeness (Post, 1921; Wójcicki, 1988),
Glivenko’s theorem, Gold’s limit-point argument, halving and weighted majority (Littlestone,
1988; Littlestone and Warmuth, 1994), the multiple-conclusion answer to Carnap (Carnap, 1943;
Shoesmith and Smiley, 1978), Belnap’s conservativity (Belnap, 1962) and the Σ1 /Π1 asymmetry
of limiting inquiry (Putnam, 1965; Gold, 1965; Kelly, 1996) are classical. New, as far as we
know, are the reduction of contradictions to coalitions, the two-sided trade-off, the denial-rank


                                                  44
trichotomy and twelve-datum tell-tale as learning results, the rule-level analysis of complete
theories, and the reading of all of these as statements about what a coherence loss can teach.
    Cn2 is classical propositional consequence (φ ∈ Cn2 (X) iff every Boolean valuation making
X true makes φ true), Taut = Cn2 (∅), and CFm (X) = Fm is the trivial operator. Hypotheses
are step sets (Definition 2.2) or finitary consequence relations h, with h(A) = {φ : A ⊢h φ}; h is
A-coherent if A ⊬h ⊥ for all A ∈ A, read as non-triviality h(A) ̸= Fm in languages without ⊥.
Unless stated otherwise A is fixed and known, independently of the target.

6.1    Coherence as negative data
Here hypotheses are step sets R in a countable class H with prior w, R w(R) = 1, and target
                                                                          P

R∗ ; every A ∈ A is target-coherent. An argument π from A to ⊥ is a derivation of ⊥ from A;
Steps(π) is its finite set of steps.

Definition 6.1 (Online coherence protocol). [T2 §2.2] In round t the learner holds a version space
VSt ⊆ H (VS0 = H) and announces an accepted set R̂t , whose steps the reasoner may chain.
The environment, possibly adversarial, possibly the learner’s own proof search, then either (P)
presents some s ∈ R∗ , and the learner deletes every R ∈ VSt with s ∈    / R; or (N) exhibits an
argument π from some A ∈ A to ⊥ with Steps(π) ⊆ R̂t , and the learner deletes every R ∈ VSt
with Steps(π) ⊆ R; or does nothing. A (P)-round with s ∈    / R̂t is an incompleteness error; an
(N)-round is a detection.

Lemma 6.2 (Negative bags; trivial). [T2 Lemma 2.1, as repaired] Let π be an argument from a

only {h : Steps(π) ⊆ h}, which can be strictly smaller even for consequence relations (target
Cn2 , A = {p}, π with steps p ▷ q, q ▷ ⊥, and h the least consequence relation containing p ▷ ⊥).

Proof. (a) Otherwise chaining gives ⊥ ∈ ClR∗ (A). (b) Chain in R. (c) h(X) = X ∪ {⊥} if p ∈ X,
else h(X) = X.

    So a contradiction is a multiple-instance label (Dietterich et al., 1997): “not all of these steps
are valid”. For a learner that can test A ▷ ⊥ ∈ h by membership it collapses to an ordinary
negative example and π is only a checkable witness; the bag structure matters for step verifiers
that are not cut-closed, such as process reward models and ensembles.

Proposition 6.3 (Caution receives no signal). [T2 Prop 2.9(a)–(c), as repaired] (a) If R̂t ⊆ R∗ , no

contradictions for the learner, and when designations are data about the target (Proposition 6.12).

Oligarchic acceptance. How should a bold learner accept, so that each contradiction teaches

6.2    Post-completeness: when coherence suffices
A consequence operator C is structural if σC(X) ⊆ C(σX) for every substitution σ: rules are
uniform schemas, so a learner that generalizes steps to schemas (Section 2.2) is a structural
learner.

Theorem 6.13 (Structural Post-completeness; known). [T2 Thm 3.1] If Fm contains ¬ and one
of ∧, ∨, →, all interpreted by their truth functions, every structural closure operator C ⊇ Cn2 ,
finitary or not, is Cn2 or CFm . The same holds for pure {→}.            Lean: Post.eq_Cn2_or_eq_trivial
Lean: Post.frag_postComplete_neg Lean: Post.impFrag_postComplete


Proof idea. Take φ ∈ C(X) \ Cn2 (X) and a falsifying row v. Substituting a tautology or a
contradiction for each atom according to v, as in the proof of Proposition 3.5, maps X into
Taut ⊆ C(∅) and φ to a contradiction, so structurality gives C(∅) = Fm. Appendix E.5.
   At the level of theorems this is Post (1921); the consequence-level form is standard too
(Pogorzelski, 1971; Wójcicki, 1988; Pogorzelski and Wojtylak, 2008). One falsifying row of one
bad rule yields a derivation of ⊥ from no premises. Without a theorem in the language there is
one more extension: in the {∧, ∨} fragment (Cn2 (∅) = ∅) let Cai (∅) = ∅ and Cai (X) = Fm for
X ̸= ∅ (almost inconsistent).

Proposition 6.14 (The theorem-free fragment; presumably folklore). [T2 Prop 3.2] In the {∧, ∨}
language the structural closure operators extending Cn2 are exactly Cn2 , Cai and CFm .

    Proof in Appendix E.5. So there coherence must be enforced on a non-empty designated
context. For sequents D let ⟨D⟩ be the least structural consequence relation containing D, and
for a designated Cn2 -consistent A0 let S(D, A0 ) = {h structural : D ⊆ h, A0 ⊬h ⊥}.

structural candidate schemas, each by an explicit derivation of ⊢ ⊥, while the non-structural ⊢ p

    Learning theorems is enough here: Cn2 is the largest structural closure operator with theorems
Taut, so a bold learner can learn the theorems and take the structural completion. For IPC,
derivability and admissibility differ (Harrop’s rule) but have the same theorems and the same
coherence profile, so theorems plus coherence data cannot tell them apart (Proposition E.1 in

Theorem 6.16 (Intuitionistic logic: coherence is blind). [T2 Thm 3.6] (a) For every intermediate
logic L and finite A: A ⊢L ⊥ iff A ⊢CPC ⊥. (b) A learner outputting a maximal coherent
structural hypothesis never outputs IPC. (c) There is a strictly increasing chain of finitely
axiomatizable intermediate logics L1 ⊊ L2 ⊊ · · · whose union Lω is intermediate, and no learner
identifies {Lk : k ≤ ω} from text plus coherence information, for any A, even with target-
dependent designations. (d) The conservative learner outputting ⟨Dn ⟩ BC-identifies every finitely
axiomatizable structural target.

Proof idea. (a) is Glivenko’s theorem (Glivenko, 1929). (c) uses Jankov formulas of an infinite
antichain of finite Heyting algebras (Jankov, 1968; Chagrov and Zakharyaschev, 1997); by (a) all
designations are the same for every member, so Corollary 6.11 applies. Appendix E.6.
    So for IPC the work is done by minimality (Section 5), not coherence: minimality is right when
the target is at the bottom of its coherent version space, coherence plus boldness when it is at the
top, and classical logic is at both ends. In Experiment B a bold learner over intuitionistic natural
deduction drifts toward CPC, accepting excluded middle, Peirce’s law and other IPC-underivable
schemas (Section 12.2).

Complete theories. Much of the algebra in a physics calculation is real-closed-field reasoning,
and RCF is complete. Is it pinned like CPC?

6.3   Arithmetic: coherence is Popperian
Arithmetic is where coherence stops being a complete test. Coherence with a Σ1 -complete base
already does everything ∆0 world feedback can (Lemma 6.18); no r.e. hypothesis is maximal, and
Turing progressions are not identifiable (Theorems 6.19 and 6.20). The right use of coherence is
Popperian: it detects false Π1 claims but not false Σ1 claims, and no computable channel decides
Σ2 truth in the limit (Theorem 6.21).
    Hypotheses are r.e. theories T ⊇ PA, world feedback is a ∆0 -oracle, and N is the intended
model; Q is Robinson arithmetic.
Lemma 6.18 (∆0 feedback is subsumed by coherence; standard). [T2 Lemma 3.7] A consistent
T ⊇ Q proves every true ∆0 sentence and no false one, so no ∆0 feedback refutes it.
Proof. Q is Σ1 -complete (Boolos et al., 2007); if T proved a false δ it would also prove ¬δ.

Theorem 6.19 (No maximal r.e. hypothesis; cited). [T2 Thm 3.8, as repaired] Every consistent r.e.
T ⊇ Q has a ρ with T + ρ and T + ¬ρ consistent (Gödel, 1931; Rosser, 1936; Tarski et al., 1953).
     So a bold learner with r.e. hypotheses and A = {∅} has no maximal choice. (If A contains all
finite sets of true sentences, T is A-coherent iff T ⊆ Th(N), and at most one refinement survives.)
Theorem 6.20 (Turing-chain impossibility). [T2 Thm 3.9, as repaired] Let T0 = PA, Tk+1 = Tk +
Con(Tk ), Tω = k Tk (Turing, 1939; Feferman, 1962), and let A be any fixed family of finite sets
               S

of true sentences. No learner identifies a class containing {Tk : k ≤ ω} from text, A-coherence
and a ∆0 -oracle.
Proof. All Tk are sound, so all side information is target-independent; the chain is strict by
Gödel II; apply Corollary 6.11.

    The Σ1 -unsound Tk +¬Con(Tk ) are natural hypotheses: consistent, unrefuted by ∆0 data, and
refuted by coherence only relative to accepted premises proving Con(Tk ). Restricting designations
to true contexts is essential: with {¬Con(Tk )} designated as data about the target, the chain
becomes identifiable (Proposition 6.12).
Theorem 6.21 (Coherence as a Π1 -truth detector; the Σ2 barrier). [T2 Thm 3.10, as repaired] (a)
For Π1 π, PA + π is consistent iff π is true. (b) For Σ1 σ, truth implies consistency of PA + σ,
not conversely (σ = ¬Con(PA)). (c) The Popperian learner (“true” on a Π1 sentence until PA
refutes it; “false” on a Σ1 sentence until PA proves it) converges to the truth on Σ1 ∪ Π1 with
at most one mind change per sentence. (d) The naively bold learner (accept φn iff consistent
with PA plus the earlier accepted sentences) converges to a Lindenbaum completion that depends
on the enumeration, and on every enumeration beginning with ¬Con(PA) it is Σ1 -unsound. (e)
Every computable learner using a computable text, coherence searches and a ∆0 -oracle fails to
converge to the truth value of some Σ2 sentence.
Proof idea. (a) A false Π1 sentence has a true, hence PA-provable, Σ1 negation. (e) Convergent
computable guesses define a ∆2 set (Shoenfield, 1959), and the true Σ2 sentences are Σ2 -complete.
Appendix E.8.

                                                50
   This is Popper’s asymmetry in its standard learning-theoretic form (Putnam, 1965; Gold,
1965; Kelly, 1996), read for coherence-learners. The same boundary appears for credences:
computable, weakly coherent, Π1 -convergent credences are dogmatic on infinitely many true Π2
sentences (Theorem E.2, a self-contained form of a theorem of Sawin and Demski 2013), and
Proposition E.3 records what weak coherence costs (both in Appendix E.9).

Reading. In arithmetic, computation adds nothing beyond coherence with a Σ1 -complete base.
What matters is where boldness is applied: on universal claims, which coherence can refute, not
on existential ones, which need a witness. Beyond ∆2 no computable channel decides truth in the
limit (Theorem 6.21(e)); only the weaker gradual verification, with credence tending to 1 exactly
on truths, reaches further (Proposition E.3). The Gödel–Rosser alternatives are a permanent
residue, removed only by accepting stronger principles (reflection, Con(PA), a stronger theory):
a justification that is not a PA-proof (Section 13).

6.4    Carnap’s problem is Gold’s problem
Under inferentialism, learning valid inferences should be learning meanings. Carnap (1943)
observed that the classical rules do not fix the truth tables: the all-true valuation, and “true iff
tautologous”, respect every classical inference.

Definition 6.22 (Meanings). [T2 §4.1] A valuation is any v : Fm → {0, 1}, identified with its
true-set in Cantor space 2Fm ; a meaning is a set V of valuations; BV is the set of Boolean ones.
For finite Γ, ∆, Γ |=1V φ iff every v ∈ V with v[Γ] = 1 has v(φ) = 1, and Γ |=m
                                                                              V ∆ iff no v ∈ V has
v[Γ] = 1, v[∆] = 0. Val(S) is the set of valuations satisfying the sequents S; V ∩ closes V under
intersections of true-sets, including the empty one v⊤ ≡ 1; vTaut is the characteristic function of
Taut. V is structural if v ∈ V implies v ◦ σ ∈ V for all substitutions σ.

    The sequent Γ ▷ ∆ excludes exactly the clopen set of valuations realizing the position [Γ : ∆].
So inference data are negative data about valuations, while coherence certifications (“[A : D] is in
bounds”) and world feedback are positive data: Restall’s reading of consequence (Restall, 2005)
turned into a statement about data.

Lemma 6.23 (Duality). [T2 Lemma 4.1] (a) Val(|=m   V ) = V . (b) For closed V , CV (X) = {v ∈ V :
                                                                                            T

X ⊆ v} is finitary and the valuations satisfying every valid single-conclusion sequent form V ∩ . (c)

Reading. “Coherence” covers two kinds of data (Table 6): certifications that a position is in
bounds (positive about V ), and 0-denial constraints such as p, ¬p▷ (negative about V ), which
remove v⊤ . Neither removes vTaut . A learner trained on imitation plus a coherence loss, in
either sense, is provably free to settle on gappy valuations: consistent, inferentially competent,
never committing on open questions. These are van Fraassen’s supervaluations (van Fraassen,
1966), the honest semantics of “settled by the premises”. Pinning classical meaning needs a loss
with two denials. Bilateral signed sequents (Smiley, 1996; Rumfitt, 2000) carry the same rank-2
information. For language-model training this raises a question the theorems do not settle, since
they concern identifiability, not training dynamics: imitation plus a contradiction penalty does
not rule out consistent but noncommittal reasoners, and whether training drifts toward them is
empirical.
    With rank-2 data finitely many data suffice. Let TT be the eleven truth-table schemata:
φ, ¬φ▷ and ▷φ, ¬φ; φ ∧ ψ ▷ φ, φ ∧ ψ ▷ ψ, φ, ψ ▷ φ ∧ ψ; φ ▷ φ ∨ ψ, ψ ▷ φ ∨ ψ, φ ∨ ψ ▷ φ, ψ;
▷φ, φ → ψ, ψ ▷ φ → ψ, φ, φ → ψ ▷ ψ. TT(p, q) are their instances in distinct atoms.

Val(TT) = BV, which is closed. (b) If V is structural, every v ∈ V satisfies the eleven sequents
TT(p, q), and V = ̸ ∅ (one coherence datum), then V = BV. (c) So among structural meanings
BV is identified finitely by twelve data; without the coherence datum V = ∅ survives, the Gold
over-generalization. (d) Without structurality BV is not identifiable in the limit from text plus
the coherence datum [ : ], or any other target-independent certifications: every finite set of valid
sequents is valid in a closed meaning BV ∪ {vχ′ }, vχ′ a Boolean valuation flipped at a formula χ
the set does not mention. (If every target-certified position is supplied, text plus certifications is
an informant, as in Proposition 6.12, and this obstruction disappears; the next one does not.)
And the dense non-structural BV \ {u0 } has the same valid sequents and in-bounds positions as

Proposition 6.27 (A compositional prior suffices). [T2 Prop 4.5] Exactly one two-element matrix
with designated value 1 validates explosion, ¬¬p ▷ p, p ▷ ¬¬p, the three ∧ rules, ∨-introduction,

never refutes V ⊇ BV; under the compositional prior it identifies the tables once every row has
been observed [T2 Prop 4.6] .

Reading. Carnap’s problem is a semantic twin of Gold’s only in part (Table 7). Gold’s trivial
logic (V = ∅) is removed by a coherence certification, Carnap’s v⊤ by a 0-denial sequent, and
vTaut , the Horn blindness of single-conclusion data, by neither. So imitation plus coherence fixes
inferential role, not classical truth conditions. That does not matter for deriving; it matters for
interpreting world feedback (“A is false” licenses ¬A only through the bilateral bridge). Rules
can be identifiable when truths are not (Section 13.2).

6.5    Tonk, harmony and conservativity
Prior (1960)’s tonk (φ ▷ φ tonk ψ, φ tonk ψ ▷ ψ) is the paradigm of a rule search exploits
(Theorem 3.2); Belnap (1962) demanded that new rules be conservative.

Proposition 6.28 (Tonk). [T2 Prop 5.1] Under cut, tonk gives φ ⊢ ψ for all φ, ψ, and coherence
refutes it in two steps (a ▷ a tonk ⊥ ▷ ⊥) if A has a non-empty context or the logic has a theorem.
In a theorem-free base with A = {∅} it survives: classical {∧, ∨} plus tonk is Cai . Without cut
tonk need not trivialize (Cook, 2005; Ripley, 2015).

Proof. One cut gives the first claim. In the theorem-free case every rule has premises, so nothing
is derivable from ∅, while from any premise tonk yields everything.



                                                  53
   Transitivity lets one bad rule poison everything, and lets coherence catch it. Boldness is
order-dependent when individually coherent rules are jointly incoherent: offered tonk’s two rules
one at a time, a bold learner keeps whichever comes first (Section 12.2).
Proposition 6.29 (Coherence is not conservativity). [T2 Prop 5.2, as repaired] Intuitionistic → plus
¬-introduction, ¬-elimination and ¬¬-elimination is the {→, ¬} fragment of CPC: coherent, but
not conservative over IPC→ (it proves Peirce’s law). ¬¬-elimination alone would be conservative.
Conservativity implies coherence when coherence is non-triviality on the old vocabulary, or ⊥
with ex falso is in the base, but not in general (IPC→ + {▷⊥}, with ⊥ new and without ex falso).
     Proof in Appendix E.11. So Belnap’s learner rejects classical negation over intuitionistic posi-
tive logic, and the coherence learner accepts it. Harmony with normalization gives conservativity
(Prawitz, 1965; Dummett, 1991), but local harmony alone does not: Read’s bullet (Read, 2000)
has local reductions yet derives ⊥ from nothing. Over a Post-complete base the two notions
coincide [L5 Cor 2.4] : if C ′ is structural on L′ ⊇ L with C ′ |L ⊇ Cn2 (L as in Theorem 6.13), then
C ′ |L is Cn2 or CFm , so C ′ is conservative iff it is coherent on one classically consistent context.
Belnap’s existence condition is, over classical logic, non-triviality; harmony matters only over
sub-classical bases.
Theorem 6.30 (Coherence is Π1 , conservativity Π2 ). [T2 Thm 5.3] For finite rule systems (ele-
mentary formal systems; Post 1943; Smullyan 1961): (a) {R : R ⊬ ⊥} is Π1 -complete; (b) for
some fixed finite base B, {N : B + N conservative over B} is Π2 -complete; (c) so coherence is
decidable in the limit with one mind change, while conservativity is not decidable in the limit by
any computable learner, only refutable in the limit (Kelly, 1996); (d) for decidable B (e.g. CPC,
IPC) conservativity is Π1 .
Proof idea. (a) Simulate φe (e) by rules and add “halt ▷⊥”. (b) Reduce totality of φe to
conservativity of one new symbol over a universal base. Appendix E.11.
    Reading. A coherence filter can be built into a convergent learner (Theorem 6.15(b)); a
conservativity filter cannot in general. Coherence plus decidable local checks such as harmony
are the learner-friendly norms. Where non-conservativity is the point, as for theoretical terms in
physics, a concept whose rules smuggle in a substantive inference (Dummett’s Boche) is coherent,
and only world feedback can test it.

6.6    Fallacies and the Kripkensteinian residue
A learner with a generalization operator G (e.g. structural closure of least generalizations) turns
finitely many fallacious human steps F into rules G(F ). Let h∗ be the target consequence relation.
Theorem 6.31 (Elimination criterion; trivial). [T2 Thm 6.1] Coherence (with data) eventually
refutes the generalized fallacy iff h∗ ⊕ G(F ) is A-incoherent; for OH the refutation is charged
to the budget of Theorem 6.5. If h∗ is sound for a class of intended structures and each A ∈ A
holds in one that also validates G(F ), the fallacy survives.
Proof. h∗ ⊕ G(F ) contains every positive datum; apply Theorem 6.9. A structure validating h∗ ,
G(F ) and A shows coherence on A.

Corollary 6.32 (All structural propositional fallacies die, quickly). [T2 Cor 6.2] If G is structural
closure and h∗ ⊇ Cn2 is structural and coherent on a designated context (so h∗ = Cn2 ), every
classically invalid rule is eliminated: substituting ⊤/⊥ along a falsifying row makes its premises

    Experiment B (Table 19) shows the negative-data role end to end: with systematic fallacies
and noise (N ≥ 50), coherence pruning cut the unsound rules left by imitation from 45.6 to 1.2
on average, and the budgeted adversary no longer derived ⊢ ⊥, at no cost in completeness. It
is not complete: 19 of 72 runs still end with an unsound rule, most surviving unsound rules
are non-structural, and at N ≤ 10 even affirming the consequent can survive, because a small
learned calculus may lack the rules needed to derive the contradiction. Outside a Post-complete
target, fallacies can survive: the quantifier swap is coherent until a context forces two objects, the
gambler’s fallacy until independence is accepted, and conditional perfection until two exclusive
laws share a consequent (Example E.4 in Appendix E.12).

Proposition 6.33 (Without uniformity, coherence is toothless; trivial). [T2 Prop 6.3] If h∗ ⊕ F
is A-coherent, the non-structural h∗ ⊕ F survives forever; e.g. Cn2 + {▷p17 }, the “quus” of
propositional logic, when every designated context is consistent with p17 .

Theorem 6.34 (The Kripkensteinian residue). [T2 Thm 6.4, as repaired] AltG (h∗ , A) = {h G-closed :
h ⊇ h∗ , h A-coherent} is, in the limit of complete data, the set of G-closed hypotheses never
refuted by positive data and coherence (Theorem 6.9). (i) G structural, h∗ = Cn2 , A =        ̸ ∅:
                                  ∗
Alt = {Cn2 }. (ii) G structural, h = IPC, A a non-empty family of classically consistent contexts:
Alt = {h structural : IPC ⊆ h ⊆ CPC}, all intermediate logics. (iii) G deductive closure, h∗ = PA,
A = {∅}: Alt is the set of all consistent closed extensions of PA (the r.e. ones, if hypotheses
are r.e.), e.g. PA + ¬Con(PA), whose completions (not r.e.) have only non-standard models.
Designating all finite sets of true sentences removes exactly the unsound ones; the sound Tk of
Theorem 6.20 remain, and by that theorem no learner identifies them together with Tω from text
plus true-context coherence.

Proof idea. (i) is Theorem 6.13. For (ii) ⊆, a classically invalid sequent in a structural h ⊇ IPC
becomes, under σv , an IPC-provable premise set with an IPC-refutable conclusion. Appendix E.12.

Division of labour. Community practice (positive data) eliminates under-generalizations.
Uniformity (structurality, least generalization) eliminates gerrymanders such as Proposition 6.33;
it is vocabulary-relative (Goodman’s point), and it turns an instance-level fallacy into a schema
that coherence can refute. Coherence eliminates uniform alternatives that conflict with accepted
uniform rules: tonk, affirming the consequent, “quus” as a second rule for +. Nothing in the setup


                                                 55
eliminates coherent uniform alternatives that agree with all data. For classical propositional
logic there are none; for arithmetic they are the Gödel–Rosser and non-standard alternatives, a
precise mathematical counterpart of Kripkenstein for arithmetic (Kripke, 1982), removable only
by accepting reflection or stronger theories on other grounds (Section 13).

6.7   A remark on eliminative versus confirmational coherence
Coherentist epistemology has impossibility results: no informative coherence measure is truth-
conducive ceteris paribus (Bovens and Hartmann, 2003b,a; Olsson, 2005a,b). They do not
threaten the use of coherence in this section, and they do refute a tempting other use.
Remark 6.35 (Three uses of coherence). [L11 §3.4, TC4] (U1) Eliminative: “h derives ⊥ from a
context certified consistent, so h has an invalid rule.” This is modus tollens, not a measure.
Conditioning a prior on “h is A-coherent” multiplies every coherent hypothesis by 1/P(coherent):
under truthful designation the target’s posterior weakly rises and odds among coherent rivals are
unchanged. The impossibility theorems, about degrees of coherence of consistent information
sets, do not apply; the prices are Theorem 6.9 and the need for truthful designation. (U2)
Probabilistic consistency of credences: de Finetti constraints, satisfied by the noncommittal
assignment, the credal analogue of gappy valuations. (U3) Agreement as evidence: annotators or
sampled derivations agree. This is the witness scenario of Lewis (1946) that the impossibility
theorems address, and they bite in full.
    Appendix E.13 makes (U3) and (U1) quantitative: unanimity among annotators who share
an error source, or among samples of one model, moves the odds that a step is valid by a bounded
factor however many agree (Remark E.5); and coherentizing credences by projection is safe
exactly when the constraints are sound, and strictly harmful when the actual world violates
them (Lemma E.6).

Reading. The setup’s use of coherence is eliminative, hence immune to the coherentist impossi-
bility theorems, but weak: it never confirms, it only removes what conflicts. Corroboration must
come from channels with independent errors: computation, randomized evaluation, measurement
(Section 2.5). Where the target is coherence-pinned, uniqueness of the coherent extension, not
truth-conduciveness of coherence, does the work. Section 13 reads this division as vindicated
wide reflective equilibrium (Goodman, 1955; Daniels, 1979).


7     An end-to-end theorem for formal mathematics: the two-tier
      learner
The first success criterion of Section 1.1 is a setup of this shape that provably works for formal
mathematics: imitate human inferences, then condition on coherence and on occasional feedback
from the world. Sections 4 to 6 supply the parts. The natural way to assemble them is a
statement of roughly this form. For every target calculus with finite anchors, human data with
sporadic noise below the margin and a systematic fallacy set F , and every adaptive prover: (i) a
cautious assertion tier is sound at all times with probability at least 1 − δ; (ii) the number of
detected incoherences is at most log2 (1/w∗ ) plus a noise cost; (iii) after N human steps the tier
equals the target plus the fallacies coherent with it; and (iv) that residue is empty for classical
propositional logic and for complete decidable theories.


                                                56
    This statement is false as stated, and the way it fails is the main finding of this section. Three
corrections are needed, and each is forced by a matching lower bound.
1. Caution is relative to a class, and fallacies break realizability. Positive data cannot tell a
   systematic fallacy from a rule (Corollary 5.19), so the realizable object is the practice, not the
   target. A tier that is cautious over the positive-data version space asserts every frequent fallacy
   (Proposition 7.5). A tier that is cautious over hypotheses allowed to declare practice rules
   fallacious asserts nothing (Proposition 7.6). What works is presumption of validity applied
   only after an audit, with abstention until then, and the waiting is necessary (Theorem 7.18).
2. Coherence condemns sets, and the blame problem is real. The practice schemas that can be
   soundly condemned as schemas are exactly those in the union of the minimal conflicts, which
   is the hitting-set duality of model-based diagnosis (Lemma 7.7). At stable depth this collateral
   damage is unavoidable for every sound learner (Theorem 7.19). The extremal witness is almost
   too clean: in the practice {modus ponens, affirming the consequent} the rival diagnosis is the
   hypothesis that “→” means “←”. World feedback with descent, or a single denial, turns bags
   into singletons (Lemma 7.8).
3. Soundness must be relativized to refutation size. No computable learner is both sound at all
   times relative to full coherence and eventually complete (Theorem 7.20).
With these corrections the theorem holds (Theorem 7.12). We call the resulting learner TTL, the
two-tier learner: a cautious, audited assertion tier and a bold sandbox that a red team attacks.
    Depth, honestly. The ingredients are known or transported from Sections 3 to 6: Lemma 7.7
is Reiter’s diagnosis theory, Lemma 7.8 is Shapiro’s contradiction backtracing, Theorem 7.18 is a
standard two-point rare-event bound, and Theorem 7.20 is a routine reduction. What is new is
diagnostic: where the natural statement breaks (Propositions 7.5 and 7.6); the audit principle;
the blame theorem with its →/← witness and its stable-depth form; the depth relativization; the
observation that world feedback earns its keep by localization, not refutation; and the assembly
into one statement with explicit constants. None of it is deep mathematics. Its value is that it pins
down, with matching lower bounds, what a setup that provably works for formal mathematics
can and cannot deliver. All results of this section passed two rounds of adversarial verification[T7] .
The second-round repairs (assumption (OE) in Theorem 7.18, the floor bound in Theorem 7.27(e),
the size convention of Definition 7.2, the ground-rule convention ρi = ci = 1 behind the N1
formula of Definition 7.9, and the oracle specification of Corollary 7.23) were then re-checked
by a third, independent referee, who found no fatal or major issue; its minor corrections are
incorporated below.

7.1    Set-up: practice, evaluation, refutations
We use the practice of Definition 2.10: a target calculus Σ∗ of genuine rules, a finite set F of
systematic fallacies, the practice ΣP = Σ∗ ⊔ F with |ΣP | ≤ K, and i.i.d. human steps tagged
by practice schemas, with sporadic noise. Fallacy tags are latent but distinct. For tag i write
βi = πi (1 − ai ) and αi = πi ai , let ρi , ci be the variability and witness count of Theorem 5.6
(ρi = ci = 1 for ground rules, so ci ≥ 1 for every tag), and let ∆i = (ρi βi − αi )/2 be the margin
of Theorem 5.14.

Assumption 7.1 (Floor). [T7 §1.2, Def 1.2] Constants ∆ > 0, c ≥ 1, K and ᾱi ≥ αi are known,
with |ΣP | ≤ K, ci ≤ c and (ρi βi − ᾱi )/2 ≥ ∆ for every tag i, fallacy tags included.



                                                  57
    The evaluation sources are those of Definition 2.13: a finite family A of designated positions
[A : D], a world W : JW → {0, 1}, and trusted steps Ttrust (for instance, first-order logic when
only non-logical axioms are learned). Each position induces the partial evaluation e[A:D] of (WS)
(Assumption 2.14): value 1 on A and on W -true judgments, value 0 on D ∪ {⊥} and on W -false
ones. When JW =   ̸ ∅, the empty position [∅ : ∅] is designated. A step is falsified under e if its
premises are e-true and its conclusion e-false. (WS) is assumed for every designated position
unless stated otherwise.
Definition 7.2 (Derivations, refutations, conflicts, oracle). [T7 Def 1.5, as repaired]
 (a) A derivation is a finite sequence of distinct judgments, each a leaf or the conclusion of one
     designated step whose premises occur earlier; its last judgment is its conclusion. Its size |π|
     is the total number of symbols in its distinct judgments. A tree derivation (Definition 2.2)
     compresses to such a sequence with the same conclusion, using only its steps and leaves
     and no larger: keep, for each judgment, the step at an occurrence of least height, order the
     judgments by that height, and cut the sequence after the tree’s conclusion.
(b) For a finite schema set B (or a step set S) a d-refutation is a derivation of size at most d,
    relative to some [A : D] ∈ A, whose leaves have e-value 1, whose steps lie in RB ∪ Ttrust
    (resp. S ∪ Ttrust ), and whose conclusion has e-value 0. This is Definition 2.19 with the size
    convention made explicit. A single falsified instance is a one-step refutation. B is d-clean if
    it has no d-refutation, and clean at every depth if it is d-clean for all d.
 (c) Conf d = {C ⊆ ΣP : C is not d-clean} is upward closed. Its minimal members Cd are the
     minimal d-conflicts, and Cd (B) denotes those contained in B. Since ΣP is finite there is d0
     with Conf d = Conf d0 for d ≥ d0 ; we write d = ∞ for these stable values.
(d) The refutation oracle Ref d (B) returns a d-refutation of B or NONE, deterministically. By
    default it returns the lexicographically least among the smallest refutations. The prefer-
    unblocked variant returns one whose descent (Lemma 7.8) is unblocked if one exists, then
    the smallest, then the lexicographically least.
    Ref d is computable by brute force when instance membership and W are decidable and there
are finitely many derivations of size at most d up to renaming the symbols that occur in neither
A nor B and on which W does not depend. Its cost is exp(O(d)), and it is accounted separately
from samples. As d → ∞ refutation search is only semi-decidable (Theorem 6.30).
                                                                                          (d)

Lemma 7.4 (Refutation is one-sided and target-blind; trivial). [T7 Lemma 2.1 and §1.3, as repaired]

    So refutations can never condemn a subset of the target, and two targets with the same
practice receive identical refutational evidence on every query. Coherence and the world can
say that a set of practice rules contains a fallacy; they can never say that a rule is genuine.
Everything positive that is ever learned about a rule comes from imitation.

7.2    Why the naive two-tier claim is false
Proposition 7.5 (Caution over practice asserts the fallacies; trivial). [T7 Prop 2.2, as repaired] Let
the positive-data tier be the per-tag trimmed version-space verifier (Theorem 5.13) over the
practice tags. On the event of Theorem 5.14 its accepted set is exactly RP = R∗ ∪ RF . So it
accepts an instance outside Sound(R∗ ) of every τ ∈ F , and an adaptive prover gets that instance
accepted by querying it. In CPC with a complete Σ∗ and a pure τ , the prover can query the closed
⊤/⊥ instance of τ with true premises and a false conclusion (Lemma 7.22), and that single step
makes every formula derivable from ∅.
Proof. Theorem 5.14 applies tag by tag, and fallacy tags are tags like any other. In the CPC
case, Σ∗ derives the closed true premises and the negation of the closed false conclusion j, both
tautologies; the step adds j, and then ⊥ and everything follow.
    Purity matters for the last clause: adding the single invalid step p ▷ q to a complete calculus
for CPC leaves Cl(∅) unchanged, and for an impure τ even all of inst(τ ) need not trivialize
(Example 3.6). The proposition is the precise sense in which “the cautious assertion tier is
sound” is false without further structure. Caution is soundness relative to the realizable class
(Theorem 4.2), and systematic fallacies make the practice, not the target, the realizable object
(Remark 5.20).
    The obvious repair is to be cautious over hypotheses that may declare practice rules fallacious.
Suppose the practice is known, and let V = {Σ : Σ ⊆ ΣP }, where a candidate Σ reads “Σ is the
target and the rest of the practice is fallacious”. All candidates explain the positive data equally
well. Let Vd be the d-clean candidates and Vt′ those consistent with the refutations found by time
t.

Reading. The dilemma is the formal shape of a familiar norm. A practice is presumed valid,

asserts nothing, because refutational evidence cannot certify a rule. “Audit, then assert” is the
only stable design, and it is the design of TTL.

7.3    Blame: from bags to culprits
A contradiction from a designated context condemns a set of steps (Lemma 6.2). Which members
should a sound learner withhold?
Lemma 7.7 (Hitting-set duality). [T7 Lemma 2.3] Let U be finite, let K ⊆ 2U be upward closed with
∅∈/ K, and let C be its minimal members; call M ⊆ U clean if M ∈  / K. (a) The maximal clean sets
are exactly the complements of the minimal transversals (hitting sets) of C. (b) An element lies in
some minimal transversal iff it lies in some member of C. Hence {maximal clean sets} = U \ C,
                                                                 T                             S

and this set is clean. (c) The minimal transversal is unique iff every member of C is a singleton.
                Lean: Blame.isMaxClean_iff Lean: Blame.iInter_maxClean_eq Lean: Blame.existsUnique_minTransversal_iff


    Proof in Appendix F.3. This is Reiter’s theory of diagnosis from first principles (Reiter, 1987;
de Kleer and Williams, 1987), and (b) is the standard fact that the vertices of the transversal
hypergraph are those of the minimal edges (Berge, 1989). Components are practice schemas,
“abnormal” means fallacious, conflicts are the negative bags of Section 6, and diagnoses are
hypotheses about which practice rules are fallacies. All three parts are formalized in Lean for a
finite universe, and checked on 4000 random families with no failure (computed). With U = ΣP
and K = Conf d , every maximal candidate keeps ΣP \ Cd . So Cd is exactly what a learner that
                                                      S        S

presumes validity, and is cautious across the remaining ambiguity at the level of schemas, must
withhold. At the level of instances it can do better (Proposition 7.6(c)); that the withholding is
forced for every sound learner is true at stable depth (Theorem 7.19(b)) but can fail at finite
depth (Theorem 7.19(c)).

Descent. Bags shrink to culprits when the argument can be evaluated line by line. Fix a
derivation π relative to [A : D] and let e+π be the partial map on the judgments of π obtained
from e[A:D] by closing under two rules that use only the trusted steps of π: forward, if all premises
of a trusted step of π have value 1 then its conclusion gets 1; backward, if a trusted step of π has
conclusion value 0 and all but one premise at 1, then the remaining premise gets 0. A worklist

                                                        60
computes this fixed point with O(|π|φ) evaluations of e, where φ is the maximal fan-in. (Closing
under all trusted steps globally is not computable in general: in arithmetic, forward closure from
the true ∆0 sentences contains, among the Σ1 sentences, exactly the true ones. It is also not
needed.) To descend on a refutation, start at its conclusion; at a node of value 0 produced by a
step s, output s if all premises of s have value 1, and otherwise move to a premise of value 0.
The descent is unblocked if at every visited node either all premises have value 1 or some premise
has value 0.
Lemma 7.8 (Descent with trusted steps). [T7 Lemma 2.5, as repaired] Assume (WS) for [A : D],
with total valuation V . Then e+  π agrees with V wherever it is defined; in particular, a judgment
receiving both values certifies that [A : D] violates (WS). Let π be a d-refutation of B relative to
[A : D] whose descent is unblocked. Then: (a) the descent outputs an untrusted step s ∈ RB with
V -true premises and a V -false conclusion, so s ∈   / R∗ ; (b) computing e+π and descending costs
O(|π|φ) ≤ O(dφ) evaluations of e; (c) every σ ∈ B with s ∈ inst(σ) is a fallacy, so removing
all of them removes no genuine rule ( certified singleton blame); (d) for each such σ, {σ} is
a d-conflict: s together with the trusted steps of π that justify the values of its premises and
conclusion forms a d-refutation of {σ}.
Proof idea. Both propagation rules are V -sound because trusted steps preserve V -truth. The
descent follows nodes of value 0 strictly downward and leaves have value 1, so it stops at a step
with V -true premises and a V -false conclusion, which by (WS) is neither trusted nor in R∗ .
Part (d) extracts the refutation from the judgments of π; this is where size must count distinct
judgments (Definition 7.2(a)). Appendix F.5.
    This is Shapiro’s contradiction backtracing from algorithmic debugging and model inference
(Shapiro, 1981, 1983), the counterexample-to-blame step of Lemma 10.17, and Lakatos’s conversion
of a global counterexample into a local one (Lakatos, 1976). Two features are specific to this setting.
Trusted steps carry values backward through unevaluable nodes, which arithmetic needs because
∀x θ is not ∆0 (Theorem 7.27(a)). And by (c) and (d), blame lands on schemas, with no collateral,
and every blamed schema is a singleton conflict. When the descent is blocked, all we have is the
bag {σ ∈ B : σ used in π}. Only the related Lemma 10.17 is formalized, for a total evaluation of a
line-list argument (Blame.LineArg.descent, Blame.LineArg.descent_not_mem); trusted-step
propagation and part (d) are not.

Reading: localization. In classical propositional logic and in arithmetic, world feedback
refutes nothing that coherence does not already refute: by Post-completeness an invalid schema
is incoherent in the empty context (Theorem 6.13), and a consistent extension of Q is ∆0 -sound
(Lemma 6.18). Its whole added value is that descent turns its refutations into singletons. World
feedback earns its keep by localization, not by refutation. Example 2.15 shows this in miniature:
the context A1 yields the bag {AC, MP}, and the valuation p = 0, q = 1 blames AC alone.

makes the separation safe; truth maintenance is the same point made across time. This resolves
the tension left by Sections 4 and 6: caution receives no signal from coherence (Proposition 6.3),
and boldness is unsound; so both tiers exist, and only the cautious one asserts.

   World-channel steps are truth-sound but need not be target-sound: for Σ∗ = {∧I, ∧E1 , ∧E2 }
the step ⊤ ▷ ⊤ ∨ ⊥ preserves truth but is not R∗ -derivable. That is why the world channel is
kept outside the tier, and why Theorem 7.12(i) concerns the tier only.

Remarks. (1) What is and is not certified. Genuine rules are never certified valid by anything in
the architecture: their assertion rests on positive data (anchoring with margin) plus presumption
after audit. Fallacies are certified invalid by descent, or implicated as a set by conflicts. Lemma 7.4
forces this asymmetry. (2) Realizability is load-bearing. If the human calculus has a rule outside
the class, identification fails, and nothing downstream repairs it; at best the audit removes an
over-general identified schema, which restores soundness but not completeness. Quantifier rules
and the induction schema are such rules (Corollary 7.26 and Theorem 7.27). If fallacies are cited
under genuine rules’ names, the per-tag class must be unions of schemas (Theorem 5.8). (3) Why
freeze. Freezing P̂ keeps the accounting to one event. Learning can continue at the cost of a
                                                   1
union bound over N ≥ N1 (an additive ≈ ln 2∆         2 inside the logarithm) and a re-audit whenever

P̂ changes. (4) Before N1 . Abstention can be softened by the world channel or by a trusted
base. Both are truth-sound (Corollary 7.13) but outside (i) unless they lie in Sound(R∗ ), and
Theorem 7.18 shows that no learner of the relevant kind can do much better on the schemas that
might be fallacies.

Reading. For the motivating question, the theorem says what “a learner of inference rules,
conditioned on coherence and the world” can deliver. It identifies the target calculus exactly when
blame is localized (no descent blocked, or (SBd )), and otherwise up to the collateral Colld (B0 ),
which every sound learner must give up at stable depth (Theorem 7.19(b)); in both cases modulo

                                                  64
a residue that no refutational channel at depth d can see. It is sound at every moment against
any amount of search. Its costs are explicit: N1 human steps, at most |F | + 1 oracle calls on
the descent path, log2 (1/w(h0 )) detections in the sandbox. And it never asserts a rule because
the rule is coherent, only because the community uses it robustly and it survived the audit.
Coherence is a filter on imitation, not a source of rules.

7.6    Every ingredient is necessary
We now show that each ingredient of TTL is forced. Here a learner is any randomized procedure
that receives the same kinds of information as TTL, possibly with one channel removed: human
samples, the queries of a prover and red team, answers of Ref d and W , its own coins and,
optionally, escalation answers. Lower bounds use a fixed prover and red team, i.e. strategies
mapping the history and their own coins to queries, the same in every scenario. Escalation
answers, if used, follow the practice: they are drawn from a law depending only on the query
and on the practice (for instance 1[q ∈ RP ]), so they have the same law in scenarios with the
same practice; for Theorem 7.20 the law is moreover computable uniformly in the practice and
the query. That covers Propositions 7.15 and 7.16 and Theorems 7.19 and 7.20; Theorem 7.18
compares different practices and needs an explicit assumption instead. A target-truthful labeller
(1[q ∈ R∗ ], the labelled setting of Section 4) is a different and stronger channel, and defeats
Theorems 7.18 and 7.19.
    Fix the practice with its frequencies, instance laws and noise law, and fix A, W, Ttrust . A target
Σ ⊆ ΣP is admissible if it satisfies (WS), equivalently is clean at every depth (Lemma 7.4(d)),
and each member of ΣP \ Σ has an instance outside Sound(RΣ ). All admissible targets share the
data law and the oracle answers (Lemma 7.4(c)) and satisfy (Floor) with the same constants.
  (d)
Fres (Σ) denotes the residue when Σ is the target.
Proposition 7.14 (Positive data are needed; trivial). [T7 Prop 5.1, as repaired] Let Σ1 ⊊ Σ2 be
calculi such that every subset of Σ2 is clean at every depth and RΣ2 ̸⊆ Sound(RΣ1 ). A learner
that receives only refutation evidence (oracle answers on schema sets of its choice, but no human
steps and no escalations) has the same view under the targets Σ1 and Σ2 . So it is unsound for
Σ1 or incomplete for Σ2 on the nonempty set RΣ2 \ Sound(RΣ1 ). Example: Σ1 = {∧I, ∧E1 , ∧E2 },
Σ2 = Σ1 ∪ {∨I1 } with classical evaluation. The non-derivability hypothesis is needed: for
Σ2 = Σ1 ∪ {A ∧ B ▷ B ∧ A}, accepting RΣ2 is both sound for Σ1 and complete for Σ2 .
    The proof is Lemma 7.4(c). This concerns soundness relative to the human calculus. In CPC,
structurality and closed evaluation decide schema validity (Lemma 7.22), so a learner wanting
only truth-soundness could enumerate schemas and assert the valid ones without human data;
positive data then only say which valid rules the practice uses. In arithmetic, positive data are
needed even for truth-completeness, because no refutational evidence ever certifies a true Π1
axiom.

Proposition 7.16 (Negative evidence is needed). [T7 Prop 5.3] Let the practice be {∧I, AC} with
fixed frequencies. In world W1 the connectives have their classical tables, AC is a fallacy and
the target is {∧I}. In W2 the tables are classical except that → is read as ↔; then AC is valid
(from B and A ↔ B infer A) and the target is {∧I, AC}. A learner without refutation evidence
sees identically distributed data in both, so it is unsound under W1 or incomplete under W2 .
The closed instance (⊤, ⊥ → ⊤ ▷ ⊥) separates them: under W1 its premises are true and its
conclusion false, while under W2 the premise ⊥ ↔ ⊤ is false.
    This is Corollary 5.19 in two-world form.
Proposition 7.17 (Structurality is needed; trivial). [T7 Prop 5.4] (a) If hypotheses are instance
sets rather than schemas, each refutation removes finitely many instances, so a fallacy with
infinitely many invalid instances keeps some invalid instance asserted at every finite time by any
learner that asserts the practice minus the refuted instances. (b) Without uniformity coherence is
toothless (Proposition 6.33: Cn2 + {▷p17 }). (c) Without structure positive data cannot generalize:
for classes of finite step sets the cautious verifier accepts exactly the data (Section 5.4).

Reading. Suppose modus ponens is rare, with frequency π. No learner that is sound whether
or not affirming the consequent is a fallacy, and that learns about the practice only from the
stream, can accept AC in the world where it is genuine before about π −1 ln(1/δ) samples: roughly
the time by which MP, the rule that would expose AC if it were a fallacy, has been seen with
confidence. TTL’s noise-free burn-in λ−1 ln(cK/δ), with λ ≤ πρMP , matches this up to the factor
ln K and the variability ρMP . This is the standard two-point rare-event bound behind PAC
sample-complexity lower bounds; the only new point is that the relevant rare event is the absence
of the refuter. Waiting is not timidity: a rule can be presumed valid only once the rules that
could impeach it have had their chance.

Theorem 7.19 (Blame: completeness needs world or bilateral evidence). [T7 Thm 5.6, as repaired]
(a) Two-point core. Let Σ0 ∪ {µ} and Σ0 ∪ {τ } be clean at every depth and {µ, τ } a d-conflict.

    scenario 1 with probability at most δ by every learner that is δ-sound in both scenarios. So
    µ, which lies in Colld in scenario 1, is collateral for every sound learner.

Proof idea. (a) A µ-instance outside Sound(RΣ0 ∪{τ } ) exists, or the refutation of {µ, τ } would
transfer to the clean set Σ0 ∪ {τ } (Lemma 3.1); in scenario 2 it is unsound and non-residual,

                                                67
The witness: → versus ←. Take A = {A1 }, no world, Σ0 = ∅, µ = MP and τ = AC.
{MP} is classically sound and A1 satisfiable; {AC} is clean, since the closure of A1 under AC
alone is {q, p → q, p → ⊥, p}; and AC followed by MP derives ⊥. Scenario 2 is literally the
hypothesis that “→” denotes converse implication. Under that reading AC is modus ponens
for ←, MP is affirming the consequent for ←, and A1 reads {q, q ⊃ p, ⊥ ⊃ p}, which is
consistent. Coherence alone cannot tell which way the arrow points. Either of two things breaks
the symmetry: world feedback, since the closed instance (⊥ → ⊥, ⊥ → (⊥ → ⊥) ▷ ⊥) of AC is
falsified; or a single denial, since in the designated position [A1 : p] AC alone derives the denied
p, and the conflict becomes {AC}. Both make scenario 2 violate (WS) (computed). In the Hilbert
practice {K, S, MP, DN, AC} the same mechanism makes K and MP necessarily collateral at full
depth; whether S or DN is collateral too is open (Appendix F.14).

Reading. This is the blame problem in its sharpest form. A community whose practice contains
both modus ponens and affirming the consequent has an incoherent practice, and coherence
correctly detects it. But coherence does not say which half of the practice is the meaning of
“if”. A learner that is sound whatever the answer must give up both as rules, keeping at most
their shared instances (Proposition 7.6(c)). What settles the direction is the world, or a denial:
the bilateralists’ rejection (Smiley, 1996; Rumfitt, 2000; Restall, 2005) does syntactically what a
counterexample object does semantically.

and (b) eventual completeness, P[∃t ∀t′ ≥ t : R∗ ⊆ accepted at t′ ] ≥ 1 − δ.

starte and contains halt ▷ ⊥ (Theorem 6.30); add the axiom τe = (▷starte ). If φe (e) diverges
the target is Σ0 ∪ {τe }; if it converges, τe is a non-residual fallacy. A learner meeting (a) and (b)
would make {e : φe (e) diverges} a Σ1 set. Appendix F.13.
    This is the Π1 -completeness of coherence turned into a statement about anytime soundness.
                                            (d )
TTL’s form of soundness (relative to Frest at time t, and to Fres only in the limit, with finitely
many changes) cannot be improved by any computable procedure.

Proposition 7.21 (Truthful designation is needed). [T7 Prop 5.8; T2 Prop 7.1, Thm 2.5] If a desig-
nated position violates (WS), descent can blame a genuine rule: with target {MP} and the bad
position [a, a → b : b], MP is blamed. Under structurality, one classically inconsistent designated
context forces the loss of a classical schema everywhere (Proposition 11.9). Proposition F.2
bounds the damage when at most m positions, not known which, violate (WS), and Theorem 6.7
is the soft version. Nothing bounds the damage of an unknown number of mis-designations.

Classical propositional logic. The language has ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ⊤, ⊥. Judgments are formulas,
or sequents whose contexts are lists with explicit structural rules (set or multiset contexts would
need anti-unification modulo associativity and commutativity, for which the bounds of Section 5
are not proved). All schemas are pure (Definition 2.4); by Proposition 7.17 this cannot be dropped.
Σ∗ is any finite set of classically valid pure schemas that is complete for classical consequence, F
any finite set of classically invalid pure schemas, the world is JW = closed formulas with W =
truth value (“computation”), and A consists of truthful positions and contains [∅ : ∅].

Lemma 7.22 (Closed-instance refutability; Post’s substitution). [T7 Lemma 6.1] A pure schema τ is
classically invalid iff some substitution of ⊤/⊥ for its metavariables yields a closed instance whose
premises are W -true and whose conclusion is W -false. As a one-step derivation this instance
has size at most |τ |, and there are at most 2v(τ ) candidates, v(τ ) the number of metavariables.
                                        Lean: Post.schema_invalid_iff_closedRefutation Lean: Post.card_candidates_le


Proof. (⇐) A falsified instance is invalid. (⇒) As in the proof of Proposition 3.5: if a valuation v
falsifies an instance τ θ, put cx = ⊤ if v(θx) = 1 and cx = ⊥ otherwise; by induction on τ , τ [cx /x]
has the values of τ θ under v, and closed formulas have the same value under every valuation.

    This is essentially Post (1921). For sequents with a context metavariable Γ, substitute the
                                           V
one-element list [⊤] or [⊥] according to v( Γθ); depending on how lists are encoded, the instance
can then exceed |τ | by a constant. A brute-force check on 30,000 random pure schemas (16,309
invalid) found no mismatch (computed), and the formula case is formalized in Lean.

    The counts are upper bounds: one falsified step can be an instance of several fallacies, as
(⊤, ⊥ → ⊤ ▷ ⊥) is of both AC and (⊤, A → ⊤ ▷ A), and one descent removes both. The
instance checks include those of the genuine schemas, which certify the final NONE. The oracle
need not return a smallest refutation; exactness and determinism are all that the audit uses, and
part (iv) of Theorem 7.12 is trivial here.

Reading. This meets the first success criterion in its strongest form. From imitation of human
proofs containing systematic fallacies, each used under its own latent tag, and sporadic slips,
plus truth-table evaluation of closed formulas, the learner identifies exactly the classical calculus
the community uses, with probability at least 1 − δ, after N1 human steps, with at most |F |
refutations. On that event it is sound against every prover at every moment, and its reasoner
derives exactly classical consequence, out of distribution.
Proposition 7.24 (Coherence alone on CPC is lossy; a denial repairs it). [T7 Prop 6.3; (b) as repaired]
Let JW = ∅ and A be truthful. (a) If [∅ : ∅] ∈ A, every τ ∈ F lies in some minimal conflict once
                                                                       (d)
d ≥ dτ , because Σ∗ ∪{τ } derives ⊥ from ∅ (Proposition 3.5). Hence Fres = ∅ for d ≥ maxτ dτ , and
TTL is truth-sound. (b) The collateral can be nonempty, and then TTL’s fallback is incomplete,
necessarily so at stable depth (Theorem 7.19(b)). For a complete Hilbert system Σ∗ for the
full language containing K and MP, F = {AC} and A = {[∅ : ∅]} or {[∅ : ∅], [A1 : ∅]}, every
descent is blocked, and K (with A1 , also MP) lies in Colld for all large d: every sound learner
using coherence alone must withhold it as a rule. (c) Bilateral repair. If for each τ ∈ F , A
contains a counterexample position [Π′ : φ′ ], where Π′ ▷ φ′ is a closed falsified instance of τ , and

   Proof in Appendix F.14. Reading. In CPC closed evaluation refutes exactly the schemas
that coherence refutes; by Post, both refute all invalid ones. The whole difference between the
channels is localization: computation names the culprit, a contradiction only a list of suspects.
A counterexample position is a syntactic object, a partial valuation, so “bilateral coherence with
denials” and “world feedback with descent” are the same resource in two notations.

Complete decidable theories. Let T be complete and decidable, such as real closed fields
(Tarski, 1951), Presburger arithmetic (Presburger, 1929), ACFp or dense linear orders without
endpoints, with M |= T . Judgments are sequents Γ ⊢ φ of first-order formulas, with W (Γ ⊢

φ) = [M |= ∀x̄( Γ → φ)], decidable by quantifier elimination, so JW = J. Σ∗ is a finite schema

calculus, sound and complete for T -consequence on sequents, including →-introduction and
∀-introduction.

Lemma 7.25 (Validity is truth preservation). [T7 Lemma 6.4] (a) Sound(R∗ ) is exactly the set of
W -truth-preserving steps. (b) A schema is a fallacy iff it has a W -falsified instance, so each
τ ∈ F has a smallest falsified instance, of some size fτ ≥ dτ .

Proof idea. If all premises are true they are derivable, since T is complete, so ClR∗ of them is
the set of true sequents; if one is false, Σ∗ derives its false universal closure, whose negation T
proves, and then everything. Appendix F.15.

Corollary 7.26 (TTL on complete decidable theories, given realizability). [T7 Cor 6.5, as repaired]
Suppose in addition that Σ∗ and F lie in a schema class for which the identification of Theo-
rem 5.14 holds, for instance first-order patterns, possibly with decidable side conditions such as
the eigenvariable condition of ∀I. Let d ≥ maxτ fτ , [∅ : ∅] ∈ A, and let Ref d search the instances
of size at most d of the schemas of B for a W -falsified one. Then everything in Corollary 7.23
                          (d)
holds verbatim: (SBd ), Fres = ∅, A = Σ∗ , truth-soundness at all times on G, and at most |F | + 1
oracle calls.

    The realizability hypothesis is not established for the listed theories. The rule ∀E, from ∀xφ
infer φ[t/x], is not a first-order pattern, because its conclusion is a substitution result; with t
arbitrary it is not a higher-order pattern in the sense of Miller (1991) either. The lgg of three ∀E
instances is (∀x(z0 +z1 = z2 )▷z3 +z4 = z5 ), with the invalid instance (∀x(0+0 = 0)▷0+0 = S0),
and more data only generalize it further (computed). The usual axiomatizations of RCF and
ACFp contain degree-indexed families, and Presburger arithmetic an induction or congruence
schema; none is a single first-order pattern. Dense linear orders without endpoints are finitely
axiomatized, so there only the quantifier rules matter. Without realizability, the identified schema
for a non-pattern rule is in general an over-general lgg. If it has an instance outside Sound(R∗ ),
as for ∀E and induction, the total oracle W falsifies one (Lemma 7.25(b)), and an audit of
sufficient depth removes it with singleton blame. So TTL stays sound, eventually so under the
depth schedule, but A lacks the rule and exactness fails. Two repairs are open: an encoding with
auxiliary decidable judgments Sub(φ, x, t, ψ) (“ψ is φ[t/x]”) evaluated by W , carried out below
for induction; or an identification theorem for higher-order-pattern schemas. Why one should
learn at all when W already decides validity, and what changes when the oracle evaluates only
quantifier-free sentences, is discussed in Appendix F.15. The real-closed-field core of olympiad
algebra and geometry would be covered by Corollary 7.26 once its realizability hypothesis is met;
trigonometric steps are not, since (R, +, ·, sin) defines Z.

Arithmetic. The language is that of PA and M = N. Ttrust is first-order logic: the logic is
fixed, and non-logical axiom schemas are learned (its propositional fragment can be learned
first by Corollary 7.23; the quantifier rules are not first-order patterns and must be trusted,
Corollary 7.26). The world is JW = ∆0 sentences with W = computation, and A consists of
truthful positions. A practice axiom schema is genuine iff all its instances are true in N, so Σ∗
may contain PA together with true extras such as Con(PA), and (WS) holds with V = truth in
N. Since R∗ consists of axiom steps, the relevant target closure is ClR∗ ∪Ttrust (Theorem 7.12(i)).
Ground axioms (those of Q, each Con(Tj ), ¬Con(PA)) are realizable; the induction schema is
not, and part (e) encodes it. Parts (a)–(d) and (f) concern the audit and hold for any P̂ = ΣP .

Theorem 7.27 (Arithmetic is Popperian). [T7 Thm 6.6, as repaired in two rounds]
(a) False Π1 axioms get singleton blame. Let τ have a false instance ∀x̄ θ(x̄) with θ ∈ ∆0
    and least counterexample n̄. The refutation “⊢ ∀x̄θ (by τ ); ⊢ θ(n̄) (by trusted ∀E)”, with

    ∀E. With the prefer-unblocked oracle, τ is removed and no PA axiom is put at risk. For one
                                                            (d)
    quantified variable with m free occurrences in θ, τ ∈
                                                         / Fres once d ≥ 2|θ| + m(n + 1) + O(1);
    for k variables (k + 1) |θ| + m(n + 1) + O(k) suffices, n the largest component of n̄.
(b) Under presumption of validity, false Σ1 axioms survive. For the practice ΣP = PA ∪ {τ } with
    τ = (▷¬Con(PA)) (so Σ∗ = PA, F = {τ }) and positions with ∆0 assertions and denials,
    Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is clean at every depth, so τ ∈ Fres is asserted forever.
(c) Popperian Σ1 -caution removes syntactically Σ1 residue. Asserting an instance of a practice
    axiom with Σ1 normal form only once W has verified a witness never asserts a false such
    axiom, ¬Con(PA) included. The policy is syntactic: an equivalent sentence with a Π2 normal
    form escapes it and is residual.
(d) Beyond Σ1 there is a permanent residue. False Π2 or Σ2 axioms τ with Σ∗ ∪ {τ } clean at
    every depth (for example, Σ∗ ⊇ Q and Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ∪ A ∪ ¬D consistent for every designated
    [A : D]) admit no finite refutation and survive, and no computable policy sorts the true from
    the false ones in the limit (Theorem 6.21(e)). The same holds for randomized learners that
    are correct in the limit with probability above 12 (proof sketch).
(e) Finite reflection-extended practices are learned under the floor, given a realizable encoding
    of induction. Under (Floor) a practice has at most min(K, ⌊1/(2∆)⌋) axiom schemas,
    and, with induction written as a first-order pattern through decidable Sub judgments, Tk =
    PA + Con(PA) + · · · + Con(Tk−1 ) is identified from positive data for every k within that
    bound. Without a floor there is no uniform sample bound, by a tight two-point bound that
    mirrors Theorem 7.18.
 (f) Reflection as designation. If A asserts Con(PA), then ¬Con(PA) becomes a singleton conflict.

Proof idea. (a) is Lemma 7.8. (b) PA + ¬Con(PA) is consistent by Gödel’s second theorem (Gödel,
1931) and proves every true ∆0 sentence and no false one (Lemma 6.18); so the audit’s first call
returns NONE. (d) reduces to Shoenfield’s limit lemma (Shoenfield, 1959) and Post’s hierarchy
theorem. (e) is the mirror image of Theorem 7.18. Appendix F.16 gives the proofs, the precise
forms of (c) and (e), and computed checks of (a) and (e).

Reading. In arithmetic TTL achieves exact, localized, Popperian falsification of false Π1 axioms;
exclusion of syntactically Σ1 errors under Σ1 -caution; identification of finite reflection-extended
practices, given a realizable induction schema; and soundness at all times relative to the stated
residue. It does not achieve, and no computable procedure can achieve, the elimination of false
Σ2 axioms consistent with the practice, or uniform sample bounds without a frequency floor; and
under presumption of validity it keeps false Σ1 axioms such as ¬Con(PA). The Gödel–Rosser
alternatives are the Kripkensteinian residue of arithmetic (Theorem 6.34(iii)), and TTL leaves
it exactly where Section 6 located it, now with explicit sample sizes, refutation budgets and
soundness against adaptive provers. Reflection enters as a designation, a justification beyond
PA-proof that is made explicit rather than smuggled in as a rule.
