7.8   Simulation evidence
The two-tier learner on a propositional practice. A simulation runs TTL in the setting
of Corollary 7.23. The practice has nine genuine tagged natural-deduction rules (∧I, ∧E1,2 , ∨I1,2 ,
MP, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism, double-negation elimination) and four fallacies with
their own tags (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, conversion, “or” as “xor”).
Sporadic noise at rate α = 0.01 is mis-tagged at random, and the trim budget is e = 2. The
audit is the per-schema closed-instance oracle. An adversarial prover enumerates every step over
a pool of ten formulas and checks it by truth table. Table 10 shows the result (seed 0; the run is
deterministic across hash seeds).
    The positive-only cautious tier asserts the fallacies as soon as they are anchored (Proposi-
tion 7.5): it is unsound in 72 of 80 runs. TTL is unsound in none of the 80, and exact in all 20
runs at N = 250 and at N = 500. Excess noise on a fallacy tag is harmless, since whatever schema
the trimmed lgg produces for that tag is world-refuted and dropped anyway. The untrimmed
learner is kept sound by the audit, which refutes the collapsed lgg of Proposition 5.12, but it
loses whole tags, and loses more of them as N grows. The simulation’s scope is limited: it tests
the singleton-conflict case of CPC with a fixed budget and a per-schema world audit. It does not
exercise descent on multi-step refutations, the fallback, or the N1 formula; a simulation of the
full audit is future work.

The propositional experiment. Experiment B (Section 12.2) runs a related pipeline, not an
implementation of TTL, and shows this section’s phenomena: coherence pruning closes every
route to ⊢ ⊥, Post probes refute all 118 invalid structural candidate schemas, non-structural rules
escape (Proposition 7.17), and world feedback mainly speeds up blame (5.0 versus 9.1 pruning
rounds): localization, not refutation.

7.9   Summary
Learning which inferences are valid is learning the audited practice. Imitation finds the prac-
tice’s rules, fallacies included, and is the only channel that says anything positive about a rule
(Lemma 7.4 and Proposition 7.14). Confrontation with designated positions and the world sorts
them, withholding every rule in a minimal conflict and, where descent applies, only the culprit
(Lemmas 7.7 and 7.8). Descent makes an algorithm, with a guarantee, out of a lesson recorded
in the motivating notes (Hänni, 2026): “one way to resolve a tension/contradiction is to go back
to what caused one (or each) of the contradicting views/predictions/claims” (philosophy/
philosophy of thinking/how do i resolve contradictions, tensions?.md). Assertion


                                                73
comes last, after the burn-in (Theorem 7.18). Coherence fixes the learned role only up to
which member of a conflicting set is given up: in the MP/AC example only the world or a denial
decides whether “→” means → or ←. This gives one precise sense to the notes’ question about
“the hooking of a model onto the world” (philosophy/philosophy of language/meaning and
truth/individual sentences being meaningful.md): the hooking is needed not to make the
role coherent, but to make it the intended one when practice conflicts with itself. The residue Fres
is empty for CPC and, given realizability, for complete decidable theories; in arithmetic it contains
¬Con(PA) under presumption of validity. Section 13 discusses the resulting warrant. Open here
are the query complexity of sound blame, the full-depth status of the Hilbert rival {S, DN, AC}
(Appendix F.14), blame with priors, the size of coherence witnesses in first-order logic, and TTL
with anchored physical contexts as designated positions (see also Section 14).


8       Simplicity and normativity from imitation
Imitation identifies practice, errors included: for positive data, a systematic error generated by
a schema is a rule (Corollary 5.19). This section examines a different remedy, proposed in the
motivating notes (Hänni, 2026), and answers the question it raises.2 The note asks how one can
understand “what someone means when using a word. as opposed to becoming a predictor of
what they would say”. It proposes
        “an even stronger simplicity prior than solomonoff. eg if there are explainable mistakes on a
        simple model, you want the simple model that doesn’t predict the mistakes. [. . . ] let’s just
        do a version of the simple hypothesis with noise, and then penalize the likelihood term less.”

The note anticipates an objection: in sequence prediction, a steeper penalty favours a universal
hypothesis that absorbs everything. It suggests, while “very much uncertain”, that this pathology
“is not present in the function case, if [. . . ] each input has to sample its own random bits”. It
asks whether, given the models it lists, the good model “could be a vertex of the convex hull of
the set of attainable (hypothesis complexity, expected neg log likelihood) tuples”. And it adds:
“I consider it very much plausible that there is some other pathology”.

Answers in brief. The function-case intuition and the convex-hull argument are both right:
private randomness makes every hypothesis pay for mixing per input, the product-model frontier
has the hoped-for kink (proved for parity models), and selection is a threshold on rates (risk
reduction per bit) along the lower hull (Theorems 8.2, 8.4 and G.6 and Lemma 8.6). But there
are other pathologies: universality returns at block granularity, selection is by rate rather than
validity, and the right steepness is not identifiable from imitation data. Steeper simplicity is
a good third filter beside coherence and the world; the note’s own alternative, “you specify
properties of the thing or notion”, removes cheap fallacies at every steepness. Section 8.7 gives
the verdict in the note’s terms, with references.
    As far as we know, three results are mildly new: the product-model frontier and its kink,
the rate threshold for arbitrary hypotheses, and the realizability of every convex frontier after
rescaling.
    2
   The source is the public working note philosophy/philosophy of thinking/beating solomonoff induction
at grokking a notion.md, which lists this proposal as one of several ideas. Quotations are verbatim.

8.1    The proposal, formalized
Inputs x ∈ X are drawn from µ, and labels lie in a finite set Y . The teacher is a channel P ∗ (y | x).
In the note’s picture, P ∗ arises from an intended norm h◦ through sporadic noise and systematic
error. Data are i.i.d. from µ × P ∗ . Normativity asks the learner to output h◦ , or its deterministic
core, rather than P ∗ . In Section 8.6, x is a proof context and y the next human step; then P ∗ is
the practice RP of Definition 2.10, viewed as a channel.

Definition 8.1 (Randomness and objective). [T5 Def 1.1, §1.3] A product hypothesis (private
randomness) is a conditional distribution h(· | x), with likelihood i h(yi | xi ). A shared-
                                                                        Q

randomness hypothesis is a distribution P (y1:N | x1:N ); sequence prediction is its causally
conditioned case. In a block hypothesis, the input at position i of a block (e.g. a document)
includes the block’s earlier pairs. The note’s loss is λℓ(h) + i≤N − log2 h(yi | xi ), with λ > 1
                                                               P

growing with N . Writing λ = cN and dividing by N gives Jˆc = cℓ + R̂N , and its population
version Jc = cℓ + R, where R(h) = Eµ×P ∗ [− log2 h(y | x)]. Let Φ(c) = inf h Jc (h). In the idealized
version, ℓ = K (prefix complexity) over total programs with rational outputs, and ph is a shortest
program for h. In the computable version, ℓ is a prefix code on a countable class. A component
costing k bits that lowers R by r has rate r/k.

     The steepness c is measured in bits per sample per bit of description. In the computable
                                             −B

1 − δ and for every fixed h0 ; so we work with Jc .
     Fixed versus growing steepness. With fixed λ, c → 0, so every component of positive rate
is eventually absorbed, error or not [T4 Prop 7.1(i); L11 Prop 2.2] : imitation with a fixed simplicity
weight converges to the teacher’s practice, the learner’s version of Cohen’s view that normative
standards are a systematization of ordinary judgments (Cohen, 1981). With λ ∝ N , as the note
proposes, selection is asymptotically stable, so the obstruction found below is rate inversion, not
sample size.

Relation to the literature. The note’s λ is the inverse 1/η of a learning rate η < 1 in a
tempered posterior (Grünwald, 2012; Grünwald and van Ommen, 2017; Zhang, 2006; Bissiri
et al., 2016; Bhattacharya et al., 2019), and cℓ + R is the algorithmic rate–distortion Lagrangian
with log-loss distortion (Vereshchagin and Vitányi, 2010). Appendix G.2 gives the details and
relates the proposal to SafeBayes and to Kolmogorov’s structure function.

8.2    No universal hypothesis in the function case
The note asks whether it is “just failing to construct the right ‘universal hypothesis’ ”. The
answer is no as long as randomness is private and inputs carry no other labels, and yes as soon
as they do.

    In sequence prediction, by contrast, a universal semimeasure M beats every model whose

case even the universal conditional semimeasure is a fixed predictor, with positive risk against
every teacher with binary labels (Appendix G.4).

8.3    The kink: shared versus private randomness
In sequence prediction, the note says, “it’s pretty much just 1 bit paying for 1 bit”. In the
function case one might instead “see some point at which the derivative changes”. We prove this
for the note’s example, made rigorous.

Setting. Let X = {0, 1}d , n = 2d and µ uniform. The simple model is a parity fa (x) =
⟨a, x⟩ mod 2 with K(a) ≥ d. The error set E has |E| = pn, p < 1/4 and K(p) = O(log d), and

the randomness deficiency of E, which is O(log n) for most E. Write ŝh (a′ ) for the correlation of

h’s vote h(0 | x) − h(1 | x) with (−1)⟨a ,x⟩ . The good model is fa with flip rate p; it has K ≤ d + κ′

Theorem 8.4 (Kink). [T5 Thm 2.5, as repaired] There is a machine constant κ such that the following
hold.
 (a) Shared randomness has (almost) no kink. Let Pu be the uniform shared-randomness
     mixture of the 2u noisy parities that agree with a on its first d − u coordinates. Then
     |K(Pu ) − (d − u)| ≤ κ′ and − log Pu (y ∗ ) = u + nH(p) − o(1), where the o(1) term is
     nonnegative and exponentially small in n (so super-exponentially small in d). So the total
     K(Pu ) − log Pu (y ∗ ) is d + nH(p) up to ±(κ′ + o(1)) for every u, and every minimizer u∗
     of λK(Pu ) − log Pu (y ∗ ) has d − u∗ ≤ λ−1
                                              λ
                                                 (2κ′ + o(1)).
 (b) Private randomness has a kink. For every product h and t ∈ N with K(h) ≤ d − 2t −
     2 log2 (t + 1) − 2 log2 d − κ,

                                 R(h) ≥ 1 − log2 (1 + βt ) ≥ 1 − βt / ln 2,

      where βt = min{2−t + 2p, (1 − 2p)2−t + εE }, with εE =                  32 ln 2 · p(δE + d + κn )/n,

 (c) The error segment. For every product h, K(h) + nR(h) ≥ d + LE − δE − 2 log2 d − κ.
     The proof (Appendix G.5) combines the list-size bound for the Hadamard code (Goldreich
and Levin, 1989; Kushilevitz and Mansour, 1993), which makes a short h correlating with fa
encode a in fewer than d bits, with Jensen’s inequality and the coding theorem; the slack 2p
arises because h may be right on E for free, and the randomness of E relative to h replaces it by
εE .

Reading. Part (a) is the note’s “1 bit paying for 1 bit”: the shared frontier is the sufficiency
line, so a steeper penalty selects a mixture that knows almost nothing of a and learns the rest
from the data, as any Bayes mixture does. Part (b) makes the note’s hope quantitative. A
product hypothesis missing u = d − K(h) bits gains at most about 2−u/2+O(log d) bits per sample
over the coin, plus slack: exponentially little, though not nothing (list mixtures missing u = 1, 2, 3
bits gain 0.454, 0.221, 0.110 bits (computed)). So on the scale of d bits the product frontier is flat
near the coin and drops at the simple model; that drop is the change of derivative.
    Two caveats. The kink is resolved only up to O(log d) bits next to the simple model. And
the slack 2p alone gives a kink only for p < 0.1421, where 1 − 2p/ ln 2 > H(p); the slack εE gives
one for every p < 1/4 once n is large and δE = O(log n) (at p = 0.2, d = 20 and δE = κ = 0,
εE = 0.014).

8.4    Selection traces the hull: rate thresholds
Let zh = (ℓ(h), R(h)), Z = {zh } and Ĉ = conv(Z + R2≥0 ). Only finitely many h have ℓ ≤ L, and
R ≥ 0, so each Jc with c > 0 attains its minimum.

Definition 8.5 (Lower hull). [T5 §3.1, as repaired] hull− (Z) is the set of boundary points of Ĉ
supported by a line of slope −c with 0 < c < ∞. A vertex is an extreme point of Ĉ that lies in
hull− (Z); vertices belong to Z.

Lemma 8.6 (Selection traces the lower hull; standard). [T5 Lemma 3.1, as repaired] (i) For c > 0,
the minimizers of Jc are the h with zh ∈ hull− (Z) on a supporting line of slope −c, and every
point of hull− (Z) in Z arises this way. (ii) If c < c′ , and h and h′ minimize Jc and Jc′ , then
ℓ(h) ≥ ℓ(h′ ) and R(h) ≤ R(h′ ). (iii) A point z ∈ Z is the unique minimizing point for all c
in some nonempty open interval iff it is a vertex. The interval is then (s+ , s− ), given by the
absolute slopes of the adjacent edges. A hypothesis is the unique minimizer there iff, in addition,
no other hypothesis has the same point.
        Lean: RateThreshold.onLowerHull_iff Lean: RateThreshold.lemma_3_1_ii Lean: RateThreshold.lemma_3_1_iii_hyp


   Part (i) holds because Jc (h) = ⟨(c, 1), zh ⟩ has the same minimum over Z as over Ĉ; (ii) follows
by adding the two optimality inequalities; (iii) is proved in Appendix G.6. The Lean proofs of (i)
and (iii) cover finite classes.

Reading. The note’s convex-hull argument is correct, with two refinements. The intended
model must be a vertex, and the only hypothesis at its point. And λ must lie in (s+ N, s− N ).
The note’s alternative, to “set abs bound on model complexity”, selects every model the penalty
selects (bound it at that model’s length), as the note observes. The converse fails: a hard bound
can also select points of the staircase ρ× (k) = min{R(h) : ℓ(h) ≤ k} that lie off the hull, though
never a Pareto-dominated point such as that of Proposition 8.10.

Arbitrary hypotheses. With ℓ = K and all hypotheses allowed, which may share information
across regions or learn components partially, independent parities behave as separable components:
the rate threshold of Theorem 8.7 survives up to explicit O(log) slack (Theorem G.6). Every
convex, decreasing, piecewise-linear frontier that starts at height 1, has rational slopes and drops
by at most one bit is, after rescaling and up to logarithmic bands, the product-model frontier
of a teacher made of independent parities and a fair-coin region (Corollary G.7); so whether a
good model is a vertex is a property of the data, not a theorem. And in the note’s example, for
small p and c well inside the window (≈ 1/n, ≈ (1 − H(p))/d), every near-optimal hypothesis
correlates strongly with the parity and memorizes almost none of the errors (Theorem G.8
and Corollary G.9). All four results are stated and proved in Appendix G.
     The note’s own numbers (computed). These are a 100-bit simple model (plus 10 bits for
the flip rate, our stand-in for the note’s “something small”), and a 10 000-bit error on a 2−10
fraction of inputs, with H(2−10 ) = 0.0112 bits per sample (about 1/100, as the note says). The
rates are 8.99 · 10−3 for the model and 1.12 · 10−6 for the error. So the good model is selected
iff c lies between these, a window spanning a factor of about 8000. At N = 106 this means
λ ∈ (1.12, 8990). Standard MDL (λ = 1) switches to the error model at N ≈ 8.9 · 105 .

Reading. The error’s rate is about 1/n: a K-random error set costs one bit per 1/n of risk,
the slowest possible rate. So the note’s example is the most favourable case for the proposal.
Normativity is achieved there because the errors are incompressible relative to the norm.

   For (ii) in the separable case: if v is selected and c is not a tie, then c < rv /kv ≤ re /ke ; and if
c = rv /kv < re /ke , then e is strictly selected. The idealized case is proved in Appendix G.10.

is new is the quantitative criterion: the penalty separates errors from rules by rate, not validity.
    For instance, a 200-bit valid rule used in 10−4 of steps, gaining at most 2.2 bits per use, has
a lower rate than the note’s 10 000-bit error, so every c that rejects the error discards it; rarely
used irregular verbs likewise regularize first (Lieberman et al., 2007).

                                                   79
Cheap fallacies [T5 Prop 4.2] . In step imitation (Section 8.6), a schema used in a fraction π of
steps has rate πg/ℓ. Affirming the consequent (AC: q, p → q / p) has the size of modus ponens.
The freshman’s dream (FD: (a + b)2 → a2 + b2 ) is shorter than the correct expansion.
    Take a toy with M = 64 candidate steps and slip rate ε = 0.05, so that the gain is g = 5.42
bits (computed). AC, at frequency 0.02 and 20 bits, then has rate 5.4 · 10−3 . That beats proof
by cases (1.4 · 10−3 ), reductio (1.6 · 10−3 ), ex falso (7.2 · 10−4 ) and induction (1.2 · 10−4 ). So no
steepness keeps every valid rule while removing every error.
    We conjecture that this is no accident (conjecture; empirical). A fallacy becomes systematic
because it is a short, natural variant of a valid pattern.

    This answers the note’s vertex question in general. The hull mechanism is right, but the
intended model is a vertex only if every valid component out-rates every error (Corollary 8.8).

Theorem 8.11 (The steepness is not identifiable from imitation data). [T5 Thm 4.3, as repaired]
  (i) Along the population path, R(hc ) is non-increasing as c decreases. So, for a fixed finite
      grid in the computable version with a noise floor, choosing c by held-out log-loss picks,
      with probability tending to one as N → ∞, a grid value whose selected hypothesis has least
      risk among the selected ones; the smallest grid value always qualifies. (At a grid value
      lying exactly at a hull breakpoint, the hypothesis selected there may alternate between co-
      minimizers of different risk.) At finite N this can fail, through the B/c term of Lemma G.1.
 (ii) For every strictly proper scoring rule, the teacher channel strictly maximizes the expected
      score at every x (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). So every validation criterion that is an
      empirical proper score on fresh imitation data targets P ∗ , errors included.
(iii) No imitation-data statistic picks a good c in both worlds of Theorem 8.9(iv).

   The proof is in Appendix G.11. In the note’s example, cross-validation picks the error model:
held-out log-loss is 1.0 at c = 10−1 , 0.0112 on [10−5 , 10−3 ], and 0 at c = 10−7 (computed). A
non-proper “knee” heuristic (the interior vertex with the widest log c-interval) picks the good
model in this example; by (iii), no such rule is right in both twin worlds.

Reading. Choosing c is a normative act, not an estimate. The note says that “is this a chair?”
is “much closer to ‘should the person who taught me the chair notion consider it a chair?’ ” than
to what that person would say. Part (iii) makes literal the claim that this target is not a function
of P ∗ .

Proposition 8.12 (Guard erosion). [T5 Prop 4.4, as repaired] Let σ|G guard a schema σ (e.g. x/x → 1
if x ̸= 0). Humans apply σ in G-contexts (frequency πG , per-step gain g). In contexts where
σ applies but G fails (frequency π¬G ), they play a non-σ step. In the σ-applicable region a
hypothesis has three options: none: uniform over the M candidates, at cost 0; unguarded: mass
1 − ε + ε/M on the σ-step, at cost kσ ; and guarded: the same as unguarded in G-contexts, and
uniform on the non-σ steps otherwise, at cost kσ + kG . Define

             πG g − π¬G log2 (1/ε)              π¬G ∆G
      ρσ =                         ,     ρG =          ,       ∆G = log2 (M/ε) − log2 (M − 1).
                      kσ                          kG

If ρG < ρσ , then for c ∈ (ρG , ρσ ) the unguarded, unsound σ is selected, although the teacher
never errs. For c < ρG the guarded rule is selected, and for c > ρσ neither is. If ρG ≥ ρσ , then
apart from ties the path goes from guarded to none, and the learner stays sound.

    In (bits, risk) relative to none, the unguarded option is a vertex of the lower hull of the three
options iff ρσ > ρG ; the proof is in Appendix G.12.
    Take πG = 0.05, π¬G = 5 · 10−4 , kσ = 22, kG = 12, M = 64 and ε = 0.05 (computed). Then
ρG = 1.8 · 10−4 and ρσ = 1.22 · 10−2 , so the unguarded rule is selected on (1.8 · 10−4 , 1.22 · 10−2 ), a
range that includes steepnesses at which ex falso (rate 7.2 · 10−4 ) is kept. With πG = π¬G = 0.002
instead, ρσ < ρG and there is no unsound phase.

Reading. What a careful teacher exhibits most rarely is what goes first: side conditions,
eigenvariable conditions, edge cases. One unsound schema can trivialize a classical calculus
(Proposition 3.5). With field rules, 0/0 = 1 and 0/0 = 0 · 0−1 = 0 give 1 = 0, a negative bag
(Lemma 6.2). So coherence must restore what simplicity erodes.

Further pathologies [T5 §4.4] . Four more are stated precisely in Appendix G.13. Error
envelopes: errors concentrated in a cheaply describable region are learned at the envelope’s own
rate, and where their density there exceeds 12 the learner predicts the error label throughout the
region. Parasitic errors: an error that is cheap given a valid rule (K(e | v) ≪ K(e), as FD is
given (ab)n = an bn ) can enter the hull bundled with it, so a valid rule may be kept only because
of the error it subsidizes. Distribution dependence: a valid rule that is rare in training stays
discarded as N → ∞. Language relativity: for any c > 0, some prefix code makes any given set
of positive-gain separable components the unique selection; between universal machines marginal
costs move by at most 2cU V , negligible for 10 000-bit errors but decisive for 20-bit schemas, so
the note’s “simplicity prior defined in terms of existing understanding” cuts both ways.

8.6    Inference rules: the division of labour
In situation-typed step imitation, a context x is a premise set and a goal (Section 2), and y is
the next human step among Mτ candidates. Contexts fall into computable situation types τ
of frequency πτ . In type τ the human applies a schema στ ∈ ΣP , genuine or fallacious, with
probability 1 − ε, and otherwise moves uniformly.
    Modelling type τ costs ℓ(στ ) + O(1) bits and gains gτ = log2 Mτ − Hτ per step. Its rate is
therefore ρτ = πτ gτ /(ℓ(στ ) + O(1)), and by Theorem 8.7 it is selected iff ρτ > c. The induced
verifier accepts the instances of the selected schemas. It is sound (Definition 2.18) iff no error
schema is selected and no guard has eroded.

Definition 8.13 (Admissible family, witnesses). [T5 §5.2, as repaired] The components are V ⊔ F
(valid, erroneous), with net values νj = rj − c kj . The admissible family A ⊆ 2V ⊔F is the
intersection of the filters in use: A-coherence (Definition 2.13), W-adequacy, and coherence with
designated meaning postulates Ax. Here W-adequacy means that no claim the world refutes is
derivable. The family is down-closed and contains 2V . A witness for e ∈ F is a minimal W ⊆ V
with W ∪{e} ∈  / A. It is the negative bag of Lemma 6.2, seen from the rules. Let V+ = {v : νv > 0}
and F+ = {e : νe > 0}. At a given c we impose two conditions. Error-independence: for U ⊆ V ,
U ∪ F ′ ∈ A iff U ∪ {e} ∈ A for each e ∈ F ′ . Valid dominance: every e ∈ F+ with a witness inside
V+ has β(e) > F+ ν. Here β(e) is the least value of B ν over sets B ⊆ V+ meeting all of e’s
                 P                                       P

witnesses inside V+ .
Theorem 8.14 (Division of labour). [T5 Thm 5.2, as repaired] Fix c, and assume separability, error-
independence and valid dominance at c. Then the optimal admissible sets are exactly the admissible
sets S ∗ (c) ∪ Z with Z ⊆ {ν = 0}, where
                              S ∗ (c) = V+ ∪ {e ∈ F+ : V+ ∪ {e} ∈ A}.
So, up to zero-value ties, simplicity removes exactly the errors of rate at most c, coherent or not;
coherence, the world and postulates remove exactly the errors that clash with the valid rules
actually kept (V+ , plus Ax), whatever their rate; the residue is the high-rate errors that pass
every filter; and valid rules of rate at most c are lost, whatever the other filters do.
    The proof is in Appendix G.14: valid dominance makes it better to restore the valid rules an
error’s witnesses need than to keep the error. A brute-force check of 17 806 instances found no
violation (computed).

Reading: avowal versus performance. Postulates are the teacher’s avowals (“1+1=2”,
“MP is valid, AC is not”, “a chair is for sitting”), not the teacher’s performance. The steeper
penalty sees only performance. This is where the debate between Stich and Nisbett (1980) and
Cohen (1981) lands [L11 §2] .
     Cohen grounds norms in a systematization of ordinary judgments; Stich and Nisbett had
argued, against reflective equilibrium as a test of justification, that systematic fallacies such
as the gambler’s fallacy can survive such a systematization. Performance data indeed cannot
separate a fallacy from a rule with the same profile (Theorem 8.9(iv)). Avowals are a second
channel: few bits that exclude whole high-rate classes of errors. Where an avowal is itself wrong,
as with naive comprehension, coherence catches it (Section 10).
     The note’s abstract/concrete example, “if something is abstract, then it usually helps a lot
to study examples to understand it”, is a cross-notion postulate: it ties the notion to another
notion with independent evidence, turning a labelling error into a W-refutation. This makes
“should the person who taught me [. . . ] consider it a chair” operational: the norm is whatever
fits the notion’s avowed role, checked against the other channels.
     Table 11 puts the pieces together. The residue is the alternative meanings of Theorem 6.34

8.7     Verdict
Where the proposal is vindicated. Function induction with private randomness has no universal-
hypothesis pathology, by exactly the mechanism the note names: “you have to pay the likelihood
term separately at every x” (Theorem 8.2). Shared randomness pays for partial knowledge once,
product models gain exponentially little from it, so the product frontier kinks, as proved for
parity teachers (Theorem 8.4). The convex-hull argument is correct; the change of derivative
is the vertex condition, plus uniqueness at the vertex (Lemma 8.6). The note’s example works,
asymptotically, on a window of more than three orders of magnitude (Corollary G.9).
    Where it fails. The penalty is validity-blind: it sorts by rate, betting that norms are high-rate
structure and errors low-rate structure (Theorem 8.9). The bet is right for idiosyncratic slips
and wrong for cheap, frequent fallacies (Proposition 8.10). It costs rare valid rules and, worse,
rarely exercised guards, so the learner can be less sound than its teacher (Proposition 8.12). The
good c cannot be estimated from imitation data (Theorem 8.11), and private randomness fails
whenever inputs carry the same person’s earlier labels (Proposition 8.3).
    What does the normativity work. Of the note’s other ideas, “you specify properties of the thing
or notion” is decisive: postulates are avowal rather than performance, and they remove high-rate
fallacies at every c, provided the valid rules in a witness out-rate the fallacy (Proposition 8.17).
The idea “what is it that this person is trying to teach me” calls for a teacher model with a
competence/performance split. Armstrong and Mindermann (2018) show that a policy does
not determine its decomposition into planner and reward, and that a simplicity prior over
decompositions does not single out the intended one. That is Theorem 8.9(iv) in another guise.
    The division of labour comes to this: simplicity removes the expensive errors; coherence
removes the incoherent ones; the world removes the refutable ones; postulates remove those
that violate avowed properties. What survives is the meanings humans actually use. Steeper
simplicity still has a job no other channel does: removing idiosyncratic, coherent, unrefutable
errors (Table 11, first row). It is a good third filter, not a route to normativity on its own.
    In the terms of Section 13, a learner fitted to practice alone is in narrow reflective equilibrium
with its teacher, with or without a simplicity penalty. Stich’s objection applies to it exactly.
What removes coherent systematic fallacies is information that is not a function of performance:
avowed postulates, and an independent world channel. That world channel is what makes the
equilibrium wide.
    Besides the open problems of Section 14, a product-model algorithmic statistics and the best
block size for a step imitator remain open. The simulations are in Section 12.

9       Coherence and existence: a “philosophical completeness theo-
        rem”
Sections 6 and 7 used coherence as a learning signal. This section asks what coherence means: if
a learned mode of talking is coherent, is there something it is talking about? The motivating
notes (Hänni, 2026) pose exactly this question:3
        “a mode of talking makes sense (is coherent) iff there is something it could be talking about”
        as long as the ‘mode of talking’ is a first-order theory and ‘something’ is a model of it, then
        this is literally the completeness theorem
        is a generalization of the completeness thm available that justifies this philosophical proposition
        more broadly?

The note suggests further instances (“probabilities describe world iff coherent”, after Christiano
et al. 2013; “maybe something could be said about vnm stuff also?”). Under the heading “from
sam”4 it records a colleague’s remark, “completeness is an adjunction between sentences and
models”, the observation “if you are in image, then round trip is just identity”, the question
“what is this image?” and its answer, “this is all sets of sentences closed under inference rules.
this is by the completeness theorem”. Elsewhere the notes add the caveat that “there might only
be such a thing in the same sense that there is a ‘proof’ of the Gödel sentence G”.5

Answer in brief. There is a whole family of “coherent iff there is something it could be talking
about” theorems with one anatomy: completeness holds iff the points of a calculus are realized
by models (§9.1). The adjunction remark, as the note answers it, is strong completeness; the
note’s proposition is weak completeness; the two differ. Every calculus is complete for models
built from its own syntax, so the proposition has content only for an independently specified
semantics. Instances: positions (Stone duality, §9.2), credences (de Finetti with counting sequents;
no bounded-arity, CCS-style constraint family characterizes coherence, §9.3), and contexts (the
somethings are belief states, not worlds, §9.4). A coherent learned calculus has a model, but a
syntactic one; the Kripkensteinian residue of Section 6 becomes a set of non-isomorphic things
talked about; and a compactness and a computability barrier show that coherence cannot in
general deliver the intended model (§9.5; verdict in §9.6).
    Credit. Almost everything here is a standard result, reorganized; the organization is the
contribution. The Galois connection is Birkhoff (1940) and Ore (1944); bilateral completeness
is Scott (1974) and Shoesmith and Smiley (1978); probabilistic coherence is de Finetti (1937)
and Gaifman (1964); local-models semantics is Ghidini and Giunchiglia (2001). The arity result
Theorem 9.14 is an instance of the classical fact that locally consistent marginals need not admit
a joint distribution (the marginal problem of Vorob’ev 1962; the correlation polytopes of Pitowsky
1991), and NP-hardness of probabilistic satisfiability is due to Georgakopoulos et al. (1988).
New as far as we know, and all elementary: the counting-sequent form of de Finetti’s theorem
(probably folklore; cf. Paris 1994); the threshold hierarchy for counting-sequent constraints
(Theorem H.1); the simplest monotone case of multi-context completeness, fitted to context
calculi like that of Section 11 (Theorem 9.19; completeness results for local-models semantics
already exist, Ghidini and Giunchiglia 2001; Serafini and Bouquet 2004); and the corollary on
    3
     logic/a ’philosophical version’ of gödel’s completeness theorem.md.
    4
     The README of the notes acknowledges discussions with Sam Eisenstat.
   5
     philosophy/philosophy of thinking/advent of reason/real attempt 2024/3f math, thinking, and

9.1    The adjunction, and the anatomy of a completeness theorem
Definition 9.1 (Semantic frames and completeness). [T6 Def 1.1, §1.1] A semantic frame (S, M, |=)
consists of a set S of “sentences”, a set or class M of “models” and a relation |= ⊆ M × S. Put
Mod(Σ) = {m : m |= σ ∀σ ∈ Σ} and Th(K) = {σ : m |= σ ∀m ∈ K}. A deductive system is
a closure operator C on P(S) (extensive, monotone, idempotent), with closed sets (theories)
Fix(C); it is finitary if C(X) is the union of the C(X0 ) over finite X0 ⊆ X. C is sound if
C ≤ Th ◦ Mod pointwise, strongly complete if C = Th ◦ Mod, and weakly complete if every
coherent X (i.e. C(X) ̸= S) has Mod(X) ̸= ∅.
Lemma 9.2 (Galois connection). [T6 Fact 1.2] (known) K ⊆ Mod(Σ) iff Σ ⊆ Th(K). Hence
Th ◦ Mod and Mod ◦ Th are closure operators, and Mod, Th are mutually inverse inclusion-
reversing bijections between their fixed points (Birkhoff, 1940; Ore, 1944).
    Read as an adjunction between (P(S), ⊆) and (P(M ), ⊇), this is Mod ⊣ Th: the precise
content of “completeness is an adjunction between sentences and models”. The adjunction exists
for every frame; a completeness theorem is a statement about its fixed points.
Proposition 9.3 (The image of the round trip). [T6 Prop 1.3] For every closure operator C:
{Th(K) : K ⊆ M } = Fix(C) iff C is strongly complete.
Proof. The image of Th is Fix(Th ◦ Mod), as ThModTh = Th; and a closure operator is
determined by its fixed points, C(X) = {T ∈ Fix(C) : X ⊆ T }.
                                      T

   This is the note’s own answer, for arbitrary closure operators (soundness is not needed): the
round trip fixes exactly the sets closed under the rules iff the rules are complete.
Theorem 9.4 (Tautological completeness). [T6 Thm 1.4] Every closure operator C is strongly
complete for its canonical frame (S, Fix(C), ∋), whose models are the theories T , with T |= σ iff
σ ∈ T.

Reading. If “something it could be talking about” may be any object, the note’s proposition
is trivially true: every mode of talking is about its own theories. Real completeness theorems
have content because their models (truth tables, structures, points of k̄ n , measures) are specified
independently of the calculus. For a learner of inference rules, that a learned calculus is “about
something” is cheap; what matters is whether it is about something we can access independently.
Theorem 9.5 (Completeness is realization of points). [T6 Thm 1.5, as repaired] Call a theory T
a point if T ̸= S and, for some σ ∈      / T , T is maximal among theories omitting σ; write
Pt(C). Let C be finitary. (a) Lindenbaum. Every theory is the intersection of the points
containing it. (b) If C is sound, it is strongly complete iff every point is the theory of a model:
Pt(C) ⊆ {Th({m}) : m ∈ M }. (c) If C is sound, some finite F has C(F ) = S, and Th({m}) ̸= S
for all m, then C is weakly complete iff every maximal proper theory is the theory of a model.
Without soundness, (⇒) fails.

9.2     Positions: bilateral completeness is Stone duality
Fix any set Fm; until Theorem 9.11 connectives play no role. A sequent Γ ▷ ∆ has finite
Γ, ∆ ⊆ Fm; a valuation is any v : Fm → {0, 1}, and v |= Γ ▷ ∆ iff v falsifies some γ ∈ Γ or verifies
some δ ∈ ∆. A position [X : Y ] asserts all of X and denies all of Y ; it is incoherent for a set ⊢ of
sequents if some Γ ▷ ∆ ∈ ⊢ has Γ ⊆ X, ∆ ⊆ Y (Restall 2005; Definition 6.22). A Scott relation
is a set of sequents closed under (Ov) Γ ▷ ∆ if Γ ∩ ∆ ̸= ∅; (Wk) from Γ ▷ ∆ infer Γ ∪ Γ′ ▷ ∆ ∪ ∆′ ;
(Cut) from Γ, φ ▷ ∆ and Γ ▷ φ, ∆ infer Γ ▷ ∆. ⟨S⟩ is the least Scott relation containing S, and
Val(⊢) the set of valuations satisfying ⊢.
Theorem 9.8 (Bilateral Lindenbaum). [T6 Thm 2.2] (known) Let ⊢ be a Scott relation. (a) Every
coherent position [X : Y ] is realized by some v ∈ Val(⊢): v[X] = 1, v[Y ] = 0. (b) The maximal
coherent positions are exactly the [v −1 (1) : v −1 (0)] with v ∈ Val(⊢).    Lean: Bilateral.thm_2_2_a

sequents valid in every valuation that satisfies S are exactly those in ⟨S⟩: Th(Mod(S)) = ⟨S⟩.

Reading. Theorem 9.8 is the cleanest form of the note’s proposition: a position is coherent
iff it partially describes an admissible valuation, “some way the sentences could all come out”.
Theorem 9.11 upgrades the something to a compositional model whose algebra is the language
itself, the multiple-conclusion analogue of Łoś and Suszko (1958) and Wójcicki (1988). Whether
the intended semantics is reached depends on the rules: with the truth-table sequents and one
coherence datum, Val(⊢) = BV (Theorem 6.26); with single-conclusion data only, the admissible
valuations include the “gappy” BV∩ (Theorem 6.24), so a single-conclusion coherence loss licenses
talk about undecided worlds.

9.3       Credences: de Finetti, counting sequents, and why local constraints fail
Let F be a finite agenda that is a union of complementary pairs {φ, φ∗ }, φ∗ ≡ ¬φ (a finite
agenda cannot be closed under ¬); BV the Boolean valuations of its atoms; v̄ = (v(φ))φ∈F . A
credence P : F → [0, 1] is negation-coherent if P (φ∗ ) = 1 − P (φ), and coherent if P = v µ(v)v̄
                                                                                        P

for a probability µ on BV, i.e. P lies in the coherence polytope ΠF = conv{v̄}. A counting
sequent (Φ, m) is a finite multiset Φ of members of F with an integer threshold m; it is valid
if every v ∈ BV makes at least m members of Φ true (with multiplicity), and P satisfies it if
                                                                           ∗
   φ∈Φ P (φ) ≥ m. An ordinary sequent Γ ▷ ∆ is the case m = 1, Φ = {γ : γ ∈ Γ} ∪ ∆.
P


Theorem 9.12 (de Finetti, with counting sequents). [T6 Thm 3.1, as repaired] For negation-coherent
P the following are equivalent: (i) P is coherent; (ii) there is no Dutch book, i.e. no λ ∈ RF with
λ · (v̄ − P ) < 0 for all v ∈ BV; (iii) for rational λ, c, if λ · v̄ ≥ c for all v then λ · P ≥ c; (iv) P
satisfies every valid counting sequent. Negation coherence is needed: P ≡ 1 satisfies (iv) but is
incoherent.

    Proof idea. ΠF is a rational polytope, so a point outside it violates one of finitely many
rational defining inequalities, which gives a Dutch book; clearing denominators and moving
negative coefficients from φ to φ∗ turns the inequality into a counting sequent. Appendix H.3.

Reading. The probabilistic completeness theorem says a credence is coherent iff it is a mixture
of worlds. Its proof-theoretic side is not ordinary sequents but counting sequents, graded positions
such as “at least two of these six claims hold”. An ordinary sequent gives only the union bound
   Γ (1 − P (γ)) +  ∆ P (δ) ≥ 1, the multiple-conclusion form of Adams’s uncertainty-sum bound
P                  P

(Adams, 1966).

Which consistency constraints suffice? The motivating notes on a consistency-based
probing project6 record candidate constraints: negation coherence P (¬Q) = 1 − P (Q) (the
CCS loss), the identity P (A ∧ B) + P (A ∨ B) = P (A) + P (B) (listed alongside a collaborator’s
suggestion), and, tentatively (“one choice would e.g. be”), modus ponens read as the tautology
¬P ∨ ¬(P → Q) ∨ Q, i.e. the union bound P (Q) ≥ P (P ) + P (P → Q) − 1. Contrast-consistent
search (CCS) trains a probe with exactly a negation-consistency loss plus a confidence loss (Burns
et al., 2023).

P (p) = P (q) = 0.2, P (p ∧ q) = 0.9 is negation-coherent but violates the union bound of p ∧ q ▷ p.

    This persists if Fk is enlarged to all formulas in at most two atoms, valued by the two-atom
marginals of the µ in (a), which do not depend on J: every pair of atoms has a genuine joint
distribution, yet Pk is globally incoherent. This is the frustration in Specker’s parable of the
three boxes (Specker, 1960).
    The hierarchy by threshold is strict too: Pk violates a repetition-free valid counting sequent
of threshold k − 1 but satisfies every valid one of threshold at most k − 2, including the union
bounds of all valid ordinary sequents (Theorem H.1). For negation-coherent credences any single
agenda is characterized by finitely many counting sequents, read off its facets; what is ruled out is
a bound on arity or threshold that works uniformly across agendas. On agendas forming a finite
Boolean algebra up to equivalence, the three-formula identities P (φ) = P (φ ∧ ψ) + P (φ ∧ ¬ψ)
with P ≥ 0, P (⊤) = 1 suffice (Proposition H.2). Both results are in Appendix H.3.

A caution for consistency-based probing. A CCS-style probe reads credences off a model
on an unclosed list of statements and enforces negation consistency, perhaps with further local
constraints. By Example 9.13 and Theorems 9.14 and H.1, no fixed stock of constraint types
(pairwise, k-wise for fixed k, or all union bounds of ordinary sequents) guarantees that the probe’s
credences are a mixture of worlds, i.e. “about” anything at all; that needs the agenda’s facets, or
an agenda closed under the connectives. And even global coherence buys only some distribution
over some worlds (Theorem 9.15): coherence is eliminative, not confirmational (Section 6.7).
An untested experiment: train probes with negation-only, pairwise and counting-sequent losses
on agendas with k-way exclusive alternatives, and measure their distance from the coherence
polytope.

First-order credences. For a countable first-order language L, P : SentL → [0, 1] is (Gaifman-
)coherent if (G1) P (φ) = 1 whenever ⊢ φ, and (G2) P (φ∨ψ) = P (φ)+P (ψ) whenever ⊢ ¬(φ∧ψ)
(Gaifman, 1964); this is the notion of the draft cited in the note (Christiano et al., 2013).

Theorem 9.15 (Coherent credences are mixtures of complete theories). [T6 Thm 3.7] (known) Let
SL be the Stone space of complete consistent L-theories, with clopens [φ] = {T : φ ∈ T }. Then P
is coherent iff P (φ) = µ([φ]) for a (unique) Borel probability µ on SL .


                                                 90
   Proof idea. P is a finitely additive probability on the clopen algebra; by compactness this is
automatically countably additive there, and Carathéodory extends it (Appendix H.3). By Gödel
completeness, a coherent credence is the expected truth value of φ in a random model: the note’s
proposition holds verbatim. So does the notes’ caveat: for complete T ⊇ PA + ¬Con(PA), δT is
coherent, gives 1 to every true quantifier-free sentence, and “believes” there is a proof of 0 = 1.

Theorem 9.16 (The Gaifman condition is a probabilistic ω-rule). [T6 Thm 3.8, as repaired] In the
language of arithmetic, let P be coherent, give probability 1 to every true
                                                                         
                                                                            quantifier-free sentence,
                                                               W
and satisfy the Gaifman condition P (∃x φ(x)) = supn P i≤n φ(i) . Then P = δTh(N) . No

    Proof idea. Induction on logical symbols: coherence forces {0, 1}-values through ¬, ∧; numerals
carry no logical symbols, and every number is a numeral’s value (Appendix H.3). This is essentially

Corollary 9.17 (Logical inductors’ limits are non-standard). [T6 Cor 3.9, as repaired] Let P be
a logical inductor (Garrabrant et al., 2016) over a consistent r.e. Γ ⊇ Q in the language of
arithmetic. Then P∞ violates the Gaifman condition. More generally, no limit-computable
coherent credence giving 1 to every true quantifier-free sentence satisfies it; the quantifier-free
hypothesis cannot be dropped.

    Proof idea. By Convergence and Limit Coherence, P∞ exists, is coherent and gives 1 to true
quantifier-free sentences, so Theorem 9.16 would make it δTh(N) . Non-Dogmatism refutes this
(the false member of a Gödel–Rosser pair gets positive probability), and so, independently, does
Tarski’s theorem, as Th(N) would be ∆2 . Appendix H.3.

Reading. The probabilistic “something” is always available; a standard something is fixed by
an infinitary condition that no limit-computable coherent credence of this kind meets. A Gaifman-
style probe of a language model’s arithmetic would compare P (∃x φ(x)) with maxi≤n P (φ(i)): a
large gap marks belief in a witness that is never named.
    Finally, the note’s “vnm stuff” has the same anatomy: finitely many strict and weak compar-
isons of lotteries have an expected-utility representation iff no nonnegative combination of them
derives L ≻ L by mixing and transitivity (Proposition H.4, by Motzkin’s transposition theorem).

9.4    Contexts: a completeness theorem for “true in the context at hand”
What is a coherent system of contexts (Section 11) about? We use a monotone multi-context
calculus whose labelled formulas i:φ are McCarthy’s ist(i, φ) (McCarthy, 1993), with a simplified
local-models semantics (Ghidini and Giunchiglia, 2001).

Definition 9.18 (Multi-context systems, MC, belief states). [T6 Def 4.0, as repaired; §4.1] For each
context i ∈ I fix a language Li , local models Mi with Ci = Thi ◦ Modi (e.g. classical logic; for a
learned logic Ci , the proper theories Mi = Fix(Ci ) \ {Li } with T |=i φ iff φ ∈ T ), local axioms
Ki , and a falsum ⊥i with Modi (⊥i ) = ∅. A bridge rule is j1 :φ1 , . . . , jn :φn ⇒ i:ψ. For labelled
premises Γ, Der(Γ) = (Ti )i is the least family with Ti ⊇ Ki ∪ Γi , each Ti Ci -closed, and closed
under bridges; Γ ⊢MC i:φ iff φ ∈ Ti . A belief state is c = (ci ), ci ⊆ Mi , with c |= i:φ iff every
m ∈ ci satisfies φ. It is a model if it satisfies every Ki and is bridge-compatible (if c |= jk :φk for
all premises then c |= i:ψ); Γ |=LMS i:φ iff every model of Γ satisfies i:φ.

                                                  91
Theorem 9.19 (Soundness and completeness; the canonical chain). [T6 Thm 4.1] Let cΓi =
Modi (Ti ) for (Ti ) = Der(Γ). (a) cΓ is a model of Γ. (b) Every model c of Γ has ci ⊆ cΓi : cΓ is
the least committal model. (c) Γ ⊢MC i:φ iff Γ |=LMS i:φ.

    Proof idea. cΓ |= i:φ iff φ ∈ Thi Modi (Ti ) = Ti ; and the theories Thi (ci ) of any model form a
closed, bridge-closed family containing K ∪ Γ, hence contain Der(Γ). Appendix H.4.

Corollary 9.20 (Context coherence iff existence). [T6 Cor 4.2] Let D ⊆ I be the designated
contexts (Definition 2.13). Γ ⊬MC i:⊥i for every i ∈ D iff some model c of Γ has ci ̸= ∅ for every
i ∈ D.

Proof. ⊥i ∈ Ti iff cΓi = ∅ by Theorem 9.19(a), and cΓ is the largest model by (b).

Remark 9.21 (Learned local logics). [T6 remark after Cor 4.2, as repaired] With the semantics Mi =
Fix(Ci ) \ {Li }, cΓi ̸= ∅ iff Ti ̸= Li , so for learned local logics designated coherence must be read
as non-triviality of Ti ; this coincides with ⊥i ∈    / Ti exactly when ⊥i is Ci -explosive.
    Non-designated contexts, such as suppositions under reductio, may have ci = ∅: they are about
nothing, which is what a successful reductio shows; this is the designation discipline of Section 6
as an existence theorem. The canonical chain is the least equilibrium in the sense of Brewka
and Eiter (2007); with non-monotone (default) bridges equilibria can fail to exist even when
every Ki is consistent, so coherence alone does not guarantee existence there (Proposition H.5,
Appendix H.4).

Rules of proof versus conditionals between worlds. A world family w = (wi ) picks a
single model wi ∈ Mi of Ki for each i and satisfies each bridge as a material conditional: if
wjk |= φk for all k then wi |= ψ. Write |=W for consequence over world families.

Theorem 9.22 (Belief states, not worlds). [T6 Thm 4.5, as repaired] (a) |=LMS ⊆ |=W . (b) The
inclusion is strict: with classical local logics, Kj = {p ∨ q}, Ki = {¬r} and bridges j:p ⇒ i:r,
j:q ⇒ i:r, MC does not derive i:⊥, but there is no world family. (c) For classical propositional
local logics, |=W is classical consequence in the disjoint union of the local languages from the
                  (i)                                            V (j )
tagged axioms Ki , the tagged premises and the bridge axioms k φk k → ψ (i) (the “eternalist”
translation).

    Proof idea. In (b), Tj = Cn2 (p ∨ q) contains neither p nor q, so no bridge fires; but every wj
satisfies p or q, forcing wi |= r (Appendix H.4).
    This is the context-logic instance of a standard distinction, rule of proof versus conditional
(global versus local consequence): c |= j:φ is a box over cj , and (b) is the failure of □(p ∨ q) |=
□p ∨ □q; it is why Ghidini and Giunchiglia (2001) use sets of local models. New is only its use
as a criterion for physics bridges.

Reading. MC reads a bridge as “export what context j establishes”; the eternalist translation
reads it as a conditional between worlds. Only the first is right for idealizations: a physics bridge
(“if the idealized model establishes Q = q, then in the world Q ≈ q ± ε”, Section 11.4) is certified
for what the idealization establishes, not for case splits over its undetermined possibilities, none
of which is actual. So a context system makes sense iff there is something it could be about holds
with belief states as the somethings (Corollary 9.20) and fails with worlds (Theorem 9.22(b)).



                                                  92
Local coherence versus a global world. The motivating notes hold that claims always sit
in background frames, that “there are many different background contexts, not one, and it is
very useful that this is so”, and that “these different frames needn’t be easily reconcilable”.7
The following makes precise when locally coherent frames nevertheless glue into one world, and
when they cannot. On a finite tree of classical propositional contexts with running intersection
and mutually conservative edges, every local model extends to a global valuation (Theorem H.6,
Appendix H.4; the join-tree argument, cf. Beeri et al. 1983). On a cycle this fails:

Proposition 9.23 (The frustrated triangle). [T6 Prop 4.7] On atoms {a, b}, {b, c}, {c, a} let
Tab = Cn2 (a ↔ ¬b), Tbc = Cn2 (b ↔ ¬c), Tca = Cn2 (c ↔ ¬a). Each is consistent, each
pair is mutually conservative on its shared atom, and the union is inconsistent; likewise pair
marginals uniform on {01, 10} agree on all single marginals but have no joint distribution.
Lean: Specker.frustrated_triangle (probabilistic part)


Proof. An odd cycle of negations has no Boolean solution; each theory has only tautologies in a
single atom.

    This is Specker’s parable in logical form (Specker, 1960) and the simplest instance of contex-
tuality: local sections agreeing on overlaps with no global section (Abramsky and Brandenburger,
2011); acyclicity of the cover rules it out (Beeri et al., 1983). So an olympiad solution’s contexts
need not be reconcilable into one world. Coherence of the designated contexts guarantees local
belief states, nonempty where designated (Corollary 9.20); one world for all contexts is strictly
stronger and cover-dependent.

Definition 9.24 (True in the context at hand). [T6 Def 4.8, as repaired] φ is true in context c iff
Γ ⊢MC c:φ, i.e. (Theorem 9.19) φ holds in every local model that c’s canonical belief state leaves
open. φ is true enough in c for a world claim ε iff (i) φ is true in c; (ii) a bridge c:φ ⇒ @:ε,
possibly with side conditions σ, is in the system and σ holds in the actual world (for a checker,
Γ ⊢MC @:σ); and (iii) that bridge is sound in the sense of Definition 11.13: every instance of it
preserves truth at every world w ∈ Wρ admitted by the background, i.e. whenever c establishes
φ and σ holds at w, ε holds at w. (Quantifying over the actual world alone would make (iii)
equivalent to the truth of ε.)

   This is the multi-context counterpart of the answer given in Theorem 11.29: truth in the
context at hand is supervaluational truth over the context’s admissible local models, and a
checker accepting exactly MC-derivations accepts exactly what is true in this sense. It does
not justify bridges: bridge soundness is world-relative and is certified by stability arguments or
world feedback (Section 11.4), never by coherence, which can only demand cΓi ̸= ∅ at designated
contexts. The context-tree calculus[L7 §8] from which Definition 11.13 is adapted is an MC system,
and its own semantics agrees with ours when every step and export instance is sound (proof sketch;
Appendix H.4).

9.5      What coherence of a learned calculus buys, and what pins the model
         down
We return to the learner. Coherence of a learned structural calculus on a designated context
always yields a model, but a syntactic one (Theorem 9.25); it reduces to the intended one
  7
      philosophy/philosophy of thinking/a few notes on frames.md.


                                                 93
exactly when the intended semantics is a surjective image of the language (Theorem 9.26).
Compactness and computability bound how far coherence can pin down an intended infinite
structure (Theorems H.8 and H.9).
    Let R be a learned set of rule schemas, CR the least structural finitary consequence operation
containing it, and ⟨R⟩ the least structural Scott relation. The designated contexts A ∈ A are
certified coherent: ⊥ ∈
                      / CR (A), or [A : D] is ⟨R⟩-coherent. As in Section 6, this is all the learner
knows.

Theorem 9.25 (What coherence buys). [T6 Thm 5.1] For each designated A: (a) some CR -theory
T ⊇ A is maximal among theories omitting ⊥; (b) the Lindenbaum matrix ⟨Fm, T ⟩ validates
every rule of CR under every assignment, and the identity assignment designates all of A and
not ⊥ (Łoś and Suszko, 1958; Wójcicki, 1988); (c) bilaterally, each designated coherent [A : D]
is realized by some v ∈ Val⟨R⟩, and Lv is a matrix model of ⟨R⟩.

    Proof idea. (a) is the Zorn step of Theorem 9.5(a), (b) is structurality, and (c) is Theorems 9.8
and 9.11; (b) holds for any CR -theory T ⊇ A omitting ⊥ (Appendix H.5).
    So if a learned mode of talking is coherent on a context, there is something it is talking about
there. But the model’s universe is the language: the formal content of the notes’ caveat about
the “proof” of the Gödel sentence. When is the syntactic something the intended one? For a
matrix ⟨A, D⟩ the Leibniz congruence ΩA (D) is the largest congruence compatible with D (a θ b
and a ∈ D imply b ∈ D), and the reduction ⟨A/Ω, D/Ω⟩ identifies elements no formula context
can tell apart (Blok and Pigozzi, 1989; Font, 2016); write Ω(T ) for ΩFm (T ).

Theorem 9.26 (The syntactic model collapses to the intended one). [T6 Thm 5.2] (a) If h : Fm →
A is a surjective homomorphism and T = h−1 (D), then

                        ⟨Fm/Ω(T ), T /Ω(T )⟩ ∼
                                             = ⟨A/ΩA (D), D/ΩA (D)⟩;

if ⟨A, D⟩ is reduced, the reduced Lindenbaum matrix of T is ⟨A, D⟩. (b) Every maximal consistent
theory of CPC has reduced Lindenbaum matrix ∼  = ⟨2, {1}⟩.
   Proof idea. Ω(T ) = h−1 (ΩA D), because a congruence compatible with T , joined with ker h,
pushes forward along h to one compatible with D (Appendix H.5). Surjectivity matters: in
general one gets the reduction of the generated submatrix.

Proposition 9.27 (What the points of a finite-matrix logic talk about). [T6 Prop 5.3, as repaired] Let
C be the consequence of a finite matrix ⟨A, D⟩. Every point of C has reduced Lindenbaum matrix
isomorphic to the reduction of a generated submatrix ⟨h(Fm), D ∩ h(Fm)⟩ (a strict homomorphic
image of a submatrix, not necessarily a submatrix); up to isomorphism there are finitely many.

     Proof idea. Every point is some h−1 (D) by Theorem 9.5(b); apply Theorem 9.26(a) to h onto
its image (Appendix H.5).
     So for classical logic every coherent position is, after identifying indiscernibles, about the
two truth values, because every point of CPC is maximal (Lemma 9.7) and maximal theories
are Boolean. The reason is not Post-completeness: IPC is not Post-complete, yet its maximal
consistent theories reduce to 2 (Proposition 9.6); calculi differ in their non-maximal points.

Example 9.28 (The residue as a set of things talked about). [T6 Ex 5.4] (i) Map Fm onto the
three-element Heyting chain H3 = {0 < 12 < 1} with h(p) = 12 . Then T = h−1 (1) is a non-
maximal point of IPC (maximal among theories omitting p) whose reduced matrix is ⟨H3 , {1}⟩:

                                                 94
one coherent intuitionistic position talks about the three-element chain while the maximal ones
talk about 2. (ii) First-order logic with equality plus the fallacy ∀x∃y R ▷ ∃y∀x R is coherent
(Example E.4); its models are exactly the one-element structures, which is what the learned
fallacy is “about”.

    In general, for multiple-conclusion hypotheses, Theorems 9.10 and 9.11 put the residue
Alt(h∗ , A) of coherent uniform alternatives (Theorem 6.34) in exact correspondence with the
closed, substitution-invariant V ⊆ Val(h∗ ) realizing every designated position. Non-identifiability
of meaning is non-uniqueness of the thing talked about.

What pins the intended model. Two layers of non-standardness remain. Coherent but
false theories such as PA + ¬Con(PA) have a prime model containing a definable non-standard
“proof of 0 = 1” (Theorem H.7). True theories need not be categorical, since by compactness no
first-order mode of talking pins down an infinite structure (Theorem H.8). For any computable
coherence notion, “coherent iff there is something it could be talking about” can hold only if
having such a something is Π1 (Theorem H.9): “having some model” is Π1 , while “having the
standard model”, “having an integer solution” and “having a finite model” are not. Anchoring a
vocabulary pins, uniformly over anchorings, exactly what is definable from it (Proposition H.10).
Every known pin of N (second-order induction, initiality, the ω-rule, and Tennenbaum’s theorem,
Theorem H.11) adds something beyond finitary computable coherence (Appendix H.6).

9.6     Verdict
Where yes. In each row of Table 12, “coherent iff there is something it could be talking about”
is a theorem, with a realization step that is non-trivial except for positions, where points already
are valuations; for the modes of talking that matter to the learner, see Theorems 9.8, 9.12, 9.15
and 9.25, Proposition H.4, and Corollary 9.20. The adjunction slogan holds in each strongly
complete case (Proposition 9.3 and Theorem 9.10).

Where no. (1) The something may be made of syntax (Theorems 9.4 and 9.25); the proposition
is substantive only for an independently specified semantics, and which semantics is right is
answered by which models we can independently access: the truth values, N through computation,
the world through observation. (2) Weak ̸= strong (Proposition 9.6). (3) Intended existence
needs more than coherence: the coherent-but-false layer is defeated only by truth-tracking
principles (reflection, stronger theories, Popperian policies, Theorem 6.21), the non-categorical
layer only by infinitary, second-order or meta-level ingredients, and both limits are forced
(Theorems H.8 and H.9). (4) The something for a context system is a family of belief states, not
of worlds (Theorem 9.22), and a global world exists automatically only on tree-like covers with
conservative overlaps (Theorem H.6 and Proposition 9.23). (5) Probabilistic coherence is global:
local constraints on an unclosed agenda need not make a probe about any mixture of worlds
(Theorems 9.14 and H.1).

What this means for the learner. The notes ask about “the hooking of a model onto the
world”;8 against coherence this becomes two precise questions. Coherence answers “is there any
world this way of talking could be about?”: yes, canonically, but partly syntactically. Hooking
  8
      philosophy/philosophy of language/meaning and truth/individual sentences being meaningful.md.



                                                 95
answers “is it this world?”: world feedback is positive data in valuation space (Section 6.4), and
uniformly over anchorings it pins exactly the definable vocabulary (Proposition H.10). Neither
does the other’s job: as in Sections 6, 7 and 11, coherence removes what is incoherent with the
target, and only world channels or extra pins select among the non-isomorphic somethings of
its residue Alt. A draft comment in the notes, marked “text below now disendorsed probably”,
imagines a conception (a C-model) given with “axioms and inference rules” for which no model
can be constructed.9 In our terms such a conception is an incoherent calculus used only through
coherent chunks: local belief states (Corollary 9.20) without a global section (Proposition 9.23).
And by the computability barrier there is no final formula for N: further pins, such as reflection,
must be added on other grounds, as in the open-ended picture of justification of Section 13.

Verdict. The philosophical proposition is true in a precise generalized sense: for positions,
credences, preferences, context systems and learned structural calculi, coherence is equivalent to
the existence of a model of the kind the semantics allows. It does not deliver intended-model
existence, which the notes’ Gödel-sentence footnote already anticipates: standard or intended
existence needs categoricity, anchoring or an infinitary condition, and no computable coherence
notion can certify it beyond Π1 .


10     Informal mathematics: learning a latent formalization
This section is the paper’s answer to the second success criterion: a setup that would have worked
for mathematical proofs before anyone knew how to formalize them. The motivating notes (Hänni,
2026) ask it in two sharper forms.10 “How come mathematicians ended up with such a nice
notion of proof? . . . this nice structure of a formal proof is sorta there in their activities. how
did it come to be there?” And, offered as “an attempt at an explanation” for the case of early
theorems about functions: mathematicians used only the part of the concept that later survived
formalization, because “the ‘rest of the concept’ . . . was untrustworthy/messy . . . and for this
reason unusable whenever people were proving things”. We call its generalization to pre-formal
practice the robust-core hypothesis.
    We model a pre-formal practice as the shadow of an unknown latent formalization: a
language, a calculus with a library, a partial reading of informal sentences into the language,
and an intended semantics (Section 10.1). We show that a verifier checking steps and re-
uses of sentences across contexts against every surviving latent formalization is sound against
adaptive provers (Section 10.2); that practice identifies meaning at best up to sameness of
informal consequence, and ontology not at all (Section 10.3); that counterexample objects can be
exponentially more informative than paradoxes (Section 10.4); that Frege → Russell → Zermelo
is a theorem about simplicity, coherence and coverage in a toy (Section 10.5); and that steps
valid under every admissible sharpening survive every formalization, while selection by objects
plus Gödel completeness explains why surviving steps are derivable, though not why they are
short (Section 10.6).
    Two caveats govern the section. Every positive result assumes realizability (the target lies
in the learner’s fixed class), whereas the decisive historical steps (ε-δ, uniform convergence,
   9
    philosophy/philosophy of thinking/analogy/logical models as distinct from mental models.md.
  10
   The quotations in this paragraph are from philosophy/emergence of structures/how come mathematicians
ended up with such a nice notion of proof?.md and philosophy/metaphilosophy/why is it a good idea
to make vague notions precise?.md.



                                                  96
ideals) were inventions of language; affordable soundness with language invention is the hardest
open problem we leave (Section 14). And most results are simple once the definitions are in
place. The genuine mathematical content is the paradox side of the object–paradox separation
(Theorem 10.20 and Proposition 10.22; its novelty relative to the Littlestone-dimension literature
is uncertain) and the comprehension-toy facts (Lemma 10.27); the deep ingredients are cited
(Gödel completeness, Robinson’s transfer, Nelson’s conservativity, Incurvati and Murzi’s theorem).

10.1    The model
Definition 10.1 (Occurrences, steps, arguments, links). [T4 §1.1] Ξ is a countable set of informal
sentence strings and C a set of contexts (definitions, conventions, notation and local suppositions
in force). An occurrence is x = (c, ξ) ∈ X := C × Ξ, with str(x) := ξ. An informal step is Γ ▷ y
with Γ ⊆fin X, y ∈ X. An informal argument α is a list of lines y1 , . . . , ym ∈ X, each a premise,
an inference Γj ▷ yj with Γj among earlier lines, or a link yi ⇝ yj with i < j and str(yi ) = str(yj )
(“the same claim, used in another context”). Prem(α) is its set of premises, ym its conclusion,
and its depth the length of its longest dependency path.
   Links are the formal locus of equivocation: a sentence proved in one context is re-used in
another, where it may be read differently.
Definition 10.2 (Latent formalization). [T4 Def 1.1, §1.2] A latent formalization is a quadruple
h = (Lh , Rh , ρh , Mh ) consisting of a countable language Lh with a sentence ⊥; a set Rh of formal
steps Π ▷ φ over Sent(Lh ) (instances of finitely many schemas plus a library of definitions and
derived lemmas); a partial reading ρh : X ⇀ Sent(Lh ) with domain Dh ; and a class Mh of
Lh -structures for which Rh is sound and ⊥ is false.
  (i) Γ ▷ y is valid under h, written (Γ ▷ y) ∈ |=h or Γ |=h y, iff Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ Dh and ρh (y) ∈
      ClRh (ρh Γ).
 (ii) It is g-valid, (Γ ▷ y) ∈ Stgh , iff moreover ρh (y) has an Rh -derivation from ρh Γ with at most
      g rule applications and formulas of size bounded by a fixed function of g and the input.
      We assume ρh computable with decidable domain, Rh decidable, and derivations restricted
      to the input’s symbols plus a finite, computably given part of Lh depending on g; then Stgh
      is decidable and Stgh ⊆ |=h , which is all that is used.
 (iii) A link yi ⇝ yj is valid under h iff ({yi } ▷ yj ) ∈ Stgh (typically ρh (yi ) = ρh (yj ): zero
       applications).
 (iv) The admissible valuations are Vh := {vM ◦ ρh : M ∈ Mh }, with vM (φ) = [M |= φ].
 (v) h is first-order complete if Lh is first-order, Mh = Mod(Th ), and ClRh (Γ) = {φ : Th ∪Γ |= φ}.
   De Bruijn’s ratio of formal to informal proof size is roughly constant (about 4, Wiedijk 2000)
only relative to a definitional library, as Mathias’s 4.5 × 1012 -symbol term for Bourbaki’s “1”
shows (Mathias, 2002); so g is measured over Rh with its library.
Assumption 10.3 ((BG), bounded gap). [T4 §1.3] There is a target h∗ = (L∗ , R∗ , ρ∗ , M∗ ), with
D∗ := Dh∗ , such that (BG1) h∗ ∈ H (realizability); (BG2) each accepted human step is, with
probability 1 − η, drawn from a distribution over Stgh∗ , and otherwise noise, sporadic or systematic
(instances of a fallacy schema); (BG3) human links are h∗ -valid up to the same noise.
   Steps that are valid but not g-short are routed out of the practice stream: they are escalated
with a request to expand them (Proposition 10.11), or count as noise.

Definition 10.4 (The three channels). [T4 §1.4] (P) Practice: the stream of (BG2); escalation
answers are practice data labelled by Stgh∗ . (C) Coherence: a family A of finite designated

ρh A, A ∈ A, and refutes h. Suppositions are not designated, so reductio is never penalized. (O)

10.2    Sound bounded-gap verification
At time t, h is consistent with the data if it labels every practice step and escalation answer
correctly by Stgh , agrees with every link answer, and has not been refuted by a paradox or an
object datum found within the search budget so far. VSt is the set of such h. Every refutation is
a certificate, so budgeted search never refutes an unrefutable hypothesis.

Definition 10.5 (Bounded-gap conservative verifier). [T4 Def 2.1] On a query q (an informal step
or a link), Vtg answers ACCEPT iff q is g-valid, resp. link-valid, under every h ∈ VSt , with a
certificate for each; otherwise ESCALATE (ask the oracle, or ask the prover to expand q).

    Vtg is computable for finite H; for infinite H unanimity is a Π1 condition, and the effective
version is the Bayesian verifier below, truncated to finitely many hypotheses. Any budgeted
proof search that counts “not found” as “not valid” only shrinks the accepted set, so it preserves
the soundness results below, though not the escalation bounds.

Lemma 10.6 (Argument soundness). [T4 Lemma 2.2, repaired] If every line of α lies in Dh and every
inference and link of α (a link as the step {yi } ▷ yj ) lies in |=h , then ρh (yj ) ∈ ClRh (ρh Prem(α))
for every line yj . Hence every line is true in every M ∈ Mh that makes the premises true.

    Induction on lines, by monotonicity and idempotence of ClRh (Appendix I.1).

Proposition 10.7 (Equivocation: step-checking alone is unsound; trivial). [T4 Prop 2.3] There
are h and α such that every inference of α is h-valid and every link joins equal strings, yet
Prem(α) ▷ ym is h-invalid.

   So the verifier checks links. Lakatos’s “hidden lemma” in Cauchy’s proof (Lakatos, 1976,

Theorem 10.8 (Deterministic soundness; trivial once set up). [T4 Thm 2.4] Assume (BG1) and
noise-free truthful data: practice and escalation answers lie in and are labelled by Stgh∗ , link
answers agree with h∗ , designated contexts are h∗ -coherent, object data are h∗ -admissible. Then
for every prover (randomized, adaptive, unbounded, knowing h∗ , the verifier and the history) and
every t, everything Vtg accepts lies in Stgh∗ ⊆ |=h∗ ; so every argument assembled from accepted
items has an h∗ -valid conclusion (unused premises outside D∗ dropped), true in every M ∈ M∗
satisfying its premises.

Proof. No datum can refute h∗ , so h∗ ∈ VSt , and unanimity implies g-validity under h∗ ; then
apply Lemma 10.6.

   Incoherent survivors only shrink the intersection: Frege’s inconsistent 1903 “way out” (Quine,
1955) would have made a conservative verifier timid, never unsound. With noisy practice h∗
can be refuted, so we use a posterior; the threshold then involves the prior mass of the target’s
observational-equivalence class [h∗ ] (Definition 10.12).

Theorem 10.9 (Time-uniform soundness with a class prior). [T4 Thm 2.5; T1 Thm 4.2] Let H be
countable with prior w and assume (BG1). Each h has a practice likelihood ph (including noise);
practice data are i.i.d. from ph∗ , each independent of everything before it (the prover does not
foresee them); likelihoods are shadow-measurable (ph = ph′ whenever h ≡g h′ ); all other data
(escalation and link answers, paradoxes, objects) are truthful and multiply the weight of h by 1
if consistent with h, by 0 otherwise. Let Vtg,δ accept q iff the posterior gives {h : q ∈
                                                                                        / Stgh } mass
below δ, and put W := w([h ]). If δ ≤ W δ , there is an event of probability at least 1 − δ ′ ,

depending only on the practice data, on which no prover ever gets a query outside Stgh∗ accepted.

    The proof (Appendix I.1) is that of Theorem 4.15, with shadow-measurability giving the
whole class [h∗ ] the likelihood of h∗ . W ∗ counts the ≡g -class (renamings; the ontological variants
of Proposition 10.16), not the meaning class: at gap g, soundness is paid for at the level of
g-shadows. Its price is escalations. Let Hg := {Stgh : h ∈ H}, with positive elasticity el(Hg , Stgh∗ )

    Proof in Appendix I.1, by reduction to the escalation theorems of Section 4. Expansion closes
the gap. Call h∗ step-expressive if every (Γ ▷ y) ∈ |=h∗ is the conclusion of an informal argument
from Γ whose inferences lie in St1h∗ (one rule application each) and whose links join occurrences
with equal ρ∗ -readings.

10.3     What practice can identify
Definition 10.12 (Equivalences). [T4 Def 3.1] h ≈ h′ iff |=h = |=h′ (this fixes Dh = {x : {x} |=h
x}); h ≈D h′ iff they agree on steps with all occurrences in D. h ≡g h′ iff Stgh = Stgh′ , Vh = Vh′ ,
and h, h′ are coherent on the same A ∈ A; ≡∞ is the same with |= for Stg .
    If all data and queries depend on the target only through its g-shadow, no learner distinguishes
≡g -equivalent targets (Proposition I.1, stated and proved in Appendix I.2). Which shadow
determines which? Call Dh negation-closed if an informal operation x 7→ ∼x (“it is not the
case that . . . ”) preserves Dh with Th ⊢ ρh (∼x) ↔ ¬ρh (x), and call v : Dh → {0, 1} a coherent
valuation of |=h if v(∼x) = 1 − v(x) and v(y) = 1 whenever Γ |=h y for a finite Γ ⊆ v −1 (1).
Lemma 10.13 (Informal completeness). [T4 Lemma 3.3, repaired] (standard corollary of compactness
                                                                        ̸ ∅. (i) Vh is exactly the
and completeness) Let h be first-order complete with negation-closed Dh =
set of coherent valuations of |=h . (ii) Γ |=h y iff Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ Dh and every v ∈ Vh with v(Γ) = 1
has v(y) = 1. (iii) A finite A ⊆ Dh is h-coherent iff v(A) = 1 for some v ∈ Vh , iff A ̸|=h y for
some y ∈ Dh . So |=h determines Vh and coherence; conversely Vh determines |=h if Vh ̸= ∅, and
coherence of all finite subsets of Dh determines it, but coherence on a fixed family A does not.

Reading. This is the notes’ “philosophical version” of the completeness theorem (“a mode
of talking makes sense (is coherent) iff there is something it could be talking about”) for a
practice’s informal shadow: the coherent ways of evaluating the practice’s sentences are exactly
its admissible objects. It is a direct corollary of Lindenbaum, compactness and completeness
(Gödel, 1930) (proof in Appendix I.2). The notes’ caveat (“as long as the ‘mode of talking’ is a
first-order theory and ‘something’ is a model of it”) is visible in Mh = Mod(Th ): if only standard
objects are presented, strengthenings such as T + Con(T ) survive, over-generalizations of the
practice’s validity relation though not errors about truth (Section 9).
     For a step set S and D ⊆ X, let ChD (S) be the steps Γ ▷ y derivable from Γ by an argument
whose lines lie in D and whose inferences and links lie in S. h∗ is step-expressive on D∗ at gap g
if ChD∗ (Stgh∗ ) = |=h∗ (implied by step-expressiveness, for g ≥ 1).

Example 10.15 (A weaker rival survives bounded-gap data). [T4 Thm 3.4(d), verification A1] Read
D∗ as p0 , ¬p0 , p3 , ¬p3 ; let T ∗ = {p0 → p1 , p1 → p2 , p2 → p3 } with axiom steps plus one-step
tautological consequence, and let the rival have Th = ∅. For g ≤ 3 the g-step relations agree on D∗ ,
but (p0 ▷ p3 ) ∈ |=h∗ \ |=h , and neither objects nor paradoxes refute the rival (Mod(T ∗ ) ⊆ Mod(∅));
at g = 4 it is refuted. Verified in Appendix I.2, together with a random test of (d).

Reading. Bounded-gap data identify the g-step relation and bracket meaning: practice bounds
it from below, objects from above (they refute a hypothesis for validating too much, never too
little). Coarser rivals (same inferences, larger steps) survive by Gold’s asymmetry (Gold, 1967),
now about obviousness; weaker rivals miss inferences of h∗ that are not chains of short steps
through the practice’s own sentences. So a practice is guaranteed to fix its meaning when its
long inferences so decompose, and otherwise it may not; expansion is the remedy.
     The equivalence classes are large: practices fix inferential role and leave ontology and latent
language open.

Proposition 10.16 (Ontology is unidentifiable at every gap). [T4 Prop 3.5, repaired] Let h =
(L, R, ρ, M) and h′ = (L, R, ρ, M′ ) be latent formalizations such that every member of M′ agrees
with some member of M on all sentences in ρ(Dh ), and vice versa. Then h ≡g h′ for every g,
and h ≡∞ h′ .

Proof. R, ρ are shared, so Stg , |= and paradoxes are; and vM ◦ ρ depends only on the truth values
of ρ(Dh ) in M .

   Instance (modulo the cited transfer principle). For readings into bounded sentences over the
superstructure V (R), Robinson’s transfer principle (Robinson, 1966) makes {V (R)} and {∗ V (R)}
such a pair, so whether the intended reals of practice contain infinitesimals cannot be learned


                                                101
from any data in this language. Likewise ε-δ analysis and a literal reading in Nelson’s internal set
theory agree in informal consequence on sentences with standard parameters (Proposition I.3),
and von Neumann and Zermelo numerals on arithmetic sentences (Proposition I.4), which
turns Benacerraf (1965) into a non-identifiability theorem. Details for all three cases are in
Appendix I.2.

Reading: ≈ is inferentialist meaning. Inferential role, incompatibility (here incoher-
ence, Lemma 10.13(iii)) and Sellarsian language-entry transitions (here object evaluations,
Lemma 10.13(i)) are all functions of |=h on D∗ , and soundness refers only to |=h∗ . Everything
finer (ontology, latent language, junk like “1 ∈ 3”) never changes a practice inference and is
unidentifiable. Granularity is partly identifiable, but it is pragmatics (which steps are acceptable),
not semantics (which are valid). Whether ε-δ and infinitesimals differ in what they are about
the practice cannot settle; the verifier needs only ≈.

10.4     Counterexample objects versus paradoxes
Lemma 10.17 (Descent along false lines). [T4 Lemma 4.1] If v is defined on the lines of α,
true on the premises and false on the conclusion, then α contains an inference with true an-
tecedents and false conclusion, or a link with true source and false target, found within depth(α)
moves evaluating only antecedents of visited lines. If v is h-admissible, the item is h-invalid.
Lean: Blame.LineArg.descent_depth Lean: Blame.ArgTree.descent_tree_not_mem


   From the false conclusion, repeatedly move to a false antecedent or link source (Appendix I.3).
This is Shapiro’s contradiction backtracing (Shapiro, 1983) for informal arguments, Lakatos’s
conversion of a global counterexample into a local one (Lakatos, 1976), and Easwaran’s demand
that proofs be fine enough to convert rebutting into undercutting defeaters (Easwaran, 2015).
Descent can end at a link: the blame then falls on an equivocation, not a rule (Lakatos’s “global
but not local” case).
