    Objects can also be neutralized. A step blamed by an object can be repaired by changing R
(lemma-incorporation), changing ρ so that the monster no longer satisfies the premise (monster-
barring by redefinition), rejecting or re-interpreting the datum (monster-barring by exclusion,
monster-adjustment), or extending L (a proof-generated concept naming the hidden lemma)
(Lakatos, 1976).
    If barring is free, objects constrain nothing; if each barred datum costs c > 0 bits, a hypothesis
that must bar m truthful data loses to h∗ in description length once m > (ℓ(h∗ ) − ℓ(h))/c

                                                    103
(Proposition I.5, Appendix I.3). So objects are powerful only if certified independently (by the
community, or by computation) or if revisions of ρ are paid for, which is Lakatos’s own preference
ordering.

Reading. Coherence says that some step of a paradox is bad; an object says which. The sorites
is the canonical uninformative paradox. The oligarchic halving of Section 6 bounds detected
incoherences by log2 (1/w(h∗ )), yet total corrections, counting rejections of valid steps, can still
be |H| − 1: coherence bounds the price of boldness, not of learning; objects bound both. Russell’s
paradox, by contrast, is a bag of size one; what it could not do is choose the generalization
(Section 10.5). A learner of inference rules must generate and evaluate objects, not only search
for ⊥.

10.5    Frege → Russell → Zermelo
Definition 10.25 (Repair setting). [T4 §5.1] I is a set of rule instances; Coh ⊆ P(I) is a coherence
predicate, downward closed and of finite character; R ⊆ P(I) is a finite class of uniformly specified
restrictions with description lengths ℓ. Practice at time t is a finitely supported weight wt : I →
[0, ∞), with coverage covt (c) := i∈c wt (i). Budget-t ⊥-search refutes c iff c has a refutation of
                                  P

size ≤ t; incoherent c has one of size k(c) < ∞. MDLt := arg min{ℓ(c) : c ∈ R, supp(wt ) ⊆ c},
and REPt is the lexicographic arg max of (covt , −ℓ) over the members of R not refuted with
budget t.

Theorem 10.26 (Abstract repair; trivial). [T4 Thm 5.1, repaired] (a) If I ∈ R is strictly shortest,
MDLt = I for all t. (b) Coherent members are never refuted; incoherent c is refuted for t ≥ k(c).
(c) For t ≥ t0 := max{k(c) : c ∈ R incoherent}, REPt maximizes (covt , −ℓ) over the coherent
members of R. (d) If wt /∥wt ∥1 → w∞ in ℓ1 and the coherent maximizer of cov∞ is unique,
REPt is eventually equal to it. (e) If c1 , c2 ∈ R are coherent and c1 ∪ c2 is not, no coherent set
contains both, and while supp(wt ) ⊆ c1 ∩ c2 only ℓ chooses between them.

    Proof in Appendix I.4. The content is in an instance that makes every step of the story
checkable. In first-order logic with ∈, =, let Comp(φ) := ∀a∀b∃y∀x (x ∈ y ↔ φ(x, a, b)), with φ
from the menu Φ of Table 13. A formula is stratified (as in Quine’s NF, Quine 1937) if it has a
typing t with t(v) = t(u) + 1 for u ∈ v and t(u) = t(v) for u = v; x ∈ x has none. R consists
of NC (the whole menu), POS (positive formulas), STRAT (stratified; NF-like), SEP (of the
form x ∈ a ∧ ψ), and Z := SEP ∪ {EMP, PAIR, UNI} (Zermelo-like). The description lengths are
stipulated: ℓ(NC) < ℓ(POS) < ℓ(SEP) < ℓ(STRAT) < ℓ(Z), and outcomes depend on this choice.

Lemma 10.27 (Comprehension facts). [T4 §5.2, F1–F6] (F1) NC is incoherent (Comp(R) with
x := y refutes it in four lines). (F2) POS is coherent, even for all positive formulas. (F3)
STRAT ∩ Φ is coherent. (F4) Z ∩ Φ is coherent. (F5) POS, STRAT, Z are pairwise jointly
incoherent. (F6) SEP ⊊ Z, and POS, STRAT, Z are pairwise ⊆-incomparable.

   The models are a one-element u ∈ u (F2), N coding the finite and cofinite sets (F3) and
the hereditarily finite sets (F4); {V, ZR} and {S, CMP} each yield Russell’s set (F5). Proof in
Appendix I.4.

has an extension”. (ii) Coherence refutes it with a four-line budget. (iii) The maximal coherent

    Historical reading (“a nice thing shadowed in” practice, not a claim about what Zermelo did).
Zermelo (1908) proves from Separation that every set M has a subset {x ∈ M : x ∈  / x} not in M :
ZR at arbitrary a, the diagonal argument as a theorem. So practice containing Zermelo-style
diagonal subsets selects Separation over stratification, and Frege’s universal extension is the
price. Without diagonal practice, and under the stipulated ℓ, NF-like stratification (on NF’s
consistency see Holmes 2015) would have won only for a practice using difference or ∅ and also
union, pairs or ∅; a purely positive practice selects positive set theory. A second separating
datum lies outside the toy: NF refutes choice (Specker, 1953), which Zermelo defended by its
uses (Moore, 1982). His stated method, to restrict “sufficiently to exclude all contradictions”
yet keep “all that is valuable” (Zermelo, 1908) (trans. van Heijenoort 1967, p. 200), is REP’s
constrained optimization; the theorem adds that the optimum exists only in a uniform class and
is chosen by coverage. Without uniformity it is far worse.
    The instances of naive comprehension have exactly 2ℵ0 maximal consistent subsets, and even
Comp(x ̸= x) alone has 2ℵ0 pairwise incompatible maximal consistent extensions (Proposition I.6,


                                               105
Appendix I.4). Incurvati and Murzi (2017) prove more: under minimal assumptions, multiple
incompatible maximal consistent sets of instances of naive comprehension exist and none is
recursively axiomatizable, generalizing McGee’s theorem for the T-schema (McGee, 1992). So
“the maximal repair” does not exist and no learner can output a recursive axiomatization of one.
Uniformity of the restriction class is what makes the learning problem well posed. The toy omits
Replacement (coverage of a conclusion), the cumulative-hierarchy conception (a choice of ℓ), and
undecidable coherence, which by Theorem 10.8 costs escalations, never soundness.

Reading. Imitation plus simplicity produces the over-general rule (Section 3); coherence refutes
it, here with sharp blame; but coherence cannot choose the repair, since the maximal coherent
generalizations are several. Coverage of what the practice does chooses: Lakatos’s “heuristic
falsifiers”, Zermelo’s “all that is valuable”. What coverage leaves open is a Kripkensteinian
residue (Section 6): coherent meanings of “set” that agree on everything the practice has used.

10.6    The robust core and the emergence of a notion of proof
Definition 10.29 (Sharpenings; robust core). [T4 Def 6.1] Fix a first-order L, a base theory T0
and vague words W . A sharpening σ gives each w ∈ W an explicit L-definition; Σ is the set
of admissible joint sharpenings. Each σ gives a first-order complete hσ = (L, Rσ , ρσ , Mod(Tσ )),
with Tσ = T0 plus σ’s definitions and ρσ reading each w by its definition. Local supervaluational
validity is |=SV := σ |=σ ; put StgSV := σ Stgσ . A precise object M |= T0 expands uniquely to
                    T                     T

Mσ |= Tσ ; an occurrence is super-determinate at M if all Mσ agree on it, and object data are
SV-truthful if reported only for super-determinate occurrences. The robust-core hypothesis RCHg :
every non-noise practice step lies in StgSV and every practice link is valid under every σ.

    Local validity (truth-preservation at each sharpening) differs from the global validity (preser-
vation of supertruth) usually called supervaluational (Fine, 1975; Williamson, 1994; Keefe, 2000;
Varzi, 2007); local validity is the right notion for “survives every formalization”.

Theorem 10.30 (Robust core). [T4 Thm 6.2, repaired]
 (a) Survival. Under RCHg , an argument whose inferences and links are non-noise practice
     items has, for every σ, its conclusion in ClRσ (ρσ Prem); a theorem so proved from premises
     every Tσ proves is a theorem of every admissible sharpening, whichever a later formalization
     adopts.
  (b) SV-truthful data never refute a sharpening. Let {hσ } ⊆ H, and let practice lie in StgSV ,
      escalation and link answers be given only when all σ agree (“yes” on StgSV , “no” outside
      S     g
        σ Stσ ), designated contexts be coherent under every σ, and objects be SV-truthful. Then
      every hσ survives forever, and Vtg accepts only steps in StgSV : it is sound for every sharpening
      at once. If moreover H is finite and every element of StgSV eventually appears in (P), then
      Vtg eventually accepts exactly StgSV .
  (c) Nothing more is soundly acceptable. Under these data, (c1) an acceptance set sound for
      every possible target hσ lies in |=SV ; (c2) one that is g-sound for every target lies in StgSV ,
      which Vtg attains when H = {hσ }. The gap |=SV \ StgSV is in general nonempty.
 (d) Permanent abstention. Steps in σ Stgσ \ StgSV are never accepted. (d1) Those outside
                                           S

     |=SV are invalid under some admissible sharpening, and only a definition (shrinking Σ) or
     lemma-incorporation removes them; (d2) those in |=SV are valid but not short under every

                                                 106
      sharpening; adding the step as a library lemma to every Rσ removes them, and so does an
      expansion into steps of StgSV when one exists.
    Proof in Appendix I.5, which also shows the gap in (c) and that for infinite Σ the robust core
can be undecidable.
    A step in the domain that is invalid under an admissible σ has a σ-monster, a model of Tσ
making its premises true and its conclusion false (Theorem I.7, by completeness; Appendix I.5).
Steps in |=SV \ StgSV have none, and a monster need not be presentable under SV-truthful
reporting. Cauchy, again: the sum-theorem step is valid only under the uniform sharpening of
“converges”, so it lies outside the robust core, and Abel’s series is a monster for the pointwise one.
Lakatos’s responses change Σ or the language: monster-barring drops the pointwise sharpening;
lemma-incorporation adds “uniformly”; a proof-generated concept introduces a word whose
only sharpening is uniform convergence. The robust-core hypothesis predicts where pre-formal
mathematics broke: at the non-robust steps.
    Only unanimity chains: if each of n steps is valid with probability ≥ 1 − ε under a measure
on sharpenings, the argument is guaranteed validity only with probability 1 − nε, and a sorites
valid under no sharpening attains this at ε = 1/n (Proposition I.8, known; Appendix I.5). The
bound is Adams’s (Adams, 1966), its use for the sorites is Edgington’s, with her verities in place
of a measure over precisifications (Edgington, 1997), and the disjoint-failure tightness is the
lottery paradox’s (Kyburg, 1961). “Valid on most readings” is to vagueness what majority vote
is to verifier ensembles (the doctrinal paradox of Section 3): it does not compose, and unanimity
is the weakest property that guarantees validity whatever the admissible sharpening turns out to
be.
Proposition 10.31 (How the nice notion of proof came to be there). [T4 Prop 6.5, repaired] Let T
be an r.e. first-order theory, ρ∗ a reading, and A0 the practice’s initial repertoire of steps (within
D∗ ). Suppose the community drops any step refuted by a presented monster (a model of T ), and
every step outside |=T is eventually refuted.
 (a) Derivability: the survivors are A∞ = A0 ∩ |=T , and the ρ∗ -images of any argument chained
     from them interpolate into a derivation in any complete calculus for T .
  (b) No gap bound follows: for A0 the instances of the single schema “from χ infer θ” (χ, θ
      arithmetic sentences) and T = PA, A∞ is undecidable and no g has A∞ ⊆ Stg for any
      complete calculus for PA meeting the effectivity assumptions of Definition 10.2.
  (c) A bounded gap needs two extra hypotheses: if A0 is the instance set of finitely many
      schemas, selection acts on schemas (a schema is dropped when any instance is refuted),
      and each surviving schema is uniformly derivable (a derivation template with at most g rule
      applications, in the schema’s metavariables, instantiates to a derivation of each instance),
      then all surviving steps are in Stg of a complete calculus for T , the shadow of finitely many
      derived rules. Uniform derivability is automatic for pure propositional schemas and fails
      in general: in a standard Hilbert calculus for PA (rules closed under substituting a fresh
      variable for a numeral), “infer θ(n̄)” with θ(n) = “n codes no PA-proof of 0 = 1” has all
      instances provable, but a uniform template would yield a PA-proof of Con(PA); uniform
      derivability is relative to the calculus and its library.
    Proof in Appendix I.5: (a) is completeness, and in (b) a gap bound would make A∞ decidable.
In the vague case, (a) applied to each (Tσ , ρσ ) gives survivors A0 ∩ |=SV , though complete monster
presentation is then in tension with SV-truthful reporting.

Reading: how the nice notion of proof came to be there. The model’s partial answer has
three ingredients. (1) Local checkability: steps are checked on objects line by line (Lemma 10.17),
so monster pressure selects steps that preserve truth in every object. (2) Completeness: for
r.e. T , Gödel’s theorem turns “truth-preserving in every object of an elementary class” into
“derivable in a finite calculus”, with no bound on length. (3) Schema-level selection of uniformly
derivable schemas, an extra hypothesis not derived here, which alone yields a bounded gap.
So the formal structure is “sorta there” in the activity because the activity was selected by
objects, and completeness says that being so selected is being shadowed by a calculus. Caveats:
complete monster presentation is an idealization (the selection took centuries); for intended-model
semantics such as {N}, (2) fails and selection heads toward true arithmetic, which no calculus
captures; and selection only removes steps, so the surviving calculus need not be complete for
T . With Theorem 10.30 this also answers the robust-core question: if pre-formal practice used
only steps valid under every admissible sharpening, its proofs survive every formalization among
them, and the conservative verifier never accepts beyond that core.
    The notes suggest looking at Euclid, who “didn’t have a full set of axioms”; reading a
diagram’s sharpenings as nearby configurations, Manders’s co-exact properties and the system E
of Avigad, Dean and Mumma give an analogue, not an instance, of the robust core (Remark I.9,
Appendix I.5).




                                                 108
10.7    Historical reading, and what a learner before formalization needed
How informal mathematics stayed reliable (Table 14). (i) The dominant negative datum was
an object, not a contradiction; only the set-theoretic antinomies were pure derivations of ⊥.
Objects localize blame, at logarithmic rather than linear cost (Theorems 10.19 and 10.20);
mathematicians still check how particular steps apply to specific examples (Weber and Mejía-
Ramos, 2011), and Euler accepted π 2 /6 on six-decimal agreement. (ii) The faulty rules were
average-case sound: right on the tame objects practitioners had in mind, wrong on degenerate
ones (Steiner’s count fails for every input, because of an excess component). Rigour arrived
when mathematicians became adversarial over objects (Weierstrass, Peano, Russell). This is
Section 3 in history: a checker trained on human steps inherits the tameness assumption, and
a strong prover finds the monsters. (iii) Lags ran from weeks to decades, so guarantees must
be time-uniform (Theorem 10.9). (iv) Labels are noisy both ways; some “known errors” are
not errors (Hales, 2007), and whether Cauchy’s theorem was false depends on the reading
(Proposition 10.7 and Theorem I.7). Modularity (Avigad, 2021), a track record of heavy use, and
a social process good at locating weak points (Thurston, 1994) tell the object search where to
look. Kreisel’s squeezing argument (Kreisel, 1967) pins informal logical validity to derivability;
the axioms cannot be squeezed, and they are what coherence and coverage leave non-unique.
    What a learner before formalization would have needed: (1) a class of latent formalizations with
a growing definitional library, so that practice has a bounded gap; (2) conservative acceptance by
unanimity, applied to links as well as steps, with a time-uniform Bayesian version (Theorems 10.8
and 10.9); (3) an expansion protocol (Proposition 10.11); (4) an object generator, adversarial
over objects, with descent (Lemma 10.17 and Theorem 10.19); (5) paid revisions of readings
(Proposition I.5); (6) coverage of practice to choose among coherent repairs within a uniform class
(Theorem 10.28 and Proposition I.6); (7) acceptance restricted to the robust core when concepts
are vague, with non-robust steps flagged as where monsters live (Theorems 10.30 and I.7); (8) a
human corpus treated as noisy and corrigible.
    The answer to success criterion 2 is yes, in a precise and conditional sense. A learner with
(1)–(8) whose class contains the practice’s latent formalization is sound at all times against
adaptive provers; for a finite class under complete presentation it identifies the practice’s step
relation, brackets its meaning and converges to the robust core; and in the comprehension toy
it reproduces Frege–Russell–Zermelo, with coverage, not coherence, choosing the repair. But
soundness is relative to realizability of the latent formalization class (BG1), and history violated
realizability at every decisive step: ε-δ, uniform convergence, ideals and the fundamental group
were inventions of language. Compare the observation in the notes that in mathematics “we
created a language in which formal proofs can be written” rather than translating existing proofs.
The hardest open problem, affordable soundness with language invention, is the first problem of
Section 14; Appendix I.6 records what this section adds to it.


11     Contexts, idealization, and checking physics
Physics is where the programme of the motivating question meets its hardest test, and where
the problem of contexts cannot be postponed. Existing olympiad solutions, the motivating
notes observe, often do not reduce the problem to one clear mathematical problem: “there’s
more of a dance with many clear setups, with some relations to the physical problem of inter-
est” (Hänni, 2026, ai/verification and generation/verification of physics olympiad
solutions/the structure of physics olympiad solutions.md). Some setups are supposi-

                                                109
tions made for reductio. Some are idealizations that contradict known facts (“assume the air
pressure is 0”). Some complete a problem that leaves something open (the sun’s elevation is
not given). A coherence loss that penalizes good arguments for both P and ¬P would pe-
nalize all three. A checker that asks whether each claim is true fails at once, because good
solutions are full of literally false claims; the motivating notes ask what else it could check:
“check that a claim is true in the context at hand. but wtf is that???” (ai/verification and
generation/verification from truth.md).
    This section answers with a semantics of contexts (§11.2), a theory of coherence, export and
tolerances (§§11.3–11.5), and a checker that is sound against every solver relative to a provably
ineliminable judgment layer, with a worked run (§§11.6–11.7).
    We build a checker, not a solver. Gold-level scores on IPhO 2025 theory under rubric grading
have been reported for current AI systems (Yu et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025), though in the
benchmark’s September 2025 data not on the modelling-heavy EuPhO 2025 of our worked example
(best model 14.9 of 29, gold threshold 16.5; a later update reports gold on all its olympiads).
The unmet target is principled checking. The motivating notes also hold that publishing
insightful research on AI theorem provers is gravely dangerous (“in my opinion, publishing such
research is omnicidal”, ai/verification and generation/formalizing philosophy.pdf, a
July 2024 draft). We have therefore avoided solver-side contributions, and leave the decision
about publication to the author of the notes.
    Most results here are trivial once the definitions are in place, or import standard tools
(Łoś’s theorem, Gronwall’s inequality, split conformal prediction, information-based complexity,
Lipschitz covering bounds, interval arithmetic). New, as far as we know, are the frame-free
realizability criterion (Theorem 11.11(a)), the two-sided analysis of adversarial stipulation
(Theorem 11.22), the table of one-sided signals (Table 15), and a rigorous thin-leg certificate
with a complete worked checker run (Section 11.7). Proofs not given inline are in Appendix J.

11.1    The problem: eternalism, contexts, and three import regimes
The simplest coherence constraint is eternalist: each proposition is true or false independently of
context, and a learner is penalized whenever it can argue for both P and ¬P . Physics reasoning
violates this constantly and correctly. A hydrostatics problem stipulates patm = 0, while the
background derives patm ≈ 1.0 × 105 Pa. A reductio derives ⊥ under a supposition. One exam
treats the same physics in incompatible models: at IPhO 2025, Theory Problem 2 excludes
surface tension and lets a gas phase appear exactly at the equilibrium threshold, while Theory
Problem 3 makes surface tension the mechanism of bubble growth. The motivating notes record
the difficulty with two obvious moves. Conjoining every sentence with the whole background
framework “leads to just assigning probability 0 to everything”; and proofs by contradiction
inside a framework known to be inadequate “might . . . really involve subverting the back-
ground framework” (philosophy/epistemology/probabilities/assigning probabilities
in a conception of the world you know to be inadequate.md).

Three import regimes. “Suppose” covers three operations that differ in what the new context
imports from its parent:




                                               110
Regime           Example               Imports              ⊥ inside means        What leaves the
                                                                                  context

                 √                     everything           success (reductio)    ¬A, or A → B
                   2 = p/q”

Physics idealizations are not counterfactuals. “If the air pressure were 0, the water in the
beaker would boil” is true and irrelevant: the problem asks what follows in a designated model
that imports incompressible hydrostatics and the data, and nothing else. Similarity semantics
(Stalnaker, 1968; Lewis, 1973) or AGM revision (Alchourrón et al., 1985) imports exactly the
background (the vapour pressure of water) that makes the context degenerate. Idealization is
designated minimal import, as in chunk-and-permeate (Brown and Priest, 2004), McCarthy’s
ist(c, φ) (McCarthy, 1993), local-models semantics (Ghidini and Giunchiglia, 2001), Cartwright’s
models (Cartwright, 1983), and compositional modelling (Falkenhainer and Forbus, 1991). We
keep their shape, “classical inside, filtered between”; what none of them supplies, as far as we
know, is different coherence obligations for suppositions and idealizations, and rigorous certificates
on the bridges.

Anatomy of a solution. Three decomposed olympiad solutions (IPhO 2012 Theory Problem 1,
part A; EuPhO 2025 Theory Problem 1(a); IPhO 2025 Theory Problem 2) share one structure.
A root cP holds the problem text, figures and conventions; for grading, the “world” is cP ,
not the actual world. A reading ρ maps cP to an admissible model family, possibly with free
completion parameters, and types the query (“express in terms of a, I0 , r, φ”). Local models
are clear mathematical problems, joined by bridges: exact ones (symmetry, decomposition,
isomorphism) and approximate ones (a small parameter set to its limit, with an error claim),
ending in an export. Only approximate bridges introduced by the solver, rather than stipulated
or regime-stated by the problem, need a certificate from the solver. The notes’ hypothesis that
“there’s a local setting up of a clear thing” holds in all three: the unclear part concentrates in the
reading and in a few approximate bridges.

11.2     Filter semantics for contexts
Definition 11.1 (Frames, worlds, readings). [T3 Def 1.1] Let L be a many-sorted first-order
language with a sort R and parameter constants p1 , . . . , pn of that sort. (i) A deformation frame
                                                   M(λ)
is a partial map M : Λ ⇀ Str(L), Λ ⊆ Rn , with pi       = λi ; dom M is where the model exists (is
well-posed). In every M(λ) the sort R is the ordered field of reals with standard numerals; K is
the class of L-structures with this standard real sort. Ideal values at infinity are reparametrized
(m → ∞ as 1/m → 0). (ii) A world is w = (Mw , λ∗w ) with λ∗w ∈ dom Mw : a top-model family
and the actual (or intended) parameter point. (iii) A reading ρ yields a set Wρ of worlds, the
admissible completions (given parameters fixed, measured ones in intervals, free ones in ranges);
a query term Q; and a set Axρ of sentences true at Mw (λ∗w ) for every w ∈ Wρ . The laws of a
frame are the sentences true at every Mw (λ), λ ∈ dom Mw .

   For a projectile, M(λ) solves ẍ = −gẑ − k|ẋ|ẋ with parameters (g, v0 , θ, k), and “neglect air”
deforms k toward 0.
Definition 11.2 (Contexts; filter semantics). [T3 Defs 1.2–1.3] A context tree has root @ and parent
map π; each other context is SUP(A), a supposition of a sentence A; or DEF(D, λ◦ , G), a declared
deformation with deformed parameters D ⊆ {1, . . . , n}, ideal values λ◦ ∈ RD , and a proper filter
G on RD converging to λ◦ (the path); or AUX, a definitional extension that shares its parent’s
semantics. A DEF context uses limit semantics if G is principal at λ◦ , and germ semantics if
G is the punctured neighbourhood filter, possibly restricted to a curve. Fix a world w, write
∥φ∥w = {λ ∈ dom Mw : Mw (λ) |= φ} and λ[D:=µ] for λ with its D-coordinates replaced by µ.
Each context c gets a (possibly improper) filter Fc (w) on dom Mw : F@ (w) is principal at λ∗w ;
for c = SUP(A) with parent p, Fc (w) is generated by Fp (w) ∪ {∥A∥w }; for c = DEF(D, λ◦ , G),
it is generated by the sets {λ[D:=µ] : λ ∈ F, µ ∈ G} ∩ dom Mw , F ∈ Fp (w), G ∈ G. Truth in
a context is c |=w φ iff ∥φ∥w ∈ Fc (w), and the context-free proposition ist(c, φ) is true at w iff
c |=w φ. A context is proper at w if ∅ ∈
                                       / Fc (w). A claim is supertrue under ρ if it is true at every
w ∈ Wρ .
    Below a root parent, a germ context makes φ true iff φ holds for all deformed parameters
close enough to the ideal along the path, at the actual values of everything else; a limit context
is evaluated at the single point λ∗ [D:=λ◦ ], and is improper if no model exists there.

Proposition 11.5 (What idealized contexts may do). [T3 Prop 1.6, rev.] (a) Contradicting the root.
In a hydrostatics frame whose laws do not mention phase change (so the model exists at patm = 0),
let c deform patm toward 0 (limit semantics). Then c |= patm = 0 and @ |= patm = 1.0 × 105 ,
both contexts are proper, and no sentence is both true and false in one context. (b) Inconsistent
limit, consistent germ. A rope of mass mr is pulled by a force Φ ̸= 0, with dom = {mr > 0};

                                                  112
deform mr toward 0 below the root. The limit context is improper; the germ context is proper and
proves |a| > K for every numeral K. (c) Norton’s distinction. Let clim , cgerm be the limit and
germ children of the root for the same D, λ◦ , with λ∗ [D:=λ◦ ] ∈ dom, and let q(µ) be the value of
Q at λ∗ [D:=µ]. Then cgerm |= Q ∈ I for every open interval I ∋ q(λ◦ ) iff q(µ) → q(λ◦ ) along G
(where the deformed models exist).

    Part (c) is Norton’s “limit property versus property of the limit system” (Norton, 2012):
reasoning inside the limit model justifies a value exactly when the query is continuous along the
path; d’Alembert’s paradox is the failure case. Part (b) is the shape of idealizations that are
inconsistent at the limit but consistent along it, such as Painlevé’s rigid bodies with Coulomb
friction (Stewart, 2000) or a uniform isothermal gas ball in vacuum; germ semantics requires
well-posedness along the family, not at the limit. Different filters on one family give different
contexts, so the path to the limit is part of the reading.

Imports are fixed by the deformation. The import filter of an idealized context is not a
third object to learn besides rules and tolerances.

Definition 11.6 (Stability). [T3 Def 1.7] φ is D-stable in w if Mw (λ) |= φ ⇐⇒ Mw (λ′ ) |= φ for
all λ, λ′ ∈ dom Mw differing only in coordinates in D. Laws are D-stable, and so are undeformed
data: arithmetic formulas in the pi , i ∈
                                        / D.

Lemma 11.7 (Import soundness). [T3 Lemma 1.8, rev.: (b), (c) added] (a) If φ is D-stable in w and
p |=w φ, then c |=w φ for every DEF child c of p deforming D, for any parent filter and path.
(b) Uniform converse. Fix Mw and D. If for every actual point λ∗ ∈ dom Mw and every ideal
value λ◦ ∈ RD the limit child c of the root satisfies @ |= φ ⇒ c |= φ, then φ is D-stable. (c)
Scope. For one fixed deformation the converse of (a) fails (e.g. φ := (k ≤ 1) under “k → 0”,
limit semantics; Appendix J).                         Lean: Contexts.import_sound ((a); propositional)


Proof idea. (a) The generator built from F = ∥φ∥ lies in ∥φ∥. (b) Put the actual point at a φ-point
λ and the ideal value at λ′D . (c) The child always satisfies k = 0. Details in Appendix J.

Reading. The imports that are sound uniformly in the actual point and the ideal value are
exactly what the declared top-model family makes stable. “Water’s vapour pressure is 2.3 kPa”
is a law of a frame with phase equilibrium, where the patm → 0 context correctly boils; in
incompressible hydrostatics it is not in the language. So learning sound import filters reduces to
learning which top-model family the problem intends: part of the reading (§11.6).

11.3     What coherence should constrain
Theorem 11.8 (No truth-functional eternal reading). [T3 Thm 2.1, rev.] Let c be a DEF context,
proper at w, with a stipulation Sc such that c |=w Sc and Sc is false at Mw (λ∗w ) (e.g. patm = 0).
Let τ (c, φ) translate “φ holds in c” into a world sentence whose truth value at w is f (Scw , φw ) for
some f : {0, 1}2 → {0, 1}. Then τ does not track in-context truth at w: c |=w ⊤ and c ̸|=w ¬Sc ,
but τ (c, ⊤)w = τ (c, ¬Sc )w .        Lean: Contexts.not_exists_truthFunctional_reading (propositional filters)


Proof. ⊤ and ¬Sc are both true at w, so both translations have value f (0, 1). And c |=w Sc with
Thw (c) consistent (Proposition 11.3(b)).



                                                     113
    Stripping (f = ∧) makes every in-context claim false at w, hence incoherent with the
root; conditionalizing (f =→) makes every one true, hence vacuous; the other two choices
collapse “in c” into “at w” or its negation. Properness is needed: for the improper rope limit of
Proposition 11.5(b), conditionalizing tracks in-context truth perfectly.
    Consequently an eternalist check, which deletes context indices and flags unsatisfiable sets of
recorded judgments, flags every recorded sound reductio, every sound idealization contradicting
a recorded root judgment, and every pair of sound contexts that record different answers to one
query (IPhO 2025 Theory Problems 2 and 3); what is penalized depends on how much of the
reasoning is recorded (Corollary J.2, Appendix J).
    A learner trained to keep such sets coherent loses classical logic, and not only in the offending
context. This is a formal version of the air-pressure worry of Section 1.1.

Proof idea. (a) Chaining valid instances would give A ⊢C ⊥. (b) Substitution and weakening.

Reading. Designate “patm = 0 plus the full background” as coherent, and a coherence loss
teaches a sub-classical logic for all reasoning: atomic paraconsistency if the background states
patm ≠ 0 outright, the loss of some classical schema if it only derives it. The fix has three parts.
Designate only consistent chunks (Brown and Priest, 2004). Keep the root phenomenological
(interval claims about measurables, observations, exports), with laws living in model contexts
(Cartwright, 1983; Wilson, 2006); a root holding unrestricted laws may itself be inconsistent.
And adopt meta-level eternalism: ist(c, φ) is an eternal proposition about a finitely specified
context (McCarthy, 1993), by Theorem 11.8 necessarily non-truth-functional in the world’s facts.
Which contexts, then, must be consistent?

11.3.1     The right constraint: realizability
Definition 11.10 (Judgment sets, bridges, realizations). [T3 Def 2.3, rev.] “Model” and “satisfiable”
refer to K; for a set M of structures, M |= χ means N |= χ for all N ∈ M . A judgment set J is a
finite set of triples (c, Γ, φ) over a context tree in which SUP contexts have only SUP descendants;
a set Ccert of DEF contexts is certified (claimed well-posed). A bridge β has a pattern ϕβ (v), a
side condition σβ and an export formula εβ (v), v ∈ V . It is a value-export bridge for Q if ϕβ (v)
is Q = v̄ with standard names (distinct values denote distinct objects in K) and σβ does not
depend on v; it is informative if {σβ } ∪ {εβ (v) : v ∈ V0 } has no model for some finite V0 ⊆ V
(e.g. interval exports over unbounded V ). A bridge use is (c, β, t) ∈ U with c a DEF context
and (c, ∅, ϕβ (t)), (πc, ∅, σβ ), (πc, ∅, εβ (t)) ∈ J. A (frame-free) realization assigns each context
a set Mc ⊆ K with (R0) M@ ̸= ∅; (R1) Mc = Mπc ∩ ∥A∥ for c = SUP(A); (R2) Mc arbitrary,
possibly empty, for DEF contexts; (R3) every judgment holds: for N ∈ Mc , N |= Γ implies
                                                                                           V

N |= φ; (R4) every used bridge is sound: for all v, Mc |= ϕβ (v) implies Mπc |= σβ → εβ (v);
(R5) Mc =  ̸ ∅ for c ∈ Ccert . The SUP-collapse J ∗ replaces each (c, Γ, φ) with c a SUP context by

(b, Γ ∪ Asm(c), φ), where b is the nearest non-SUP ancestor and Asm(c) the suppositions on the
path; Th∗ (c) := { Γ → φ : (c, Γ, φ) ∈ J ∗ }. The anchored set Anc is the least set of non-SUP
                   V

contexts containing @ and Ccert and containing c whenever (c, β, t) ∈ U with β informative and
πc ∈ Anc.

Theorem 11.11 (Realizability criterion). [T3 Thm 2.4, rev.: (a) frame-free; (b), (c) new] Suppose every
used bridge is an informative value-export bridge. (a) Frame-free. J has a realization satisfying
(R0)–(R5) iff Th∗ (c) is satisfiable for every c ∈ Anc. (b) Necessity in the frame semantics. Call
J frame-realizable if for some world w, with the filters of Definition 11.2, every judgment holds
(c |=w Γ → φ), every c ∈ Ccert is proper, and every bridge use is sound at w (c |=w ϕβ (v)
        V

implies πc |=w σβ → εβ (v)). If J is frame-realizable, the criterion of (a) holds, for limit or germ
paths. (c) Non-sufficiency. The converse of (b) fails. CE1: a certified limit child c of the root
deforms D = {2} toward 0, and J = {(@, ∅, p1 = 1), (c, ∅, p1 = 0)}; the criterion holds, but the
root forces λ∗1 = 1, and c, proper because certified, sits at λ∗ [2:=0], so c |= p1 = 1. CE2: two
certified siblings with the same declaration have equal filters, so Q = 1 in one and Q = 2 in the
other cannot both hold.

Proof idea. By (R1), SUP contexts impose on their base exactly the constraints Th∗ . An
anchoring lemma says every anchored context has Mc =   ̸ ∅: from an empty Mc an informative
bridge would export every εβ (v). Conversely, put one model of Th∗ (c) at each anchored context
and ∅ elsewhere. Part (b) uses properness for nonemptiness. Full proof in Appendix J.

    Brute-force checks agree with (a), show that informativeness is needed, and find no violation
of (b) (computed) (Appendix J). Bridge soundness here is ω-free; for judgment sets produced
by the calculus of Definition 11.13, add (πc, ∅, ωc ) to each bridge use and read (R4) as Mπc |=
σβ ∧ ωc → εβ (v); the anchoring arguments are unchanged. The locality of (a) is a consequence of
(R2): in the frame semantics rigid parameters and shared filters force cross-context constraints,
which under limit semantics are a pointwise adjunction (Proposition J.3), the structural core
of discussive and preservationist logics (Jaśkowski, 1969; Schotch and Jennings, 1980). Germ
semantics is open.
    Consequences for reductio and ill-posed contexts are collected in Corollary J.4 (Appendix J):
a SUP context deriving ⊥ contributes exactly the negation of its suppositions, an idealized one
deriving ⊥ constrains frame-free realizability only if anchored, and eternalist coherence is strictly
stronger than frame-free realizability.

Reading. Arguments for P and ¬P in contradictory contexts should not be penalized, and
Theorem 11.11(a) says exactly which contexts must be consistent: the root, and idealizations
that are certified or export informatively. Ill-posed idealizations must not export, and this is now
an iff. The frame-semantic constraints CE1, CE2 are enforced in the checker by a declaration
discipline, not by coherence (§11.6).
Remark 11.12 (Belief states, worlds, contextuality). Section 9 gives the multi-context counterpart:
coherence on designated contexts is equivalent to a model nonempty there (Theorem 9.19
and Corollary 9.20); bridges must be read as rules of proof over belief states, not conditionals
between worlds (Theorem 9.22); and locally coherent contexts need not glue into one world
(Proposition 9.23), a logical form of contextuality (Abramsky and Brandenburger, 2011).

11.3.2    A calculus, its soundness, and blame localization
Definition 11.13 (Context calculus). [T3 §2.3, rev.] Judgments are c ⊩ φ; R̂ is the (learned) rule
set and Impc the declared import set of c. (Ax) c ⊩ φ for φ ∈ Ax(c), where Ax(@) = Axρ ,
Ax(SUP(A)) = {A}, and Ax(DEF(D, λ◦ , G)) is the set of canonical stipulations: pi = λ◦i (i ∈ D)
under limit semantics, pD ∈ U for definable U ∈ G under germ semantics; stipulations about
undeclared parameters are not axioms. (Step) From c ⊩ φ1 , . . . , c ⊩ φk and an instance
φ1 , . . . , φk ▷ ψ of R̂, infer c ⊩ ψ. (Imp) From πc ⊩ φ with φ ∈ Impc , infer c ⊩ φ. (Dis) For
c = SUP(A): from c ⊩ ψ infer πc ⊩ A → ψ. (Exp) For a DEF context c: from c ⊩ ϕβ (t), πc ⊩ σβ
and πc ⊩ ωc , infer πc ⊩ εβ (t); here the well-posedness certificate ωc is a sentence such that for
every w and λ ∈ ∥ωc ∥w , {µ : λ[D:=µ] ∈ dom Mw } ∈ G. An instance is sound at w if it preserves
truth there (for Step: c |=w i φi → ψ), and sound if sound at every w ∈ Wρ .
                                  V


   Step soundness is context-relative: time reversal is sound in a drag-free DEF context and
unsound at the root.

Theorem 11.14 (Soundness). [T3 Thm 2.5] If every Ax in a derivation of c ⊩ φ is true at w and
every Step, Imp and Exp instance in it is sound at w, then c |=w φ.

Proof. Induction: Ax and Step by hypothesis and filter closure (Proposition 11.3(a)); Imp and
Exp by soundness of the instance; Dis by Proposition 11.4.

Corollary 11.15 (Blame localization). [T3 Cor 2.6, rev.] Let Wρ ≠ ∅. Call d designated if it is
the root, or a certified DEF context with a properness witness wd ∈ Wρ at which d is proper.
Let D derive d ⊩ ⊥, and let its cone be all instances in its derivation tree, including those in
sub-contexts whose conclusions reach d by Dis or Exp. (a) At every w at which d is proper
(every w ∈ Wρ if d = @), the cone contains an Ax false at w or an instance unsound at w.
(b) Items outside the cone are never implicated: an undischarged SUP contradiction, or a pair
of contradictory ist-claims. (c) If πd |=w ωd and πd is proper at w, then d is proper at w; so
parent-derived certificates are properness witnesses.

Proof idea. (a) is the contrapositive of Theorem 11.14; (b) follows. (c) In each parent filter set
pick λ ∈ ∥ωd ∥. Proposition J.5 adds how ⊥ in an anchored DEF context propagates toward the
root or a certified context, and where the blame then falls.

     The cone is a negative bag in the sense of Section 6, and by (a) a correct target never contains
it whole. So with the designated contexts of Corollary 11.15 (the root, and certified contexts
with properness witnesses) as the only designated contexts, an oligarchic-halving learner makes
at most log2 (1/w∗ ) detections and no false alarms while the reading and the certifications are
correct (Theorem 6.5; false alarms are priced by Theorem 6.7). What root coherence cannot see
is silent unsoundness: exports that are false but consistent with everything else (§11.5).

11.3.3    Reductio hygiene, and 100 = 99.9
The motivating notes’ second worry (§11.1) continues: “and there’s a chance such an argument
could equally be provided starting from the statement itself”. Let c have an explicit imported
fragment Kc , a finite set of premises. A reductio of A in c is an R̂-derivation of ⊥ from Kc ∪ {A}
in SUP(A); accepting it yields c ⊩ ¬A. An instance is c-sound at w if c |=w φi → ψ.
                                                                                 V




                                                116
Theorem 11.16 (Reductio hygiene). [T3 Thm 1.9, rev.: (c)–(e)] (a) Soundness. If c |=w Kc and
every instance used is c-sound at w, every accepted reductio of A yields c |=w ¬A. (b) Inconsistent
imports refute everything. If Kc ⊢R̂ ⊥, every sentence, A and ¬A alike, has a reductio in c,
whatever the world. (c) Derivation-local tests fail. Let K = {A → q, ¬A → q, ¬q}. K is
unsatisfiable, but the reductio of A uses only the satisfiable {A → q, ¬q} and that of ¬A only the
satisfiable {¬A → q, ¬q}; any test that is a function of the derivation alone and accepts every
sound reductio from a consistent premise set accepts both. (d) A consistency certificate suffices. If
a structure N satisfies Kc and every instance used (N |= φi → ψ), every reductio-refuted A is
                                                                          V

false in N , so no A and ¬A are both refuted. The condition on instances is automatic for logically
sound R̂ and needed otherwise. If c is proper at w, c |=w Kc and the instances are c-sound at w,
a suitable N = Mw (λ) exists: a properness witness is a certificate. (e) Learning consequence. A
coherence loss fed with reductios from a context whose fragment is R̂-inconsistent receives “A
false” and “¬A false” for every A: jointly unsatisfiable, systematic, world-independent labels.

Proof idea. (a) SUP(A) refines c’s filter, so induction gives SUP(A) |=w ⊥, and Proposition 11.4

Reading. A reductio in an inadequate framework can indeed be spurious, as the notes suggest;
the remedy is not to abandon reductio. Hygiene is a global certificate on the imported fragment,
not a syntactic relevance condition on the derivation, which (c) shows cannot work. In physics
the certificate is a well-posedness witness: an explicit or validated-numerical solution of the local
model.

Proposition 11.17 (The continuity asymmetry). [T3 Prop 1.10] Let premises xi = mi hold only
to tolerance, xi ∈ [mi ± ri ], with box B. (a) A direct derivation of y = g(x), g continuous on B,
errs by at most supx∈B |g(x) − g(m)|, which tends to 0 with the tolerances by continuity of g. (b)
Exact-equality reasoning derives ⊥ from approximately true premises read as exact: x = 100 m
(flat Earth) and x = 99.9 m (sphere), both true to ±0.2 m, give 0 = 0.1 by substitution, while as
intervals they give x ∈ [99.8, 100.1] ̸= ∅. (c) Sound replacement. If A with the exact laws implies
f (x) = 0, and F is an inclusion-monotone interval extension of f with 0 ∈    / F (B), the interval
premises refute A soundly; the condition is sufficient, not necessary.

Proof. (a) Definition. (b) Arithmetic. (c) Inclusion monotonicity (Moore, 1966) gives f (B) ⊆
F (B) ̸∋ 0.

Reading. The notes ask: “how come we usually avoid this sort of catastrophic reasoning [100 =
99.9]? i don’t think any nice ‘formal criterion’ is going to be right?” (philosophy/philosophy of
science/the domain of applicability of a scientific mode(l).md). Here is a partial
answer, a sufficient condition rather than a definition of good reasoning: “x = y” defines a closed
set of data with empty interior, so derivability of ⊥ is a discontinuous function of the data, while
derived values are continuous ones. This gives one precise reason behind a tentative suggestion in
the notes, that the danger of reductio in inadequate frameworks is “maybe . . . some argument in
favor of trusting ‘constructive’ reasoning more than ‘non-constructive’ reasoning, at least in messy
domains” (the note quoted in §11.1). The fix is interval typing with a margin (Theorem J.8(c)).



                                                       117
11.4      Export: what can justify leaving a context
Contexts let an idealized model contradict the world; exports carry its conclusions back. No
export is free: information about the idealized model alone, however complete (its jet, its germ,
finitely many values elsewhere), never justifies a finite-tolerance claim at the actual parameter
(Theorem 11.19). What justifies one is information of small radius about the de-idealized family
(Proposition 11.20). A solver who may choose contexts can then stipulate any answer unless side
conditions are evaluated in the parent and contexts are declared deformations (Theorem 11.22).
    Fix a one-parameter deformation (the multi-parameter case is identical) with ideal value 0
and actual value λ∗ ∈ (0, Λ]. A family is represented by its query function Q : [0, Λ] → R; a
family class is a set C of them. An information map I gives what an export rule may use (the
jet at 0, the germ, a restriction Q|S , finitely many values). An export rule E maps (I(Q), λ∗ ) to
“abstain” or a finite interval [q ± ϵ], and is sound on C if Q(λ∗ ) ∈ E(I(Q), λ∗ ) whenever it does
not abstain.

Lemma 11.18 (Invisible perturbation). [T3 Lemma 3.2; Traub et al. 1988] If some f with f (λ∗ ) ̸= 0
has Q + Af ∈ C and I(Q + Af ) = I(Q) for all Q ∈ C, A ∈ R, then every export rule sound on C
abstains at λ∗ on every Q ∈ C.                                         Lean: Export.invisible_perturbation


Proof. An output [q ± ϵ] on I(Q) = I(Q + Af ) would have to contain Q(λ∗ ) + Af (λ∗ ) for every
A.

Theorem 11.19 (No free export). [T3 Thm 3.3, rev.: closure hypothesis] Every rule sound on C abstains
at every λ∗ > 0, on every Q ∈ C, if (a) C + C ∞ [0, Λ] ⊆ C and I is the full jet at 0; or (b)
C + C ∞ [0, Λ] ⊆ C and I is the germ at 0, or Q|S for any S whose closure omits λ∗ ; or (c)
C + {polynomials} ⊆ C (e.g. C is the class of all restrictions of entire functions) and I is the jet
up to a finite order N ; or (d) C + C ∞ [0, Λ] ⊆ C and I is any finite set of values Q(λj ), λj ̸= λ∗ .

    So an export certificate is information of small radius: a uniform derivative bound, a Gronwall

Theorem 11.21 (Certified-neighbourhood and rate-qualified export). [T3 Thm 3.5] (a) If the
parent proves λ∗ ∈ U and a frame theorem gives supλ∈U |Q(M(λ)) − q| ≤ ϵ, the parent may
soundly assert Q ∈ [q ± ϵ]. (b) A germ claim Q ∼ q exports nothing at a fixed λ∗ ; with a rate
|Q/q − 1| ≤ C∥λ∥k on U it exports |Q/q − 1| ≤ C supU ∥λ∥k . (c) If the problem declares a regime,
the root is a germ context and asymptotic equivalence is the correctness relation itself; for exp-log
expressions in one parameter it is decidable modulo zero-equivalence of constants (Gruntz, 1996;
Richardson, 1968).

   Part (a) fixes the logical form of every side condition: a parent-certified set plus a uniform
bound over it, not a value at a guessed point. Certificates of this form include a checkable
Gronwall bound for finite-horizon exports (Theorem J.6); a rigorous range certificate for projectiles
under any drag dominated by quadratic drag (Theorem J.7), which for a steel ball certifies
R ∈ [9.653, 10.483] m against a simulated 9.978 m and for a ping-pong ball is silent; and error
budgets for chains of bridges (Theorem J.8), under which “100 − 99.9” with tolerances 0.2 certifies
not even a sign. All three are stated and proved in Appendix J.5.

Theorem 11.22 (Where side conditions live, and what contexts may be). [T3 Thm 3.9, rev.: (c)] (a)
Child-evaluated side conditions are unsound. If Exp accepts c ⊩ s ≤ η in place of πc ⊩ s ≤ η, the
export fires on every world (at pD = 0, s = 0); on any C ∞ -closed class this is unsound for every
ϵ. The ping-pong ball gets the drag-free range ±5%, while its true range is 49% short. (b) Free
stipulations are unsound even with parent evaluation. If contexts may set undeclared parameters,
a solver stipulates pD = 0 and gc = g ′ ; the parent condition holds for the steel ball, and the child’s
Q = R0 (g ′ ) is any desired value. (c) Sufficiency. Suppose contexts are declared deformations with
only canonical stipulations as axioms; σβ and a well-posedness certificate ωc are derived in the
parent; and the schema is a theorem of the frame: for all w, all λ ∈ dom Mw with Mw (λ) |= σβ
and all v, if {µ : λ[D:=µ] ∈ dom Mw , Q(Mw (λ[D:=µ])) = v} ∈ G then Mw (λ) |= εβ (v). Then
every accepted export is sound, for every solver. Without ωc , (c) is false: in the rope frame of
Proposition 11.5(b) under limit semantics, the improper child proves a = 0, the schema holds
vacuously, the parent proves mr ≤ η, and Exp would accept |a| ≤ ϵ while |a| = |Φ|/mr ≥ |Φ|/η.

Proof idea. (a), (b) are the constructions. For (c), the child-filter generator witnessing Q = v̄,
intersected with the parent sets for σβ and ωc , puts the schema’s antecedent at every point of a
parent filter set. Details in Appendix J.

     Theorem J.7 is such a schema (Appendix J.5). Germ contexts naturally conclude Q ≃ v
(standard part v); the analogous asymptotic schema is sound below a principal parent given ωc
(Lemma J.9), and under a nested germ parent it also needs uniform convergence on a parent
filter set.

Reading. This is the search problem of Section 3 transplanted to idealizations: a solver
chooses contexts as a prover chooses steps. The remedy is the analogue of cautious acceptance:
contexts restricted to declared deformations with canonical stipulations (Strevens’s “default values”
made into a syntactic discipline; Strevens 2008), side conditions evaluated in the parent, and a
parent-derived well-posedness certificate supplied by the trusted catalogue (Assumption 11.26).

                                                  119
11.5     Learning tolerances and validity regions
Export certificates need tolerances and validity regions, which are natural targets for learning. This
subsection asks which signals learn them soundly against a solver who picks the regime. Coherence
among exports catches only tolerances that are too narrow (Theorem 11.23); exchangeable
calibration gives average coverage and nothing under selection; and only a proved regularity
property turns validated simulation of the top model into a sound certifier. A bridge schema s
has a dimensionless regime parameter π ∈ Π and an error function es (π), the relative difference
between top model and idealization; the task is to learn where es ≤ τ .

Theorem 11.23 (Coherence cannot calibrate tolerances). [T3 Thm 4.1] Schemas s = 1, . . . , m
export [qs,i ± ϵs ] for true values Vi ; a coherence-only calibrator chooses ϵ̂ from the discrepancies
(qs,i − qs′ ,i ) alone. If the environment class is closed under common shifts ((q, V ) admissible
implies (q, V + b) admissible for |b| ≤ β: all models may share an omitted effect), every ϵ̂ sound
on the class has ϵ̂s ≥ β; with unbounded shifts, ϵ̂ = ∞.              Lean: Export.coherence_cannot_calibrate


Proof. (q, V ± β) give the same data, hence the same ϵ̂, and soundness for both signs gives
2β ≤ 2ϵ̂s .

    Worse, coherent tolerance vectors form an up-set, so a minimal coherent repair only ever
widens tolerances and never restricts a schema’s regime, and two schemas sharing an idealization
never disagree: their agreement is common-mode, not independent evidence (Levins, 1966;
Odenbaugh and Alexandrova, 2011). Appendix J.6 gives pendulum numbers for both effects
(computed).
    The other signals are treated in Appendix J.6: split conformal calibration fails under selection
(Theorem J.10); without regularity, finitely many simulations certify only the queried points
(Theorem J.11); a proved Lipschitz constant or monotonicity gives a sound certifier at a matching
query cost (Theorems J.12 and J.13); and monotonicity can fail, for a damped pendulum
(Proposition J.14).

Reading. The monotonicity that Laymon (1987) uses to explicate idealized data (better data,
better predictions) is a property of a model–query pair, to be proved, not assumed. Once such
a property is proved, simulation of the top model is a sound oracle for validity regions; world
feedback proper is needed only to calibrate the top model itself, and for olympiad grading, where
the root is cP , not even that.

11.6     The Structured Physics Solution checker
Definition 11.24 (Structured Physics Solution). [T3 Def 5.1; L9 §7.1] An SPS is a tuple (ρ, T , D, X):
a purported reading ρ (frame class and parameter roles: given, measured, free, deformable; the
query, its dimension and allowed symbols; conventions), which, if the setter supplies a formal
specification, must be that specification or agree with it (Wρ , Q and its type equal, Axρ its
axioms or kernel-derivable from them); a context tree T ; a derivation D in the calculus of
Definition 11.13 whose Exp instances cite schemas from a catalogue B; and a final judgment
X = (@ ⊩ Q ∈ [q ± δ]). A declared-regime problem uses a top-level germ context d whose
declaration belongs to the trusted specification, and X = (d ⊩ χ).

Definition 11.25 (The checker). [T3 Def 5.2, rev.: Ax legality, schema indexing] The checker accepts iff
all of the following hold. Reading: if a formal specification is supplied, ρ is it or passes the

                                                    120
comparison of Definition 11.24 (check C0 in §11.7). Ax legality: every Ax at the root is in Axρ ,
every Ax in SUP(A) is A, every Ax in a DEF context is a canonical stipulation of its declaration.
Kernel and laws: every Step is accepted by the kernel, and every law it cites is in the trusted
law catalogue. Schema indexing: every Exp cites a β ∈ B whose catalogue entry is indexed by
exactly the context’s declaration (D, λ◦ , G); σβ and the well-posedness certificate ωβ listed in
the catalogue entry of β (used as ωc ) are derived in the parent, so the solver may not choose
ωc ; asymptotic schemas are cited only below a principal parent (the root, or a limit-semantics
context all of whose DEF ancestors use limit semantics). Imports: every Imp into a DEF context
is a catalogue law or an undeformed datum for its D (imports into SUP children are unrestricted).
Shape: every non-root context is SUP, DEF or AUX, every AUX bridge is a kernel-checked theorem,
and X is derived at the root (or the declared germ root). All checks are deterministic.

    Ax legality and schema indexing are necessary: without them the checker accepts the attack
of Theorem 11.22(b). The list of “deformable” parameters need not be trusted: if a solver uses
DEF({k, g}, (0, g ′ )), the “neglect k” schema, indexed by DEF({k}, 0), cannot be cited.

Assumption 11.26 (Trusted base). [T3 §5, rev.] (TB1) The kernel and the law catalogue are sound:
every accepted Step instance and every catalogue law is valid in every Mw (λ), λ ∈ dom Mw , w ∈
Wρ (including top-model theorems used as certified-neighbourhood bridges). (TB2) Every β ∈ B
is a theorem of the frame for its indexed declaration, in the pointwise form of Theorem 11.22(c) or
the asymptotic form of Lemma J.9; and each catalogue entry carries a well-posedness certificate
ωβ for its declaration: for every w and λ ∈ ∥ωβ ∥w , {µ : λ[D:=µ] ∈ dom Mw } ∈ G. (TB3)
Validated numerics return correct enclosures.

Theorem 11.27 (Relative soundness of the SPS checker). [T3 Thm 5.3, rev.] Assume (TB1)–(TB3),
and that ρ is a reading in the sense of Definition 11.1, i.e. Axρ holds at every w ∈ Wρ (guaranteed
when the Reading check compares ρ with a formal specification). For every solver whatsoever,
                                                                               ∗
if the checker accepts (ρ, T , D, X) with a root judgment X, then QMw (λw ) ∈ [q ± δ] for every
w ∈ Wρ (for a germ root, d |=w χ). Hence if the intended reading satisfies Wρ∗ ⊆ Wρ the export
is supertrue for the intended problem, and if the actual system is in Wρ∗ it is true of the world.

Proof idea. Theorem 11.14 at each w ∈ Wρ : Step by (TB1); root axioms because ρ is a
reading; DEF axioms because canonical stipulations hold in the child filter (the check that blocks
Theorem 11.22(b)); imports by Lemma 11.7(a); exports by Theorem 11.22(c) with (TB2), (TB3)
and schema indexing (by (TB2), ωc is a genuine certificate). Nothing depends on how D was
produced. Details in Appendix J.

    The residual judgment layer is exactly (J1) reading adequacy: ρ is a reading (Axρ holds
at every w ∈ Wρ ) and Wρ∗ ⊆ Wρ ; when ρ is the setter’s formal specification only the second
half remains; (J2) top-model adequacy, that the actual system is a world in Wρ∗ (needed only
for world claims, not for olympiad grading, where cP is the root); and (J3) the trusted base
(TB1)–(TB3). (J3) is the trusted core of any proof checker. (J1) and (J2) cannot be removed:

Theorem 11.29 (Supervaluational correctness; completion invariance). [T3 Thm 5.5, rev.] Write
              ∗
Qw = QMw (λw ) , with Wρ ranging over all admissible completions (free parameters θf ∈ Θf ,
measured ones in their intervals). (a) “Q ∈ [q ± δ]” is supertrue iff supw∈Wρ |Qw − q| ≤ δ;
a supertrue answer at precision δ exists iff oscWρ Q ≤ 2δ, and the midrange is one. (b) A
completion-invariance certificate is a root derivation of Q ∈ [q ± δ] from Axρ in which θf enters
only through “θf ∈ Θf ”. By Theorem 11.27 the conclusion of every accepted root derivation holds
at every completion, so in the formal checker completion invariance is not a separate obligation
but the content of deriving from Axρ rather than from a narrowed axiom set. Informal forms
are ∂Q/∂θf = 0 on a connected Θf where Q is differentiable in θf , or a variation bound; in
§11.7, E is constant in α only while the point stays lit for every admissible α, and jumps to 0 at
s = L tan α. (c) Supertruth over R is the largest acceptance criterion sound under reading
                                    S

uncertainty.

Reading. This answers the question quoted at the opening of this section: a claim is true in the
context at hand iff it holds on the context’s filter in every admissible completion of the reading.
It is supervaluation (Fine, 1975) over completions of an underspecified problem. Checking it de-
composes into kernel steps, stable imports, certified bridges with parent-evaluated side conditions,
and a reading; only the reading is not mechanizable. Hence our strongest recommendation: the
problem setter should supply a formal specification of the admissible completions, after which the
checker is sound relative to the top model and the trusted base (TB1)–(TB3) alone. An episode in
the notes’ introspective solution of the problem of §11.7 (“i suspected [the angle doesn’t matter]
but then i messed up a calculation”, introspection/introspect-solving physics olympiad
problems/introspect-solving eupho 2025-T1.md) is a failed completion-invariance obliga-
tion that a checker would flag at once.
Proposition 11.30 (Gricean determinacy is one-sided). [T3 Prop 5.6] Call ρ determinate at δ
if oscWρ Q ≤ 2δ. If Wρ′ ⊆ Wρ then oscρ′ Q ≤ oscρ Q. So “the problem is well-posed” can refute
only (some) over-wide readings, never over-narrow ones; and silent narrowing (fixing the sun’s
angle, choosing a specular mirror, importing an extra law, deciding “the finger is horizontal”)
never decreases determinacy, while it violates (J1).
Proof. A supremum over a subset is at most the supremum over the set; dually for infima.

     The free internal signal for readings thus pushes toward the unsafe error: silent narrowing is
the solver’s natural attack. With Section 6 and Theorem 11.23 this completes a table of three
one-sided signals: The opposite signal must come from outside: a formal specification by the
setter (which moves (J1) into the checked part); intended-completion data (official solutions,
marking schemes; the introspection note, on whether a finger in the part-(b) photograph is
tilted: “ok i peeked at the solution and it seems to assume that’s not the case”); and round-trip
checks such as rendering the model’s observable and comparing it with the figure, which are also
one-sided: passing one does not certify a reading. Section 13 returns to the table.

11.7    Worked example: EuPhO 2025 Theory 1(a), the polished chair leg
The setup is reconstructed from the introspection note of §11.6 and has not been checked against
the official text; the answer E = aI20 | sin φ2 |/r is the one reached in that note, which records
it as matching the official answer. Specification: a vertical specular cylinder of radius a, lit
over height L, stands on a flat floor; the sun is a parallel beam of irradiance I at zenith angle
α, travelling in +x; the floor’s direct illuminance is I0 = I cos α. The query is the reflected
illuminance (“surplus”) E(r, φ), with φ measured from the anti-sun direction +x. Given a, I0 , L;
free completion α ∈ [30◦ , 60◦ ], which the photograph does not fix; conventions: perfect specular
reflectance, geometric optics, incoherent addition, sun radius δs = 4.65 mrad, leg vertical; answer
type: a function of (a, I0 , r, φ) with the dimension of I0 . Write e(ϑ) = (cos ϑ, sin ϑ).

Proposition 11.31 (Exact reflected illuminance). [T3 Prop 6.1] (SymPy-verified) Parametrize the
lit side by ϑ ∈ (π/2, 3π/2) and the reflection height by h ∈ [0, L]; let ψ = 2ϑ − π, s = h tan α and
c = sin ψ2 . (a) The reflected ray lands at P = a e(ϑ) + s e(ψ) = (s + ac) e(ψ) + a cos ψ2 e(ψ + π2 ).
(b) (ϑ, s) 7→ P is injective with | det ∂P/∂(ϑ, s)| = 2s + ac. (c) E(P ) = I0 ac/(2s + ac) for
s ≤ L tan α, and E = 0 off the image and where the preimage has s > L tan α; the total reflected
flux 2aLI sin α equals the intercepted flux. (d) At a fixed floor point E does not depend on α;
only the lit domain s ≤ L tan α does.

    Part (d) is the completion-invariance certificate, exact in the top model. Injectivity (the
caustic of a convex cylindrical mirror is virtual) is proved in Appendix J; a Monte Carlo agrees
to its ≈0.6% noise (computed). The formula is elementary catoptrics; we have not found it in the
sources checked, but the official solution may contain it, so its novelty is uncertain.

Proposition 11.32 (Thin-leg bridge, rigorous). [T3 Prop 6.2, rev.: lit domain] Let E0 = aI20 σ/r,

1− m       E      √ 1+m/σ
   σ ≤ E0 ≤ 1−ϵ2 −ϵ/2 .

   The bound is rigorous but conservative (computed); its export domain is an annulus a ≪
r < L tan α, an instance of intermediate asymptotics (Barenblatt, 1996). A finite-sun bridge
(Proposition J.15, Appendix J.8) widens it by the sun’s azimuth spread, for any radiance profile
over the solar disc.

What remains judgment. The photo-to-model reading (a specular cylinder, lit over its full
height, its unsupplied reflectance, the meaning of “illuminance surplus”, the α range) and the
open world (taper, tilt, floor roughness, the seat’s shadow). Each effect could be added as a
declared deformation with its own bridge, moving it from judgment to checking; what cannot
be moved is the claim that these are all the effects the setters intend (Theorem 11.28); the
reading can only be tested by round trips such as rendering the predicted floor pattern. A second,
germ-root example from IPhO 2025 is in Appendix J.8.

11.8     The four logical roles of physicists’ checks
Dimensional analysis, limiting cases, symmetry and conservation are often grouped together as
“coherence checks”. They play at least four logical roles, and only the first two are coherence in
the sense of Section 6:
    Dimensions are a type system (Kennedy, 1994), and the Buckingham Π theorem (Buck-
ingham, 1914) turns “express in terms of” into a type signature; but dropping a small Π
group is a bridge (role 4), not a type fact. Symmetry needs uniqueness, as the notes observe
(physics/symmetry.md): a symmetric problem implies only a symmetric set of solutions, and

                        Table 17: Logical roles of the physicist’s checks.[L9 §3]

                        symmetries                 equations
2. in-model theorem     conservation laws          a computation inside one   worst case within the
                                                   local model                model; silent on exports
3. regression against   limiting cases             agreement with solved      sound only for regular
another context                                    sub-models                 limits (Norton)
4. export side          order of magnitude; “the   a bridge at a stated       sound with explicit

a declared symmetry gives free negative data. Limiting cases are valid only under Norton’s
continuity (Proposition 11.5(c)), and order-of-magnitude checks are export side conditions (The-
orem J.8). Appendix J.9 gives the details and the closest precedent, the Andes tutor (VanLehn
et al., 2005).

What is and is not established. Contradictory contexts are fine, and realizability says
which must be consistent. Reductio in inadequate frameworks needs a consistency certificate,
and with approximate premises a margin. Untrusted solvers are handled for everything except
the reading, whose characteristic attack, silent narrowing, no internal signal sees. Not established
(Section 14): any theorem about learning readings (the deep part, J1); frame realizability under
germ semantics; idealizations inside suppositions and non-value exports; automated proofs of
the regularity constants of Theorems J.12 and J.13; a checker beyond one worked problem. The
mini-checker illustrates the checks on one problem and twelve variants (ten attacks, one control
and one completeness test); it is not a system, and its own soundness is argued, not proved.


12     Experiments
This section reports three small computational experiments (A–C) and re-runs of four check
scripts of the theory (D–G). They illustrate theorems of the earlier sections in settings where the
target calculus is known, validity can be decided or tested, and adversaries can be run. They are
not evidence that the methods scale, whether to real human mathematics, to neural verifiers, or
to domains where world feedback is scarce. Experiments A–C use the Python package cil in
code/. All runs are deterministic given the seeds. A–C use seeds 0, 1, 2 throughout, and “a ± b”
is the mean and the population standard deviation over these three seeds, not a confidence
interval; rows that pool several values of N give the standard deviation over the pooled runs. Full
tables are in the reports code/results/*.md; reproduction instructions and run times are in
code/README.md. An independent review of the code re-ran everything and fixed two reporting
errors in B and a latent one in A. The fallacy-fate counts in B’s report changed (for example, for
affirming the consequent at N = 10); no other number changed (computed).




                                                   125
12.1     A: algebra, from imitation to a sound calculus, and the meadow
Setup. The target has 41 oriented rewrite schemas for field algebra over partial terms (Ex-
ample 2.12). Eleven carry guards built from defined, nonzero and nonneg atoms on schematic
variables, such as x/x → 1 if nonzero(x); numeral arithmetic is trusted, not learned. A simulator
writes N human derivations in which every valid step instantiates a target schema and cites its
name. Noise is sporadic (5% random mutations under random rule names), fallacies (each
opportunity for one of five systematic
                                  √ fallacies taken with probability 0.3: the freshman’s dream,
unguarded x/x → 1, unguarded x2 → x, (a + b)/(c + d) → a/c + b/d, −(a + b) → −a + b),
both, or none. The learner clusters rewrite cores by MDL and takes Plotkin’s least general
generalization (Plotkin, 1970) of each cluster, bucketing by the cited rule (tagged) or by shape
(untagged). The verifier is conservative: it accepts a numeral evaluation or an instance of an
active schema with human support m ≥ 2 whose guard follows from the context. A Lakatos-style
loop (Lakatos, 1976) of at most six rounds probes the schemas, derives with them, detects
contradictions, blames and repairs (minimal guard, else split the cluster, else delete). In mode
numeral the only signal is coherence (C): two derivations of distinct numerals from one ground
term, or a derivation contradicting arithmetic. Modes bag and step add a world oracle (W), on
whole derivations with blame by spectrum fault localization (Abreu et al., 2007), or on single
steps. The oracle compares partial values with Kleene equality at boundary and random rational
points (Schwartz, 1980; Zippel, 1979). Held-out valid and invalid steps in distribution (ID, about
10-node terms) and out of it (OOD, about 40 nodes) are labelled by an independent 60-point
oracle, and a white-box attack targets every active schema.

Coherence without a world: the meadow. Pure coherence removes the errors that change
the value of a numeral expression. In paired runs of the tagged learner it deleted the freshman’s
dream in all 11 runs in which imitation had produced it, (a + b)/(c + d) → a/c + b/d in 17/17
and −(a + b) → −a + b in 20/21, and repaired unguarded x/x → 1 into the guarded rule in
31/35. It almost never learned a guard that concerns only definedness: a · 0 → 0 ended with a
guard weaker than defined(a) in all 54 runs with N ≥ 100. Of the 90 pure-coherence runs, 88
end with an unsound schema (Figure 1).
    What survives has a meaning. Every unsound learned schema was re-tested in a total
semantics: complex values, x/0 := 0, the principal square root, non-integer powers set to 0. This
is a version of the meadows of Bergstra and Tucker (2007); its division convention x/0 = 0 is also
that of Lean’s Mathlib (Section 13). All 41 target rules hold in it, all five fallacies fail in it, and
seven of the 11 guards are unnecessary in it. For N ≥ 200, 304 of the 315 schemas that survive
pure coherence (96.5%) are sound in it. Of the other eleven, ten mention an object constant (as
in x · z → x; pure coherence compares only numeral expressions) and one is a value error. For
N < 200 the share is 86.3%, since a smaller calculus derives fewer contradictions. Conversely,
apart from one run, the guards

12.2      B: natural deduction, Post probes and the bold extension of IPC
Setup. Formulas use atoms p, q, r (s only out of distribution) and →, ∧, ∨, ¬, ⊥; steps are
sequent-style natural-deduction inferences (Example 2.11). The target is classical natural
deduction with 13 rules, the assumption rule carrying the side condition A ∈ Γ as a mem guard;
IPC drops reductio. Simulated humans prove random tautologies backwards. Their fallacies,
each taken with probability 0.3 and cited as →E, are affirming the consequent (AC), denying the
antecedent (DA) and an illegitimate discharge (ID); noise corrupts 5% of steps. The learner vs
buckets steps by cited rule, anti-unifies them under an MDL criterion, adds most-specific mem
guards and verifies with support m = 2. Coherence pruning uses five designated contexts: ∅ and
four satisfiable premise sets. Negative bags (Lemma 6.2) come from blind search for Γd ⊢ ⊥ and
from Post probes, which substitute ⊥ or ¬⊥ for a rule’s metavariables, prove its premises and
refute its conclusion (Proposition 3.5 and Lemma 7.22). Blame is a minimum-weight hitting set,
weighted by the human steps the cheapest repair loses. The world phase adds two observed
valuations of the 16. Rule soundness is decided exactly by truth tables. An adversary searches
with the learned rules for derivations of 34 invalid goals, ⊢ ⊥ among them; sound completeness is
the share of 25 random tautologies the sound active rules prove within budget (target calculus:
0.88 ± 0.03).

one too. At N ≤ 10 coherence leaves unsound rules in 4 of 18 runs, AC itself among them: a

with completeness 0.87 ± 0.04.

Post-completeness probes. A bold learner over classical natural deduction adds a candidate
schema iff no derivation of ⊢ ⊥ is found with it. Of 177 structural candidates (19 hand-picked, 8
pairwise LGGs of target rules, 150 random), the 59 classically valid ones were all accepted, and
the 118 invalid ones were all refuted by an explicit derivation of ⊢ ⊥, as Theorems 6.13 and 6.15
predict. The derivations are short: median 2.5 and maximum 6 steps for the LGGs of target
rules, median 6 and maximum 17 for the random schemas. For AC, the probe A := ⊥, B := ¬⊥
gives
           ⊥ ⊢ ⊥ (ax), ⊥ ⊢ ¬⊥ (¬I), ⊢ ⊥ → ¬⊥ (→I), ⊢ ¬⊥ (¬I), ⊢ ⊥ (AC).
Non-structural rules escape (Proposition 7.17): ⊢ p is coherent with every designated context
and falls only to an observed valuation, and p ⊢ q falls to the designated context {p, ¬q}. Of
the 45 unsound rules that survive pruning in any run, 38 mention specific atoms. Offered
tonk’s two rules one at a time, the bold learner accepts whichever comes first and rejects the
other (Proposition 6.28). One observed valuation is a complete test for a schematic rule with k
metavariables only if all 2k literal instantiations are probed. The code probes at most eight, and
the three schematic rules that survive the world phase in some run each have k ≥ 4; probing all
instantiations removed them. What world feedback adds is exact blame, since a refuted step
names its rule: 5.0 ± 2.1 pruning rounds against 9.1 ± 5.9 without it (N ≥ 20, 36 runs).

The bold extension of intuitionistic logic. Over intuitionistic natural deduction the bold
learner accepted excluded middle, double-negation elimination, reductio, Peirce’s law, weak
excluded middle and Dummett’s linearity, each underivable in IPC (a Kripke countermodel
was found for each), and rejected the classically invalid candidates by derivations of ⊢ ⊥.
Completeness on classical tautologies rose from 0.72 to 0.80 (classical natural deduction: 0.84).
The same happens when IPC is first learned: from 60 simulated intuitionistic proofs, vs with
coherence recovers the 12 rules (10 exactly, 2 with a stronger guard), never learns reductio, has
no classically or Kripke-unsound rule, and its bold phase then accepts the same six principles.
This is Theorem 6.16: coherence cannot separate the intermediate logics, so a maximal coherent
structural learner never outputs IPC, and the residue of Theorem 6.34(ii) shows up as a drift
toward CPC. Only the cautious, imitation-based tier keeps IPC.

Caveats. The designated contexts are certified satisfiable with ground-truth satisfiability, a
modelling assumption (Assumption 2.14). Most-specific guards make ∧E and ∨E stronger than
the target, since the simulated humans only eliminate from open assumptions: sound, but
incomplete out of distribution. Fresh seeds 3 and 4 (N = 50, both) reproduce the pattern.




                                               129
12.3       C: an adversarial prover against statistical and rule-learned verifiers
Setup. All verifiers are trained on the same N = 500 noisy algebra derivations of Experiment A,
except one trained on a clean corpus. The statistical verifiers, akin to process reward models,
are logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees and a random forest from scikit-learn (Pedregosa
et al., 2011) on hashed subterm-shape n-grams, rule signatures and tree-edit features. They
receive oracle labels for positives and for negatives (refuted human steps, perturbations, fallacy
instances), so they get more supervision than the positive-only rule learner. Thresholds are
calibrated in distribution to a balanced precision TPR/(TPR + FPR); “@pX” means precision
X. The rule-learned verifiers are A’s learner without guards (lgg_pos), with most-specific guards

Accuracy in distribution does not transfer to the search distribution. The boosted-
tree verifier reaches test AUC 0.995 on held-out human-like steps. Calibrated to in-distribution
balanced precision 0.9925, it still lets the prover prove 16.3 ± 2.4 of the 23 false goals, with a
median of 514 queries to a false proof (Table 20 and Figure 2). At the strictest threshold, with
no false accept on the calibration set, recall falls to 0.45; it then proves 4.7 of 33 true identities,
and still 1.7 false goals. All 11 statistical configurations derive false equations under search. Of
their 1082 invalid proof edges, 81% come from goal-directed leaps, grafts and random mutations,
and only 1% from the known fallacies: steps that look like human steps and are not. This is
Theorem 3.2 and Lemma 3.11(ii) in a closed domain: in-distribution accuracy is a property of
a measure fixed before the prover moves, soundness a property of a set. That learned reward
models are exploited by optimization is documented at scale, notably by the overoptimization
scaling laws of Gao et al. (2023); the experiment adds a domain in which every exploited step
can be certified invalid.

Rule-learned verifiers fail only through named schemas. All 154 invalid proof edges
of the rule-learned verifiers are licensed by a schema that the soundness test flags; the most
used is the noise-born projection x + y → y, which alone collapses arithmetic (1 = 1 + 1 = 2).
A counterexample deletes or guards such a schema and removes its whole family of exploits; a
classifier has no such unit of repair. After world feedback the learned calculus proves no false goal
and 32.3 of 33 true identities, like the ground-truth calculus. With clean data and an adequate
guard language positive data suffice: lgg_ms_clean proves no false goal, as the version-space
verifier of Theorem 4.2 should, although in one seed an over-specialized schema 0/(y + 3) → 0,
whose true guard the guard language cannot express, is active and was not reached. Together, the
four rule-based verifiers with no false goal derive no false equation in 900,305 queries. Coherence
without a world leaves A’s residue: in-distribution balanced precision 1.0000, yet 5 false goals
per seed, all definedness errors such as 0/x = 0 and (x − x)/y = 0, each true when 1/0 = 0.
In-distribution precision does not rank verifiers by soundness, even among rule-based ones.

Patching the classifier with its own exploits. The natural remedy is adversarial data
collection, as for PRM800K (Lightman et al., 2023): harvest the certainly invalid accepted steps
from the searches on the 23 false goals, add them as negatives, retrain and recalibrate. Over
four rounds (boosted trees at p0.99, seeds 0 and 1 only), false goals proved on the harvested set
fell from 15.5 to 0.0 and false equations per thousand queries from 195.7 to 14.3. The patched
verifier still proved 1.5 of 12 fresh false goals and 2.0 of 35 goals against a second, differently
configured prover, while true identities proved fell from 28.0 to 24.5. Retraining is an effective
practical mitigation; its soundness is relative to the attacks it was patched against.

Four check scripts were re-run for this section and reproduce the numbers quoted where the results
are stated (computed): ttl_sim.py, the two-tier learner, in the singleton-conflict case of CPC only
