(D, Table 10); sps_checker.py, the physics mini-checker on the chair-leg solution (E, Table 16);
the simplicity scripts c1–c5 (F, the computed figures of Section 8); and comprehension_toy.py,
the Frege–Russell–Zermelo trajectory (G, Theorem 10.28(iv)). Three outputs are not quoted
elsewhere. In F, c2 confirms the kink of Theorem 8.4 on parities over {0, 1}10 with N = 200

while shared-randomness code lengths stay in [0.116, 0.126]; and c3 finds no violation of the rate
threshold of Theorem 8.7 in 6000 (instance, c) pairs. In G, on the Dedekind–Cantor operations
alone, stratification (STRAT) and the Zermelo-like class (Z: separation plus elementary sets) tie
on coverage, and description length selects STRAT; once Zermelo’s diagonal subsets outweigh
Frege’s universal extension, Z is selected; with the weights reversed, STRAT is.

12.5    What the experiments do and do not show
They show the mechanisms of the theorems at work in small, fully checkable domains: positive
data fix shapes but not guards (A, B); systematic errors reach support (A, B, D); coherence refutes
uniform errors through Post’s substitution and leaves a residue of coherent alternative meanings
(the meadow in A and C, intermediate logics in B); a world channel that can see the residue
removes it (A–C); and accuracy in distribution says nothing about soundness under search (C).
They show no more than that. Realizability is assumed: valid human steps are exact instances
of the target rules, the guard language contains the true guards, and the simulated humans
are the target plus known fallacies and noise; real practice satisfies none of this (Section 10).
Soundness is measured, not proved: in A and C it is random testing, and “0” means that no
counterexample was found; B decides rule soundness exactly, but its coherence verdicts and
adversaries are budgeted searches. World feedback is cheap in algebra: random evaluation is
an almost perfect oracle for polynomial identities, and a run of A uses about 104 queries; in
physics, and in mathematics with undecidable fragments, B’s two observed valuations or the
certified bridges of Section 11 are the more realistic picture. Few seeds: three per configuration
(two for C’s retraining), although fresh seeds reproduce the patterns of A and B. Toy scale:
closed small domains, heuristic and informed black-box adversaries (for which “not proved” is
not “unprovable”), small statistical baselines on hand-built features. Nothing here measures
how often larger learned verifiers are exploited, and the theorems do not predict that rate; they
explain only why accuracy cannot rule it out.


13     Justification beyond proof
The investigation began with a question about principled justification. What does it look like,
once we go beyond mathematical proof? This section steps back from the theorems and says
what they show about that question. It also says what they do not show. Throughout, “we”
means the authors of this report. The view argued for is deliberately modest. The theorems do
not deliver a theory of justification. They make precise one shape that justification can take,
and they locate exactly where that shape runs out.

13.1    The setup is Goodman’s circle, made into a learning problem
The setup we studied has three parts:
   • learn inference rules from accepted inferences;


                                               132
   • revise them when they generate unacceptable conclusions;
   • revise accepted inferences when they conflict with rules one is unwilling to give up.
This is, almost verbatim, Goodman’s account of the justification of deduction and induction:

     “Rules and particular inferences alike are justified by being brought into agreement
     with each other. A rule is amended if it yields an inference we are unwilling to accept;
     an inference is rejected if it violates a rule we are unwilling to amend.” (Goodman,
     1955, ch. III)

In our vocabulary, the channels correspond to Goodman’s account as follows:
   • Imitation (P) supplies the accepted particular inferences.
   • Rule schemas, learned by least generalization, are the rules.
   • Coherence (C) is the mechanism by which a rule “yields an inference we are unwilling to
     accept”. A derivation of ⊥ from a context certified consistent is a negative bag, and some
     rule in it must go.
   • World feedback (W) adds a channel whose errors are independent of human errors.
Without (W), the process is narrow reflective equilibrium (Rawls, 1971, 1974). With (W) it is
wide reflective equilibrium in the sense of Daniels (1979). Daniels’ “independence constraint”
requires that the background theories not rest on the same considered judgments as the principles.
It can be read as requiring that the corroborating channel’s errors be independent of the human
ones. Without such independence, agreement moves the odds by at most a bounded factor
(Section 6.7). Even with it, no informative coherence measure is truth-conducive in general.
    What our theorems add to Goodman’s picture is a set of vindications with explicit conditions.
Under stated channel assumptions, mutual adjustment is sound against every adaptive arguer,
with explicit costs:
   • realizability of the target in a structured hypothesis class;
   • truthful designation of the contexts that are certified consistent;
   • a world channel of the right kind.
For several of these assumptions there is a matching impossibility result (Table 9). Realizability
is shown to be load-bearing by example rather than by a theorem. World feedback or bilateral
evidence (a designated denial) is needed for completeness under ambiguous blame, not for
soundness (Theorem 7.19 and Proposition 7.24). This is the sense in which the theorems are
conditional reliabilist meta-justifications of reflective equilibrium. They are not a non-circular
foundation for logic. As Dummett (1973) observed, any justification of deduction is explanatory
rather than suasive: it uses deduction. What they provide is an explicit list of what the stated
guarantees rely on, with proofs that the guarantees hold under them. The list consists of the
three items above, together with the technical hypotheses of Theorem 7.12: a known frequency
floor, fallacies used under their own latent tags, and an exact depth-d refutation oracle.
    Two features of the guarantees matter philosophically.
   • First, they are anytime, not merely in the limit. Limit theorems are Reichenbachian
     vindications (Reichenbach, 1938). They fall to the objection of Salmon (1967) that infinitely
     many methods share the same limit while disagreeing at every finite stage. Our soundness
     guarantees hold at every time, with probability over the data (Theorem 4.15). Our costs

                                               133
       are explicit finite quantities: escalations, detections, samples. The motivating notes are
       suspicious of limit framings, and hold that thinking and mathematics are “infinite endeavors”
       with no final formula. They also propose “trajectories of moral-reflective flight” as an
       alternative to reflective equilibrium, which they find “pretty flat/dead” as a picture of a
       mind’s development (philosophy/ethics/Trajectories of moral-reflective flight
       — an alternative to reflective equilibrium.md). Our results bear on that view only
       in a limited way. They concern a fixed target calculus, for which convergence is the right
       notion. They say nothing about the open-ended development of concepts and calculi that
       the notes have in mind (language invention, Section 14).
   • Second, they are worst case over arguers. A step checker that is accurate on the distribution
     of human steps can be exploited by search (Theorem 3.2). Justification that is to survive an
     untrusted or adversarial generator must be uniform over what the generator may propose.
     This is the case that motivates the question in the first place.

13.2     What each signal can do, and the residue it leaves
The main results combine into a division of labour. Table 21 summarizes it.
    Two observations about this table seem to us to be the real philosophical content of the
investigation.

Every signal is one-sided. Each learning signal we studied can refute errors in only one
direction:
   • Positive data never refute an over-generalization (Gold).
   • Coherence never refutes over-caution: a cautious learner never sees a contradiction (Propo-
     sition 6.3). Nor does it refute a coherent over-generalization (Theorem 6.9).
   • Coherence among exported tolerances never refutes a tolerance that is too wide. Coherent
     tolerance vectors form an up-set, so minimal coherent repairs only widen (Table 15). And
     when all models may share an omitted effect, no coherence-only calibrator can certify a
     tolerance below the size of that effect (Theorem 11.23).
   • The demand that a problem be well posed refutes readings that are too wide, but it rewards
     readings that are too narrow (Proposition 11.30).
Each one-sided signal is an attack surface for an adversarial arguer, and it calls for a complementary
signal that refutes errors in the other direction. Principled justification, on this picture, is not
one master criterion. It is a set of signals that together cover every direction of error, plus an
explicit statement of the directions that remain uncovered. Table 15 lists the pairs for physics.
The same structure appears in mathematics. Imitation proposes and caution guards. Coherence
condemns, but only bold hypotheses. Objects localize.

Each residue has a name, and different philosophies disagree only about the residue.
Outside the residue of coherent, uniform, world-adequate alternatives, every position we know of
counts the learner as correct:
   • the realist;
   • the Peircean, for whom truth is the limit of inquiry;

Inside the residue, they disagree. The realist sees undetectable error. The Peircean or Dummettian
sees no fact of the matter. Carnap sees a free choice of language. Quine sees a choice made on
pragmatic grounds. The theorems make the residue precise in several cases:
   • It is empty for classical propositional logic.
   • It contains all intermediate logics for an intuitionistic practice.
   • It contains PA + ¬Con(PA) for arithmetic.
   • In the algebra experiment it contains the total semantics with 1/0 = 0, which pure
     coherence converged to for N ≥ 200, up to 11 of 315 surviving schemas (Section 12). Its
     division convention x/0 = 0 is, as it happens, the one adopted by Lean’s Mathlib and
     by Isabelle/HOL. Its other total conventions, such as complex square roots, differ from
     Mathlib’s.
A theorem can say exactly where these philosophies part ways. It cannot settle who is right
inside the residue. We think that is the correct division of labour between mathematics and
philosophy here.
     One consequence deserves to be stated on its own. Rules can be identifiable when truths
are not. Among structural meanings, the bilateral tell-tale identifies the classical ones from
finitely many data (Theorem 6.26). Yet in arithmetic, no computable learner using a computable
text, coherence searches and a ∆0 oracle decides Σ2 truth in the limit (Theorem 6.21). This
bears on Dummett’s acquisition argument but does not refute it. That argument targets truth-
conditional meaning: a meaning one could acquire must be manifestable in use, so meaning cannot
outrun decidability. What the learner acquires is the rules, for the propositional connectives
(Theorem 6.26), and Dummett agrees that rules are manifestable. The theorems show only that
acquiring rules exactly is compatible with truth values, here of arithmetic Σ2 sentences, staying
beyond computable reach.

13.3    Rules are not premises
The tortoise of Carroll (1895) refused to infer Z from A, B and “if A and B then Z” until that
inference was itself added as a premise, and so on forever. For a learner the lesson has a precise
form:
   • A learned rule is a schema. Its validity is a universally quantified claim over all instances,
     of Π form.
   • No finite amount of world feedback verifies such a claim. Feedback can only refute it.
   • The justification for using a learned rule therefore cannot be further premises. It has to be
     a guarantee about the process that accepted it: cautious acceptance, and an anchor that
     has been observed.
This is why the right acceptance policy for learned rules is Popperian. Accept tentatively. Assert
only what every surviving hypothesis licenses. Treat each refutation as permanent. It is also
why self-certification must never feed back into acceptance:


                                                136
  • a learned verifier that “proves its own soundness” has provided no evidence that distinguishes
    it from an unsound verifier sharing the certifying rule;
  • in arithmetic, by Löb’s theorem a theory that proves the reflection schema ProvT (⌜φ⌝) → φ
    for its own provability predicate, for all φ, proves everything. By contrast, the corresponding
    reflection rule is admissible for Σ1 -sound theories.
Reflection is a principled source of genuinely new inferences, beyond imitation, that a learner
who has accepted a calculus is committed to. Where it is used, it must enter as a stratified rule,
never as a self-referential premise.

13.4     What principled justification beyond proof looks like
Putting the pieces together, the results suggest the following shape for a principled justification
of a claim about something other than pure mathematics. A physics olympiad answer is the
running case.
  1. Proof inside contexts. Each step inside a context is checked against a calculus. The
     calculus is formal where possible. Where it is learned, acceptance is cautious, so the check
     is sound against an arguer who searches for weaknesses (Sections 4 and 10).
  2. Certified bridges between contexts. Moving a conclusion from an idealized context
     to the claim of interest is not a logical step. It needs a certificate carrying information of
     finite radius about how the quantity behaves away from the idealization. Facts about the
     idealized model alone never suffice (no free export, Theorem 11.19). Side conditions are
     evaluated where they are true, in the parent context, and contexts are declared deformations.
     Otherwise an arguer can “stipulate” its way to anything (Theorem 11.22).
  3. An explicit judgment layer. What remains is a judgment layer of three parts. The first
     two are provably ineliminable (Theorem 11.28). The third is the trusted core of any proof
     checker.

         • that the problem was read correctly, i.e. the admissible worlds were not narrowed;
         • that the top model is adequate for the world claims;
         • that the trusted base is trustworthy.

       A principled justification does not hide this layer. It minimizes it and declares it.
  4. Correctness as supertruth. For underspecified questions, “true in the context at hand”
     means true in every admissible completion of the intended model, to the demanded precision.
     This is the largest acceptance criterion that stays sound under uncertainty about the reading
     (Theorem 11.29). Answer-invariance under unspecified features, which experienced solvers
     notice and rely on, is exactly a certificate of supertruth.
  5. Learning signals with known limits. Every learned component comes with a statement
     of the signal that trained it and the residue that signal leaves. The learned components are
     the calculus, the bridge validity regions and the tolerances.
   Measured against this shape, mathematical proof is the limiting case in which:
  • the judgment layer has shrunk to the reading of the formal statement and trust in the
    axioms;


                                                137
  • every bridge is exact;
  • the calculus is fixed rather than learned.
Informal mathematics before formalization sits in between. In our model it is a bounded-gap
practice over a latent calculus. If the robust-core hypothesis holds, its proofs survive every
admissible formalization. In the historical episodes we examined, counterexample objects did
most of the corrective work, and the few paradoxes were the set-theoretic antinomies (Section 10).
Physics adds a nonempty, explicit judgment layer and non-logical bridges, but the shape is the
same. On this view the difference between mathematical and physical justification is one of
degree, measured by the size of the declared residue, not one of kind.

13.5     What this says about meaning
The inferentialist premise of the question was that learning which inferences are valid is roughly
learning meanings. The results support a qualified version:
  • Inferential roles are learnable, exactly, from finite use. A finite anchor fixes the
    inferential role of a vocabulary for unbounded use (Corollary 5.10). This is a precise, if
    modest, answer to the rule-following question of how finite training fixes an infinite norm.
    The answer is: through structure (schemas) plus a small set of telling instances. The
    skeptic’s “quus” survives only as a non-uniform patch, which uniformity rules out, or as
    a coherent uniform alternative, which is a named residue. This answer is relative to the
    hypothesis class and its vocabulary, which the data do not fix. That is Goodman’s point,
    and it is exactly where Kripke’s skeptic presses (Section 5.5).
  • More than role is not identifiable. Under complete closure-level data, practice, co-
    herence and object data identify a latent formalization exactly up to informal-validity
    equivalence, and no further. Bounded-gap data only bracket it (Theorem 10.14). Ontology
    is not identifiable: standard and nonstandard reals are observationally equivalent on the
    practice (Proposition 10.16). Neither is the choice of set-theoretic reduction (Proposi-
    tion I.4).
  • Coherence buys existence, but not intended existence. Every coherent mode
    of talking has something it could be talking about. That is a generalized completeness
    theorem, true for positions, credences and context systems alike (Section 9). But that
    something may be a syntactic or nonstandard model. Intended existence needs one of three
    additional things:

         – categoricity;
         – anchoring of the vocabulary to the world (Beth definability);
         – an infinitary condition, such as the probabilistic ω-rule.

       No computable coherence notion can certify intended existence beyond Π1 .
Inferential role is one aspect of meaning, and the project captures that aspect precisely. Other
aspects are not captured by anything studied here:
  • the “hooking” of a conception onto the world;
  • the activities a concept supports;
  • the questions it lets one ask.

                                               138
We do not claim otherwise. All three aspects are emphasized in the motivating notes. These
treat inferential role (“compositional inference warranting”) as one aspect of meaning among sev-
eral (philosophy/philosophy of language/meaning and truth/; philosophy/philosophy
of thinking/beating solomonoff induction at grokking a notion.md).

13.6    The motivating questions
The questions that prompted this investigation are recorded in Hänni’s public working notes
(Hänni, 2026). Section 1.2 and Table 1 list them, with pointers to where each is answered or
partly answered. The readings of the notes given there are ours.


14     Limits and open problems
We collect the main limitations of the results and the open problems they leave. The hardest of
them is the first.

1. Affordable soundness when the learner must invent language. Every soundness
guarantee here is relative to realizability: the target calculus, or the latent formalization, must lie
in the hypothesis class. History did not respect any fixed class. It invented uniform convergence,
ideals, ε–δ and the fundamental group as proof-generated concepts.
   • A universal, language-inventing class restores realizability, but sound verification then costs
                         ∗
     on the order of 2K(h ) escalations (Theorems 4.12 and 10.10).
   • What is needed is a class that is closed under the definitional extensions mathematics
     actually made, and that still has small escalation dimension. Equivalently, we need a theory
     of when concept invention, for example by anti-unification over definitions or by naming
     the hidden lemma found by descent, is cheap.

2. Computational cost. Our bounds count samples, escalations, detections and refutation-
oracle calls, not computation.
   • Membership in the version-space intersection for untagged unions is likely NP-hard.
   • Consistency with negative bags is a multiple-instance problem. Its hardness is the formal
     shadow of the obfuscated-arguments problem in debate.
   • Refutation search is only semi-decidable. Our depth-relative soundness (Theorem 7.20) is
     the honest form of what can be had.
A complexity-theoretic version of the two-tier theorem would be valuable. It would identify
which audits are polynomial and for which classes.

3. The reading layer. In physics the irreducible judgment is the reading: which admissible
worlds the problem text determines (Theorem 11.28).
   • Determinacy refutes only over-wide readings (Proposition 11.30).
   • What positive data identify the intended admissible class? We conjecture that official
     solutions together with marking schemes form a tell-tale within a class of “minimal
     completions consistent with the intended imports”.


                                                 139
  • Learning readings soundly is, we think, the central open problem for principled checking
    beyond mathematics.

4. Sharp combinatorics. Several bounds have gaps:
  • The binomial conjecture for k-unions of intersection-closed classes (Conjecture 4.11) would
    close the gap for untagged schema learning.
                                 (r)
  • The bag-price conjecture Mbag ≤ r · Ldim (Conjecture 10.24) would give the exact exchange
    rate between paradoxes and counterexample objects.
  • The query complexity of sound blame, i.e. computing the union of the minimal conflicts
    with a conflict oracle, is open.

5. Coherence beyond Post-completeness.
  • For which first-order or modal targets does every invalid uniform rule have a short coherence
    witness in a natural designated context?
  • Is there a hierarchy of coherence-witness complexity?
  • Which logics and theories are coherence-pinned, meaning that the residue is empty for
    natural families of designated contexts?
  • For arithmetic: is there a principled learner over reflection progressions that converges to
    “the right amount of reflection” under a natural feedback notion?

6. Simplicity and normativity.
  • For which classes of simple models does the product-model frontier kink, beyond parities?
  • Is there a principled, data-free choice of the simplicity coefficient, for example one tied to
    the cheapest postulate-violating error?
  • Which assumptions on a performance model, such as errors being time-bounded shortcuts,
    make joint description length identify competence despite the known non-identifiability of
    preferences from behaviour?

7. Probabilistic and contextual coherence.
  • Find a finitely presented proof system for valid counting sequents that is complete for de
    Finetti coherence.
  • Prove a probabilistic local-to-global theorem for context systems on tree covers.
  • Decide whether contextual frustration between idealized contexts should be penalized or
    tolerated.

8. Scale.
  • Our experiments are illustrations in small symbolic domains with realizable targets, cheap
    world feedback and few seeds.




                                              140
  • Whether learned calculi with cautious acceptance remain affordable at the scale of real
    mathematical corpora (for example Lean or Metamath step data with injected fallacies at
    measured human rates) is an empirical question we have not addressed.
  • We have deliberately not built a strong prover. The motivating notes regard publishing
    insightful research on AI theorem provers as gravely dangerous. The results here concern
    checking, and we make no recommendations for prover development.

A     Proofs for Section 2
Theorem 2.5 is due to Plotkin (1970) and Reynolds (1970), and the rank lemma is folklore in
their lattice of schemas. All other statements of Section 2 are proved here.

A.1    Proof of Lemma 2.3 (closure facts)
(a) Let D be the set of judgments with an R-derivation from B. D contains B (one-node
derivations) and is closed under R: if P ▷ j ∈ R and P ⊆ D, graft derivations of the finitely
many members of P under a new root j. So ClR (B) ⊆ D. Conversely, if X ⊇ B is R-closed,
induction on the height of derivations shows that every node of every derivation from B lies
in X; so D ⊆ ClR (B). Extensivity and monotonicity in B and in R hold because a derivation
from B using steps of R is also one from any B ′ ⊇ B using steps of any R′ ⊇ R. Idempotence: a
derivation from ClR (B) becomes a derivation from B after grafting a derivation from B above



                                                156
each leaf. Finitarity: a derivation has finitely many leaves, so it is a derivation from a finite
B0 ⊆ B.
    (b) A single step P ▷ j ∈ R is a derivation of j from P , so R ⊆ Sound(R), and monotonicity
in the rule set gives ClR (B) ⊆ ClSound(R) (B). Conversely, ClR (B) is closed under Sound(R):
if P ⊆ ClR (B) and j ∈ ClR (P ), then by (a) j ∈ ClR (ClR (B)) = ClR (B); it contains B, so it
contains ClSound(R) (B). Finally, Sound(A) = {P ▷ j : j ∈ ClA (P )} depends only on ClA , so
ClA = ClR gives A ⊆ Sound(A) = Sound(R); and Sound(R) itself has the closure ClR .

A.2    Proof of Lemma 2.6 (rank)
Throughout, |t| is the number of symbol occurrences in t, metavariable occurrences included,
and vars(t) is the set of distinct metavariables of t. A renaming of a set X of metavariables is a
substitution whose restriction to X is an injective map into metavariables. If τ = σθ with θ a
renaming of vars(σ), then σ = τ θ−1 , so σ ≡ τ ; conversely, σ ≡ τ means equality up to such a
renaming, and then µ(σ) = µ(τ ).
    Let τ = σθ. Let x1 , . . . , xk be the distinct metavariables of σ, and let xi occur mi ≥ 1 times
in σ.
    Size. Replacing each of the mi occurrences of xi (one symbol) by θxi (with |θxi | symbols)
gives

We bound each summand.
   • If θxi is a metavariable, then |θxi | = 1 = |vars(θxi )| and the summand is 0.
   • Otherwise θxi contains at least one function or constant symbol and at least one occurrence
     of each of its metavariables, so |θxi | ≥ |vars(θxi )| + 1. Using mi ≥ 1, the summand is at
     least (|θxi | − 1) + 1 − |vars(θxi )| ≥ 1.
Hence µ(τ ) ≥ µ(σ).
    Equality. If µ(τ ) = µ(σ), then every summand in (1) is 0 and the inequality there is tight.
The first forces every θxi to be a metavariable; the second forces the sets vars(θxi ) = {θxi } to
be pairwise disjoint, i.e. the θxi to be pairwise distinct. So θ restricted to vars(σ) is a renaming.
Conversely, if it is a renaming, then |τ | = |σ| and |vars(τ )| = |vars(σ)|, so µ(τ ) = µ(σ).
    Chains. Suppose σl+1 ≻ σl strictly, i.e. σl = σl+1 θl and σl ̸≡ σl+1 . Then θl is not a renaming
of vars(σl+1 ) (otherwise the two would be equivalent), so µ(σl ) > µ(σl+1 ), i.e. µ(σl ) ≥ µ(σl+1 ) + 1.
Summing along τ = σ0 ≺ σ1 ≺ · · · ≺ σm gives µ(τ ) ≥ µ(σm ) + m, and µ(σm ) ≥ 0.

A.3     Proof of Lemma 2.7 (when the lgg recovers the schema)
Idea. Substituting θx for the occurrences of x adds more symbols than distinct metavariables
unless θx is a metavariable, which is the rank lemma. Anti-unifying the tj copies σ and puts
A(θ1 x, . . . , θn x) at x; this is a metavariable iff (R) holds, and two of them coincide iff (D) fails.
In detail:
    Let σ have metavariables x1 , . . . , xv , let θ1 , . . . , θn be ground substitutions (n ≥ 1), and let
tj = σθj . For each metavariable x of σ write cx = (θ1 x, . . . , θn x) for its column, and let η be the
substitution η(x) := A(cx ).
    Claim. For every subterm σ ′ of σ, A(σ ′ θ1 , . . . , σ ′ θn ) = σ ′ η.
    By induction on σ ′ . If σ ′ = x is a metavariable, both sides are A(cx ). If σ ′ = f (σ1′ , . . . , σr′ )
(with r = 0 for a constant), then every σ ′ θj = f (σ1′ θj , . . . , σr′ θj ) has root f , so by definition
A outputs f applied to A of the argument columns (σk′ θ1 , . . . , σk′ θn ), which by the induction
hypothesis are σk′ η. Hence the output is f (σ1′ η, . . . , σr′ η) = σ ′ η.
    Taking σ ′ = σ and using Theorem 2.5,

                                lgg(t1 , . . . , tn ) = A(t1 , . . . , tn ) = ση ⪯ σ.

    When η is a renaming. By the definition of A:
   • η(x) = A(cx ) is a metavariable iff the entries of cx do not all have the same root, i.e. iff (R)
     holds at x. If (R) fails at x, η(x) is a compound term or a constant.
   • If (R) holds at x and at y, then η(x) = zcx and η(y) = zcy , and these coincide iff cx = cy ,
     i.e. iff (D) fails for the pair x, y.
So η restricted to vars(σ) is a renaming iff (R) holds for every x and (D) holds for every pair
x ̸= y.
    Conclusion. If (R) and (D) hold, η is a renaming and lgg(t1 , . . . , tn ) = ση ≡ σ. If either fails,
η is not a renaming of vars(σ), so by Lemma 2.6 µ(ση) > µ(σ); since equivalent schemas have
equal rank, lgg(t1 , . . . , tn ) ̸≡ σ, and it is strictly more specific.

A.4     Least general generalizations of infinite sets
Every nonempty set P of ground terms, finite or not, has a least general generalization, unique
up to renaming. To see this, choose a nonempty finite Q ⊆ P for which µ(lgg(Q)) is minimal
(µ takes values in N). Let p ∈ P . Since Q ⊆ Q ∪ {p} ⊆ inst(lgg(Q ∪ {p})), Theorem 2.5 gives
lgg(Q) ⪯ lgg(Q ∪ {p}), so by Lemma 2.6 µ(lgg(Q ∪ {p})) ≤ µ(lgg(Q)). By minimality the two
ranks are equal, so by the equality case of Lemma 2.6 lgg(Q ∪ {p}) ≡ lgg(Q) and p ∈ inst(lgg(Q)).
Hence P ⊆ inst(lgg(Q)). If P ⊆ inst(τ ), then Q ⊆ inst(τ ) and lgg(Q) ⪯ τ . So lgg(Q) is a least
general generalization of P ; any two are ⪯ each other, hence equivalent.

A.5     Proof of Lemma 2.8 (guarded closure)
P ⊆ inst(lgg(P )) by Theorem 2.5, and every ϕ ∈ ΨP holds on P , so P ⊆ inst(lgg(P ), ΨP ). Let
P ⊆ inst(σ, Ψ). Then P ⊆ inst(σ), so σ ⪰ lgg(P ) and inst(lgg(P )) ⊆ inst(σ). Every ϕ ∈ Ψ holds
on all of P , so Ψ ⊆ ΨP and ϕ∈ΨP ϕ−1 (1) ⊆ ϕ∈Ψ ϕ−1 (1). Intersecting, inst(lgg(P ), ΨP ) ⊆
                             T                 T

inst(σ, Ψ).




                                                        158
A.6     Sound evaluation and coherence
Lemma A.1 ((WS) and coherence; trivial). [T7 §1.3] Under (WS) every designated position is in
bounds for R∗ ∪ Ttrust , hence for R∗ . Conversely, if JW = ∅ and every designated position is in
bounds for R∗ ∪ Ttrust (for instance, in bounds for R∗ with Ttrust ⊆ Sound(R∗ )), then (WS) holds.

    Remarks. (WS) does not require Ttrust ⊆ Sound(R∗ ): in arithmetic the target may consist of
non-logical axioms with first-order logic trusted (Section 7), and the relevant target closure is
then ClR∗ ∪Ttrust . In formal mathematics V is truth in the intended structure M: (WS) holds
when designated positions are true of M, W is truth in M on its fragment, and target and
trusted steps are M-sound.

Proof. Write R+ = R∗ ∪ Ttrust . Let [Γ : ∆] be designated and V as in (WS). V makes every
member of Γ true, and no step of R+ has true premises and a false conclusion, so the set of V -true
judgments is an R+ -closed superset of Γ and contains ClR+ (Γ). Since V makes ⊥ and every
member of ∆ false, ⊥ ∈ / ClR+ (Γ) and ∆ ∩ ClR+ (Γ) = ∅. As ClR∗ (Γ) ⊆ ClR+ (Γ) (Lemma 2.3(a),
monotonicity in the rule set), the position is also in bounds for R∗ .
   Conversely, let JW = ∅ and let [Γ : ∆] be a designated position that is in bounds for R+ .
Then e is well defined, because Γ ⊆ ClR+ (Γ) is disjoint from ∆ ∪ {⊥}. Let V be the indicator
function of ClR+ (Γ). It extends e: it is 1 on Γ and 0 on ∆ ∪ {⊥}. The set ClR+ (Γ) is closed
under R+ , so no step of R+ has V -true premises and a V -false conclusion, and (WS) holds.
For the parenthetical instance: if Ttrust ⊆ Sound(R∗ ), then R∗ ⊆ R+ ⊆ Sound(R∗ ), so by
Lemma 2.3(a),(b) ClR+ = ClR∗ , and being in bounds for R∗ is the same as being in bounds for
R+ .


B      Proofs for Section 3
Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.5 and Proposition 3.9 are proved in full in the main text.
This appendix proves the remaining results of Section 3, verifies the claims of Example 3.6, and
records the examples showing that the hypotheses of Lemma 3.11 and Theorem 3.12 are needed.
Notation is as in Section 3; in particular S is the set of all steps (Definition 2.2). Throughout, |=
is classical propositional consequence, and a step Π ▷ φ over formulas is sound if Π |= φ.

B.1     PAC learners can be maximally unsound
Proof of Corollary 3.3. For N ≥ 0 let S≥N := {s ∈ S : |s| ≥ N }.
    Step 1: Tj ⊆ S≥j . Every step of Tj has the premise A ∨ ⊤(j) , and ⊤(j) contains j occurrences
of ⊤. So every step of Tj has size at least j.
    Step 2: the tail bound. The sets S≥N decrease in N and have empty intersection, so
Q(S≥N ) ↓ 0 by continuity from above. Fix ε ∈ (0, 1) and let Nε := min{N ≥ 0 : Q(S≥N ) ≤ ε}.
    • If ȷ̂ ≥ Nε , then Q(Tȷ̂ ) ≤ Q(S≥ȷ̂ ) ≤ Q(S≥Nε ) ≤ ε, by Step 1 and monotonicity.
    • If ȷ̂ < Nε , then Nε ≥ 2, because ȷ̂ ≥ 1. By minimality of Nε , Q(S≥Nε −1 ) > ε. Moreover
      ȷ̂ < Nε means |Xi | ≤ Nε − 2 for every i, i.e. no sample lies in S≥Nε −1 . Since the Xi are
      i.i.d. from Q, this event has probability (1 − Q(S≥Nε −1 ))m < (1 − ε)m .
Hence Pr[Q(Tȷ̂ ) > ε] ≤ Pr[ȷ̂ < Nε ] ≤ (1 − ε)m .
    Step 3: the error decomposition. Write h = L(X1..m ) and Y = inst(⊤I, ∧I, ∨I2 ) ⊆ R∗ . An
element of (h ∪ Tȷ̂ ∪ Y ) \ R∗ lies in h \ R∗ or in Tȷ̂ , because Y ⊆ R∗ . An element of R∗ \ (h ∪ Tȷ̂ ∪ Y )

                                                   159
lies in R∗ \ h. So (h ∪ Tȷ̂ ∪ Y ) △ R∗ ⊆ (h △ R∗ ) ∪ Tȷ̂ , and errQ (L+ ) ≤ errQ (L) + Q(Tȷ̂ ) pointwise
in the sample. This proves (a).
     Step 4: PAC. Let m ≥ max{mL (ε/2, δ/2), ⌈(2/ε) ln(2/δ)⌉}. Then Pr[errQ (L) > ε/2] ≤ δ/2,
since as usual the guarantee of L holds for every sample size m ≥ mL (ε, δ). By Step 2 applied
with ε/2, Pr[Q(Tȷ̂ ) > ε/2] ≤ (1 − ε/2)m ≤ e−mε/2 ≤ δ/2. By Step 3 and a union bound,
Pr[errQ (L+ ) > ε] ≤ δ. Both events are computed from the same sample, so no extra samples
beyond the maximum are needed. The outputs of L+ need not lie in the hypothesis class of L,
so the guarantee is improper. This proves (b).
     Step 5: trivialization. Every output of L+ contains Y ∪ Tȷ̂ . The derivation in the proof of
Theorem 3.2(i), with j = ȷ̂, uses only steps of Y (namely ⊤I, ∧I and ∨I2 ) and one step of Tȷ̂ . So
ClL+ (X1..m ) (∅) = Fm for every sample. This proves (c).

Remark B.1. Step 5 is where the three added schemas are needed. If L ≡ ∅ and they are omitted,
the output is Tȷ̂ alone. Every step of Tȷ̂ has a premise, so ∅ is closed under it and ClTȷ̂ (∅) = ∅.

B.3    The commitment-order lemma
Recall Definition 3.10. An R-derivation is a finite tree of sequents in which each node is either
a leaf marked as a premise (chosen freely by the prover) or, together with its children, forms
an instance of some rule of R: the children are the instance’s premise sequents (none, for a
premise-free rule) and the node is its conclusion sequent. The conclusion of the derivation is the
sequent at the root.

Proof of Lemma 3.11(i). Let G := {x : ρi is valid in x for every i ≤ m}. By the union bound
over the whole library,
                                        m
                                        X                                   m
                                                                            X
                       Pr [x ∈
                             / G] ≤           Pr [ρi is not valid in x] ≤         εi .
                      x∼D                     x∼D
                                        i=1                                 i=1

Fix x ∈ G and any R-derivation whose premises are all true in x. We show by induction on
height that every sequent in the tree is true in x. Premise nodes are true by assumption. Every
other node is the conclusion of an instance ι of some ρi , whose premise sequents are its children
(possibly none) and are true in x by the induction hypothesis. Since x ∈ G, ρi is valid in x, so ι
holds in x and its conclusion is true in x. In particular the conclusion of the derivation is true
in x.
     So the event “some R-derivation from premises true in x has a conclusion false in x” is
contained in the complement of G. Its probability (its outer probability, if it is not measurable)
                      P
is therefore at most i εi . The event G is determined by x and the library R alone. Because R
is fixed before x is drawn, G does not depend on the prover, and the bound holds simultaneously
for every prover, including one that sees x and chooses any number of derivations of any length.
The sum runs over the whole library, not over the rules a particular derivation uses.

Remark B.2 (Per-pair guarantees do not give per-scene validity). Suppose each scene in the
support of D falsifies exactly one of M instances of a rule ρ, and the instance is drawn uniformly
from these M . Then Pr(x,ι) [ι holds in x] = 1 − 1/M , but ρ is valid in no scene, so its per-scene


                                                    161
validity is 0. A prover that sees x submits the falsified instance; this is regime (ii) inside each
scene.

Proof of Lemma 3.11(ii). Let ι0 be an instance of ρ that fails in x0 : its premise sequents are
true in x0 and its conclusion sequent is false in x0 . The tree consisting of ι0 alone (its conclusion
at the root, its premises as leaves) is a {ρ}-derivation from premises true in x0 with a conclusion
false in x0 . A prover that knows x0 submits it, and nothing in this regime is random, so this
happens with probability 1. If µ{ι : ι fails in x0 } > 0, such an ι0 exists. If µ is supported on
instances that hold in x0 , the average validity is 1, i.e. ε = 0, but a failing instance off the support
of µ may still exist, and the same prover uses it. So no bound in terms of ε holds.

   For part (iii) we use the Schwartz–Zippel lemma (Schwartz, 1980; Zippel, 1979; DeMillo and
Lipton, 1978): if f ∈ F [z1 , . . . , zn ] is nonzero of total degree at most d and U ⊆ F is finite, then
Pra∼Unif(U n ) [f (a) = 0] ≤ d/|U |.

Proof of Lemma 3.11(iii). Formalize the protocol as follows. In round k the prover, which may
be randomized, adaptive and computationally unbounded, commits to explicit expressions for

B.4    The doctrinal paradox
We use the online protocol of Definition 6.1: (P)- and (N)-data, arguments π and their step sets
Steps(π) are as defined there.

Proof of Theorem 3.12. Step 1: each hi is a coherent, cut-closed calculus. The sets T1 , T2 , T3
are satisfied by the valuations (v(p), v(q)) = (1, 1), (1, 0), (0, 1) respectively. For every set Γ,
Clhi (Γ) = CnCPC (Ti ∪Γ). For ⊇: if Ti ∪Γ |= φ, compactness gives a finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ with Ti ∪Γ0 |= φ,
so Γ0 ▷ φ ∈ hi and φ ∈ Clhi (Γ). For ⊆: CnCPC (Ti ∪ Γ) contains Γ and is closed under hi , since
Π ⊆ CnCPC (Ti ∪ Γ) and Ti ∪ Π |= φ imply Ti ∪ Γ |= φ. In particular Clhi (∅) = CnCPC (Ti ), which
does not contain ⊥ because Ti is satisfiable. So every hi is A-coherent and is a possible target.
    Step 2: memberships. The following table records which hi contain each step of π.
                       step                  h1 (p, q)   h2 (p, ¬q)   h3 (¬p, q)
                       ▷p                       ✓            ✓            –
                       ▷q                       ✓            –            ✓
                       p, q ▷ p ∧ q             ✓            ✓            ✓
                       ▷¬(p ∧ q)                –            ✓            ✓
                       p ∧ q, ¬(p ∧ q) ▷ ⊥      ✓            ✓            ✓

The checkmarks are immediate: p ∈ T1 , T2 ; q ∈ T1 , T3 ; ¬q |= ¬(p ∧ q) and ¬p |= ¬(p ∧ q); and
the third and fifth steps are valid outright. For the dashes: T3 |= ¬p, T2 |= ¬q and T1 |= p ∧ q,
and each Ti is satisfiable, so T3 ̸|= p, T2 ̸|= q and T1 ̸|= ¬(p ∧ q).
    Step 3: π is a legal detection that deletes nothing. The five steps form an argument π from ∅
to ⊥: the first two yield p and q, the third yields p ∧ q, the fourth yields ¬(p ∧ q), and the
fifth yields ⊥. With uniform weights, s is in the majority set over H iff s lies in at least two
of the hi , since 2/3 > 1/2 > 1/3. By the table, every step of π lies in at least two hi , so
Steps(π) ⊆ R̂maj , the majority set over H. Also by the table, Steps(π) ̸⊆ hi for each i. So the
deletion set {R ∈ H : Steps(π) ⊆ R} is empty.
    Step 4: induction on rounds. Fix any target hi∗ . Consider the environment that, in each
round, exhibits π or presents the positive datum ▷p ∨ ¬p, in any order. We show VSt = H for
all t. Initially VS1 = H. If VSt = H, then R̂t = R̂maj ⊇ Steps(π). So π is a legal (N)-datum,
since ∅ ∈ A, and by Step 3 it deletes nothing. The datum ▷p ∨ ¬p lies in every hi , so it is a legal
(P)-datum for the target and deletes {R : ▷p ∨ ¬p ∈        / R} = ∅. Hence VSt+1 = H. So VSt = H
and R̂t = R̂maj for all t, and π is available in every round.

Consequences recorded in the main text.
   • The vote is unsound relative to every target. By Step 3, ⊥ ∈ ClR̂maj (∅). By Step 1,
      ⊥∈
       / Clhi (∅) for each i. By Lemma 3.1 with B = ∅, R̂maj ̸⊆ Sound(hi ) for each i.
   • Discriminating data break the paradox. Let the target be h1 and present ▷p ∈ h1 . This
     deletes h3 , since ▷p ∈ / h3 . Over VS = {h1 , h2 }, with weight 1/3 each, a step is a strict
     majority iff it lies in both, so R̂ = h1 ∩ h2 . Since ▷q ∈
                                                              / h2 , π is no longer available. The
     hi are pairwise incomparable: ▷p ∧ q lies only in h1 , ▷p ∧ ¬q only in h2 , and ▷¬p ∧ q


                                                 163
      only in h3 . So on a text enumerating all of the target, each wrong hypothesis is eventually
      deleted by a datum it lacks, and from then on the uninformative detections stop.

Relation to judgment aggregation. Theorem 3.12 is the doctrinal paradox of Kornhauser
and Sager (1986) and the discursive dilemma of Pettit (2001), with verifiers in place of judges.
Its general form is the theorem of List and Pettit (2002): no aggregation function satisfies
universal domain, anonymity and systematicity while producing consistent and complete collective
judgments, for agendas with at least two atoms and their conjunction (or disjunction, or material
conditional). For oligarchic aggregation under mere deductive closure, see Gärdenfors (2006) and
Dietrich and List (2008); Proposition 6.6 is its learning-theoretic counterpart.


C     Proofs for Section 4
The following are proved in full in the main text: Theorem 4.2(a) and (c), Theorem 4.12,
Theorem 4.14 and Corollary 4.17. This appendix proves the remaining results, states two results
that the main text only summarizes (Propositions C.2 and C.5), checks the examples of Section 4,
and records the evidence for Conjecture 4.11. All statements are the versions repaired during
adversarial verification; the repairs are listed at the end of this appendix (Appendix C.12). The
scripts cited below are in research/theory/T1-code/ of the accompanying repository. We
re-ran them for this paper, and all values reproduce; the exceptions are the hill-climbing run
with h ≤ 5 and the independent search of Appendix C.8, which we report as recorded.
    Throughout, a verifier’s internal randomness is a single draw ω ∼ Λ on a space ΩV , made
before the first round. Nothing is lost by this, since coins drawn later can be drawn up front.
Steps are ground terms, |t| is the number of symbol occurrences of t, and µ(t) = |t| − |vars(t)|.
We use the rank lemma (Lemma 2.6) and the characterization of the lgg (Theorem 2.5).

shows. The deterministic form (c) follows because Λ(E) ∈ {0, 1} when Λ is a point mass. Any
history that a deterministic verifier produces against a target is consistent with that target, since
the oracle is truthful.
    The reckless verifier. Let H = {R1 = {a, c}, R2 = {a, b, c}, R3 = {a, b}} and P0 = ∅. The
verifier draws B ∼ Bernoulli(ε). If B = 1 it accepts every query; otherwise it runs the VS verifier.
   • It is ε-sound. When B = 0 no invalid query is ever accepted, by Theorem 4.2(a), so the
     probability of an invalid acceptance is at most P[B = 1] = ε.
   • Take target R2 , and let the prover query c and then b. Initially VS = {a}, so when

    Random human data. Suppose instead that P0 is random, with a countable range and a

as above with VSh computed from P0 = d. The coupling, applied conditionally on P0 = d, gives

          p(d) := PR∗ [h, then q accepted | P0 = d] = PR′ [h, then q accepted | P0 = d].

Hence PR′ [P0 = d] · p(d) ≤ δ, which is the weaker bound stated in the main text.

C.3    Intersection-closed classes; single schemas
Proof of Proposition 4.5. (i) By definition, VS(P ) is the intersection of the members of H that
                                               T

contain P , which is cl(P ). Intersection-closure puts it in H ∪ {∅}. It contains P , and every

Proof of Lemma 4.6. (1) Two schemas. Let σ, τ be schemas, renamed apart. A ground term t
lies in inst(σ) ∩ inst(τ ) iff t = σθ = τ θ′ for ground substitutions θ, θ′ . Since the variables are
disjoint, θ ∪ θ′ then unifies σ and τ . If σ and τ are not unifiable, the intersection is empty.
Otherwise let η be a most general unifier. Every unifier factors through η, so t = σηρ for
some ρ, and t ∈ inst(ση). Conversely, every ground instance σηρ = τ ηρ lies in both sets. So
inst(σ) ∩ inst(τ ) = inst(ση) ∈ H1 .
    (2) Arbitrary families. Let F ⊆ H1 . The empty family has intersection S = inst(x) ∈ H1 .
If F = ∅, it lies in H1 . Otherwise F contains a ground term t, and every member of F
   T                                      T

is inst(σ) with σθ = t for some θ. Then |σ| ≤ |t|, and every function or constant symbol of σ
occurs in t. So, up to renaming, there are finitely many such σ, and F has finitely many distinct
members. Its intersection is a finite intersection, which lies in H1 by (1).
    (3) Lggs of arbitrary nonempty sets. Let P ̸= ∅. For finite F ⊆ F ′ ⊆ P we have lggF ⪯ lggF ′ ,
since F ⊆ F ′ ⊆ inst(lggF ′ ). By the rank lemma, a strictly increasing chain of lggs has length
at most µ(lgg{t}) = |t| for any t ∈ P . So there is a finite F0 ⊆ P such that lggF ≡ lggF0
for every finite F with F0 ⊆ F ⊆ P . Put g := lggF0 . For each s ∈ P , lgg(F0 ∪ {s}) ≡ g,
so s ∈ inst(g). If P ⊆ inst(τ ), then F0 ⊆ inst(τ ), so g ⪯ τ . Thus g is the lgg of P , and
inst(g) = {inst(τ ) : P ⊆ inst(τ )}.
           T



                                                   166
   (4) The closure. For nonempty P , the members of H1 that contain P are the sets inst(τ ) with
P ⊆ inst(τ ) (the empty set does not contain P ). So cl(P ) = inst(lggP ) by (3), or by Theorem 2.5
when P is finite.

Proof of Proposition C.2. Identify a, b with 0, 1, so that steps are points x ∈ {0, 1}n . A linear
flat schema denotes a subcube, which fixes some coordinates and leaves the others free. For
points y, p and a set J of coordinates, say y agrees with p on J if yj = pj for all j ∈ J. The pair
(J, p|J ) with |J| = k is a pattern, and a set P of points realizes it if some y ∈ P agrees with p
on J.
     Escape criterion. Let P be the set of earlier chain elements. A subcube Q with p ∈         / Q fixes
some coordinate j to 1 − pj , since otherwise p ∈ Q. So Q lies in the half-cube {xj = 1 − pj },
which is itself a subcube avoiding p. Hence p escapes iff some union of at most k half-cubes
{xj ≠ pj }, j ∈ J, covers P . That holds iff no y ∈ P agrees with p on J. Padding J to size k
(possible since n ≥ k) preserves this.   So p escapes iff some pattern of p is not realized     by P .
     Upper bound. There are 2k nk patterns. The first chain element realizes nk of them. Each
                                                                                        

later element escapes, so it realizes at least one pattern not realized     before, and realized patterns
                                                           k        n
stay realized. So the chain has length at most 1 + (2 − 1) k .
     Lower bound. The target is the full cube f (x1 , . . . , xn ). Query all points of weight at most k
in order of non-decreasing weight. Let x have weight w ≤ k, and choose J ⊇ supp(x) with
|J| = k. An earlier point y that agrees with x on J has yj = 1 on supp(x), so supp(y) ⊇ supp(x).
Its weight is at most w, so y = x, which is impossible      for an earlier, distinct point. So every such
                                            Pk     n
point escapes, and the chain has length w=0 w .
     Repeated metavariables. A flat schema with repeated metavariables denotes the points that
satisfy its constants and the equalities xi = xj for positions sharing a metavariable. If such a
schema avoids p, then either a constant position j has pj ̸= the constant, so the schema lies in
{xj ̸= pj }, or all constants agree with p and some pair i, j sharing a metavariable has pi ̸= pj ,
so the schema lies in {xi = xj }. Each such set is determined by at most two coordinates of p,
and each of its points disagrees with p on one of them. If p escapes, there is therefore a set J
of at most 2k coordinates on which no earlier point agrees with p. Padding J to size 2k               (for
                                                                                                 n
n ≥ 2k) and counting patterns as above gives a chain length of at most 1 + (22k − 1) 2k             . The
class contains the linear one, and elastic chains stay elastic in a larger class, so the lower bound
persists.

Proposition C.3 (Conjecture 4.11 for (k, h) = (2, 3)). [T1 Conj 3.8, case proved during verification] Let
C be a family of subsets of U , closed under arbitrary intersections, with U ∈ C and of height 3.
Then every elastic sequence for the class of unions of one or two members of C, relative to ∅, has
                     4
length at most 6 = 2 .

Proof. Reduction. Let C0 = C. Its points lie in every member, so they never escape and
                                   T

never occur in an elastic sequence. Removing C0 from U and from every member preserves
intersection-closure, height and elastic sequences. So we may assume C0 = ∅.
    Ranks. Let the rank r(X) of a member be the length of the longest strict chain of members
from ∅ to X. If X ⊊ Y are members, then r(X) < r(Y ). Since r(U ) = 3, every member X ̸= U
has r(X) ≤ 2. The only member of rank 0 is ∅. Members of rank 1 are atoms and members of
rank 2 are planes.
    Fact 1. If X, Y are members with X ̸⊆ Y , then X ∩ Y is a member with r(X ∩ Y ) < r(X). So
the intersection of a plane with a member not containing it is ∅ or an atom, and the intersection
of an atom with a member not containing it is ∅.
    Let s1 , . . . , sm be elastic, with witnesses Yi1 ∪ Yi2 (taking Yi1 = Yi2 for a single member) that
cover s1 , . . . , si−1 and miss si .
    Claim A: each atom contains at most one si . Suppose si , sj ∈ A with i < j. Then si ∈ Yjl
for some l, and sj ∈     / Yjl , so A ̸⊆ Yjl . By Fact 1, A ∩ Yjl = ∅, contradicting si ∈ A ∩ Yjl .
    Claim B: each plane contains at most three si . Let X be a plane and sj the last sequence
element in X. The earlier elements of X are covered by Yj1 ∪ Yj2 . Since sj ∈        / Yjl , X ̸⊆ Yjl , so each
       l
X ∩ Yj is ∅ or an atom. By Claim A, each contains at most one sequence element. So X has at
most two elements before sj .
    By Claims A and B, every member other than U contains at most three sequence elements.
    The contradiction. Suppose m ≥ 7. The members Y71 , Y72 miss s7 , so they differ from U , and
together they cover s1 , . . . , s6 . Each covers at most three, so each covers exactly three, disjointly.
Atoms cover at most one, so both are planes; call them X and Y . Moreover, X contains no
element covered only by Y , since it would then contain four sequence elements, contrary to
Claim B; and likewise for Y . Say s6 ∈ Y . The witness Z1 ∪ Z2 of s6 misses s6 and covers the
three X-elements, which all lie among s1 , . . . , s5 .


                                                     171
    Let Z be a member with s6 ∈ / Z. If Z ̸⊇ X, then Z ∩ X is ∅ or an atom, so Z covers at most

  • Graphic matroids: the bound      would be tight at k = 2. The ground set of M (Kh+1 ) is the
                                h+1
    edge set of Kh+1 , with 2 points. Its flats are the edge sets that are unions of complete
    graphs on the blocks of a partition of the vertices. Flats are closed under intersection, and
    the rank of the matroid is h, so the family has height h. graphic.py computes the 2-union

  • Search. Randomized hill-climbing with k = 2 (icclimb.py) found exactly the conjectured
    maxima 6 and 10 for h ≤ 3 and h ≤ 4, on universes of 9 and 12 points. A run with h ≤ 5
    used a universe of only 14 points. Elasticity never exceeds the number of points, so its
    maximum of 14 is a ceiling artifact: it is not evidence of slack below 15, and it does not test
    the conjecture, since a counterexample needs at least 16 points. An independent search on
    11–12 points with h ≤ 4 found no counterexample.

C.9    Time-uniform soundness
Lemma C.4 (Ville’s inequality (Ville, 1939)). If (Mt )t≥0 is a nonnegative supermartingale with
EM0 ≤ 1, then P[∃t : Mt ≥ 1/δ ′ ] ≤ δ ′ for every δ ′ ∈ (0, 1].
Proof of Theorem 4.15. Observations and likelihoods. In round u there is at most one observa-
tion Ou : a human datum X ∈ S, an oracle answer y ∈ {0, 1} to an escalated query qu , or nothing.
For each R let λR (Ou ) be pR (X), ℓR (y | qu ) or 1 accordingly, and let Lt (R) = u≤t λR (Ou ).

    A prover that foresees the noise. Let H = 2{0,1} with the uniform prior, so w∗ = 1/4, and
let R∗ = {0}. There are no human data. The oracle flips the true label with probability η,
independently at each query, so ℓR (y | q) = 1 − η if y = 1[q ∈ R] and η otherwise. Set δ ′ = 0.05
and δ = w∗ δ ′ . The prover knows in advance whether the next answer will be flipped. If it will
be, the prover queries the invalid step 1, and the answer reads “valid”. If not, it queries the valid
step 0, and the answer again reads “valid”. So every answer is “valid”, and each answer to a
query of 1 multiplies the likelihood ratio of {0, 1} to {0} by (1 − η)/η > 1. No answer ever lowers
that ratio. Flips occur infinitely often, so the posterior mass of the hypotheses that exclude 1
eventually falls below δ, and the next query of 1 is accepted. The simulation prescient.py
gives acceptance probability 1.0 at η = 0.1 and at η = 0.3, against the bound 0.05. This prover
violates the hypothesis of (a), because Ft would have to contain the future noise. In (b) no such
prover exists, because there is no noise to foresee.

C.12     Repairs made during verification
The results of Section 4 went through adversarial verification; the referee reports and the repair log
are in research/verification/T1-soundness-under-search-verification.md, and a second
round is in research/verification/reverification-round2.md. The repairs that changed a
statement or a proof are these.
   • Theorem 4.2(b) first bounded the acceptance probability conditionally on the history. That
     reading is false (the reckless verifier of Appendix C.1); the statement now bounds the joint
     probability, and the deterministic case (c) was added.
   • The lower bound of Theorem 4.4 first cited the conditional reading; it now uses the coupling
     of Lemma C.1 directly.
   • Theorem 4.7: the displays were restated with the target-relative quantity el(H1 , σ ∗ | ∅; N ),
     and the proof of (i) now uses the lgg representatives, so that inclusion gives strict generality
     without assumptions on the signature. The second round noted the degenerate case of (ii)
     in which no instance of σ ∗ has size at most N ; hence the maximum with 0 there and in the
     corresponding case of Theorem 4.9.
   • Proposition 4.8 first claimed super-exponential cost without qualification; the growing
     signature and the fixed-signature bound were made explicit.
   • The justification of Theorem 4.9 first asserted that Hktag is intersection-closed, which is
     false (Appendix C.6); it now uses the factorization of the version space.
   • Theorem 4.10(iii) first said “Θ(nk ) for flat schemas”. This is proved only for linear flat
     schemas and needs n ≥ k (Proposition C.2).
   • The evidence for Conjecture 4.11 was corrected. A claim that “a natural one-step decompo-
     sition proof fails on some extremal sequences” had no surviving script and was withdrawn;
     the h ≤ 5 search was recognized as a ceiling artifact; the graphic-matroid data were added.
     The case (k, h) = (2, 3) (Proposition C.3) was sketched by a referee and written out in full.
   • The hypothesis of Theorem 4.15(a), that the prover cannot foresee the data or the noise,
     was implicit; the prescient prover of Appendix C.9 shows that it is needed. Part (a) is
     credited to Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2020).
   • Corollary 4.18 first called the verifier 0-sound; the guarantee covers only targets with
     w(R∗ ) ≥ δ.

Theorem 5.3, Corollary 5.10, Proposition 5.12, Theorem 5.16 and Corollary 5.19 are proved

    Notation is as in Sections 2 and 5. Steps are ground terms over a signature Ω with at least
two constants a = ̸ b. For a schema σ, vars(σ) is its set of metavariables and v = |vars(σ)|. A
substitution θ for σ maps vars(σ) to ground terms. Anti-unification is the map A of Section 2.2,
and lgg is computed by it (Theorem 2.5).

D.1    Three elementary facts
Lemma D.1. (F1) If τ = σθ and θ restricted to vars(σ) is not a renaming, then inst(τ ) ⊊ inst(σ).
(F2) The intersection of the instance sets of all schemas is empty. (F3) For tagged calculi Hktag
and clean data D, VS(D) = i≤k {i} × R̂i , where R̂i = inst(lgg(D(i) )) if D(i) ̸= ∅ and R̂i = ∅
                   T           S

otherwise.

Proof. (F1) Inclusion holds because instances of τ are instances of σ. For strictness there are two
cases. First, suppose some θx is not a metavariable, say with root g. Choose a constant c ̸= g; it
exists because there are two constants. Let t = σθ′ with θ′ x = c and θ′ ground elsewhere. At a
position of σ where x occurs, t carries c, while every instance of τ carries a term with root g. So
t∈/ inst(τ ). Second, suppose every θx is a metavariable. Then θ is not injective on vars(σ), say
θx = θy with x ̸= y. Let θ′ x = a and θ′ y = b. Every instance of τ has equal subterms at the
positions of x and y, and σθ′ does not. So σθ′ ∈  / inst(τ ).
    (F2) The ground schemas a and b have disjoint instance sets {a} and {b}.
    (F3) Write I for the family of single-schema instance sets. Then Hktag = { i {i}×Ai : Ai ∈ I},
                                                                               S

D.2    Proofs of Propositions 5.4 and 5.5
Proof of Proposition 5.4. (a) If T is an anchor and T ⊆ R ∈ H, then R ⊇ R∗ , so R ̸⊊ R∗ .
    (b) Let T ̸= ∅ be a tell-tale, and suppose T ⊆ R ∈ H with R ̸⊇ R∗ . Then R ∩ R∗ ⊇ T is
nonempty, so it is a member of H by intersection-closure of H ∪ {∅}. And T ⊆ R ∩ R∗ ⊊ R∗ ,
which contradicts the tell-tale property. For H = {{1}, {2}} and R∗ = {1}: no member lies
strictly inside {1}, so ∅ is a tell-tale; {2} ⊇ ∅ does not contain R∗ , so ∅ is not an anchor. Here
H ∪ {∅} is intersection-closed. For the existence claim, if T is a tell-tale and r ∈ R∗ , then T ∪ {r}
is a nonempty tell-tale (fewer members contain it), hence an anchor; anchors are tell-tales by (a).



                                                176
    (c) The class is an indexed family of uniformly recursive sets. {0} is a tell-tale for 2N, since
every Rn contains the odd number 2n + 1 and so no member lies strictly inside 2N. Rn is a
tell-tale for itself. By Angluin’s theorem (Angluin, 1980) the class is identifiable in the limit from
text. Every finite T ⊆ 2N lies in Rn for any n with 2n ≥ max T , and Rn ̸⊇ 2N. So 2N has no
anchor, and by Theorem 5.3(b) the cautious verifier is never complete on a text for 2N. The
same example shows that “finite” is needed in Theorem 5.3(a): every member containing 2N is
2N, so R̂(2N) = 2N.

Proof of Proposition 5.5. If R∗ = ∅, then ∅ is an anchor. Otherwise suppose R∗ has no anchor,
and pick w0 ∈ R∗ . Given w0 , . . . , wn−1 ∈ R∗ , the finite set {w0 , . . . , wn−1 } ⊆ R∗ is not an anchor.
So some Rn ∈ H contains it with Rn ̸⊇ R∗ ; pick wn ∈ R∗ \ Rn . Then {w0 , . . . , wn−1 } ⊆ Rn ̸∋ wn
for all n ≥ 1, which is infinite elasticity.

    This is the standard argument in direct form. The facts used after the proposition in the
main text are standard: finite thickness implies finite elasticity, and the union theorem of Wright
(1989) with the corrected definition of Motoki et al. (1991).

D.4     Proof of the claims in Remark 5.7
Teaching sets. Let θ1 , θ2 map the vi metavariables of σi to 2vi pairwise distinct constants. For
each x, θ1 x ̸= θ2 x are distinct constants, so their roots differ and (R) holds. For x ̸= y, θ1 x ̸= θ1 y,
so (D) holds. By Lemma 2.7, lgg(σi θ1 , σi θ2 ) ≡ σi . In a tagged class this set (one per rule) is an
anchor, by (F3).
     No distribution-free completeness rate. Let g be binary, h ≥ 1, m = 2h , and let uj (1 ≤ j ≤ m)
be the complete g-tree of depth h with leaf j equal to a and all other leaves equal to b. Let
J ⊆ [m] with |J| ≥ 2, and anti-unify {uj : j ∈ J}. All internal positions carry g and are copied.
At leaf ℓ ∈ J the column contains a (from uℓ ) and b (from any other uj , j ∈ J), so it becomes a
metavariable zℓ . Columns at distinct leaves ℓ, ℓ′ ∈ J differ (at index ℓ one has a, the other b), so
zℓ ̸= zℓ′ . At leaves ℓ ∈
                        / J the column is constantly b. Hence the lgg has distinct metavariables
exactly at the leaves in J and b elsewhere. Its instances among the u’s are exactly {uj : j ∈ J},
because uk with k ∈   / J has a at a leaf where the lgg has b. For |J| = 1 the lgg is uj itself.
     Take the target inst(x) ∈ H1 and the uniform law Q on {u1 , . . . , um }. A sample of n < m/2
draws hits a set J of at most n indices, and by the above R̂(D) ∩ {u1 , . . . , um } = {uj : j ∈ J}.
So Q(R∗ \ R̂(D)) ≥ (m − n)/m > 1/2 for every such sample. Any learner whose acceptance set is
sound for every target in H1 compatible with its data accepts a subset of R̂(D) (Lemma 5.1(b)),
so its completeness error is at least as large. Since h is arbitrary, no bound on the number of
samples that is independent of Q can guarantee completeness error at most 1/2.

D.5     Proof of Theorem 5.8
Part (a). Let R = l≤k inst(τl ) ∈ VS(D). Partition Subi (D) by the least l with σi θ ∈ inst(τl ). If
                     S

no class were generic, each would lie in a failure set, and k failure sets would cover Subi (D). So
some class Q is generic, and its τl ⪰ lgg{σi θ : θ ∈ Q} ≡ σi . Hence R ⊇ R∗ . A failure set contains
at most one member of a pairwise-generic set, so k + 1 such     members cannot be covered.
   Part (b). Fix a rule i with vi ≥ 1. Write M := vi + v2i and M ′ := vi2 + 1 ≥ M . Consider the
                                                             

range space on substitutions (a countable set) whose ranges are
                                      
                                Ci := F1 ∪ · · · ∪ Fk : F1 , . . . , Fk ∈ Fi .

    Step 1: traces of Fi . Let θ1 , . . . , θn be substitutions. For fixed x, the sets {θ : root(θx) = f }
for different f are pairwise disjoint. So their traces on {θ1 , . . . , θn } are pairwise disjoint subsets, of
which at most n are nonempty, giving at most n + 1 distinct traces. Each pair x ̸= y contributes
one set, hence one trace. So Fi has at most vi (n + 1) + v2i ≤ M (n + 1) distinct traces on n
points.
    Step 2: traces of Ci . The trace of F1 ∪ · · · ∪ Fk is determined by the traces of F1 , . . . , Fk . So
Ci has at most (M (n + 1))k ≤ (M ′ (n + 1))k traces on n points.


                                                     178
     Step 3: VC dimension. If Ci shatters d points, then 2d ≤ (M ′ (d + 1))k , i.e. ϕ(d) :=
d − k log2 (M ′ (d + 1)) ≤ 0. Let L := log2 (4kM ′ ) ≥ 2 and di = 2kL. Then ϕ(di ) > 0 iff
(4kM ′ )2 > M ′ (2kL + 1), iff 16k 2 M ′ > 2kL + 1. This holds because L < 4kM ′ gives 2kL + 1 <
8k 2 M ′ + 1 ≤ 16k 2 M ′ . Moreover ϕ′ (d) = 1 − k/((d + 1) ln 2) > 0 for d ≥ di ≥ 4k. So ϕ(d) > 0 for
all d ≥ di , and the VC dimension of Ci is less than di .
     Step 4: the ε-net theorem (Haussler and Welzl, 1987; Blumer et al., 1989). Let a range space
have VC dimension at most d, let µ be a probability measure, and let 0 < ε, δ ′ < 1. If
                                                n4           2 8d       13 o

                                                  ε          δ′ ε        ε
then with probability at least 1 − δ ′ an i.i.d. µ-sample of size m meets every range of µ-measure
at least ε. We use the theorem in this “measure ≥ ε” form. The symmetrization proof gives it
with the same constants. Alternatively, apply the standard “measure > ε” form with ε = ζi /2,
at the cost of a constant factor.
     Step 5: conclusion. Apply Step 4 with µ = Λi , ε = ζi , d = di and δ ′ = δ/k ′ . The sum in the
statement exceeds the maximum. By definition of ζi , every range in Ci has Λi -measure at least
ζi . So with probability at least 1 − δ/k ′ the ni rule-i substitutions meet every range in Ci , i.e.
they are not contained in any union of k failure sets. They are a subset of Subi (D), so neither is
Subi (D). For a ground rule, one sample makes Subi (D) nonempty, and Fi = ∅. A union bound
over the k ′ rules and part (a) finish the proof.

D.7     Proofs for Remark 5.11
Let Φ be finite and let the target be G∗ := inst(σ ∗ , Ψ∗ ) ̸= ∅. Write cl(P ) := inst(lgg(P ), ΨP ) for
nonempty P , the least guarded instance set containing P (Lemma 2.8).
    Anchors exist. Ascending generalization chains are finite (Lemma 2.6), so the lgg of the
(possibly infinite) set G∗ exists and equals lgg(T0 ) for some finite T0 ⊆ G∗ . For each ϕ ∈ Φ that
is not true on all of G∗ , pick tϕ ∈ G∗ with ϕ(tϕ ) = 0. Let T := T0 ∪ {tϕ }. Then lgg(T ) = lgg(G∗ ),
because lgg(T0 ) ⪯ lgg(T ) ⪯ lgg(G∗ ) = lgg(T0 ). Also ΨT is exactly the set of predicates true on
all of G∗ . Hence G∗ ⊆ inst(lgg(T ), ΨT ) = cl(T ). Conversely, cl(T ) ⊆ G∗ , since G∗ is a guarded
instance set containing T . So cl(T ) = G∗ , and every guarded instance set containing T contains
G∗ : T is an anchor.
    Chains. Let cl(P0 ) = C0 ⊊ C1 ⊊ · · · ⊊ Cm ⊆ G∗ be closures (the chain of closures of the data
plus escalated steps, for nonempty initial data P0 ⊆ G∗ ), Cj = inst(gj , Ψj ) with gj = lgg(Cj ) and
Ψj = ΨCj . Inclusion gives gj−1 ⪯ gj and Ψj−1 ⊇ Ψj . If both were equalities, then Cj−1 = Cj . So
each step either strictly generalizes the schema (at most µ(g0 ) − µ(σ ∗ ) times, by Lemma 2.6, since
gm ⪯ lgg(G∗ ) ⪯ σ ∗ ) or strictly shrinks the guard set (at most |Φ| times). By Proposition 4.5(ii)
and Theorem 4.4 this bounds the escalations by µ(lgg(P0 )) − µ(σ ∗ ) + |Φ|.

D.10     Proof of Lemma 5.17
Let F be a probability law on the countable set Ω, m = maxf F (f ) (attained, because only finitely
many atoms exceed any positive mass), fmax a maximizer, and ρ = maxG min(F (G), 1 − F (G)).
    ρ ≤ 1 − m. For any G, the side of the split that does not contain fmax has mass at most
1 − m, so the minimum is at most 1 − m.
    1 − m ≤ 2ρ. If m ≥ 1/2, the split G = {fmax } gives min(m, 1 − m) = 1 − m, so ρ ≥ 1 − m. If
m < 1/2, enumerate Ω and add symbols to G one at a time until F (G) ≥ (1−m)/2. This happens
at a finite stage, since the partial sums tend to 1. Before the last addition F (G) < (1 − m)/2,
and the last symbol has mass at most m. So finally (1 − m)/2 ≤ F (G) < (1 + m)/2, hence
1 − F (G) > (1 − m)/2, and ρ ≥ (1 − m)/2.
    Tightness. For the uniform law on 2r + 1 symbols, m = 1/(2r + 1), and the best split has r
against r + 1 symbols, so ρ = r/(2r + 1). Then 1 − m = 2r/(2r + 1) = 2ρ.
    Over random laws the ratio (1 − m)/ρ reaches 1.974 (computed; research/theory/T1-code/
rho.py).

D.11     Proof of Corollary 5.18
Suppose βi P[root(Θx) ̸= f ] ≤ α for some x, f . Let R′′ be R∗ with its tag-i component replaced
by inst(σi [x 7→ f (z̄)]), which lies in Hktag . By (F1), R′′ ⊊ R∗ . Q is a law on R∗ , and the
Q-mass of R∗ \ R′′ is the probability that a datum is a tag-i instance with root(Θx) ̸= f ,
namely βi P[root(Θx) ̸= f ] ≤ α. Apply Theorem 5.16 to R′′ ⊊ R∗ . Every q ∈ R∗ \ R′′ ̸= ∅
has PQ [∃t : q ∈ Acct ] ≤ δ. So PQ [R∗ ⊆ Acct ] ≤ δ for all t, which contradicts the hypothesis.
The pair case uses σi [y 7→ x] in the same way. All of the alternative’s “noise” sits on tag i, so
robust soundness is only needed for laws whose noise on tag i is at most α; this is the per-tag
reading.
   The factor βi in the displayed conditions is needed because α is a fraction of all data, while
the probabilities are under Λi .

D.12     Dimension inference
This subsection states the remark summarized in Section 5.7 and sketches its proof.
Remark D.2 (Dimension inference). [L9 §3.1, TC1] (proof sketch; not adversarially verified) The dimension
of a physical quantity is its inferential role: which sums and equations it may enter. Here learning
meaning from positive examples is solvable in closed form. Let q1 , . . . , qn be quantity symbols,
and let observed equations be polynomial (or Laurent) equations among them; each monomial
has an exponent vector in Zn . A grading is a homomorphism g : Zn → A into an abelian
group (deg qi = g(ei )), and an equation is g-homogeneous if all its monomials have the same
degree. For observed equations E, let K(E) ≤ Zn be generated by the differences of exponent
vectors of monomials in a common equation. (i) The gradings making E homogeneous are
the homomorphisms vanishing on K(E), so Zn → Zn /K(E) is the finest one: every consistent
grading factors through it. It is computed by Smith normal form (modulo torsion for rational
exponents). The cautious verifier for “dimensionally admissible” accepts exactly the equations
whose differences lie in K(E) (in its saturation, if gradings must be torsion-free). (ii) The
admissible sets form an intersection-closed class indexed by subgroups of Zn . Since these are
finitely generated, every target has a finite anchor, and Theorem 5.3 gives exact identification
once the data exhibit generators of the target’s relations. This is an instance of learning algebraic
closure systems from text, where Noetherianity is finite generation (Stephan and Ventsov,
2001). (iii) Gold’s limitation appears in miniature: positive data never refute a coarser grading
(“everything dimensionless” is always consistent), but the cautious learner never adopts one.
The collapse of Proposition 5.12 appears too: one wrong equation adds a spurious generator
and merges dimensions. (iv) The residue is conventional. The finest grading is fixed only up to
isomorphism, i.e. up to the choice of base dimensions, which no inference can see. Whether a
constant such as c is dimensional is a choice between data sets: natural units add c = 1 and coarsen
the grading, and Gaussian units absorb a dimension that SI keeps. These are coherent, empirically
equivalent alternative meanings, settled by convention (Section 13). Dimension types implement
the type-checking side (Kennedy, 1994); Buckingham’s Π theorem is the invariant-theoretic face
(Buckingham, 1914).
Sketch of (i)–(ii). The claims are elementary; we record only the argument.
   (i) An equation whose monomials have exponent vectors a1 , . . . , ar is g-homogeneous iff
g(aj − a1 ) = 0 for all j. So all of E is homogeneous iff g vanishes on the generators of K(E), iff it
vanishes on K(E). The projection π : Zn → Zn /K(E) is such a grading. By the homomorphism



                                                  182
theorem every such g factors uniquely as ḡ ◦π. An equation is homogeneous under every consistent
                                          T
grading iff its differences lie in g ker g = ker π = K(E).
     Smith normal form. If M is an integer matrix whose rows generate K(E) and U M V =
diag(d1 , . . . , dr , 0, . . . ) is its Smith normal form, with U, V unimodular, then Zn /K(E) =       ∼
                    n−r . If the target group is torsion-free, g(cv) = 0 with c ̸= 0 forces g(v) = 0. So g
   j Z/dj Z ⊕ Z
L

vanishes on the saturation {v : cv ∈ K(E) for some c ̸= 0}, and the finest torsion-free grading is
(Zn /K(E))/torsion.
     (ii) Let Adm(L) be the set of equations whose differences lie in L ≤ Zn . Then Adm(L) ∩
Adm(L′ ) = Adm(L ∩ L′ ), and Adm determines L: the equation 1 = q v (Laurent monomials) is
in Adm(L) iff v ∈ L. The version space of E is {Adm(L) : K(E) ≤ L}, so R̂(E) = Adm(K(E)).
For the target L∗ = ker g ∗ , choose generators v1 , . . . , vs (subgroups of Zn are finitely generated).
The equations 1 = q vj form an anchor. More generally, a finite E ⊆ Adm(L∗ ) is an anchor
iff K(E) = L∗ : if K(E) ⊊ L∗ , then Adm(K(E)) is consistent with E and misses Adm(L∗ ).
Theorem 5.3 then gives the stated identification. Claims (iii)–(iv) of the remark are direct
readings of these facts.

D.13     Experiment A: the positive-data numbers
(computed) These are the numbers behind the summary in Section 5.8, taken from code/results/
algebra_learning.md. Experiment A (Section 12.1) learns school algebra over partial terms
(Example 2.12) from simulated human derivations. The target has 41 rewrite schemas, 11 of them
guarded. The corpus has sporadic noise (5% random corruptions), five systematic fallacies (each
committed with probability 0.3 per opportunity), or both. The learner is a heuristic relative of
the cautious verifier (MDL-clustered anti-unification within rule-name buckets, support threshold
two); by default it infers no guards, and a variant takes the most specific guard true on all
instances (Lemma 2.8). Means are over three seeds; soundness is measured, not proved. Positive
data alone gave the following.
   • Shapes are recovered where Lemma 2.7 predicts. A rule’s shape was recovered in 0% of
     (rule, run) pairs with one human instance, 67% with two, 92% with three or four and 100%
     with five or more; on clean data, all 41 shapes for N ≥ 200 derivations.
   • Generalization is systematic. On clean data at N = 500, valid out-of-distribution steps
     (terms of about 40 nodes, against about 10 in human steps) are accepted as often as
     in-distribution ones (1.00 and 1.00). A gradient-boosted step classifier trained on the
     noisy corpus with validity labels accepts 89% of valid in-distribution steps, 73% of valid
     out-of-distribution ones, and about half of the invalid ones.
   • Guards are not displayed. On clean data at N = 500, the default learner ends with 11.7±0.5
     unsound active schemas (essentially the 11 guarded rules without guards) and accepts 34%
     of invalid out-of-distribution steps. Most-specific guards reduce this to 0.3 ± 0.5 unsound
     schemas (those whose guard the guard language cannot express), but with fallacies present
     the count rises to 5.3 ± 0.5, with 22% false accepts.
   • Fallacies reach support. At N = 500 each of the five fallacies is learned as an active schema
     in 6/6 runs, with and without guard inference (Corollary 5.19).
   • A fixed support threshold is no soundness guarantee. Under sporadic noise, spurious unsound
     schemas grow with N , reaching 102 ± 11 at N = 500 with threshold one and 18.5 ± 3.6 for



                                                   183
      the untagged learner with threshold two (3.0 on clean data); hence the linear budgets of
      Theorem 5.14.
    • With noise and fallacies together at N = 500, the cited-rule learner recovers all 41 shapes,
      yet 15.7 ± 0.5 active schemas are unsound, 51% of invalid out-of-distribution steps are
      accepted, and a white-box prover finds 65 ± 2 accepted invalid steps.
Experiment B shows the same pattern for propositional natural deduction (Section 12.2).

D.14     Repairs made during verification
The statements of Section 5 are the ones repaired after adversarial verification (record in
research/verification/T1-soundness-under-search-verification.md). The repairs were
these. The converse in Proposition 5.4(b) was restricted to nonempty tell-tales. Proposition 5.9
replaces an earlier claim that at most k roots at a metavariable make identification fail for good,
which is false for k ′ ≥ 2. Theorem 5.8(b) uses the ε-net theorem in its “measure ≥ ε” form.
The ground-rule conventions ρi = ci = 1 of Theorems 5.6 and 5.14 were made explicit, with the
missing ground-rule event added to the proof of Theorem 5.14. Theorem 5.13(b) gained the
clause “more than ei valid samples” and per-tag budgets. In Lemma 5.17 the constant 3 was
sharpened to the tight 2, and Corollary 5.18 gained the factor βi . Finally, the tagged case rests
on the factorization (F3) rather than on intersection-closure, which Hktag lacks.
