E.4     Proof of Proposition 6.12
(a) For the target, Γ ⊬∗ φ iff Γ∪{¬φ} is target-coherent, by classical reductio. So the designations
eventually enumerate (codes for) every finite-premise sequent not in ⊢∗ , and the text enumerates
⊢∗ : together they form an informant. Let (hi ) enumerate H, and let the learner output the least
i such that hi contains every sequent seen in the text and is coherent on every designated context
seen. Let i∗ be the least index of the target and j < i∗ , so hj ̸= ⊢∗ . If ⊢∗ ̸⊆ hj , the text eventually
shows a sequent of ⊢∗ \ hj , and j is rejected from then on. Otherwise pick Γ ▷ φ ∈ hj \ ⊢∗ . Then
Γ ∪ {¬φ} is target-coherent, hence eventually designated, and it is hj -incoherent by reductio in
hj ; so j is rejected from then on. The target’s index i∗ is never rejected. As there are finitely
many j < i∗ , the output is eventually i∗ forever. If membership in the hi is uniformly decidable,
both tests are decidable (coherence of hi on A is non-membership of A ▷ ⊥), so the learner is
computable.
     (b) {pj } is hn -coherent iff {¬pi : i < n}∪{pj } is consistent iff j ≥ n, and it is hω -incoherent for
every j. The chain is strictly increasing with union hω , and all members are ∅-coherent. Consider
the computable learner that outputs hj for the least j such that {pj } has been designated, and hω
if there is none (the enumeration learner of (a) also works). On target hn , exactly the singletons
{pj } with j ≥ n can be designated, and {pn } eventually is; from then on the least designated
j is n, and the learner outputs hn . On target hω no singleton {pj } is ever designated, and the
learner outputs hω throughout.
     Repair note. This proposition was added after verification; the referee’s counterexample (b)
showed that the first version of Corollary 6.11, stated without “A fixed”, was false.

E.5     Proofs for Section 6.2: Post-completeness
Theorem 6.13, main case. Let φ ∈ C(X) \ Cn2 (X), with v[X] = 1, v(φ) = 0. Fix a tautology
⊤0 in one atom and ⊥0 = ¬⊤0 , and let σv (p) = ⊤0 or ⊥0 as v(p) = 1 or 0. Every Boolean
u has u(σv ψ) = v(ψ), so σv X ⊆ Taut ⊆ C(∅) and σv φ is a contradiction. By structurality



                                                    186
σv φ ∈ C(σv X) ⊆ C(C(∅)) = C(∅), hence Fm = Cn2 ({σv φ}) ⊆ C(∅), and C = CFm . This is the
substitution of the proof of Proposition 3.5, at the level of consequence operators.

Theorem 6.13, pure {→}. Let φ ∈ C(X) \ Cn2 (X) and v a Boolean valuation with v[X] = 1,
v(φ) = 0. Put σv (p) = p0 → p0 if v(p) = 1 and σv (p) = p0 otherwise. By induction on ψ,
σv ψ ≡2 p0 → p0 if v(ψ) = 1 and σv ψ ≡2 p0 if v(ψ) = 0. For atoms this is the definition.
For ψ = α → β: if v(α) = 0, then σv ψ ≡2 p0 → (·), and both p0 → (p0 → p0 ) and p0 → p0
are tautologies; if v(α) = v(β) = 1, then σv ψ ≡2 ⊤ → ⊤ ≡2 ⊤; if v(α) = 1, v(β) = 0, then
σv ψ ≡2 ⊤ → p0 ≡2 p0 . Hence σv X ⊆ Taut ⊆ C(∅) and, by structurality, σv φ ∈ C(σv X) ⊆ C(∅),
with σv φ ≡2 p0 . So p0 ∈ Cn2 ({σv φ}) ⊆ C(C(∅)) = C(∅). Substituting any ψ for p0 and using
σC(∅) ⊆ C(∅) gives C(∅) = Fm.

Proposition 6.14. Cai is a closure operator, and it is structural because σX is non-empty iff
X is. In the {∧, ∨} language Cn2 (∅) = ∅, since the all-false valuation falsifies every formula; so
Cai ⊇ Cn2 . Now let C ⊋ Cn2 be structural. Case C(∅) ̸= ∅. Pick φ ∈ C(∅) and substitute p0 for
every atom. Every one-variable lattice term is ≡2 p0 , so p0 ∈ Cn2 ({σφ}) ⊆ C(C(∅)) = C(∅), and
by structurality C(∅) = Fm: C = CFm . Case C(∅) = ∅. Take φ ∈ C(X) \ Cn2 (X) (so X ̸= ∅)
and a Boolean v with v[X] = 1, v(φ) = 0. Let σ send the atoms true under v to q and the false
ones to r (distinct atoms). Each σψ is a lattice term in q, r, and its value at (q, r) = (1, 0) is
v(ψ). Up to ≡2 , the lattice terms in q, r are q, r, q ∧ r and q ∨ r. So σψ ∈ {q, q ∨ r} up to ≡2
for ψ ∈ X, and σφ ∈ {r, q ∧ r}. Hence σX ⊆ Cn2 ({q}) and r ∈ Cn2 ({σφ}), so

         r ∈ C({σφ}) ⊆ C(C(σX)) = C(σX) ⊆ C(Cn2 ({q})) ⊆ C(C({q})) = C({q}).

Substituting χ for q and ψ for r gives ψ ∈ C({χ}) for all χ, ψ, so C(Y ) = Fm for every non-empty
Y : C = Cai .

Theorem 6.15. (a) Suppose ⟨D⟩ = Cn2 . Every h ∈ S(D, A0 ) is structural and contains D,
hence contains ⟨D⟩ = Cn2 ; by Theorem 6.13, h ∈ {Cn2 , CFm }, and A0 excludes CFm . Conversely,
suppose ⟨D⟩ ⊊ Cn2 (note ⟨D⟩ ⊆ Cn2 because Cn2 is structural and contains D). Then ⟨D⟩ is
structural, contains D, and is A0 -coherent because Cn2 is; so ⟨D⟩ and Cn2 are distinct members
of S(D, A0 ).
    Explicit finite bases. For a language containing ¬ and → (possibly also ∧, ∨), with distinct
atoms p, q, r, take the axioms ▷p → (q → p), ▷(p → (q → r)) → ((p → q) → (p → r)),
▷(¬p → ¬q) → (q → p) and modus ponens p, p → q ▷ q; if ∧, ∨ are present, add their
clauses as →-axioms: ▷p ∧ q → p, ▷p ∧ q → q, ▷p → (q → p ∧ q), ▷p → p ∨ q, ▷q → p ∨ q,
▷(p → r) → ((q → r) → (p ∨ q → r)). If ⊥ or ⊤ is a primitive constant, add the axioms ▷¬⊥,
resp. ▷⊤; with the third axiom and the first these give ▷⊥ → p (from ¬⊥ and ¬⊥ → (¬p → ¬⊥)
infer ¬p → ¬⊥, then ⊥ → p). Without these axioms the constants behave like atoms that
substitution cannot reach, and ▷¬⊥ is underivable. For pure {→} take the first two axioms,
Peirce’s law ▷((p → q) → p) → p and modus ponens. For languages without →, such as {¬, ∧}
and {¬, ∨}, finite bases exist because every two-element matrix logic is finitely based (Rautenberg,
1981).
    The least structural consequence relation generated by a set of sequents is given by derivations
from substitution instances of those sequents. With the axioms and modus ponens above, these
are derivations in a Hilbert system with modus ponens as its only rule: Łukasiewicz’s axioms for
{¬, →}, extended by the usual axioms for ∧ and ∨, and for {→} the axioms K, S and Peirce’s

                                                187
law, a variant of the Tarski–Bernays axiomatization (K and S give intuitionistic implication,
and Peirce’s law makes it classical). These systems are complete for tautologies (Kleene, 1952;
Mendelson, 1964); for the ∧, ∨ axioms Kalmár’s lemma goes through because the system proves
p, q ⊢ p ∧ q, ¬p ⊢ ¬(p ∧ q), ¬q ⊢ ¬(p ∧ q), p ⊢ p ∨ q, q ⊢ p ∨ q and ¬p, ¬q ⊢ ¬(p ∨ q), and ⊢ ¬⊥, ⊢ ⊤
(base cases for the constants). Since modus ponens is the only rule and the first two axioms are
present, the deduction theorem holds. So if X |= φ, compactness gives a finite {x1 , . . . , xn } ⊆ X
with |= x1 → (· · · → (xn → φ)), which is provable, and n applications of modus ponens derive φ
from X. Hence ⟨D⟩ = Cn2 .
     (b) Let j < i∗ , so hj =
                            ̸ Cn2 . If hj ̸⊇ Cn2 , some sequent of Cn2 \ hj eventually appears in
the text, and j is ineligible from then on. If hj ⊇ Cn2 , then hj = CFm by Theorem 6.13, and
A0 ⊢hj ⊥ makes j ineligible from the start. i∗ is always eligible. So the learner’s output is
non-decreasing, never exceeds i∗ , and is eventually i∗ ; in particular it changes its mind at most
i∗ times. Uniform decidability makes the eligibility tests computable; no property of the ordering
was used.
     (c) Cn2 ⊕{▷p} with p not in A0 : its consequences of A0 are Cn2 (A0 ∪{p}), which is consistent,
and it contains every sequent of Cn2 . CFm contains every sequent. Cai contains every sequent of
Cn2 in the {∧, ∨} fragment and is non-trivial on ∅.

The sequent-rule basis fails (countermodel). The form of the basis matters: if the ∧
clauses are sequent rules (p ∧ q ▷ p, . . . ) while modus ponens is the only rule for →, then
▷p → (q → p ∧ q) is underivable; giving them as →-axioms, as above, repairs this. Take the
language {¬, →, ∧} and let D′ consist of the three {¬, →} axioms, modus ponens, and the sequent
rules p ∧ q ▷ p, p ∧ q ▷ q, p, q ▷ p ∧ q. We show ▷p → (q → p ∧ q) ∈  / ⟨D′ ⟩; this countermodel is due
to a referee and was re-checked by script. For every assignment s of truth values to atoms define
vs on all formulas, simultaneously for all s, by recursion on complexity: vs (p) = s(p); vs treats ¬
and → classically; and vs (α ∧ β) = 1 iff α ∈ Θ∗ and β ∈ Θ∗ , where Θ∗ = {φ : vs (φ) = 1 for all s}.
This is well defined, since membership of α, β in Θ∗ depends only on values at lower complexity.
Every substitution instance of a {¬, →} tautology lies in Θ∗ , because each vs evaluates ¬, →
classically and treats the substituted subformulas as atoms. Θ∗ is closed under modus ponens (if
vs (α) = vs (α → β) = 1 for all s, then vs (β) = 1 for all s), under ∧-introduction (if α, β ∈ Θ∗
then vs (α ∧ β) = 1 for all s) and under ∧-elimination (if α ∧ β ∈ Θ∗ then α, β ∈ Θ∗ by definition).
So ⟨D′ ⟩(∅) ⊆ Θ∗ . But p ∈     / Θ∗ , so vs (p ∧ q) = 0 for every s; at s(p) = s(q) = 1 this gives
vs (p → (q → p ∧ q)) = 0. Hence p → (q → p ∧ q) ∈     / Θ∗ , and ⟨D′ ⟩ =
                                                                       ̸ Cn2 .

Renaming is not enough. [L5 Prop 2.5] Let C(X) = Cn2 (X) if Cn2 (X) contains no atom, and
C(X) = Cn2 (X ∪ At) otherwise, where At is the set of atoms. C is extensive; it is monotone
because Cn2 (X) ⊆ Cn2 (Y ) for X ⊆ Y ; and it is idempotent, since in the first case Cn2 (Cn2 (X))
has no atom and in the second C(X) already contains every atom. For a renaming ρ (atoms to
atoms) we have ρC(X) ⊆ C(ρX): in the first case because Cn2 is structural, and in the second
because Cn2 (ρX) contains ρp for an atom p ∈ Cn2 (X), so C(ρX) = Cn2 (ρX∪At) ⊇ ρCn2 (X∪At).
C contains p ▷ q, and C(∅) = Taut; so C is ∅-coherent, has the classical theorems, and differs
from Cn2 . It is the least renaming-invariant closure operator above Cn2 containing p ▷ q: any
such operator puts every atom into C ′ (X) as soon as Cn2 (X) contains one. So a learner that
generalizes only by renaming atoms can settle on C.

Proposition E.1 (Theorems versus consequence). [T2 Props 3.4, 3.5, as repaired] For a substitution-
closed theorem set Th let Cadm (X) = {φ : ∀σ(σX ⊆ Th ⇒ σφ ∈ Th)}. (a) Cadm is the largest
structural closure operator with theorems Th; on finite premise sets it is the structural completion
(admissible rules). (b) For Th = Taut in a language as in Theorem 6.13, Cadm = Cn2 (structural
completeness); in the {∧, ∨} fragment Cadm = Cai . Lean: Post.le_Cn2_of_empty_eq_Taut (special case

not derivable; Harrop 1960; Rybakov 1997; Iemhoff 2001), and the two have the same theorems
and the same coherence profile, A ⊢IPCadm ⊥ iff A ⊢CPC ⊥.

    So a learner can learn the theorems and then take the structural completion; a learner that
is not bold here may settle on X 7→ X ∪ Taut, which has the right theorems but cannot chain
inferences from premises. And no learner fed theorems and coherence data can tell IPC-derivability
from IPC-admissibility.

Proposition E.1(a). Extensive and monotone: clear. Idempotent: if σX ⊆ Th, then
σCadm (X) ⊆ Th by definition, so every φ ∈ Cadm (Cadm (X)) has σφ ∈ Th. Structural: if
φ ∈ Cadm (X) and σ(τ X) ⊆ Th, then applying the definition to σ ◦ τ gives σ(τ φ) ∈ Th; so
τ φ ∈ Cadm (τ X). Cadm (∅) = Th because Th is substitution-closed. Maximal: if C is structural
with C(∅) = Th, φ ∈ C(X) and σX ⊆ Th, then σφ ∈ C(σX) ⊆ C(C(∅)) = Th. For finite X,
the defining condition is admissibility of X/φ.

Proposition E.1(b),(c). (b) Cn2 is structural with theorems Taut, so Cn2 ⊆ Cadm by (a). If

Cadm (X) = Fm for X ̸= ∅ and Cadm (∅) = ∅, i.e. Cadm = Cai .
    (c) The admissibility and non-derivability of Harrop’s rule are cited (Harrop, 1960; Rybakov,
1997; Iemhoff, 2001). The two relations have the same theorems by (a). For the coherence

induction, ⊢IPC ¬⊥; and if α, β are each provable or refutable according to their classical values,
so are α ∧ β, α ∨ β, α → β and ¬α. Now if A is classically consistent, pick a Boolean v |= A
and substitute ⊤ := ⊥ → ⊥ or ⊥ for each atom according to v. Then σv A consists of classically
true variable-free formulas, all IPC-theorems, while σv ⊥ = ⊥ is not one; so the rule A/⊥ is not
admissible, i.e. A ⊬IPC

family of RCF-consistent finite contexts, d even, and h the least parameter-structural consequence
relation containing ⊢RCF and all instances of td = 1 + 1 ▷ t > 0. Since xd − 2 is irreducible over
Q (Eisenstein), 21/d has degree d, and h is unsound: cd = 1 + 1 ⊢h c > 0 fails at c = −21/d . For
A ∈ F with parameters among c̄, the set SA = {x̄ : R |= A(x̄)} is a non-empty semialgebraic
                                                             V

set defined over Q; it has finitely many connected components, and each contains a point with
real algebraic coordinates (a standard fact of real algebraic geometry, via Tarski transfer). Choose
one such point in every component of every SA , A ∈ F, and let D bound the degrees over Q of
the fields their coordinates generate. As for h1 , an instance fires in A only if t(x̄)d = 2 on all of
SA (times Rk for parameters of t not in A). Then t takes values in {±21/d }, so it is constant on
each component, and its value at the chosen point (extended by zeros) lies in a field of degree at
most D. So for d > D no instance fires in any A ∈ F, and h(A) = CnRCF (A) is consistent: h is
F-coherent but unsound. The observation is due to a referee; we give it as a sketch.

Beyond RCF. With sin on R, which defines Z, incompleteness enters. For exp the question is
open: Th(R, exp) is model complete (Wilkie, 1996), and decidable if Schanuel’s conjecture holds
(Macintyre and Wilkie, 1996).
    Repair note. The first version claimed, from (a), that complete theories are pinned “as cleanly
as CPC” at the rule level, in contexts with parameters. A referee’s counterexamples (c) refuted
that; (b) is the repair. The algebraic facts about f were also checked with a computer algebra
system.

E.8    Proof of Theorem 6.21
(a) If π is true, PA + π ⊆ Th(N) is consistent. If π is false, ¬π is a true Σ1 sentence, so PA ⊢ ¬π
by Σ1 -completeness, and PA + π is inconsistent.


                                                  191
    (b) A true σ gives PA + σ ⊆ Th(N). By Gödel’s second theorem PA + ¬Con(PA) is consistent,
although ¬Con(PA) is a false Σ1 sentence.
    (c) On a Π1 sentence π the learner says “true” at stage t unless a PA-proof of ¬π with code
≤ t exists. By (a) and soundness of PA, such a proof exists iff π is false; so the verdict changes at
most once and converges to the truth. On a Σ1 sentence σ it says “false” unless a PA-refutation
of ¬σ (equivalently a proof of σ) with code ≤ t exists; apply (a) to the Π1 sentence ¬σ.
    (d) At stage t the learner accepts φn iff no PA-proof with code ≤ t refutes the conjunction
of φn with the sentences among φ0 , . . . , φn−1 accepted at stage t. By induction on n: once
the statuses of φ0 , . . . , φn−1 have stabilized, the status of φn is a Π1 question (consistency
of a fixed finite extension of PA), answered by proof search with at most one change. So all
statuses converge. In the limit φn is accepted iff it is consistent with PA plus the accepted earlier
sentences: this is Lindenbaum’s construction along the enumeration, so the limit is a complete
consistent extension of PA, and it depends on the enumeration. If φ0 = ¬Con(PA), no refutation
of PA + ¬Con(PA) exists (Gödel II), so φ0 is accepted forever and the limit contains a false Σ1
sentence. On the enumeration Con(PA) ∧ 0=0, ¬Con(PA), Con(PA), . . . , the first sentence is
consistent with PA (it is true) and stays accepted; the second is inconsistent with it, which proof
search finds, so it is rejected.
    (e) On a computable presentation, the learner’s guesses about each sentence form a computable
function g(φ, n). If they converged to the truth value on every Σ2 sentence, then by Shoenfield’s
limit lemma (Shoenfield, 1959) the set of true Σ2 sentences would be ∆2 ; but it is Σ2 -complete,
hence not ∆2 , by the arithmetical hierarchy theorem (Kleene, 1952, §57).
    Repair note. The first version of (d) said that the naive learner accepts whichever of Con(PA)
and ¬Con(PA) comes first; a referee’s enumeration above refutes that, and (d) now states the
Lindenbaum form.

E.9    Credences: the trilemma and what weak coherence costs
The arithmetic boundary of Theorem 6.21 has a counterpart for credences. Quantifier blocks
may be empty, so Π1 sentences also count as Π2 and Σ2 .

Theorem E.2 (The coherence/Π1 /Π2 trilemma; cf. Sawin and Demski 2013). [L3 Thm D, as repaired]
Let Pt (φ) ∈ Q ∩ [0, 1] be computable uniformly in t, φ, with (i) limt Pt (π) = 1 for every true Π1
π, and (ii) lim supt (Pt (π) + Pt (φ)) ≤ 1 whenever π is Π1 and PA ⊢ π → ¬φ. Then infinitely
many true Π2 sentences have lim inf t Pt (φ) = 0.

Proof. A false Π2 φ = ∀x∃yR has a true Π1 refuter ∀y¬R(x̄0 , y), so lim supt Pt (φ) = 0 by (i),
(ii). Thus {φ ∈ Π2 : lim inf t Pt (φ) > 0}, a Σ2 set, contains no false Π2 sentence. If it contained
all but finitely many true ones, the Π2 -complete set of true Π2 sentences would be Σ2 (a finite
modification of a Σ2 set is Σ2 ), contradicting the arithmetical hierarchy theorem (Kleene, 1952,
§57).

    So one can have at most three of: computability, weak coherence, Π1 -convergence, and
non-dogmatism on true Π2 sentences; logical induction drops Π1 -convergence. Coherence does
not, however, confine credences to ∆2 :
                                                             ′
Proposition E.3 (What weak coherence costs). [L3 Thm D , as repaired] Say computable credences
gradually verify C if Pt (φ) → 1 iff φ is true, for φ ∈ C. (a) Convergent credences, coherent
or not, have a Π2 success set, so never gradually verify the Σ2 sentences. (b) Credences as in


                                                192
Theorem E.2(ii) never gradually verify all Π2 sentences. (c) Some computable credences, weakly
coherent for all pairs, gradually verify the Σ2 sentences (necessarily without converging on all of
them).

Proof of Proposition E.3. (a) If limits exist on C, then for φ ∈ C: limt Pt (φ) = 1 iff
∀q ∈ Q+ ∀s ∃t ≥ s Pt (φ) > 1 − q, a Π2 condition. The set of true Σ2 sentences is Σ2 -complete,
so it is not Π2 (else it would be ∆2 ), and no convergent computable credences have it as their
success set.
    (b) By the convention on empty quantifier blocks every Π1 sentence is Π2 . If weakly coherent
credences gradually verified all Π2 sentences, they would be Π1 -convergent, and Theorem E.2
would give a true Π2 sentence with lim inf t Pt = 0, contradicting Pt → 1 on true Π2 sentences.
    (c) Enumerate the sentences of Σ2 form, σ = ∃x∀y R(x, y) with R in ∆0 (quantifier blocks
coded as single variables; an empty block is a dummy variable), with indices ind(σ). At stage t:
• xt (σ) is the least x ≤ t with R(x, y) for all y ≤ t, or t + 1 if there is none;
• ct (σ) is the last stage s ≤ t with xs (σ) ̸= xs−1 (σ), or −1 if there is none;
• at (σ) := t − max(ind(σ), ct (σ)), the age of the current witness, for t ≥ ind(σ);
• It is the symmetric set of pairs (σ, σ ′ ) of Σ2 sentences with indices ≤ t that have a PA-proof
  of ¬(σ ∧ σ ′ ) with code ≤ t (including σ ′ = σ);
                                               ′
• Pt (σ) := min 1 − 2−at (σ) , min{2−at (σ ) : (σ, σ ′ ) ∈ It , at (σ ′ ) ≥ at (σ)} .
                                                                                   

Set Pt := 0 on sentences not of Σ2 form, and on σ before stage ind(σ).
     Weak coherence. If PA ⊢ ψ → ¬φ and one of them is not of Σ2 form, it has credence 0
and the sum is at most 1. Otherwise (ψ, φ) ∈ It from some stage on. At such a stage, say
at (ψ) ≤ at (φ); then Pt (ψ) ≤ 2−at (φ) and Pt (φ) ≤ 1 − 2−at (φ) , so the sum is at most 1. False
σ. Every x is eventually refuted, so xt (σ) → ∞ and changes infinitely often. At each change
at (σ) = 0 and Pt (σ) ≤ 1 − 20 = 0. So Pt (σ) ̸→ 1. True σ. Let x∗ be its least witness. Once every
x < x∗ is refuted and t ≥ x∗ , xt (σ) = x∗ forever. Let T0 = max(ind(σ), last change); for t > T0 ,
at (σ) = t − T0 → ∞. A competitor σ ′ with (σ, σ ′ ) ∈ It is PA-incompatible with the true σ, hence
false since PA is sound. If ind(σ ′ ) > T0 then at (σ ′ ) ≤ t − ind(σ ′ ) < at (σ). The finitely many
competitors with index ≤ T0 are false, so each changes its witness at some stage c > T0 , after
which at (σ ′ ) ≤ t − c < at (σ). So from some stage on no competitor enters the inner minimum,
and Pt (σ) = 1 − 2−at (σ) → 1. Non-convergence. By (a), these credences cannot converge on every
Σ2 sentence.
     The construction is due to a referee and was sanity-checked by script (L3-scripts/sigma2_
weak_coherence.py). It assigns 0 to every sentence not of Σ2 form, so it is dogmatic on the
strictly Π2 truths, consistent with Theorem E.2.

Incoherent credences reach the Π2 class convergently. For a sentence φ = ∀x∃y R(x, y)
of Π2 form (R in ∆0 , blocks coded as single variables) let kt (φ) be the largest k ≤ t such that
every x < k has some y ≤ t with R(x, y), put Pt (φ) = 1 − 2−kt (φ) , and Pt = 0 on other sentences.
These credences are computable, and kt (φ) is non-decreasing in t, so Pt (φ) converges. If φ is
true, kt (φ) → ∞ and Pt (φ) → 1; if x0 is the least x without a witness, kt (φ) ≤ x0 for all t, so
limt Pt (φ) ≤ 1 − 2−x0 < 1. So these credences gradually verify the Π2 sentences and converge on
all of them; by Proposition E.3(b) they are not weakly coherent. On the other side, the sentences
of Σ1 form, of Π1 form, and Boolean combinations of Σ1 sentences are decidable in the limit

                                                     193
(Theorem 6.21(c), applied componentwise), and the 0/1 output of such a decider, with 0 on other
sentences, is computable, convergent and weakly coherent, since its limits are truth values and
PA is sound.
    Reading. Take the classes Σ1 , Π1 , B(Σ1 ), Σ2 , Π2 and Π3 as full syntactic classes. Among
convergent credences, the first three are gradually verifiable with or without weak coherence,
Σ2 and Π3 by neither (a convergent success set is Π2 , as in part (a), and neither set of true
sentences is Π2 ), and Π2 only incoherently. So among convergent credences weak coherence costs
exactly the Π2 class. Without convergence, weakly coherent credences reach the Σ2 class (part
(c)), which is not ∆2 ; so what a learner gains beyond ∆2 by giving up convergence is not all
lost to coherence. These are statements about full classes; which proper subclasses of Π2 weakly
coherent credences can gradually verify we leave open.

E.10    Proofs for Section 6.4: Carnap’s problem
For finite Γ, ∆ write U (Γ, ∆) = {v : v[Γ] = 1, v[∆] = 0}; these sets form a clopen basis of 2Fm ,
and a valuation satisfies the sequent Γ ▷ ∆ iff it lies outside U (Γ, ∆). So Val(S) is closed for
every set S of sequents.

Lemma 6.23. (a) If v ∈     / V , some basic neighbourhood U (Γ, ∆) ∋ v misses V ; then Γ |=m V ∆
and v violates it. If v ∈ V violates a valid Γ ▷ ∆, then U (Γ, ∆) is a neighbourhood of v, so it
contains some u ∈ V , which violates the sequent too; contradiction.
    (b) Finitary: if φ ∈ CV (X), the closed sets V ∩ {v : v(φ) = 0} and {v : v(x) = 1},
x ∈ X, have empty intersection; by compactness a finite subfamily already does, so φ ∈ CV (X0 )
for a finite X0 ⊆ X. Hence a valuation respects every valid finite-premise single-conclusion
sequent iff CV (v) = v (identifying v with its true-set). Fix(CV ) = V ∩ : a fixed point X equals
  {v ∈ V : X ⊆ v}, an intersection of members of V (the empty intersection being Fm); conversely,
T

for X = W with W ⊆ V , CV (X) ⊆ W = X.
          T                            T

    (c) An intersection of classical theories is a theory, and Fm is the empty intersection.
Conversely, a consistent theory T is the intersection of the Boolean valuations extending it: if
φ∈ / T , completeness gives a Boolean v ⊇ T with v(φ) = 0.

Theorem 6.24. BV is closed (Theorem 6.26(a)), so by Lemma 6.23(b) every w ∈ BV∩ , hence
every w ∈ W , satisfies every sequent valid in |=1BV ; so |=1BV ⊆ |=1W , and W ⊇ BV gives the
converse. By Lemma 6.23(c) the members of BV∩ are the vT for classical theories T (including
Fm), and vT is Boolean iff T is maximal consistent. v⊤ = vFm makes φ and ¬φ both true. For
consistent non-maximal T , some φ has φ, ¬φ ∈    / T while φ ∨ ¬φ ∈ T , which violates the tables
for ¬ and ∨; and φ → ¬φ ∈     / T (it entails ¬φ), which violates the table for → at vT (φ) = 0.
Theories are closed under the ∧ rules, so every vT respects the table for ∧. BV∩ is closed, because
“Γ ⊆ v implies φ ∈ v” for each finite Γ |= φ is a closed condition; and it is structural, because
{ψ : σψ ∈ T } is a classical theory whenever T is, Cn2 being structural.

Theorem 6.25. d(v) = 0 means that v violates some valid Γ▷, i.e. some finite subset of its
true-set is inconsistent. For consistent v, d(v) ≤ 1 means that some finite Γ ⊆ v classically entails
some φ ∈ / v, i.e. the true-set is not closed. A consistent closed non-maximal T omits some φ
and ¬φ, violating the valid ▷φ, ¬φ, so d(vT ) = 2. Maximal consistent theories are Boolean, and
Boolean valuations satisfy every valid sequent, so d = ∞ exactly on BV.


                                                194
Theorem 6.26. (a) Each schema enforces one row condition. For ¬: φ, ¬φ▷ excludes both
true and ▷φ, ¬φ excludes both false, so v(¬φ) = 1 − v(φ). For ∧: the two eliminations give
v(φ ∧ ψ) ≤ min, introduction gives ≥. For ∨: the introductions give v(φ ∨ ψ) ≥ max, and
φ ∨ ψ ▷ φ, ψ gives ≤. For →: ▷φ, φ → ψ gives v(φ → ψ) = 1 when v(φ) = 0; ψ ▷ φ → ψ gives
it when v(ψ) = 1; modus ponens gives v(φ → ψ) = 0 when v(φ) = 1, v(ψ) = 0. So v satisfies
all instances iff it is a homomorphism into the two-element Boolean algebra. (With ⊥, ⊤ in the
language, ⊥▷ and ▷⊤ fix their values.) BV = Val(TT) is closed, and |=m           BV determines BV by
Lemma 6.23(a).
     (b) For any substitution σ and sequent s = Γ ▷ ∆, v satisfies σs iff v ◦ σ satisfies s. Let
v ∈ V . Every instance of a schema in TT is σ(TTj (p, q)) for some σ and j, and v ◦ σ ∈ V satisfies
TTj (p, q); so v satisfies all instances and V ⊆ Val(TT) = BV. For equality, take any v ∈ V
(there is one, as V ̸= ∅) and any u ∈ BV. Let σ(p) = p0 ∨ ¬p0 if u(p) = 1 and σ(p) = ¬(p0 ∨ ¬p0 )
otherwise. Then v ◦ σ ∈ V ⊆ BV is Boolean and agrees with u on atoms (v is Boolean, so
v(p0 ∨ ¬p0 ) = 1), hence v ◦ σ = u and u ∈ V .
     (c) The learner that outputs BV once the eleven sequents TT(p, q) and the coherence datum
have appeared is correct by (b), and it never needs to change its mind. V = ∅ satisfies every
sequent vacuously, so without the coherence datum no finite set of positive data excludes it.
     (d) Pointwise refutation. A text for LBV := |=m    BV eventually presents every instance of TT,
and by (a) every non-Boolean valuation violates one. No tell-tale. Fix a Boolean u0 , and for
a formula χ let vχ′ agree with u0 except at χ. Then vχ′ (¬χ) = u0 (¬χ) = 1 − u0 (χ) = vχ′ (χ),
so vχ′ ∈ / BV = BV. BV ∪ {vχ′ } is closed, and by Lemma 6.23(a) its relation Lχ satisfies
Val(Lχ ) = BV ∪ {vχ′ } =  ̸ BV, so Lχ ⊊ LBV . Given a finite T ⊆ LBV , choose χ occurring in no
                        ′
sequent of T ; then vχ agrees with u0 on every formula T mentions and satisfies T , so T ⊆ Lχ .
Non-learnability. Suppose a learner, computable or not, BC-identifies (a fortiori if it EX-identifies)
every meaning in a class containing BV and all BV ∪ {vχ′ } from texts of their relations, plus the
coherence datum [ : ] or any other fixed, target-independent certifications; these can be folded
into the learner, as in Corollary 6.11. (The datum [ : ] is in bounds for every member and carries
no information.) By the locking-sequence argument (Blum and Blum, 1975; Angluin, 1980),
which needs no effectivity, there is a finite σ of LBV -data such that the learner conjectures BV
on every extension of σ by LBV -data. Choose χ not mentioned in σ; then σ consists of Lχ -data,
and on a text for Lχ beginning with σ the learner conjectures BV ̸= BV ∪ {vχ′ } forever. Scope.
The argument needs the certifications to be target-independent. If every position in bounds for
the target is eventually certified, text plus certifications is an informant (a sequent Γ ▷ ∆ is valid
iff [Γ : ∆] is not in bounds), as in Proposition 6.12; then a certification of [χ, ¬χ : ] or of [ : χ, ¬χ],
whichever vχ′ realizes, separates BV ∪ {vχ′ } from BV, and this obstruction disappears. Density.
A Boolean valuation is determined by its values on atoms, and the map from atom assignments
to BV is a homeomorphism from 2ω , which has no isolated points. So BV \ {u0 } is dense in BV;
by Lemma 6.23(a) it has the same multiple-conclusion relation, and a basic open set meets BV
iff it meets BV \ {u0 }, so the two meanings have the same in-bounds positions. Composing any
Boolean v with the constant substitution along u0 yields u0 , so BV \ {u0 } is not structural.
     Repair note. The first version of (d) ended “identification in the limit still holds via the
text”. That was false and has been retracted; (d) now proves non-identifiability, and its scope
(target-independent certifications) was made explicit in a second round. The Lean formalization
proves (d) for BC-identification from texts with pauses and arbitrary learners.

Computational checks. (computed) Brute force over the sixteen formulas of depth ≤ 1 in

Proposition 6.27. Row by row, with designated set {1}. ¬: explosion p, ¬p ▷ q at p = 1,
q = 0 forces f¬ (1) = 0; then p ▷ ¬¬p at p = 1 forces f¬ (0) = 1. ∧: p ∧ q ▷ p forces f∧ (0, b) = 0,
p ∧ q ▷ q forces f∧ (a, 0) = 0, and p, q ▷ p ∧ q forces f∧ (1, 1) = 1. ∨: the introductions force
f∨ (a, 1) = f∨ (1, b) = 1, and disjunctive syllogism at p = q = 0 (where ¬p = 1) forces f∨ (0, 0) = 0.
→: modus ponens forces f→ (1, 0) = 0; q ▷ p → q forces f→ (a, 1) = 1; ¬p ▷ p → q at p = 0
forces f→ (0, b) = 1. So only the standard matrix can validate all twelve rules, and it does.
A brute-force check over all 4 · 163 matrices confirms that exactly one matrix validates them
(T2-checks/matrix_check.py).

E.11     Proofs for Section 6.5: tonk and conservativity
Proposition 6.29. Intuitionistic implication with ¬-introduction, ¬-elimination and ¬¬-
elimination is a standard natural-deduction system for the {→, ¬} fragment of classical logic
(Prawitz, 1965), so it is coherent and proves Peirce’s law ((p → q) → p) → p. Peirce’s law is not
intuitionistically valid: in the two-world Kripke model w ≤ w′ with p true only at w′ and q true
nowhere, p → q fails at both worlds, so (p → q) → p holds at w vacuously, while p fails at w.
So the extension is not conservative over IPC→ . ¬¬-elimination alone is conservative. Let τ
erase negations (τ (¬φ) = τ (φ), τ commuting with →, identity on atoms). It maps each instance
of ¬¬φ ▷ φ to the identity step τ φ ▷ τ φ and each instance of an IPC→ rule to an instance of
the same rule, and it fixes ¬-free formulas. So a derivation of a ¬-free sequent in the extension
maps to an IPC→ -derivation of the same sequent. Conservativity and coherence. If the base is
non-trivial and coherence means non-triviality on the old vocabulary, a conservative extension
proves no new old-vocabulary sequent, so it is non-trivial; likewise if ⊥ with ex falso is in the
base. If ⊥ is new and has no rules, IPC→ + {▷⊥} adds no ⊥-free theorem and so is conservative,
yet derives ⊥.

Theorem 6.30. (a) “R ⊬ ⊥” says that no finite derivation in R ends in ⊥, a Π1 condition.
For hardness, given e build a finite system Re that derives the successive configurations of the
computation of φe (e) (elementary formal systems simulate Turing machines; Post 1943; Smullyan
1961), and add the rule “halting configuration ▷⊥”. Then Re ⊬ ⊥ iff φe (e) diverges, which
reduces the Π1 -complete complement of the halting set.
    (b) Membership: “for every old-vocabulary s and every derivation of s in B + N there is a
derivation of s in B” is Π2 . Hardness, from the Π2 -complete set Tot = {e : φe total}. Let B
be a universal elementary formal system that derives T (x̄, ē) iff φe (x) ↓ (unary numerals x̄, ē)
and derives Num(n̄) for exactly the unary numerals, designed so that T -strings never occur as
premises of its rules. Its productions must also match only predicate-tagged strings over the old
alphabet; in pure Post-string format a projection such as xy ▷ y could otherwise strip a new
symbol, while in an elementary formal system with predicates this is automatic. Let Ne add
a new symbol c with the rules ▷c ē and c y, Num(x) ▷ T (x, y) (schematic in x, y). The only
derivable c-string is c ē, so the new old-vocabulary theorems are exactly T (n̄, ē) for n ∈ N, and
since T -strings are never premises nothing further follows. So the old-vocabulary theorems of

                                                 196
B + Ne are Thm(B) ∪ {T (n̄, ē) : n ∈ N}, and B + Ne is conservative over B iff φe (n) ↓ for every
n, iff e ∈ Tot.
    (c) A set is decidable in the limit by a computable learner iff it is ∆2 (Shoenfield, 1959;
Putnam, 1965; Gold, 1965); a Π1 set is decided in the limit with at most one mind change; a
Π2 -complete set is not ∆2 . Refutability in the limit corresponds to Π2 (Kelly, 1996).
    (d) If B is decidable, “every old-vocabulary theorem of B + N is a theorem of B” quantifies
universally over derivations and then checks a decidable property: Π1 .

E.12    Proof of Theorem 6.34, and survivors
The characterization of Alt as the never-refuted G-closed hypotheses is Theorem 6.9(ii), restricted
to G-closed h.
    (i) A structural h ⊇ Cn2 is Cn2 or CFm by Theorem 6.13, and CFm is incoherent on every
context, so on the non-empty A.
    (ii) ⊇: if h is structural with IPC ⊆ h ⊆ CPC and A is classically consistent, then A ⊬CPC ⊥,
so A ⊬h ⊥. ⊆: let h ⊇ IPC be structural and suppose Γ ⊢h φ with Γ finite and Γ ̸|= φ. Take a
Boolean v with v[Γ] = 1, v(φ) = 0, and let σv map each atom to ⊥ → ⊥ or ⊥ according to v. As
shown in the proof of Proposition E.1(c), IPC proves every classically true variable-free formula
and refutes every classically false one. So IPC proves each member of σv Γ and proves ¬σv φ. By
structurality σv Γ ⊢h σv φ; by cut with the IPC-theorems σv Γ, ∅ ⊢h σv φ; with ∅ ⊢h ¬σv φ and
σv φ, ¬σv φ ⊢IPC ⊥, ∅ ⊢h ⊥. By monotonicity h is incoherent on every A ∈ A, which is non-empty.
So every coherent structural h ⊇ IPC lies inside CPC.
    (iii) With G deductive closure, h∗ = PA and A = {∅}, the hypotheses above the target
are the deductively closed theories containing PA (the r.e. ones, if hypotheses are restricted to
r.e. theories as in Section 6.3), and ∅-coherence is consistency. PA + ¬Con(PA) is consistent
by Gödel II; its completions are not r.e., and they have only non-standard models, since they
contain the false ¬Con(PA). Designating {Con(PA)} removes PA + ¬Con(PA). If every finite set
of true sentences is designated, a theory containing a false φ is incoherent on {¬φ}, and a theory
T ⊆ Th(N) is coherent on every true context; so exactly the unsound ones are removed. The
theories Tk (k ≤ ω) of Theorem 6.20 contain PA and are sound, so they remain, and by that
theorem no learner identifies them all from text plus true-context coherence. Any two of them
have different theorems (for j < k, Tk proves Con(Tj ) and Tj does not), and any finite subclass
is identifiable from text; what fails is identification of the whole chain together with Tω .
    Repair note. Part (ii) was strengthened from “⊇” to equality after verification, with the σv
argument above; part (iii) was made precise (G, h∗ and A specified, and the claim about the Tk
restricted to what Theorem 6.20 proves).

Survivors. Outside a Post-complete target, generalized fallacies can be coherent. The main
text summarizes the following examples.

Example E.4 (Survivors). [T2 §6, as repaired] (1) Quantifier swap ∀x∃yR / ∃y∀xR is sound in
one-element structures, hence ∅-coherent; its alternative meaning is “the domain is a singleton”,
and any designated context with 0 ̸= 1 kills it. (2) The gambler’s fallacy is incoherent with
independence, but coherent without it: an anti-persistent stationary Markov chain with switching
probability 0.6 has fair marginals and validates it. Only frequencies or an accepted independence
premise remove it. (3) Base-rate neglect as a uniform schema P (E|H) = a / P (H|E) = a yields
P (H|E) + P (¬H|E) = 1.8 when P (E|H) = P (E|¬H) = 0.9, and dies with additivity. (4)


                                               197
Conditional perfection (from q and a law p → q ∈ K, infer p; Geis and Zwicky 1971) is coherent
whenever the per-law converse {q → p : (p → q) ∈ K} is consistent with K ∪ A; this is sufficient,
not necessary (K = {p1 → q1 , p2 → q2 }, A = {q1 ∨ q2 , ¬p1 , ¬p2 }: the converse is inconsistent
with K ∪ A, yet neither qi is derivable, so the step rule never fires and the fallacy survives, for
step-set hypotheses without proof by cases). It dies when two exclusive laws share a consequent
(rain → wet, sprinkler → wet, ¬(rain ∧ sprinkler), A = {wet}). The per-law converse is not
Clark’s completion (Clark, 1978): completing only the head wet (with rain, sprinkler abducible)
gives wet ↔ rain ∨ sprinkler, which is consistent there.

E.13    Consensus and coherentizing
These two results make the uses (U3) and (U1) of Remark 6.35 quantitative.
Remark E.5 (Consensus does not amplify under a common cause). [L11 TC3] Let m annotators
judge a step. With probability π > 0, independently of validity, they all copy one shared judgment
that says “valid” with probability a for valid and b > 0 for invalid steps; otherwise they judge
independently with rates p > q. Then

                         P(all say valid | valid)    πa + (1 − π)pm    1
                                                   =               m
                                                                     ≤
                        P(all say valid | invalid)   πb + (1 − π)q     πb

for every m, against (p/q)m when π = 0. So unanimity among annotators sharing an error source,
or self-consistency across samples of one model, moves the odds by a bounded factor. Human
errors in mathematics are often systematic in this sense, which is why corroboration must come
from channels whose errors are independent of the human ones, Daniels’ independence constraint
(Daniels, 1979).
   The eliminative use (U1) has a quantitative safety guarantee whose converse shows what it
depends on. Let W ⊆ {0, 1}S be the worlds allowed by constraints on a finite set S of sentences,
K their convex hull, and score credences x in world w by ∥x − w∥2 .
                                                                                   ′
Lemma E.6 (Coherentizing is safe iff the constraints are sound). [L3 Lemma E , as repaired] For
x∈/ K with Euclidean projection x∗ onto K, every w ∈ K has ∥x − w∥2 ≥ ∥x − x∗ ∥2 + ∥x∗ − w∥2 .
Conversely, if the actual world’s indicator v is not in W, then v ∈
                                                                  / K, and projecting x = v raises
the actual loss from 0 to ∥v − v ∗ ∥2 > 0.

Proof. ⟨x − x∗ , w − x∗ ⟩ ≤ 0. For the converse, a 0/1 vector is an extreme point of the cube, so it
lies in the convex hull of 0/1 vectors only if it is one of them.

     This is the accuracy-dominance argument of de Finetti (1974) and Joyce (1998) (Bregman
projections for other proper scores; Predd et al. 2009). It belongs to the projection, not to
arbitrary arbitrage removal: for x = (0.6, 0.6) on {φ, ¬φ}, moving to (1, 0) costs 2.0 in world
(0, 1), against 0.52 before and 0.5 for the projection. The converse is the probabilistic form of
the air-pressure example of Section 1.1: coherence pressure from an idealized context the world
violates, or from untrusted learned rules, can make credences strictly worse.

(F1) Cleanness is closed downward. If B ′ ⊆ B, every refutation of B ′ is a refutation of B, because
     RB ′ ⊆ RB . Likewise for step sets.
(F2) Transfer. If every step of a set S ′ lies in Sound(R) and π is a refutation with steps in
     S ′ ∪ R ∪ Ttrust , then replacing each S ′ -step of π by an R-derivation of its conclusion from its
     premises, and compressing (Definition 7.2(a)), gives a refutation with steps in R ∪ Ttrust , from
     the same leaves to the same conclusion, of some finite size. In particular, if R is clean at every
     depth, then every refutation using S ′ transfers to a refutation of R, which is impossible.

  F.1     Proof of Lemma 7.4
  Fix a designated position [A : D] and its valuation V , and let X = V −1 (1). Since V falsifies no
  step of R∗ , X is closed under R∗ , so ClR∗ (X) = X. Hence if P ▷ j ∈ Sound(R∗ ) and P ⊆ X,
  then j ∈ ClR∗ (P ) ⊆ ClR∗ (X) = X: V falsifies no step of Sound(R∗ ).
      (a) Let S ⊆ Sound(R∗ ), and let π be a derivation relative to [A : D] whose leaves have
  e-value 1 and whose steps lie in S ∪ Ttrust . By induction along the sequence π, every judgment
  of π is V -true. A leaf is e-true, hence V -true because V extends e. A judgment produced by a
  step of S ∪ Ttrust from earlier, V -true judgments is V -true, by the claim for S and by (WS) for
  Ttrust . So the conclusion of π is V -true, and since V extends e it is not e-false. Hence π is not a
  refutation; as π, its size and the position were arbitrary, S is clean at every depth. For B ⊆ Σ∗ ,
  RB ⊆ R∗ ⊆ Sound(R∗ ) (Lemma 2.3(b)).
      (b) A member of Conf d has a d-refutation, so by (a) it is not contained in Σ∗ ; as it is contained
  in ΣP = Σ∗ ⊔ F , it meets F .
      (c) The definition of a d-refutation of B mentions only e (which is determined by A and W ),
  Ttrust , d and B. So Conf d is a function of these data. Both tie-breaking rules choose among the
  d-refutations of B using only their sizes, a fixed lexicographic order, and whether their descent is
  blocked; the last depends only on π and e, because e+   π is computed from e and the trusted steps
  of π.
      (d) (⇒) The proof of (a) used (WS) only for the position of π. (⇐) Suppose e = e[A:D] is well
  defined and Σ∗ is clean at every depth relative to [A : D]. Let Y = ClR∗ ∪Ttrust (A ∪ W −1 (1)) and
  let V be the indicator of Y . Since Y is closed under R∗ ∪ Ttrust , V falsifies no step of R∗ ∪ Ttrust ,
  and V is 1 on every e-true judgment. Let j be e-false and suppose j ∈ Y . By Lemma 2.3(a), j has
  a finite (R∗ ∪ Ttrust )-derivation tree from A ∪ W −1 (1), that is, from e-true leaves. Compressing
  it gives a refutation of Σ∗ relative to [A : D] of some finite size, contradicting cleanness. So V is
  0 on every e-false judgment, V extends e, and (WS) holds for [A : D]. Nothing in the argument
  used that Σ∗ is the target.

F.2    Details for Proposition 7.5
The first two claims are Theorems 5.13 and 5.14 applied to the tagged practice, together with
Definition 2.10, which gives every fallacy an instance outside Sound(R∗ ). For the CPC claim, let
Πc ▷ jc be the closed falsified instance of the pure fallacy τ (Lemma 7.22). Each closed formula
has the same value under every valuation, so every member of Πc and ¬jc are tautologies, and
a complete Σ∗ derives them from ∅. The step adds jc , and {jc , ¬jc } classically entails every
formula, which Σ∗ derives. For the contrast: if Σ∗ is complete and s = (p ▷ q) for atoms p, q, the
set of tautologies is closed under s because p is not a tautology, so ClR∗ ∪{s} (∅) = ClR∗ (∅).

F.3    Proof of Lemma 7.7
(a) M ⊆ U is clean iff it contains no member of K, iff (by upward closure and finiteness) it contains
no member of C, iff U \ M meets every member of C, i.e. is a transversal. Complementation
reverses inclusion, so maximal clean sets correspond to minimal transversals.
    (b, ⇐) Let x ∈ C ∈ C and T = (U \ C) ∪ {x}. Let E ∈ C. If E ̸⊆ C, then E meets U \ C. If
E ⊆ C, then E = C by minimality of C, so x ∈ E. Hence T is a transversal, and it contains a
minimal transversal T ′ . Since T ′ meets C and T ′ ∩ C ⊆ T ∩ C = {x}, we get x ∈ T ′ .
    (b, ⇒) If x ∈ T for a minimal transversal T , then T \ {x} is not a transversal, so some E ∈ C
has E ∩ T = {x}, and x ∈ E.
    (b, second claim) By (a), x lies outside some maximal clean set iff x lies in some minimal
transversal, iff x ∈ C. Every clean set is contained in a maximal one, and ∅ is clean, so there
                    S

are maximal clean sets and their intersection is U \ C. It is clean because cleanness is closed
                                                        S

downward.
    (c, ⇐) If C = {{x1 }, . . . , {xr }}, every transversal contains {x1 , . . . , xr }, which is itself a
transversal.
    (c, ⇒) Let T be the unique minimal transversal. By (b), T = C. For each x ∈ T , minimality
                                                                    S

gives some E ∈ C with E ∩ T = {x}; since E ⊆ C = T , E = {x}. A member C ∈ C with
                                                      S

|C| ≥ 2 would then strictly contain the singleton member {x} for any x ∈ C, contradicting
minimality.

F.5    Proof of Lemma 7.8
Agreement. We show by induction on the order in which the fixed-point computation assigns
values that every value of e+ π agrees with V . Initial values come from e, which V extends. If the
forward rule assigns 1 to the conclusion of a trusted step whose premises have value 1, those
premises are V -true by induction, and since V falsifies no trusted step the conclusion is V -true.
If the backward rule assigns 0 to a premise π0 of a trusted step whose conclusion has value 0 and
whose other premises have value 1, then by induction the conclusion is V -false and the other
premises are V -true; if π0 were V -true the step would be falsified by V , so π0 is V -false. Hence
e+
 π never assigns both values to a judgment, and if it does, no total V as in (WS) exists for
[A : D].
    (a) Each move of the descent goes from a node of value 0 to one of its premises, which occurs
strictly earlier in the sequence π; so the descent terminates. Leaves have e-value 1, hence e+       π -value
1, while every visited node has value 0; so every visited node is the conclusion of some step of π.
Since the descent is unblocked, it ends by outputting a step s all of whose premises have value 1
and whose conclusion has value 0 (a step without premises is output at once). By agreement,
the premises of s are V -true and its conclusion V -false. By (WS), s ∈        / Ttrust and s ∈/ R∗ ; as π is
a refutation of B, s ∈ RB .
    (b) The worklist assigns each judgment of π a value at most once and re-examines a trusted
step only when one of its judgments receives a value, so the fixed point costs O(|π|φ) operations,
with one evaluation of e per judgment. The descent looks at the premises of each visited node
once, and visits at most |π| nodes. The number of judgments is at most |π| ≤ d.
    (c) If some genuine σ had s ∈ inst(σ), then s ∈ R∗ , contradicting (a).
    (d) Let σ ∈ B with s ∈ inst(σ). Let J1 be the list of judgments of π with e+          π -value 1, in the
order in which they received the value (those with initial e-value 1 first). Each member of J1 is
e-true, and then is treated as a leaf, or received value 1 by the forward rule as the conclusion
of a trusted step of π whose premises precede it in J1 . The premises of s lie in J1 . Let c0 be
the conclusion of s. Define c0 , c1 , . . . : if ci is e-false, stop; otherwise ci received value 0 by the
backward rule from a trusted step ti of π of which ci is a premise, whose conclusion ci+1 had
received value 0 strictly earlier, and whose other premises lie in J1 . Since assignment times
strictly decrease along the chain, it terminates at some e-false ck , and the ci are pairwise distinct.
They are not in J1 , because e+  π is consistent.


                                                    201
    Let πσ be the list J1 , followed by c0 (justified by s), c1 (justified by t0 ), . . . , ck (justified
by tk−1 ). Its judgments are distinct; each non-leaf judgment is the conclusion of a step whose
premises occur earlier; its leaves are e-true; its steps are s ∈ inst(σ) and trusted steps; and its
last judgment ck is e-false. So πσ is a refutation of {σ} relative to [A : D]. All its judgments are
judgments of π, and size counts distinct judgments, so |πσ | ≤ |π| ≤ d. Hence {σ} is a d-conflict.
(Under a tree-size convention this bound could fail, because the premise derivations of s and the
side premises of the chain may share judgments.)
    The Lean theorem InfLearn.Blame.LineArg.descent proves the descent for a line-list
argument under a total evaluation, with the walk length bounded by any height function that
decreases along dependencies, and LineArg.descent_not_mem proves that the step found lies
outside every rule set whose steps preserve truth. Trusted-step propagation and part (d) are not
formalized.

F.6    Proof of Lemma 7.10, and the cost of the audit
By Lemma 7.8(a),(c) each successful descent removes at least one schema, all of them fallacies,
so Σ∗ ⊆ B throughout, and there are at most |F | removals. (a) The returned B is d-clean; for
                                                       (d)
τ ∈ B \ Σ∗ , Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ⊆ B is clean by (F1), so τ ∈ Fres . (b) By Lemma 7.7 with U = B0 , A is
the intersection of the maximal clean subsets of B0 , hence clean. The left inclusion holds because
Σ∗ ⊆ B0 and Colld (B0 ) = Σ∗ ∩ Cd (B0 ). If τ ∈ A ∩ F were not residual, Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ⊆ B0 would
                                 S

contain a minimal conflict, which contains τ by Lemma 7.4(a), contradicting τ ∈ A. The last
claim is Proposition 7.6(c).
    Cost. The descent path costs at most |F | + 1 oracle calls and O((|F | + 1) d φ) evaluations
of e. The fallback needs Cd (B0 ): at most 2|B0 | oracle calls by brute force. From a cleanness
                          S

(membership) oracle, the minimal conflicts and the maximal clean sets of a monotone property
can be generated jointly in time quasi-polynomial in their total number (Bioch and Ibaraki, 1995;
Gurvich and Khachiyan, 1999), with the dualization algorithm of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996)
as the engine; the second family can be exponentially larger than the first, and both can be
exponential in |F |. At stable depth the fallback’s schema-level incompleteness is unavoidable
(Theorem 7.19(b)); its cost is the price of bags.

F.7    The voting audit
Theorem 7.12 assumes (WS) for every designated position. When some positions may be wrong,
as when an idealization is designated together with background it contradicts, the audit can vote.

Proposition F.2 (Voting audit). [T7 Prop 3.2, as repaired] Suppose at most m designated positions
violate (WS), it is not known which, and P̂ = ΣP . For each position p run the descent loop
of the audit relative to p alone, from Bp = ΣP and Blamedp = ∅, with the prefer-unblocked
oracle restricted to p. Stop when the oracle returns NONE (p is finished), when the descent
is blocked, or when ep is ill defined or e+
                                          π gives a judgment both values (then p is certified bad
and its blame is discarded); otherwise move every σ ∈ Bp with s ∈ inst(σ) into Blamedp . Let
votes(σ) = #{p : σ ∈ Blamedp }, counting blame from [∅ : ∅] as m + 1 votes if the world is known
to be truthful, and return A = ΣP \ {σ : votes(σ) ≥ m + 1}. Then (a) Σ∗ ⊆ A; (b) at most
|A|(|F | + 1) + m|Σ∗ | oracle calls are made; (c) call p complete if it is good and finished; then
A ∩ F ⊆ {τ ∈ F : #{p complete : Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is not d-clean relative to p} ≤ m}. For m = 0 and
all positions complete this is Lemma 7.10(a).


                                                  202
Proof. (a) At a good position p, every schema moved into Blamedp is a fallacy, by Lemma 7.8(c)
applied relative to p. So a genuine schema collects votes only from bad positions, of which there
are at most m. The bonus for [∅ : ∅] is used only when that position is known to be good, and
then it blames only fallacies. So every genuine schema has at most m votes and lies in A.
    (b) Every call at p either ends p’s loop or moves at least one schema out of Bp . Indeed, if
the call returns a refutation r, ep is well defined, e+  p,r is consistent and the descent is unblocked,
then the descent outputs a step s whose premises have value 1 and whose conclusion has value
0, by the argument of Lemma 7.8(a), which used only consistency and unblockedness. If s
were trusted, the forward rule would have given its conclusion value 1 as well, contradicting
consistency. So s is untrusted and lies in RBp , and some σ ∈ Bp with s ∈ inst(σ) is moved.
Hence the loop at p makes at most |Bp | + 1 ≤ |ΣP | + 1 calls, and at most |F | + 1 at a
good position, where only fallacies move. With m′ ≤ m bad positions the total is at most
(|A| − m′ )(|F | + 1) + m′ (|F | + |Σ∗ | + 1) ≤ |A|(|F | + 1) + m|Σ∗ |.
    (c) Let p be complete. Its loop ended with NONE, so its final Bp is d-clean relative to p;
and since p is good, only fallacies were moved, so Σ∗ ⊆ Bp . If τ ∈ F \ Blamedp , then τ ∈ Bp ,
and Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ⊆ Bp is d-clean relative to p by (F1). Contrapositively, each complete p relative
to which Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is not d-clean gives τ a vote. A τ ∈ A has at most m votes, which gives the
claim. For m = 0 with all positions complete, A = ΣP \ p Blamedp lies inside every final Bp , so
                                                                S

it is d-clean relative to every position; it contains Σ∗ , and each of its fallacies is residual. This is
the conclusion of Lemma 7.10(a).

    Why per-position loops (computed). One smallest-refutation query per position, followed by
voting, does not suffice. With one bad position [a, a → b : b], target {MP} and F = ∅, a
single query already makes a successful descent, which blames the genuine MP; so the number
of successful descents is not bounded by (m + 1)|F |, and votes from bad positions must be
tolerated, as in (a) and (b). With m = 1, the truthful positions p1 = [q, p → q, ¬p : p, ¬q]
and p2 = [¬r, r → t : ¬t] and the practice {MP, AC, DA}, the smallest refutation at p1 always
blames AC and hides denying the antecedent, so DA gets one vote and survives although it is
refutable at two positions. The loops above exclude already-blamed schemas, so DA is blamed at
both positions and removed, while AC, refutable at one position only, may survive.

F.8    Proof of Proposition 7.11
(a) By Definition 7.9, A is computed at t = N1 from P̂ , a function of the first N1 human steps,

most d. Primitive promoted rules would also need truth maintenance under the depth schedule.
    (b) Let h0 ∈ HS be clean at every depth with w(h0 ) > 0. A detection exhibits a refutation π

    Why joint probabilities and the residue. The conditional probability given h would be false
for randomized learners: a learner that with probability ε accepts everything from time 1 on, and
otherwise runs TTL, is (δ + ε)-sound, yet given the history “q1 accepted at time 1” it accepts
every fallacy instance. And plain Sound(RΣ ) would make the intersection trivial, since typically
∅ ∈ T , convicting TTL itself.

Proof of Proposition 7.16. Both worlds have the practice {∧I, AC} with the same frequencies
and instance laws, so a learner without refutation evidence has a view with the same law in both.

learner is incomplete under W2 . For the separation, under W1 the instance (⊤, ⊥ → ⊤ ▷ ⊥) has
true premises and a false conclusion, while under W2 its premise ⊥ ↔ ⊤ is false.

Proof of Proposition 7.17. (a) By time t at most t refutations have been exhibited, each a finite

hypothesis, the intersection of the version space of data D is D itself (Section 5.4).

Existence of s, and admissibility. If every τ -instance were in Sound(R{σ,µ} ), the refutation of

and 13 for {AC} (on A2 , where AC infers ⊥ from φ and ⊥ → φ), and {MP} is clean at every
depth. For 9 ≤ d ≤ 12 the only minimal conflict is {MP, AC}, the descent is blocked, and TTL

    Verification. These claims were computed with well-founded derivations and size counting
distinct judgments (computed), and can be checked by hand. On A1 , AC infers p from q and
p → q, and MP infers ⊥ from p and p → ⊥; the distinct judgments q, p → q, p, p → ⊥, ⊥ have
1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 9 symbols. On A2 , AC infers ⊥ from φ and ⊥ → φ, with 5 + 7 + 1 = 13
symbols. The closure of A1 under AC alone is {q, p → q, p → ⊥, p}, so {AC} has no refutation
on A1 ; and {MP} is classically sound while both contexts are satisfied by q = 1, p = 0. So for
9 ≤ d ≤ 12, Cd = {{MP, AC}}. With no world and no trusted steps e is defined only on the
assertions and on ⊥; at ⊥ the producing MP step has the unevaluated premise p and no premise
of value 0, so the descent is blocked, and the fallback returns ∅. The subsets of the practice that
are clean at every depth are ∅ and {MP}; both are admissible, since AC is classically invalid and


                                                208
MP has instances outside Sound(∅). Under ∅, MP is residual at every depth, so asserting RMP
is sound under both. For d ≥ 13, {AC} is a conflict, so {MP, AC} is no longer minimal; with
the default oracle the blocked refutation of size 9 triggers the fallback with Cd = {{AC}}, and
with the prefer-unblocked oracle the refutation on A2 has an unblocked descent that removes
AC; either way A = {MP}.

F.13     Proof of Theorem 7.20
Construction. Let Σ0 be a finite elementary formal system (Post, 1943; Smullyan, 1961) with
judgments starte that simulates the universal machine on input e from starte and contains the
rule halt ▷ ⊥, as in Theorem 6.30(a). Σ0 has no rules without premises, so without a start
judgment nothing is derivable; in particular Σ0 is clean on [∅ : ∅], and the step ▷starte is not
in Sound(RΣ0 ). Let τe = (▷starte ) and ΣPe = Σ0 ∪ {τe }, with fixed computable frequencies and
instance laws. If φe (e) diverges, ΣPe is clean and is the target, with F = ∅. If φe (e) converges,
Σ0 ∪ {τe } derives ⊥ from ∅, the target is Σ0 , F = {τe } and τe ∈ / Fres ; accepting ▷starte is then a
                 ∗
step outside R ∪ RFres = RΣ0 .
     Uniformity. For each e only one case occurs, so this is not a two-scenario argument; what
is used is that the data laws and the oracle answers Ref d (for every d, by brute force) are
computable uniformly in e.
     Reduction. Let S = {e : ∃t P(the learner accepts ▷ starte by time t) > 12 }. If φe (e) diverges,
the prover queries the genuine step ▷starte in every round, and (b) and continuity of measure give
e ∈ S. If φe (e) converges, (a) gives P(ever accepts) ≤ δ < 12 , so e ∈
                                                                      / S. Hence S is the complement
of the halting set {e : φe (e) converges}. But for a computable learner, with computable data laws,
oracle and prover, the probability of acceptance by time t is lower semicomputable uniformly
in (e, t), so S is Σ1 . This also holds if the learner escalates, because escalation answers follow
the practice by a law computable uniformly in (e, q) (Section 7.6), such as 1[q ∈ ReP ], which is
decidable by matching. Computability of the law is needed: e can be read off τe , so the law
1[φe (e) diverges] depends only on the practice, and a learner that escalates ▷starte and accepts
iff the answer is 1 would meet (a) and (b). The complement of the halting set is not Σ1 : a
contradiction.

Proof of Proposition 7.24. (a) inst(τ ) is substitution-closed and contains an unsound step, and
R∗ is complete for CPC, so by Proposition 3.5 ClR∗ ∪inst(τ ) (∅) contains ⊥. A derivation of ⊥ from
∅ is a refutation of Σ∗ ∪ {τ } relative to [∅ : ∅], so dτ is finite. For d ≥ dτ , Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ∈ Conf d
                                                                    (d)
contains some C ′ ∈ Cd , and τ ∈ C ′ by Lemma 7.4(a). Hence Fres = ∅ for d ≥ maxτ dτ , and by
Theorem 7.12(iii) and Corollary 7.13 TTL asserts only instances of Σ∗ , which are classically
valid.
     (b) {AC, K} is a conflict. K = A → (B → A) gives ⊥ → (p → ⊥) (with A = ⊥, B = p) and
(p → ⊥) → (⊥ → (p → ⊥)) (with A = p → ⊥, B = ⊥). AC, B, A → B ▷ A, applied to these
two gives p → ⊥; applied to p → ⊥ and ⊥ → (p → ⊥) it gives ⊥. This is a refutation relative to
[∅ : ∅]. It is minimal at every depth beyond its size. {K} ⊆ Σ∗ is clean (Lemma 7.4(a)). {AC} is
clean at every depth on these positions: from ∅ it derives nothing, since AC has premises, and
the closure of A1 under AC alone is {q, p → q, p → ⊥, p}. Likewise, with A1 designated, AC
followed by MP derives ⊥, and {MP} is clean, so {AC, MP} is a minimal conflict. Every descent
is blocked. With no world and no trusted steps, e is defined only on the assertions of the position


                                                 209
and on ⊥. An output step would need premises among the assertions (or none) and conclusion ⊥.
No genuine step is such a step, because the positions are satisfiable and Σ∗ is sound; and no AC
step is, because AC with premises in A1 yields only p, and AC needs premises. So the fallback
runs at B0 = ΣP , K (and with A1 also MP) lies in Colld for all large d, and Theorem 7.19(b)
applies.
     (c) τ derives the denied φ′ from the asserted Π′ in one step, a refutation of size at most
|τ | ≤ d (a closed ⊤/⊥ instance has at most the symbols of τ ). So {τ } ∈ Conf d for each τ ∈ F ,
every conflict contains a fallacy and hence a singleton conflict, and the minimal conflicts are
                                           (d)
exactly these singletons. Then Colld = ∅, Fres = ∅, and Lemma 7.10 gives A = Σ∗ on the descent
path, and also in the fallback, where Σ∗ \ Colld (B0 ) ⊆ A ⊆ Σ∗ and Colld (B0 ) ⊆ Colld = ∅.

A Hilbert illustration (computed; formulas with at most seven leaves over {p, q, ⊥}, the least bound at
which S has instances; with six leaves the conflicts are the same). Take the practice {K, S, MP, DN, AC}
with A = {[∅ : ∅], [A1 : ∅]}. The minimal conflicts are {AC, K} and {AC, MP}, the diagnoses
are {AC} and {K, MP}, and the collateral is {K, MP}. The conflict {AC, K} is the four-step
derivation from no premises in the proof of (b) above. Both conflicts are minimal at every
depth beyond their sizes, and with no world and no trusted steps every descent is blocked; so by
Theorem 7.19(b), K and MP are necessarily collateral at full depth. With the bilateral position
[A1 : p] the only minimal conflict is {AC}, and the closed instance (⊥ → ⊥, ⊥ → (⊥ → ⊥) ▷ ⊥)
of AC is falsified. Whether {S, DN, AC} is clean at every depth, i.e. whether the collateral also
contains S or DN, is open. No matrix with at most four values witnesses its cleanness, that
is, validates S and DN, with AC designation-preserving, ⊥ undesignated and A1 satisfiable
(exhaustive backtracking, 5.0M nodes for four values with three designated). A prior that prefers
fewer fallacies, Quine’s maxim of minimum mutilation, picks {AC} over {K, MP}; in the core
{MP, AC} case it is silent unless it uses frequency, which does not track validity (Section 8).

F.15     Proofs for complete decidable theories
We take Σ∗ to be a standard sequent calculus: besides being sound and complete for T -consequence,
it has →-introduction, ∀-introduction, ¬-elimination (deriving ⊢ ⊥ from ⊢ ψ and ⊢ ¬ψ), ex falso
and weakening, as derived rules at least.

Proof of Lemma 7.25. (a) Let Π ▷ j be a step. All premises W -true. Each premise Γ ⊢ φ has a
universal closure true in M; since T is complete, T proves it, and Σ∗ derives the premise from ∅.
Hence ClR∗ (Π) = ClR∗ (∅), which by soundness and completeness of Σ∗ and completeness of T
is the set of W -true sequents; so j ∈ ClR∗ (Π) iff W (j) = 1. Some premise Γ ⊢ φ W -false. By
→I and ∀I, Σ∗ derives from it the sentence ⊢ ∀x̄(γ1 → · · · → γn → φ), which is false in M. T
refutes it, so Σ∗ derives its negation; then ¬E, ex falso and weakening derive every sequent, and
ClR∗ (Π) = J. So Π ▷ j ∈ Sound(R∗ ) iff some premise is W -false or j is W -true, i.e. iff the step
preserves W -truth.
    (b) A schema is a fallacy iff it has an instance outside Sound(R∗ ), iff by (a) it has an instance
with W -true premises and a W -false conclusion. The smallest such instance is a one-step
refutation of {τ } ⊆ Σ∗ ∪ {τ } relative to [∅ : ∅], so dτ ≤ fτ .

Proof of Corollary 7.26. Under the realizability hypothesis Theorem 7.12 applies; (WS) holds
with V = truth in M (of universal closures), the positions being truthful. The oracle is exact:
if B is not d-clean it contains a fallacy (Lemma 7.4(b)), whose smallest falsified instance has


                                                  210
size fτ ≤ d and is found; if B is d-clean the search cannot find a falsified instance of size at
most d, which would be a d-refutation. Each {τ }, τ ∈ F , is then a conflict, and the proof of
Corollary 7.23 applies verbatim; truth-soundness follows from Corollary 7.13, since R∗ preserves
truth in M by Lemma 7.25(a).

Why learn at all? Here W is already a sound and complete step checker, so learning is not
needed for epistemic access. TTL adds two things. It identifies which calculus the practice uses.
And it makes deployed checking fast: schema matching takes linear time, while real quantifier
elimination is doubly exponential in the worst case (Davenport and Heintz, 1988), deciding RCF
sentences is possible in exponential space (Ben-Or et al., 1986), the first-order theory of (R, +)
                                                                    Ω(n)
already needs exponential time, and Presburger arithmetic needs 22       time (Fischer and Rabin,
1974). The audit calls W only on the few instances needed to falsify each fallacy. This dividend
is real but modest.

A restricted oracle. A restricted oracle shows the division of labour more sharply. Suppose
W evaluates only quantifier-free sentences with rational constants, and first-order logic is trusted.
The fallacy τ = (▷¬∃x (x · x = 1 + 1)) is a step without premises whose conclusion is not
quantifier-free, so it has no instance that W can evaluate: the world alone never refutes it, and
Lemma 7.25(b) fails for this oracle. The position [∃x (x · x = 1 + 1) : ∅] is truthful in R. In the
refutation “⊢ ¬∃x(x · x = 1 + 1) (by τ ); ⊢ ⊥ (by trusted ¬E, with the asserted ∃x(x · x = 1 + 1))”,
the backward rule through ¬E gives ¬∃x(. . . ) the value 0, and the descent outputs τ ’s step: {τ }
is a singleton conflict. Without trusted logic the conflict is the bag {τ, ¬E}; with the bilateral
position [∅ :⊢ ¬∃x(x · x = 1 + 1)] it is {τ }, by a one-step refutation. The position must assert
the closed sentence: under the universal-closure semantics, [x · x = 1 + 1 : ∅] would assert the
false ∀x (x · x = 2) and violate (WS). Over R, then, coherence with a designated truth catches
what this computation misses. Over N there is no converse: ∆0 computation refutes nothing
that coherence from Q does not already refute (Lemma 6.18); what it adds there is localization
(Theorem 7.27(a)).

F.16    Proof of Theorem 7.27
(a) In the refutation, τ ’s step has no premises and ∀E is trusted. The conclusion θ(n̄) is a false
∆0 sentence, so it has value 0; the backward rule through ∀E (whose only premise is ∀x̄θ; for
k variables, through each of the k instantiation steps) gives ∀x̄θ the value 0; and the descent
outputs τ ’s step, whose (empty) premise set has value 1 vacuously. The descent is unblocked, so
by Lemma 7.8(c) only schemas having ⊢ ∀x̄θ as an instance are removed, and these are fallacies;
no axiom of PA is one, since its instances are true. With the prefer-unblocked oracle, as long
as τ remains in B there is an unblocked refutation of size at most d, so the oracle returns an
unblocked one, every call removes at least one fallacy and no genuine schema, and the loop does
not fall back before τ is removed. Size. For one variable, |∀xθ| = |θ| + 2, and θ(n) replaces each
of the m occurrences of x (one symbol) by the numeral S n 0 (n + 1 symbols), so |θ(n)| = |θ| + mn.
The total is 2|θ| + mn + 2 ≤ 2|θ| + m(n + 1) + O(1). For k variables the refutation has k + 1
judgments, each of size at most |θ| + m(n + 1) + O(k). For θ(x) = x < S 5 0 (|θ| = 8, m = 1,
n = 5) the sizes are 10 and 13, total 23. Under the default tie-breaking rule a smaller blocked
refutation through learned axioms could trigger the fallback, and those axioms could become
collateral; and if the refutation ran through Q’s axioms by coherence instead of through W , the


                                                211
bag would contain them. So computation is subsumed by coherence as a source of refutations
(Lemma 6.18), but not as a source of blame.
     (b) PA ⊬ Con(PA) by Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem (Gödel, 1931), so PA+¬Con(PA)
is consistent. A refutation of Σ∗ ∪ {τ } relative to a position with ∆0 assertions and denials
would derive, in first-order logic, from PA + ¬Con(PA) and true ∆0 leaves, either ⊥ or a false ∆0
sentence. Q ⊆ PA proves every true ∆0 sentence and refutes every false one (Lemma 6.18), so in
either case PA + ¬Con(PA) would be inconsistent. Hence Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is clean at every depth and
τ ∈ Fres . Since ΣP = Σ∗ ∪ {τ } is clean at every depth, the first call Ref d (ΣP ) returns NONE at
every d, so A = ΣP ∋ τ at every depth (given P̂ = ΣP ).
     (c) Precise form. Fix a computable prenex normal form with negations pushed into the ∆0
matrix, and assert an instance of a practice axiom with Σ1 normal form ∃x̄ θ only once W has
verified a witness. Then false axioms with Σ1 normal form, ¬Con(PA) included, are never asserted,
and true ones are asserted after a witness search, with no uniform time bound; for schematic
axioms, acceptance becomes a semi-decision. The sentence ∀y ∃p (Prf PA (p, ⌜⊥⌝) ∨ y ̸= y),
equivalent to ¬Con(PA) but with a Π2 normal form, escapes the policy and is residual.
     Proof. A false sentence with Σ1 normal form ∃x̄ θ has no witness, so W never verifies one and
the instance is never asserted. A true one has a witness, which enumeration finds after finitely
many W -evaluations, with no computable bound on its size. The disguise ∀y ∃p (Prf PA (p, ⌜⊥⌝) ∨
y ̸= y) is logically equivalent to ∃p Prf PA (p, ⌜⊥⌝), i.e. to ¬Con(PA), because y ̸= y is refutable;
its prenex normal form is Π2 , so the policy does not apply; and PA plus it is consistent and
∆0 -sound, so by the argument of (b) it is residual.
     (d) Cleanness. Suppose Σ∗ ⊇ Q and Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ∪ A ∪ ¬D is consistent for every designated
[A : D]. A refutation relative to [A : D] would derive, from Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ∪ A and true ∆0 leaves,
either ⊥, or some δ ∈ D, or a false ∆0 sentence. Q proves the true ∆0 leaves and refutes false
∆0 sentences, so in each case Σ∗ ∪ {τ } ∪ A ∪ ¬D would be inconsistent. Impossibility. Let (φe )
enumerate the Σ2 sentences, let Σ∗ = PA, and consider the practices PA∪{⊢ φe }, with the practice
data given as a computable text. Suppose a computable learner, using the data, Ref d at every
depth and the ∆0 oracle, eventually and permanently asserts ⊢ φe if φe is true, and eventually
and permanently withholds it if φe is false and PA ∪ {⊢ φe } is clean at every depth. Define g(e, s):
if a refutation of PA ∪ {⊢ φe } has been found by stage s of a systematic search (computable, since
each Ref d is), output “false”; otherwise output the learner’s current verdict. A true φe makes
the practice sound, hence clean (Lemma 7.4(a)), so the search never succeeds and g converges to
“true”. A false φe either has a refutation, which the search eventually finds, or is clean, and then
the learner converges to “false”. So lims g(e, s) exists and is the truth value of φe , which makes
Σ2 -truth ∆2 by Shoenfield’s limit lemma (Shoenfield, 1959). But the set of true Σ2 sentences is
Σ2 -complete and therefore not Π2 , let alone ∆2 , by Post’s hierarchy theorem (Theorem 6.21(e)).
Randomized learners (proof sketch). If the learner is randomized and correct in the limit with
probability above 12 , the sets {e : P(eventually and permanently withholds ⊢ φe ) > 12 } and the
corresponding set for assertion are Σ2 , and the same combination would make Σ2 -truth ∆2 .
     (e) Precise form. The induction schema is not a first-order pattern: its lgg has false
instances, and the audit refutes it with singleton blame, so the asserted calculus would lack
induction. Add auxiliary decidable judgments Sub(φ, x, t, ψ) to JW and write induction as
Sub(φ, x, 0, a), Sub(φ, x, Sx, b)▷ ⊢ a ∧ ∀x(φ → b) → ∀xφ, with the human data recording the
Sub premises. This is a first-order pattern, recovered by the lgg of generic instances. Then under
(Floor) a practice has at most min(K, ⌊1/(2∆)⌋) axiom schemas, and Tk = PA + Con(PA) + · · · +
Con(Tk−1 ) is identified from positive data for every k within that bound. Without a floor there

G        Further results and proofs for Section 8
This appendix states the secondary results that Section 8 only summarizes: Lemma G.1,
Proposition G.2, Theorems G.6 and G.8, and Corollaries G.7 and G.9, the relation to the
literature on algorithmic statistics, and the further pathologies. It also proves the results of the
main text whose proofs are not given there. Proved in full in the main text are Theorem 8.7,
Corollary 8.8, and Proposition 8.10, Lemma 8.6(i)–(ii), and Theorem 8.9 outside its idealized
case. The kink rests on three lemmas, stated and proved in Appendix G.5. Appendix G.15 lists
the scripts behind the computed figures and the statements changed during verification.
    Conventions:
    • Logarithms are base 2 unless written ln.
    • κ denotes a machine constant. It absorbs O(1) terms and may grow from one result to the
      next, but it is fixed before d, n or m.
    • ph is a shortest program for h, and K(ph ) = K(h) + O(1) (Li and Vitányi, 2008).
    • Prefix complexities of concatenated self-delimiting descriptions add, up to O(1).
    • Where a result compares the class with a semimeasure or an infinite mixture, the class is
      enlarged to lower-semicomputable semimeasures and computable real-valued predictors.

Lemma G.1 (Empirical selection tracks population selection). [T5 Lemma 1.2] In the computable
version, suppose h(y | x) ≥p2−B for all h. With probability at least 1 − δ, simultaneously for
all h, |R̂N (h) − R(h)| ≤ B (ℓ(h) ln 2 + ln(2/δ))/(2N ). On this event, each minimizer ĥ of Jˆc
satisfies, for every fixed h0 ,
                                          q
                    Jc (ĥ) ≤ Φ(c) + 2B ((ℓ(h0 ) + B/c) ln 2 + ln(2/δ))/(2N ).

In particular, a unique population minimizer with gap γ is recovered once this bound is below γ.

    This is a standard Occam-type bound: Hoeffding’s inequality with a Kraft union bound.

Proof. Both minimizers exist. By Kraft, {h : ℓ(h) ≤ L} has at most 2L elements. Fix h0 . Losses
lie in [0, B], so R(h0 ), R̂N (h0 ) ≤ B. Any h with ℓ(h) > ℓ(h0 ) + B/c therefore has

                       Jc (h), Jˆc (h) ≥ cℓ(h) > cℓ(h0 ) + B ≥ Jc (h0 ), Jˆc (h0 ).

So both infima are minima over a finite set. In particular a population minimizer hc exists, and
both ℓ(hc ) and ℓ(ĥ) are at most ℓ(h0 ) + B/c.
   Uniform deviation. For a fixed h, − log h(yi | xi ) are i.i.d. in [0, B]. By Hoeffding’s inequality,

G.2    Relation to the literature
Tempered posteriors. The tempered posterior ∝ 2−ℓ i h(yi | xi )η has its MAP at the minimizer
                                                           Q

of ℓ/η + N R̂N , so the note’s λ is 1/η: a learning rate η < 1 (Grünwald, 2012; Grünwald and
van Ommen, 2017; Zhang, 2006; Bissiri et al., 2016; Bhattacharya et al., 2019). With λ = cN
the posterior tends to the non-concentrating Gibbs measure ∝ 2−(ℓ+R/c) (Catoni, 2007), whose
mode the proposal selects. SafeBayes learns η from data to repair misspecification; Theorem 8.11
suggests why no such criterion finds the note’s η, since an imitation model is well specified for
the teacher (our reading, not checked against the papers).
    Algorithmic statistics. Kolmogorov’s structure function hx (α) = min{log |S| : x ∈ S, K(S) ≤
α} lies, to logarithmic precision, above the sufficiency line K(x) − α, and, within these constraints
and to logarithmic precision, every shape is realized by the structure function of some data
(Vereshchagin and Vitányi, 2004); see also Gács et al. (2001); Vereshchagin and Shen (2017).
Set and probability models share randomness. The product-model structure function ρ× (k) =
min{R(h) : ℓ(h) ≤ k} need not have slope −1 and can kink (Theorem 8.4): that is the note’s
insight in this language. All sufficient statistics tie at λ = 1, so λ = 1 + ϵ selects roughly the

                                                    215
minimal one and larger λ selects insufficient models (proof sketch), as the note wants, since the
errors are structure. The objective cℓ + R is the algorithmic rate–distortion Lagrangian with
log-loss distortion (Vereshchagin and Vitányi, 2010); classical two-part MDL (Rissanen, 1978;
Barron and Cover, 1991; Grünwald, 2007) has λ = 1 (whether Barron and Cover also use λ > 1
we have not checked).

G.4     Universality: sequences and blocks
Proposition G.2 (The sequence pathology, exactly). [T5 Prop 2.3, as repaired] Let M be a universal
lower-semicomputable conditional semimeasure on label sequences, with M ≥ 2−K(q)−c0 q for
every computable q (Li and Vitányi, 2008), and let cM = K(M). For every λ > 1,
               λK(M) − log M(y1:N | x1:N ) ≤ λcM + K(q) + c0 − log q(y1:N | x1:N ).
This beats q’s own objective whenever K(q) > cM + (cM + c0 )/(λ − 1).
Proof. Take logarithms in the dominance inequality and add λcM .

   As λ → ∞ the threshold tends to cM , not 0. In the function case, even the universal
conditional semimeasure m(y | x) ≍ 2−K(y|x) is a fixed predictor [T5 Thm 2.4] . For binary Y we
have K(y | x) = O(1), so R(m) ≥ log2 1−21−κU > 0 for every teacher, where κU is a machine
constant.

G.5     The kink
The setting is that of Section 8.3. For a product h put sh (x) = h(0 | x) − h(1 | x) and
                ′
χa′ (x) = (−1)⟨a ,x⟩ , so that ŝh (a′ ) = Ex [sh χa′ ]. Put σh := sh χa ∈ [−1, 1], so that ŝh (a) = Ex σh .
     Overview. In (a), the true component of Pu has weight 2−u and likelihood exactly 2−nH(p) ,
and every other component disagrees with y ∗ on at least n/2 − pn points. In (b), Parseval allows
at most 22t parities to correlate at least 2−t with h, so a short h that correlated with fa would
encode a in fewer than d bits; Jensen’s inequality turns small correlation into risk near one bit;
and Hoeffding’s inequality for sampling without replacement (Hoeffding, 1963), with a counting
argument, uses the randomness of E relative to h to remove the slack 2p. Part (c) is the coding
theorem.
Lemma G.3 (List decoding; standard). [T5 Lemma 2.5a] For t ∈ N, |{a′ : ŝh (a′ ) ≥ 2−t }| ≤ 22t .
Hence, if ŝh (a) ≥ 2−t , then
                            K(a | ph ) ≤ 2t + 2 log2 (t + 1) + 2 log2 d + O(1).
Proof. Parseval gives a′ ŝh (a′ )2 = Ex [s2h ] ≤ 1, so at most 22t coefficients are at least 2−t . Given
                        P

ph , compute every ŝh (a′ ) exactly (finite rational sums), and list those that are at least 2−t . Then
specify d and t self-delimitingly, followed by the 2t-bit index of a in the list. The 2 log2 d term is
