Proof of Theorem 8.4. (a), upper bounds.
   • Pu is computable from the d − u known bits of a together with d, u and p. So K(Pu ) ≤
     d − u + κ′ , using K(p) = O(log d).
   • The true parity is a component of weight 2−u . Its likelihood is exactly (1 − p)n−pn ppn =
     2−nH(p) , because |E| = pn. Hence − log Pu (y ∗ ) ≤ u + nH(p).
   (a), lower bound on − log Pu (y ∗ ). Every other component fa′ disagrees with y ∗ on w ≥
n/2 − pn points. This is because fa ⊕ fa′ has weight n/2, and flipping E changes at most pn of
them. So the likelihood of fa′ is

                      2−nH(p) (p/(1 − p))w−pn ≤ 2−nH(p) (p/(1 − p))n(1/2−2p) ,

and therefore − log Pu (y ∗ ) ≥ u + nH(p) − log2 1 + 2u (p/(1 − p))n(1/2−2p) . The exponent is
                                                                                 

positive because p < 1/4. The last term is below 2−2800 already at d = 10, p = 1/64 (computed).
    (a), lower bound on K(Pu ). Given a program for Pu and (d, u), compute the a′ that maximizes
Pu (fa′ ), the probability of the label vector fa′ .
   • Every a′ with the true (d − u)-prefix has Pu (fa′ ) ≥ 2−u (1 − p)n , from its own component.
   • Every other a′ is at Hamming distance exactly n/2 from every component, so Pu (fa′ ) =
     (p(1 − p))n/2 .
   • The first is larger, because n2 log2 1−p  n
                                           p > 2 ≥ d ≥ u.
So the argmax has the true prefix, and d ≤ K(a) ≤ K(Pu ) + u + O(log d).
   (a), selection. For every u,

                    λK(Pu ) − log Pu (y ∗ ) ≥ λ(d − u − κ′ ) + u + nH(p) − o(1),

while the value at u = d is at most λκ′ + d + nH(p). A minimizer u∗ therefore satisfies
(λ − 1)(d − u∗ ) ≤ 2λκ′ + o(1). In the computable version the code length is exactly d − u.

G.6       Proof of Lemma 8.6(iii)
Fix z = (ℓz , rz ) ∈ Z and c > 0, and write φc (y) = ⟨(c, 1), y⟩. Compare z with the other points of
Z:
  • Points to the left, Z< = {z ′ : ℓ′ < ℓz }, a finite set. Here φc (z) ≤ φc (z ′ ) iff c ≤ σ(z ′ ) :=
    (r′ − rz )/(ℓz − ℓ′ ), strictly iff c < σ(z ′ ).
  • Points to the right, Z> = {z ′ : ℓ′ > ℓz }. Here φc (z) ≤ φc (z ′ ) iff c ≥ τ (z ′ ) := (rz −r′ )/(ℓ′ −ℓz ),
    strictly iff c > τ (z ′ ).
  • Other points with the same ℓ have a different r, and z beats them iff rz < r′ , for every c.
Let s− := minZ< σ, with s− = ∞ if Z< = ∅, and s+ := max(0, supZ> τ ). If supZ> τ > 0,
the supremum is attained, because τ (z ′ ) ≤ rz /(ℓ′ − ℓz ) and only finitely many points have
ℓ′ ≤ ℓz + rz /s for any s > 0.
    So the set of c > 0 at which z is the unique minimizing point is the open interval (s+ , s− )
when rz < r′ for all same-ℓ points, and is empty otherwise.
    If (s+ , s− ) ̸= ∅, then z is a vertex. Take c in the interval.
  • On Z + R2≥0 , φc is uniquely minimized at z, because φc (z ′ + v) > φc (z ′ ) for v ≥ 0, v ̸= 0.

  • A point of Ĉ is a finite convex combination of points of Z + R2≥0 . Its φc -value equals φc (z)
    only if every point in the combination is z. So z is the unique minimizer of φc over Ĉ.
  • Hence z is an extreme point of Ĉ, supported by a line of slope −c, i.e. a vertex of hull− (Z).
     If z is a vertex, then (s+ , s− ) ̸= ∅. First, extreme points of conv(S) lie in S, and a point
z ′ + v with v ̸= 0 is the midpoint of z ′ + v/2 and z ′ + 3v/2. So vertices lie in Z.
  • Since z ∈ hull− (Z), some c0 > 0 has z minimizing φc0 . So s+ ≤ c0 ≤ s− , and same-ℓ points
    have r′ > rz .
  • Suppose s+ = s− = c0 . Then some zL ∈ Z< has σ(zL ) = c0 , since Z< is finite, and some
    zR ∈ Z> has τ (zR ) = c0 , since the supremum is attained when positive.



                                                     220
    • Then zL , z and zR lie on one line of slope −c0 , with ℓL < ℓz < ℓR . So z is a proper convex
      combination of zL and zR , and not extreme. This is a contradiction.
     The interval and the hypothesis-level claim. The interval is (s+ , s− ), where s∓ are the absolute
slopes of the edges to the adjacent vertices; at a risk-minimal vertex s+ = 0. Hypotheses with
the same point have equal Jc for every c, so a hypothesis is the unique minimizer on the interval
iff no other hypothesis has its point.
A computed check (computed): 300 random point sets and 400 values of c each gave no minimizer
off the hull, no monotonicity violation, and every vertex selectable.

G.7     The rate threshold for arbitrary hypotheses
With ℓ = K and all hypotheses allowed, a hypothesis might share information across regions, or
learn components only partially. For independent parities neither helps, up to explicit slack.
     Take regions Xj = {j} × {0, 1}dj , j ≤ m, with µ(j, z) = πj 2−dj , and teacher y ∗ (j, z) =
⟨aj , z⟩ mod 2, with K(a1 , . . . , am ) ≥ j dj . The rate of component j is πj /dj , and ŝh,j is the
                                          P

correlation of h with aj on region j. The function ω(t) = 1 − log2 (1 + 21−t ) is the exact per-region
risk floor (Lemma G.4 with p = 0). It is increasing and concave, with ω(2) = 0.415.

G.8    Every convex frontier is realizable
Corollary G.7 (Every convex frontier is realizable, after rescaling). [T5 Cor 3.4, as repaired] Let
s1 > · · · > sm > 0 be rational and dj ≥ 1 integers, with j sj dj ≤ 1. Set πj = sj dj , and add a
                                                         P

fair-coin region of mass π0 = 1 − j πj . Let P be the convex polygon from (0, 1) whose successive
                                  P

edges have slope −sj and horizontal length dj , and which is flat at height π0 afterwards. Then
the lower boundary ρ̆ of the closure of Ĉ satisfies

                              P (k + C ′ ) − ϵ ≤ ρ̆(k) ≤ P (k − C ′ ) + ϵ,

where C ′ = O(                                                  1−dj /4 .
               P                                        P
                  j log dj + m log m + mκ) and ϵ =        j πj 2

   Scaling every dj up by L and every sj down by L makes the bands negligible. So every convex,
decreasing, piecewise-linear frontier that starts at height 1, has rational slopes and drops by at
most one bit is realized after rescaling, up to the bands. This is the product-model analogue of
the “all shapes” theorem of Vereshchagin and Vitányi (2004), with the same moral: whether a
good model is a vertex is a property of the data, not a theorem. The proof is Legendre duality.

Proof. The coin region. On the coin region every hypothesis has cross-entropy at least one bit
per unit mass, with equality iff it is uniform there. So R(h) ≥ π0 + j≥1 πj Rj (h), and the region
                                                                       P

plays no role in the complexity argument. The lower bound of Theorem G.6 therefore holds with
π0 added. The witnesses hS are uniform on the coin region, at an extra O(1) bits to recognize it.
Hence |Φ(c) − Ψ(c)| ≤ cC ′ + ϵ with Ψ(c) := π0 + j min(c dj , πj ), for all c ≥ 0. At c = 0 both
                                                       P

sides equal π0 .
    Legendre duality. Φ(c) = inf y∈Ĉ ⟨(c, 1), y⟩ is the support function of Ĉ. The lower boundary
ρ̆ of its closure is convex and lower semicontinuous, so ρ̆(k) = supc≥0 [Φ(c) − ck]. Likewise
P (k) := supc≥0 [Ψ(c) − ck].
                                                                                  P
   • Ψ is concave and piecewise linear, with breakpoints at c = sj and slope         j:sj >c dj between
     them.
   • Its conjugate P is the polygon described in the statement: it starts at P (0) = Ψ(∞) = 1,
     has an edge of slope −sj and length dj for each j in decreasing order of sj , and is flat at
     π0 afterwards. For k < 0, P (k) = +∞.
   The sandwich. Then

G.9      The note’s example, verified
Return to the setting of Theorem 8.4. Let τt = 2t + 2 log2 (t + 1) + 2 log2 d + κ and Ktot =
d + LE − δE − 2 log2 d − κ.

Theorem G.8 (Parity version of the note’s example). [T5 Thm 3.5, as repaired] For every c > 0 and
t ∈ N,
              Φ(c) ≤ min{1 + cκ, c(d + κ′ ) + H(p), c(d + LE + κ log n)}

The terms correspond to the coin, the good model and the bad model, which switch near c =
(1 − H(p))/d and c = H(p)/LE ≈ 1/n.

                  ′

where Λ = log2 (n + 1) + δE + 2 log2 d + κ + κ′ .

    So for c well inside the window (≈ 1/n, ≈ (1 − H(p))/d), i.e. with cn ≫ 1, c d ≪ 1 and p
small (the bound on ŝh (a) is vacuous once 21−H(p) − 1 ≤ 2p, e.g. at p = 0.2), every near-optimal
hypothesis (small ξ) correlates strongly with fa and memorizes almost none of the errors. Near
either end of the window the bounds become vacuous. For example, at d = 20, p = 2−10 and
κ = κ′ = ξ = 0, c = 10−4 gives ŝ ≥ 0.980 and R ≥ H(p) − 2.8 · 10−5 , and c = 10−3 gives ŝ ≥ 0.955
(computed).

Proof of Theorem G.8. Upper bound. We list the three models.
  • The coin has K ≤ κ and R = 1.
  • The good model has K ≤ d + κ′ and R = H(p) exactly, since |E| = pn.
  • The error-memorizing model y ∗ has K ≤ d + LE + κ log n (index E among the pn-subsets,
    and give pn) and R = 0.
      Lower bound. Fix h and t.
  • If K(h) ≤ d − τt , then Theorem 8.4(b) gives Jc (h) ≥ R(h) ≥ 1 − βt / ln 2.
  • Otherwise, Theorem 8.4(c) and R ≥ 0 give Jc (h) ≥ cK + max(0, (Ktot − K)/n) with
    K = K(h) > d − τt . As a function of K this is piecewise linear: its slope is c − 1/n below
    Ktot and c above. Note that Ktot − d + τt = LE − δE + s(t) ≥ 0, because LE − δE = K(E |
    a, K(a)) ≥ 0.

          – If c ≥ 1/n, the minimum over K ≥ d − τt is at K = d − τt , with value c(d − τt ) +
            (LE − δE + s(t))/n ≥ c(d − τt ) + (LE − δE − κ)/n.
          – If c < 1/n, the minimum is at K = Ktot , with value cKtot .

In every case Jc (h) is at least the minimum of the three lower-bound terms. The 2 log2 d in Ktot
and the slack in βt move the switch points only within their O(log) slack.

G.10     Proof of Theorem 8.9(ii) in the idealized setting
Let h be near-optimal, and let c be such that each of v and e satisfies the hypothesis of clause
(a) or that of clause (b) of Theorem G.6. Suppose v is learned, i.e. ŝh,v ≥ 21 .
   • Then v does not satisfy the hypothesis of (a), so it satisfies that of (b). In particular
     πv ≥ πv ω(dv /4) > c dv , i.e. πv /dv > c.
   • If e satisfied the hypothesis of (a), then πe < c de . That would give πe /de < c < πv /dv ,
     contradicting πv /dv ≤ πe /de .
   • So e satisfies the hypothesis of (b), and is learned.



G.11     Proof of Theorem 8.11
(i).
   • Monotone risk. By Lemma 8.6(ii), for grid values c1 < ci and any population minimizers h
     at c1 and h′ at ci , R(h) ≤ R(h′ ).
   • Eventually exact. For each grid value, Lemma G.1 gives Jc (ĥc ) → Φ(c) in probability.
     Only finitely many hypotheses have ℓ ≤ ℓ(h0 ) + B/c, so the gap between Φ(c) and the
     best non-minimizer is positive. Hence, with probability tending to one, ĥc is a population
     minimizer for every grid value simultaneously. Without a unique population minimizer,
     which minimizer is selected may change with N ; with one, ĥc = hc eventually.
   • Uniform validation. The selected hypotheses lie, with probability tending to one, in the
     finite set of population minimizers at the grid values. Held-out log-losses converge uniformly
     to risks over that set, since losses lie in [0, B], and its distinct risk values are separated by
     a positive gap.
So, with probability tending to one, selection by held-out log-loss picks a grid value whose selected
hypothesis has least risk among the selected ones. By the first item, which holds for any choice
of minimizers (including ties at a hull breakpoint), the smallest grid value always attains this
least risk, and it is the unique choice when its risk is strictly smallest. At finite N the second
item may fail at small c, where the bound of Lemma G.1 is weakest. That is the caveat in the
statement.
    (ii). Strict propriety holds pointwise in x (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Integrating over µ,
the teacher channel strictly maximizes the expected score among channels that differ from it

                                                 225
on a set of positive µ-mass. With a growing held-out set, empirical scores converge uniformly
over finitely many candidates. So the criterion selects, among candidates, one with the largest
expected score, i.e. the smallest divergence from P ∗ in the score’s divergence.
   (iii). Any statistic of imitation data has the same law in the two worlds of Theorem 8.9(iv),
while the good c differs between them.

G.12     Proof of Proposition 8.12
Measure log-loss relative to the option none, which gives every candidate probability 1/M .
   • G-contexts, unguarded or guarded. The σ-model gains g per step, by the definition of the
     per-step gain. Mass πG .
   • ¬G-contexts, unguarded. The teacher’s step is a non-σ step. It receives probability ε/M
     instead of 1/M , a loss of log2 (1/ε) per step. Mass π¬G .
   • ¬G-contexts, guarded. The teacher’s step receives 1/(M − 1) instead of the unguarded
     ε/M , a gain of ∆G = log2 (M/ε) − log2 (M − 1) per step over the unguarded option. Note
     ∆G > log2 (1/ε), by log2 MM−1 .
So the unguarded option lowers risk by πG g − π¬G log2 (1/ε) = kσ ρσ at cost kσ . The guard lowers
it by a further π¬G ∆G = kG ρG at cost kG . If the guarded option also models the teacher’s
alternative step in ¬G-contexts, its gain there only increases, and the argument is unchanged
with the larger ∆G .
    In (bits, risk) relative to none, the three options are therefore the points (0, 0), (kσ , −kσ ρσ )
and (kσ + kG , −kσ ρσ − kG ρG ). The middle point is a vertex of their lower hull iff ρσ > ρG .
Within the σ-applicable region apply Lemma 8.6, and across regions Theorem 8.7: if ρG < ρσ ,
the guarded option is selected for c < ρG , the unguarded one for c ∈ (ρG , ρσ ), and none for
c > ρσ .
    For the case ρG ≥ ρσ : the middle point lies on or above the chord from (0, 0) to the guarded
point. The lower hull of the three points is then that chord, with slope −(kσ ρσ + kG ρG )/(kσ + kG ),
and apart from ties the selection jumps from guarded to none at that c. In the second numerical
instance of the main text the jump is at c = (0.0022 + 0.0087)/34 ≈ 3.2 · 10−4 .

G.13     Further pathologies
These four complement Proposition 8.12 [T5 §4.4] .
    Error envelopes [T5 Prop 4.5] . Suppose the error set E lies inside a region S with K(S | f ) = kS ,
µ(S) = σ and error density θ = µ(E)/σ in S, and let p = µ(E). The hypothesis “f , with flip
rate θ on S and 0 off S” costs kS + O(1) bits more than the good model and lowers its risk from
H(p) to σH(θ) (a direct computation). So it is learned at its own rate, which can far exceed the
rate of the full error component; and if θ > 12 , the learner predicts the error label on all of S,
imitating a coarse version of the error. For example, p = 2−10 , σ = 2−8 , θ = 14 and kS = 30 give
a risk reduction of 0.0112 − 0.0032 = 0.0080 bits, a rate of 2.7 · 10−4 , against 1.1 · 10−6 for the
full error. In the note’s example E is K-random, so no such envelope exists (Theorem 8.4(c)).
Real systematic errors are the opposite case: low-complexity patterns of exactly this kind.
    Parasitic errors [T5 §4.4(d3), as repaired] . The separability of Theorem 8.7 fails when an error
is cheap given a valid rule, K(e | v) ≪ K(e): once v is included, the marginal rate of e is
re /K(e | v). The freshman’s dream is a one-symbol mutation of (ab)n = an bn ; the unguarded rule
is the guarded one minus its guard; “or as xor” is ∨ plus one clause. Valid rules thus subsidize

                                                 226
their own mis-generalizations. The selection path is the lower hull of the subset points under
the joint code, and bundles can enter it together. For example (computed), take a valid v with
kv = 10 and rv = 0.01 (rate 10−3 ), and an error e with K(e) = 100, K(e | v) = 1 and re = 0.01.
At c = 1.5 · 10−3 , relative to the empty set, {v} changes Jc by +0.005, {e} by +0.14, and {v, e}
by 11c − 0.02 = −0.0035. So {v, e} is optimal, although v’s own rate and e’s unconditional rate
(10−4 ) are both below c: the bundle’s rate 0.02/11 ≈ 1.8 · 10−3 exceeds c, and v survives only
because it buys e cheaply.
    Distribution dependence [T5 §4.4(d7)] . Rates scale with frequency under µ. A valid rule that
is rare in the training distribution, e.g. used mainly in hard problems, is discarded, and stays
discarded as N → ∞ with λ = cN . Under a shift to a distribution where it matters, the learned
norm is wrong. The verifier of Section 8.6 then stays sound but becomes incomplete; with guard
erosion it can become unsound.
    Language relativity [T5 §4.4(d6), as repaired] . Take separable components j ≤ m with risk re-
ductions rj , a target set S ◦ with rj > 0 for j ∈ S ◦ , and c > 0. Choose integers kj ≥ 0 with
kj < rj /c on S ◦ and kj > rj /c off it, and give hS length m + j∈S kj . The Kraft sum is
                                                                       P

2−m j (1 + 2−kj ) ≤ 1, so a prefix code with these lengths exists. Then Jc (hS ) is a constant
     Q

plus j∈S (c kj − rj ), whose terms are negative exactly on S ◦ , so S ◦ is the unique selection (no
     P

failures in 3000 random instances (computed)). For universal machines U and V the invariance
theorem bounds the damage: |KU − KV | ≤ cU V , so a marginal cost K(hS∪{j} ) − K(hS ) changes
by at most 2cU V , and rates by the factor k/(k ± 2cU V ). That is negligible for 10 000-bit errors
and decisive for 20-bit schemas, which is the inference-rule regime. A learner whose description
language is shaped by human concepts, for instance by pretraining on human text, therefore
gives human-natural errors short codes, and raises exactly the rates of the fallacies humans find
natural.

0}.

H.1        The abstract frame
Proof of Lemma 9.2. Both sides of K ⊆ Mod(Σ) ⇐⇒ Σ ⊆ Th(K) say that m |= σ for all
m ∈ K, σ ∈ Σ. Both maps are inclusion-reversing. Taking K = Mod(Σ) gives Σ ⊆ ThMod(Σ),
and taking Σ = Th(K) gives K ⊆ ModTh(K); so both composites are extensive and monotone.
Applying the inclusion-reversing Mod to Σ ⊆ ThModΣ gives ModThModΣ ⊆ ModΣ, and the
converse is extensivity of ModTh at ModΣ; so ModThMod = Mod, and dually ThModTh = Th.
Idempotence of both composites follows. The fixed points of Th ◦ Mod are exactly the sets
Th(K), those of Mod ◦ Th the sets Mod(Σ), and the two identities show that Mod and Th are
mutually inverse on them. Fixed-point sets of closure operators on power sets are closed under
arbitrary intersections, so they are complete lattices.

Proof of Theorem 9.5. We first record a consequence of finitarity: the union U of a nonempty

it has a maximal member Tσ . Then Tσ =   ̸ S, and every closed T ′ ⊋ Tσ contains σ by maximality;

Details for Proposition 9.6. Soundness. Every Boolean valuation is a model of IPC, so each
Th({v}) is IPC-closed. Failure of strong completeness. p ∨ ¬p is true in every Boolean valuation,
and refuted in the three-element Heyting algebra by h(p) = 12 , so IPC ⊬ p∨¬p. Weak completeness.
The hypotheses of Theorem 9.5(c) hold with F = {⊥}, and Th({v}) ̸∋ ⊥. Let T be a maximal
proper IPC-closed set; proper means consistent, as {⊥} is explosive. If φ ∈/ T , then CIPC (T ∪ {φ})
is closed and strictly larger than T , hence equals Fm; so T, φ ⊢IPC ⊥ and, by the deduction
theorem, ¬φ = φ → ⊥ ∈ T . So φ ∈ T or ¬φ ∈ T , whence φ ∨ ¬φ ∈ T for every φ. As
consequence relations CPC = IPC + EM, where EM is the set of instances of excluded middle;
so CCPC (T ) = CIPC (T ∪ EM) = CIPC (T ) = T ̸∋ ⊥. Thus T is CPC-consistent, and maximal
CPC-consistent (any CPC-consistent superset is IPC-consistent), hence T = v −1 (1) for a Boolean
v. Theorem 9.5(c) concludes. Alternatively, weak completeness follows from Glivenko’s theorem
(Glivenko, 1929).

Proof of Lemma 9.7. Let T be maximal among Cn2 -theories omitting φ, and suppose neither ψ
nor ¬ψ is in T . By maximality φ ∈ Cn2 (T ∪ {ψ}) and φ ∈ Cn2 (T ∪ {¬ψ}). By proof by cases,
Cn2 (T ∪ {ψ}) ∩ Cn2 (T ∪ {¬ψ}) = Cn2 (T ) = T , so φ ∈ T , a contradiction. Hence T is complete
(it contains ψ or ¬ψ for every ψ). Since T ≠ Fm it is consistent, and a complete consistent
theory is maximal consistent.

Proof of Corollary 9.9. Soundness, ⟨S⟩ ⊆ Th(Mod(S)): the sequents valid in every v ∈ Mod(S)

Proof of Theorem 9.10. Syntactic closure. By Corollary 9.9, Th ◦ Mod on sets of sequents is
S 7→ ⟨S⟩, so its fixed points are exactly the Scott relations. Semantic closure. For V ⊆ 2Fm ,
Mod(Th(V )) = V . The set Mod(Th(V )) is an intersection of the sets {v : v |= Γ ▷ ∆}, each
of which is clopen (it depends on finitely many coordinates); so it is closed, and it contains V ;
hence it contains V . Conversely, let w ∈/ V . Some basic open neighbourhood of w, determined
by finitely many coordinates, misses V ; it has the form U (Γ, ∆) = {v : v[Γ] = 1, v[∆] = 0} with
Γ = w−1 (1) ∩ E, ∆ = w−1 (0) ∩ E for a finite E ⊆ Fm. Since U (Γ, ∆) ∩ V = ∅, every v ∈ V
satisfies Γ ▷ ∆, so Γ ▷ ∆ ∈ Th(V ); and w ∈ U (Γ, ∆) violates it. So w ∈    / Mod(Th(V )). This
is Lemma 6.23(a); it is formalized as Bilateral.Val_Th for sequents over an arbitrary set Fm
(and as Carnap.Val_mrel for the propositional language). Duality. By Lemma 9.2, Mod = Val
and Th are mutually inverse inclusion-reversing bijections between the fixed points on the two
sides, i.e. between Scott relations and closed subsets of 2Fm .

Scope. For any single finite agenda (a union of complementary pairs) and negation-coherent P ,
the finitely many rational inequalities defining ΠF (its facets, plus its affine hull when it is not
full-dimensional) give finitely many counting sequents that characterize coherence (Theorem 9.12;
negation coherence is needed, since counting sequents alone cannot impose P (φ) + P (φ∗ ) ≤ 1).
What Theorems 9.14 and H.1 rule out is a bound on arity or threshold that works uniformly
across agendas (Fk needs arity k and threshold k − 1). Moreover, deciding coherence on arbitrary
agendas is NP-hard (Georgakopoulos et al., 1988) (P (φ) = 1, P (φ∗ ) = 0 is coherent iff φ is
satisfiable), so no efficiently checkable constraint family characterizes it unless P = NP. Closing
the agenda changes the picture:

Proposition H.2 (On logically closed agendas, local additivity suffices). [T6 Prop 3.6] If F
represents a finite Boolean subalgebra of the Lindenbaum algebra and P respects equivalence, then P
is coherent iff P ≥ 0, P (⊤) = 1 and P (φ) = P (φ∧ψ)+P (φ∧¬ψ) for all φ, ψ ∈ F ; each constraint
mentions at most three formulas, and the additivity identity P (A ∧ B) + P (A ∨ B) = P (A) + P (B)
from the probing notes follows from them.

                   P

v(φ ∧ ¬ψ) for every Boolean v. (⇐) Taking φ = ψ = ⊤ gives P (⊤) = P (⊤) + P (⊥), so P (⊥) = 0.
Let a1 , . . . , aN be the atoms (minimal nonzero elements) of the finite Boolean algebra F ; distinct
atoms are disjoint, and every nonzero element lies above some atom. Splitting successively,

Lemma H.3 (Elementary consequences of Gaifman coherence). Let P satisfy (G1), (G2). Then:
(i) P (¬φ) = 1−P (φ); (ii) if ⊢ φ ↔ ψ then P (φ) = P (ψ); (iii) if ⊢ φ → ψ then P (φ) ≤ P (ψ); (iv)
max(P (φ), P (ψ)) ≤ P (φ∨ψ) ≤ P (φ)+P (ψ); (v) P (φ)+P (ψ)−1 ≤ P (φ∧ψ) ≤ min(P (φ), P (ψ)).

Proof. (i) Apply (G2) and (G1) to φ ∨ ¬φ. (ii) φ ∨ ¬φ and ψ ∨ ¬φ are both provable, and both
pairs are provably exclusive; so P (φ) + P (¬φ) = 1 = P (ψ) + P (¬φ). (iii) ψ is provably equivalent
to φ ∨ (ψ ∧ ¬φ), a provably exclusive disjunction, so P (ψ) = P (φ) + P (ψ ∧ ¬φ) ≥ P (φ) by (ii)
and (G2). (iv) The lower bound is (iii). For the upper bound, P (φ ∨ ψ) = P (φ) + P (ψ ∧ ¬φ) ≤

                                                 234
P (φ) + P (ψ) by (ii), (G2) and (iii). (v) The upper bound is (iii). For the lower bound,
1 − P (φ ∧ ψ) = P (¬φ ∨ ¬ψ) ≤ P (¬φ) + P (¬ψ) by (i), (ii), (iv).

Proof of Theorem 9.15. (⇐) If P (φ) = µ([φ]): a provable φ lies in every complete consistent
theory, so [φ] = SL ; and if ⊢ ¬(φ ∧ ψ), then [φ] ∩ [ψ] = ∅ and [φ ∨ ψ] = [φ] ∪ [ψ]. (⇒) By the
completeness theorem, [φ] = [ψ] iff ⊢ φ ↔ ψ, and [φ] ∩ [ψ] = ∅ iff ⊢ ¬(φ ∧ ψ). Every clopen subset
of SL is compact, hence a finite union of basic clopens, hence of the form [φ]. So µ0 ([φ]) := P (φ)
is a well-defined function on the clopen algebra (Lemma H.3(ii)), with µ0 (SL ) = P (⊤) = 1,
nonnegative, and finitely additive by (G2). It is countably additive on the clopen algebra: if
      F
[φ] = n [φn ], compactness of [φ] and openness of the [φn ] give a finite subcover, and disjointness
makes all other [φn ] empty. By Carathéodory’s extension theorem µ0 extends to a probability on
the σ-algebra generated by the clopens. Since L is countable there are countably many clopens,
and they form a basis, so every open set is a countable union of clopens and this σ-algebra is the
Borel σ-algebra. Uniqueness: the clopens form a π-system generating it (π–λ theorem).

Proof of Theorem 9.16. Every sentence is provably equivalent to one built from atomic sentences
by ¬, ∧, ∃, and both P (Lemma H.3(ii)) and truth in N respect provable equivalence; so it suffices
to treat such sentences. We show P (φ) = [N |= φ] by induction on the number of logical symbols,
simultaneously for all such sentences. Atomic sentences are quantifier-free. A true one has P = 1
by hypothesis. If σ is false, ¬σ is a true quantifier-free sentence, so P (σ) = 1 − P (¬σ) = 0.
Negation: P (¬φ) = 1 − P (φ) (Lemma H.3(i)). Conjunction: if P (φ), P (ψ) ∈ {0, 1}, the
bounds of Lemma H.3(v) coincide and give P (φ ∧ ψ) = min(P (φ), P (ψ)). Existential: numerals
i = S · · · S0 contain no logical symbols, so each instance φ(i) has fewer logical symbols than
∃x φ(x), and by induction P (φ(i)) = [N |= φ(i)]. By Lemma H.3(iv), applied repeatedly,
maxi≤n P (φ(i)) ≤ P ( i≤n φ(i)) ≤ i≤n P (φ(i)), so P ( i≤n φ(i)) = maxi≤n P (φ(i)) ∈ {0, 1}.
                        W            P                    W

By the Gaifman condition, P (∃x φ(x)) is 1 iff some φ(i) is true in N, iff N |= ∃x φ(x), because
every natural number is the value of a numeral.

Proof of Corollary 9.17. We use the following from Garrabrant et al. (2016): a market is a
computable sequence of rational pricings (Pn ); by Convergence and Limit Coherence (Garrabrant
et al. 2016, Thms 4.1.1, 4.1.2) the limit P∞ (φ) = limn Pn (φ) exists and is a coherent probability
relative to Γ; and by Non-Dogmatism (Garrabrant et al. 2016, Thm 4.6.2) Γ ⊬ ¬φ implies
P∞ (φ) > 0. By Limit Coherence, P∞ is Gaifman-coherent and gives 1 to every theorem of Γ,
in particular to every true quantifier-free sentence, which Q ⊆ Γ proves. Suppose it satisfied
the Gaifman condition. Then P∞ = δTh(N) by Theorem 9.16. Two arguments refute this. Via
Non-Dogmatism. By the Gödel–Rosser theorem (Gödel, 1931; Rosser, 1936), the consistent
r.e. Γ ⊇ Q is incomplete: some σ has Γ ⊬ σ and Γ ⊬ ¬σ. Let ψ be whichever of σ, ¬σ is false
in N. Then Γ ⊬ ¬ψ (as ¬¬σ is equivalent to σ), so P∞ (ψ) > 0 = δTh(N) (ψ). Via ∆2 . Since
(n, φ) 7→ Pn (φ) is computable, “Pn (φ) > 21 ” is decidable. If the limit were δTh(N) , then φ ∈ Th(N)
iff ∃N ∀n ≥ N Pn (φ) > 12 (a Σ2 condition) iff ∀N ∃n ≥ N Pn (φ) > 21 (a Π2 condition): if
P∞ (φ) = 1 both hold, and if P∞ (φ) = 0 neither does. So Th(N) would be ∆2 , contradicting
Tarski’s theorem that Th(N) is not arithmetical. The general statement. The ∆2 argument
used only that the credence is the pointwise limit of a computable sequence of rational-valued
functions, that it is coherent, and that it gives 1 to every true quantifier-free sentence; so no
such credence satisfies the Gaifman condition. The quantifier-free hypothesis is needed. Let T
be the theory of the one-element structure, in which S0 = 0 = 0 + 0 = 0 · 0. T is decidable,
so δT is computable and coherent; and it satisfies the Gaifman condition with respect to the


                                                 235
numerals, because the only element is the value of a numeral. It fails the hypothesis only by
giving P (0 = S0) = 1.

for every i ∈ D iff the system is D-coherent. (b) Let context i have consistent Ki with Ki ⊬ p
and no premises (Γi = ∅), and add the single non-monotone bridge “i:p if not i:p” (negation
as failure). Then Ki is consistent, so the context is coherent without its bridge, yet there is no
equilibrium. So existence for default-style bridges needs an extra condition, such as stratification
or the absence of odd loops through negation as failure; stratification is sufficient, not necessary,
and coherence alone does not supply it.

Proof of Proposition H.5. Write R(S)i for the right-hand side of the equilibrium equation, and
T = Der(Γ). (a) T ⊇ R(T ): each Ti is Ci -closed and contains Ki , Γi and, by (Br), the head of
every bridge rule whose premises lie in T . Conversely the family R(T ) contains K ∪ Γ, is locally
closed, and is bridge-closed: a rule whose premises lie in R(T ) ⊆ T has its premises in T , so its
head lies in R(T ) by definition. By leastness of T , T ⊆ R(T ). So T = R(T ) is an equilibrium.
Any equilibrium S = R(S) is locally closed, contains K ∪ Γ and is bridge-closed, so S ⊇ T . Hence
a D-consistent equilibrium forces T to be D-consistent, and conversely T itself is an equilibrium.
(b) If p ∈ Si , the rule is inapplicable, so Si = Ci (Ki ) ̸∋ p; if p ∈
                                                                      / Si , the rule fires and p ∈ Si .
Either way Si ̸= R(S)i .

Theorem H.6 (Local-to-global on trees). [T6 Thm 4.6] Let the contexts be the vertices of a finite
tree, context i classical propositional over atoms Ai with a consistent closed theory Ti . Assume
running intersection ({i : a ∈ Ai } is connected for each atom a) and mutual conservativity on
edges (Ti ∩ L(Ai ∩ Aj ) = Tj ∩ L(Ai ∩ Aj )). Then every model of every Ti extends to a valuation
satisfying all Tj .

   This is the join-tree, or iterated Robinson-consistency, argument (cf. Beeri et al. 1983):
conservativity makes model sets agree on overlaps, and models glue breadth-first.

Proof. Projection lemma. For a consistent closed theory T over atoms A and B ⊆ A: Mod(T )|B =
ModB (T ∩ L(B)). The inclusion ⊆ is clear. For ⊇, let a B-valuation w satisfy T ∩ L(B), and
suppose T together with the literals over B true in w were unsatisfiable. By compactness,
T ⊢ ¬(l1 ∧ · · · ∧ lr ) for some literals lk true in w; this sentence lies in T ∩ L(B) and is false in w,
a contradiction. By the lemma, mutual conservativity on an edge {i, j} says Mod(Ti )|Ai ∩Aj =
Mod(Tj )|Ai ∩Aj . Gluing. Root the tree at i0 and let mi0 |= Ti0 be given; assign the atoms of Ai0
accordingly. Visit the remaining vertices in breadth-first order. When c is visited, its parent
p has been visited and its children have not, so p is the only visited neighbour of c and the
tree path from c to any visited vertex passes through p. If an atom a ∈ Ac is already assigned,
it lies in Ad for some visited d; by running intersection it lies in every Ae on the path from c
to d, in particular in Ap . So the assigned atoms of Ac lie in Ac ∩ Ap . After p was visited the
global assignment restricted to Ap was a model mp |= Tp , and assigned atoms never change. So
the current assignment on Ac ∩ Ap is mp |Ac ∩Ap ∈ Mod(Tp )|Ac ∩Ap = Mod(Tc )|Ac ∩Ap , and some
mc |= Tc agrees with it; extend the assignment by mc . Atoms in no Ai are assigned arbitrarily.
At the end the assignment restricted to each Ac is mc |= Tc .

    contexts_local_global.py checks the theorem on one fixed three-node path cover with
7,131 random local-theory systems and on 2,000 random tree covers with 2–5 nodes, with no
failure; a negative control without running intersection fails in 437 of 2,000 cases.




                                                  237
Relation to the context-tree calculus (proof sketch). The context-tree calculus[L7 §8] from
which Definition 11.13 is adapted has stipulations (local axioms), imports π(c):φ ⇒ c:φ for φ in the
import filter Fc , discharge c:ψ ⇒ π(c):A → ψ, and side-conditioned export c:φβ (t), π(c):σβ (t) ⇒
π(c):εβ (t). All are monotone bridge rules, so it is an MC system, and Theorem 9.19 is its
completeness theorem for local-models semantics with bridges read as compatibility constraints;
there an exported ε shrinks the parent’s belief state. The calculus’s own semantics differs: the
models of the root are fixed by background and observations and do not depend on exports, and
bridges are required to be sound; soundness for that semantics holds when every step and export
instance is sound. The two semantics coincide when the local consequence is the complete base
logic and every step and export instance is sound: then Tc = Th(Modct (c)) for every c, where
Modct is the model class of the calculus’s own semantics, ⊆ is its soundness proposition, and ⊇
goes by induction down the tree (at the root by local completeness; an idealized child imports
exactly Fc ∩ Tπ(c) ; a supposition child imports all of Tπ(c) and its assumption). Without that
hypothesis they differ: if an unsound export yields @:Q = 5 while background and observations
prove Q = 3, MC derives @:⊥ and cΓ@ = ∅, as Theorem 9.19 requires, while the root’s model class
in the calculus’s own semantics stays nonempty. For supposition contexts with full import, the
canonical chain always satisfies cΓc = cΓπ(c) ∩ Mod(A).

H.5     Learned calculi
Proof of Theorem 9.25. (a) is the Zorn step in the proof of Theorem 9.5(a), applied to the
closed set CR (A) and σ = ⊥ (§H.1). (b) If φ ∈ CR (Γ) and σΓ ⊆ T , structurality gives
σφ ∈ CR (σΓ) ⊆ CR (T ) = T ; this works for any CR -theory T ⊇ A omitting ⊥. (c) is Theorems 9.8
and 9.11.

Existence of the Leibniz congruence. The join of a family of congruences of A is the
transitive closure of their union. If each congruence in the family is compatible with D, then a
and b related by the join are connected by a chain a = c0 θ1 c1 · · · θr cr = b with each θk in the
family; each step preserves membership in D, so the join is compatible. The join of all compatible
congruences is therefore the largest one.

Proof of Theorem 9.26. (a) Claim: Ω(T ) = h−1 (ΩA D), where h−1 (θ) = {(a, b) : (ha, hb) ∈ θ}.
The preimage of a congruence under a homomorphism is a congruence. It is compatible
with T : if (ha, hb) ∈ ΩA D and a ∈ T , then ha ∈ D, so hb ∈ D and b ∈ T . Maximality:
let θ′ be any congruence of Fm compatible with T . The kernel ker h is compatible with T ,
as T = h−1 (D) is a union of ker h-classes, so θ′′ = θ′ ∨ ker h is compatible with T . Let
θA = {(ha, hb) : (a, b) ∈ θ′′ }. It is reflexive because h is onto, and symmetric. It is transitive:
if (ha, hb), (hb′ , hc) ∈ θA come from pairs in θ′′ with hb = hb′ , then b θ′′ b′ because ker h ⊆ θ′′ ,
so a θ′′ c. It is compatible with the operations: if (xl , yl ) ∈ θA come from (al , bl ) ∈ θ′′ , then for
an operation f , (f (x̄), f (ȳ)) = (hf (ā), hf (b̄)) with f (ā) θ′′ f (b̄). And it is compatible with D:
if (ha, hb) ∈ θA comes from (a, b) ∈ θ′′ and ha ∈ D, then a ∈ T , so b ∈ T and hb ∈ D. Hence
θA ⊆ ΩA D, and θ′ ⊆ θ′′ ⊆ h−1 (θA ) ⊆ h−1 (ΩA D). Isomorphism. Define [a]Ω(T ) 7→ [ha]ΩA D . By
the claim it is well defined and injective; it is onto because h is; it is a homomorphism because h
is; and it maps T /Ω(T ) onto D/ΩA D because a ∈ T iff ha ∈ D. If ⟨A, D⟩ is reduced, ΩA D is
the identity and the right-hand side is ⟨A, D⟩. (b) A maximal consistent theory of CPC is v −1 (1)
for a Boolean homomorphism v : Fm → 2. This v is onto, since v(p ∨ ¬p) = 1 and v(p ∧ ¬p) = 0.

The matrix ⟨2, {1}⟩ is reduced: the only congruence of 2 besides the identity identifies 0 with 1,
which is not compatible with {1}. Apply (a).

the models of first-order logic plus the schema are exactly the one-element structures, and a
designated context asserting two distinct objects has none.

H.6      Term models, non-standardness and pins
This subsection expands the paragraph “What pins the intended model” of §9.5.

First-order term models. For a consistent first-order theory, the Lindenbaum construction
is Henkin’s (Henkin, 1949): witnesses, a complete Henkin theory, closed terms modulo provable
equality (the Leibniz reduction). A note on consistency-based probing tentatively argues (“I
think this is an argument that”) that “any assignment of truth-values to sentences which does
not violate inference rules can be extended to a full model (this is cool because a model also
needs to assign actual functions and objects . . . )”.12 The argument goes through for complete
consistent assignments: the objects are classes of witness terms. If the assignment makes ∃x φ(x)
true and every named instance false, the model needs unnamed objects, the Gaifman failure of
Corollary 9.17.

Theorem H.7 (Prime models). [T6 Thm 5.5] (known) For complete consistent T ⊇ PA the defin-
able elements of any model of T form the prime model K(T ), unique up to isomorphism and
 12
      ai/DLK/logic.md.



                                                 239
elementarily embeddable in every model of T (Kaye, 1991); K(Th(N)) = N; if ¬Con(PA) ∈ T ,
K(T ) is non-standard.

    For the last clause: “the least code of a PA-proof of 0 = 1” is definable, while T refutes each
standard instance Prf(n, ⌜0=1⌝), whose negation is a true ∆0 sentence (PA being consistent) and
so provable in Q ⊆ T . This is the precise form of the notes’ Gödel-sentence footnote: a complete
coherent theory has a canonical thing it talks about, the objects it can define, and the “proof” is
one of them, a definable non-standard number.

Two layers of non-standardness. (i) Coherent but false: PA + ¬Con(PA) is consistent, false,
and even Π1 -sound (if it proves a Π1 sentence π, then PA ⊢ Con(PA) ∨ π; were π false, PA would
prove the true Σ1 sentence ¬π and hence Con(PA), against Gödel’s second incompleteness theo-
rem). This is finitary and comes from incompleteness (coherence is not truth, Theorem 6.21(b)).
(ii) True but not categorical: Th(N) itself has non-standard models, a limit phenomenon from
compactness. Pinning comes in levels: P0 coherent (a model exists); P1 complete (all models
elementarily equivalent; for logics, Post-complete, Theorem 6.13); P2 κ-categorical; P3 categorical
(unique model up to isomorphism; for calculi, all points reduce to one matrix, Proposition 9.27).

Theorem H.8 (Compactness barrier). [T6 Thm 5.6] (known) A first-order theory with an infinite
model has models of every infinite cardinality ≥ |L| (Löwenheim–Skolem–Tarski), so no first-order
mode of talking reaches P3 for an infinite structure.

    Every finite structure in a finite language, by contrast, is characterized up to isomorphism by
one sentence. In the icosahedron example of the notes,13 after the physical icosahedron explodes
the mode of talking stays coherent and its object is still pinned up to isomorphism; the caveat
bites only for infinite objects.

Theorem H.9 (Computability barrier). [T6 Thm 5.7, as repaired] Let S be a decidable set of finite
syntactic objects and K an intended class of models. If some calculus has an r.e. set of incoherent
finite sets, and a finite X ⊆ S is incoherent iff it has no model in K, then {X : X has a K-model}
is co-r.e. (Π1 ). Consequently no such calculus exists for (a) arithmetic with K = {N} (Th(N)
is not arithmetical); (b) Diophantine equations with K = {Z} (solvability is Σ1 -complete,
Matiyasevich 1970); (c) first-order sentences in a vocabulary with a binary relation symbol, with
K the finite structures (finite satisfiability is Σ1 and undecidable, Trakhtenbrot 1950; for monadic
vocabularies it is decidable). (d) For K all structures, satisfiability is Π1 , as Gödel’s theorem
requires; for polynomial equations over k̄ it is decidable.

Proof. “No K-model” is “incoherent”, which is r.e. In (b), (c) the set is also Σ1 , hence would be
decidable; in (a) Th(N) would be Π1 , contradicting Tarski’s undefinability theorem (e.g. Boolos
et al. 2007).

    This is the textbook argument “a complete r.e. calculus makes semantic consequence r.e.”;
what is new is the framing. For any computable notion of coherence, “coherent iff there is
something it could be talking about” can hold only if having such a something is a Π1 property.
“Having some model” is Π1 ; “having the standard model”, “having an integer solution” and
“having a finite model” (in a vocabulary with a binary relation symbol) are not. The proposition
is true exactly to the extent that “something” is construed liberally.
  13
       philosophy/philosophy of language/math is a mere string game iff everything is.md.


                                                  240
Proposition H.10 (Anchoring pins exactly the definable vocabulary). [T6 Prop 5.8, reading as repaired]
Let Lo ⊆ L be the anchored (world-hooked) vocabulary and T an L-theory. Any two models of
T with the same universe and the same interpretation of Lo coincide iff every symbol of L is
explicitly T -definable from Lo (Beth, 1953).

Reading. Beth’s theorem quantifies over all models of T , i.e. over every possible anchoring
structure: anchoring determines the rest of the language uniformly, whatever the anchoring
structure iff the rest is definable. Over the actual structure pinning can hold without definability:
if T says that R is a nonempty initial segment of < without a largest element, then over (N, <)
the only expansion is R = N, while over ω + ω both R = ω and R = ω + ω work. Undefinable
theoretical terms are multiply realizable over some anchoring, though perhaps not over the actual
one (the Ramsey–Lewis situation, Lewis 1970).

How are the natural numbers pinned down? The notes ask this of numbers as pinned
down “in a brain, to a thinker, or something”, adding “is there a way they are the ‘lowest-
complexity-structure’ which satisfy some axioms??”.14 We answer only the model-theoretic
version. Coherence and first-order completeness cannot do it (Theorems H.8 and H.9). The
known pins each add something: second-order induction (Dedekind, 1888) adds quantification over
all subsets, and no complete r.e. calculus exists for its consequence, as Theorem H.9(a) predicts;
internal categoricity (Parsons, 1990; McGee, 1997; Button and Walsh, 2018) pins the structure
relative to the available language, not the theory. Initiality (N is the initial (0, S)-algebra, the
least Herbrand model of {N (0), N (x) → N (Sx)}, van Emden and Kowalski 1976, and an initial
segment of every model of PA) adds a universal property, “nothing else is a number”, which is not
first-order. The ω-rule, or Gaifman condition, adds an infinitary rule that no limit-computable
credence of the relevant kind obeys (Corollary 9.17). World anchoring by computation adds
nothing beyond coherence with Q (Lemma 6.18). And:
Theorem H.11 (Tennenbaum). [T6 §5.5] (known) In no countable non-standard model of PA is
addition computable, and in none is multiplication computable (Tennenbaum 1959; the separate
statements for + and × are due to Kreisel and McAloon, see Kaye 1991). Hence N is the unique
computable model of PA up to isomorphism.
    This is a theorem-level “yes” to the “lowest-complexity structure” question, with two caveats.
First, “computable” is defined using the meta-language’s natural numbers, a point the notes
make about the meta-syntax’s N in general.15 Second, the axioms matter: weaker theories
such as open induction have computable non-standard models (Shepherdson, 1964). Every pin
uses something beyond finitary computable coherence: second-order quantification, a universal
property, a complexity bound measured in N, or an infinitary rule. Theorems H.8 and H.9 say
this is forced.

I.2    Identification
Proposition I.1 (No learner sees past the shadow; trivial). [T4 Prop 3.2, repaired] Suppose the
law of the practice data is a function of Stgh∗ and the history, escalation and link answers are
Stgh∗ -labels, the law of the object data (which occurrences are shown or queried, and their values)
is a function of Vh∗ and the history, A does not depend on the target, and queries come from the
learner or from provers that depend on the target only through its shadow. If h ≡g h′ , every data
sequence has the same probability under target h as under h′ , so no learner distinguishes them.
The closure-level version replaces Stg by |= and ≡g by ≡∞ .

Proof of Proposition I.1. Write the interaction as a sequence of rounds. In round k + 1 the
learner (and any prover whose strategy depends on the target only through its shadow) issues
queries Qk+1 drawn from a kernel that depends only on the history Hk and its own coins; then
the environment issues a datum Dk+1 . By the assumptions, the conditional law of Dk+1 given
(Hk , Qk+1 ) is K(sh, Hk , Qk+1 ) for a kernel K and the shadow sh of the target: practice data
depend on Stgh∗ and the history; escalation and link answers are Stgh∗ -labels; object data depend


                                                       243
on Vh∗ and the history; and paradoxes are computed by the learner from the fixed family A and
the hypotheses themselves, independently of the target. (Since h ≡g h′ includes agreement on
coherence, the same A satisfies the designation promise under both targets.) Let Ph be the law
of the interaction under target h. By induction on k, Ph and Ph′ agree on (Hk , Qk+1 ): the step
from k to k + 1 composes the same kernels. Hence they agree on all cylinder sets, and so on the
whole sequence. Any learner’s output is a function of the history and its coins, so it has the same
law under h and h′ . The closure-level version is the same argument with |= in place of Stg .

Proof of Lemma 10.13. Write D = Dh and T = Th .
    (i) ⊆: let v = vM ◦ ρh with M |= T . Since T ⊢ ρh (∼x) ↔ ¬ρh (x), v(∼x) = 1 − v(x). If
Γ ⊆ v −1 (1) is finite and Γ |=h y, then M |= ρh Γ and T ∪ ρh Γ |= ρh y, so v(y) = 1.
    ⊇: let v be a coherent valuation and Θ := T ∪ {ρh (x) : v(x) = 1}. Suppose Θ is inconsistent.
By compactness some finite Γ ⊆ v −1 (1) makes T ∪ ρh Γ inconsistent, so Γ |=h y for every y ∈ D.
Pick x ∈ D (here D ̸= ∅ is used); one of x, ∼x has v-value 0, call it y; but Γ |=h y forces v(y) = 1,
a contradiction. So Θ has a model M . If v(x) = 1 then M |= ρh (x). If v(x) = 0 then v(∼x) = 1,
so M |= ρh (∼x) and hence M |= ¬ρh (x). Thus v = vM ◦ ρh ∈ Vh .
    (ii) (⇒) is (i) ⊆, together with the domain clause in the definition of |=h . (⇐) If Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ D
and Γ ̸|=h y, then T ∪ ρh Γ ∪ {¬ρh y} is consistent, by completeness; a model M of it gives
v = vM ◦ ρh ∈ Vh with v(Γ) = 1 and v(y) = 0.
    (iii) A is h-coherent iff ⊥ ∈/ ClRh (ρh A) iff T ∪ ρh A is consistent iff it has a model M , iff
vM ◦ ρh is a member of Vh with v(A) = 1. For the second equivalence: if A is coherent, pick
x ∈ D; in a model of T ∪ ρh A one of x, ∼x is false, call it y, and then A ̸|=h y. If A is incoherent,
T ∪ ρh A is inconsistent and A |=h y for every y ∈ D.
    The converses. If Vh ̸= ∅, D is the common domain of its members and (ii) recovers |=h .
Coherence of finite subsets of D recovers |=h , since for Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ D, Γ |=h y iff T ∪ ρh Γ ∪ {¬ρh y}
is inconsistent iff Γ ∪ {∼y} is incoherent. That neither holds unconditionally: two hypotheses
with inconsistent theories and different domains both have V = ∅; and two hypotheses that differ
only on steps avoiding every member of a fixed A agree on coherence on A.

   The key step in Theorem 10.14 is the following lemma.
Lemma I.2 (Upper bracket). Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 10.14, and let h ∈ H have
Dh ⊇ D∗ . Call an h∗ -datum the restriction of some u ∈ Vh∗ to a finite subset of D∗ .
  (i) If |=h |D∗ ̸⊆ |=h∗ , some h∗ -datum refutes h.
 (ii) If |=h |D∗ ⊆ |=h∗ , no h∗ -datum refutes h, and h is coherent on every finite A ⊆ D∗ on which
      h∗ is coherent.
Proof. (i) Take (Γ ▷ y) ∈ |=h \ |=h∗ with Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ D∗ . By Lemma 10.13(ii) for h∗ , some u ∈ Vh∗
has u(Γ) = 1 and u(y) = 0. Let v := u|Γ∪{y} , an h∗ -datum with dom v ⊆ Dh . If v extended to
some vM ◦ ρh ∈ Vh , then M |= Th ∪ ρh Γ and M ̸|= ρh y, contradicting Γ |=h y. So v refutes h.
   (ii) Let v = u|F with u ∈ Vh∗ and F ⊆ D∗ finite, and let Γv := {x ∈ F : v(x) = 1} ∪ {∼x : x ∈
F, v(x) = 0}, a finite subset of D∗ (which is negation-closed). Suppose v extended to no member
of Vh . Then Th ∪ ρh Γv is inconsistent, since a model of it would induce an extension of v (using
Th ⊢ ρh (∼x) ↔ ¬ρh (x)). Pick x ∈ D∗ . Then Γv |=h x and Γv |=h ∼x, and both steps have their
occurrences in D∗ , so Γv |=h∗ x and Γv |=h∗ ∼x. But u makes Γv true, so by Lemma 10.13(ii) for
h∗ it makes both x and ∼x true, which is impossible. For coherence: if h were incoherent on
A ⊆ D∗ , then A |=h x and A |=h ∼x for x ∈ D∗ , hence A |=h∗ x and A |=h∗ ∼x, and T ∗ ∪ ρ∗ A
would be inconsistent.

Practice refutation is decidable because Stgh is. An object datum v refutes h iff Th ∪ ρh Γv is
inconsistent (notation of Lemma I.2), which is semi-decidable since ClRh is r.e.; paradoxes are
found by search. Each non-member of S g is refuted by a finite datum with a finite certificate,
and H is finite, so the budgeted version space equals S g after finitely many data and a finite
budget. Example 10.15 shows that survivors can have strictly weaker meaning.

Verification of Example 10.15. Both hypotheses are propositional (a fragment of first-order logic)
and share the reading; D∗ = Dh consists of occurrences read as p0 , ¬p0 , p3 , ¬p3 , and ∼ maps the
occurrence read as pi to the one read as ¬pi and back, so D∗ is negation-closed. R∗ consists
of the zero-premise steps ▷τ for τ ∈ T ∗ and all steps Π ▷ φ with Π finite and Π tautologically
implying φ; Rh consists of the tautological steps only. Then ClR∗ (Γ) is the set of tautological
consequences of Γ ∪ T ∗ and ClRh (Γ) that of Γ, so both hypotheses are first-order complete, with
Th = ∅.
    Let 1 ≤ g ≤ 3. Since Rh ⊆ R∗ , Stgh ⊆ Stgh∗ . Conversely, let Γ ▷ y be in Stgh∗ , via an
R∗ -derivation π of ρ(y) from ρΓ with at most g applications. If ρ(y) ∈ ρΓ, the step is in Stgh
with zero applications. Otherwise the last step of π is tautological, because axiom steps conclude
members of T ∗ , which are not readings of occurrences in D∗ . So π uses at most g − 1 ≤ 2 axiom
steps, and ρ(y) is a tautological consequence of ρΓ ∪ T ′ for some T ′ ⊊ T ∗ . We claim ρ(y) is then
a tautological consequence of ρΓ alone. Otherwise some valuation v of p0 , p3 satisfies ρΓ and


                                                    245
falsifies ρ(y) (all four formulas mention only p0 , p3 ). Let pi → pi+1 be a chain axiom missing
from T ′ , and extend v by v(pk ) := v(p0 ) for k ≤ i and v(pk ) := v(p3 ) for k ≥ i + 1. Every axiom
of T ′ is then of the form pk → pk+1 with both sides equal, so v satisfies T ′ ∪ ρΓ and falsifies ρ(y),
a contradiction. Hence the single tautological step ρΓ ▷ ρ(y) is in Rh , and Γ ▷ y ∈ St1h ⊆ Stgh . So
Stgh = Stgh∗ .
    (p0 ▷ p3 ) ∈ |=h∗ , since T ∗ implies p0 → p3 ; it is not in |=h , since p0 ̸|= p3 . So |=h |D∗ ⊊ |=h∗
and h ∈ / U ∗ . Every object datum extends to an h-admissible valuation, since Mod(T ∗ ) ⊆ Mod(∅)
gives Vh∗ ⊆ Vh ; and every A on which h∗ is coherent is h-coherent, since Th ⊆ T ∗ . So h survives
every presentation in the sense of Theorem 10.14(d), although h ∈        / U ∗ . At g = 4, the derivation
from p0 by the three axiom steps and one tautological step puts (p0 ▷ p3 ) in St4h∗ \ St4h , and
practice refutes h.

The nonstandard instance of Proposition 10.16 (modulo the cited transfer principle). Let ρ
read informal analysis into bounded sentences of a countable sublanguage of the ∈-language of
the superstructure V (R), with constants for the standard objects the practice can name, and let
R be first-order logic with bounded axioms true in V (R). With M = {V (R)} and M′ = {∗ V (R)},
Robinson’s transfer principle (Robinson, 1966), which rests on Łoś’s theorem, gives the hypothesis
of Proposition 10.16: R is sound for both structures, and they agree on every sentence in ρ(Dh ).
Boundedness matters: the two structures are not elementarily equivalent in the full ∈-language
(“iterated power sets of R exist for every finite length” fails at nonstandard lengths).
Proposition I.3 (ε-δ versus internal set theory). [T4 Prop 3.6, repaired] (modulo cited theorems
of Nelson) Let ρIST read informal analysis literally in Nelson’s IST (Nelson, 1977), with ev-

∀dx (dx ≃ 0 ∧ dx ≠ 0 → ξ)). Let Dst be the occurrences read as sentences with standard parame-

reduction algorithm assigns to ρIST (x). Then hW ≈Dst hIST .
    Outside Dst nothing is claimed: f (x) = N x with N unlimited is ε-δ continuous at 0 but
fails the literal reading ∀x (x ≃ 0 → f (x) ≃ f (0)) at x = 1/N . Nor is agreement of the g-step
relations claimed: if infinitesimal proofs are shorter, noise-free bounded-gap practice generated
by hIST refutes hW as a granularity hypothesis, leaving meaning unaffected. The proof uses
Nelson’s reduction algorithm and conservativity of IST over ZFC, with transfer for the standard
parameters.

Proposition I.4 (What numbers could not be). [T4 Prop 3.7] (modulo standard facts of ZF) Let Dar
be the occurrences of informal arithmetic sentences, read into the ∈-language via von Neumann
numerals (ρvN , n + 1 = n ∪ {n}) or Zermelo numerals (ρZ , n + 1 = {n}), with +, × defined
by recursion. Then (ZF, ρvN ) ≈Dar (ZF, ρZ ), although the readings differ on “1 ∈ 3”, which lies
outside Dar .

    The proof transports along the recursion-defined isomorphism given by Dedekind’s categoricity
theorem (Dedekind, 1888). Benacerraf (1965) thus becomes a non-identifiability theorem: practice
fixes ≈ on its domain and nothing else.

Proof of Proposition I.4. Let ωvN be the set of von Neumann natural numbers, with successor
SvN (x) = x ∪ {x}, and let ωZ be the range of the function z on ωvN defined by recursion,
z(0) = ∅ and z(SvN n) = {z(n)} (Replacement), with successor SZ (x) = {x}. ZF proves that both
(ωvN , ∅, SvN ) and (ωZ , ∅, SZ ) are Dedekind–Peano systems: the successor is injective, ∅ is not a
successor, and every subset containing ∅ and closed under successor is everything (for ωZ , by
induction along z). Define +• , ×• on each by the recursion equations. By Dedekind’s categoricity
theorem (Dedekind, 1888), provable in ZF, there is a unique f : ωvN → ωZ with f (0) = 0 and
f (SvN n) = SZ f (n); it is a bijection, and by induction it preserves + and ×.
    For an arithmetic formula φ(⃗v ) let φvN and φZ be its translations: quantifiers relativized
to ω• , and 0, S, +, × interpreted as above. By induction on terms and then formulas, ZF ⊢
∀⃗n ∈ ωvN (φvN (⃗n) ↔ φZ (f⃗n)). Atomic formulas use that f commutes with the operations and is
injective; connectives are immediate; for ∃m ψ use that f is surjective. So for closed arithmetic
x, ZF ⊢ ρvN (x) ↔ ρZ (x), and for Γ ∪ {y} ⊆ Dar closed, Γ |=vN y iff ZF ⊢ ρvN Γ → ρvN y iff
                                                                                V

ZF ⊢ ρZ Γ → ρZ y iff Γ |=Z y.

I.3   Objects versus paradoxes
Proof of Lemma 10.17. From the false conclusion, repeatedly move to a false antecedent (or link
source); stop when there is none. Each move goes one step down a dependency path, so there are
at most depth(α) moves, and only antecedents of visited lines are evaluated. Premises are true,
so the walk stops at an inference or link with true antecedents (or source) and false conclusion
(or target). If v = vM ◦ ρh with M ∈ Mh , a valid item would have a true conclusion in M .



                                                  247
   In the correction games, VS is the set of surviving hypotheses. A learner is deterministic; the
environment may choose the target adaptively, as long as some target is consistent with all its
answers, and an item is legal only if it is legal for such a target.

Proof of Theorem 10.19. (a) Announce the set of steps carried by more than half of the surviving
weight. Then (+) on s ∈      / At and (−obj) on s ∈ At each keep at most half of it, and h∗
always survives; so after M corrections w(h∗ ) ≤ 2−M w(H). With the uniform prior this gives
M ≤ ⌊log2 |H|⌋.
    (b) Fix r ≥ 1. A (−obj) item s ∈ At \ h∗ is also a legal (−bagr ) item B = {s}, and it
deletes the same hypotheses (h ∋ s, i.e. h ⊇ {s}). (+) items are common to both games. So
against any learner, the object environment’s moves are a subset of the bag environment’s, and
every bag-game strategy achieves in the object game at most its bag-game worst case. Hence
           (r)
Mobj ≤ Mbag . At r = 1 a legal bag is a set B ⊆ At with |B| ≤ 1 and B ̸⊆ h∗ , i.e. B = {s} with
s ∈ At \ h∗ , so the games coincide.
    (c) Let Ldim(∅) = −1, and for nonempty C ⊆ 2S let Ldim(C) be the largest d such that there
is a complete binary tree of depth d whose internal nodes are labelled by elements of S and
such that every root-to-leaf path is realized by some h ∈ C. A path is realized if, at each node
labelled s, it goes right iff s ∈ h (Littlestone, 1988). For s ∈ S write Cs1 := {h ∈ C : s ∈ h} and
Cs0 := C \ Cs1 . If Ldim(C) = d ≥ 0, then min(Ldim(Cs0 ), Ldim(Cs1 )) < d for every s. Otherwise
both subclasses would have trees of depth d, and a root labelled s above them would give a tree
of depth d + 1 for C.
     Upper bound. Announce At := {s : Ldim(VS1s ) ≥ Ldim(VS0s )}. A (−obj) item s ∈ At leaves
VS0s , and a (+) item s ∈/ At leaves VS1s . In both cases the remaining class is the one of smaller
Littlestone dimension, which is below Ldim(VS). The target always survives, so Ldim(VS) ≥ 0,
and there are at most Ldim(H) corrections.
     Lower bound. The environment maintains VS with a tree of depth d = Ldim(VS). While
d ≥ 1, let s label the root. If s ∈ At , it answers (−obj) s and commits to VS0s . This is legal:
any h ∈ VS0s has s ∈ At \ h, and VS0s ̸= ∅ because it contains the hypotheses realizing the
left subtree. If s ∈ / At , it answers (+) s and commits to VS1s . Either way the new version
space contains a subtree of depth d − 1. So every learner suffers at least Ldim(H) corrections,
and Mobj (H) = Ldim(H). This is Littlestone’s theorem, transcribed. Equivalence queries with
arbitrary hypotheses (Angluin, 1988) are the same game.

    On 248 random classes the exact minimax value Mobj equals the Littlestone dimension
(computed) (verification_checks.py, check V4).

Proof of Proposition 10.23. Mobj (H) = 1 means some first announcement A is such that every
legal feedback leaves a single hypothesis. A feedback item s against A (either kind) leaves exactly
the hypotheses h with s ∈ A △ h. The environment may return any s ∈ A △ h∗ for any h∗ ∈ H,
so the sets A △ h, h ∈ H, are pairwise disjoint. In the bag game, announce A. A (+) item s ∈   /A
lies in exactly one A △ h and pins the target. A bag B ⊆ A with |B| ≤ r leaves the h with
B ̸⊆ h, i.e. with B ∩ (A △ h) ̸= ∅. Each element of B lies in at most one such set, so at most
r hypotheses survive. Then announce the survivors one at a time. Any feedback against an
announced h ̸= h∗ deletes h: a (+) item s ∈ h∗ \ h deletes the hypotheses lacking s, and a bag
B ⊆ h with B ̸⊆ h∗ deletes the hypotheses containing B. So at most r − 1 further corrections
occur, at most r in all. (If |H| ≤ r, plain elimination costs at most r − 1.)

Proposition I.5 (Free barring nullifies objects; trivial). [T4 Prop 4.7] If barring object data is free,
objects constrain nothing: every hypothesis consistent with (P) and (C) can survive forever. If
objects are truthful and each barred datum costs c > 0 bits, a hypothesis that must bar m data
loses to h∗ in description length once m > (ℓ(h∗ ) − ℓ(h))/c.

Proof. If barring is free, (O) refutes nothing, and only (P) and (C) remain. With cost c, h scores
ℓ(h) + mc against ℓ(h∗ ), since truthful objects never force h∗ to bar.

Proof of Theorem 10.26. Refutations are sound, so a refuted set is incoherent. (a) I contains
every support and is strictly shortest. (b) A coherent c has no refutation; an incoherent c has
one of size k(c), found by every search with budget t ≥ k(c). (c) For t ≥ t0 , by (b), the unrefuted
members of R are exactly the coherent ones. (d) Normalizing wt does not change the arg max. For
every c ∈ R, covt (c)/∥wt ∥1 −cov∞ (c) =          i∈c (wt (i)/∥wt ∥1 −w∞ (i)) ≤ ∥wt /∥wt ∥1 −w∞ ∥1 → 0,
                                               P

where cov∞ (c) := i∈c w∞ (i). Let c∗ be the unique coherent maximizer of cov∞ , and γ > 0
                     P

its margin over the other coherent members (R is finite). Once t ≥ t0 and the ℓ1 distance is
below γ/2, c∗ has strictly larger coverage than every other coherent member, so REPt = c∗ .
Pointwise convergence alone would not suffice: the members of R are typically infinite, and
mass escaping along instances inside some c breaks the convergence of coverages. (By Scheffé’s
lemma, pointwise convergence of probability vectors to a probability vector is enough.) (e) Coh
is downward closed, so any superset of the incoherent c1 ∪ c2 is incoherent. If supp(wt ) ⊆ c1 ∩ c2 ,
then covt (c1 ) = covt (c2 ) = ∥wt ∥1 , and the lexicographic comparison reduces to ℓ.

Proof of Lemma 10.27. Membership of the menu formulas in the classes (Table 13):
   • POS: V, S, INT, UNI, PAIR;
   • STRAT ∩ Φ: V, EMP, INT, UNI, PAIR, DIFF, CMP;
   • SEP: INT, DIFF, ZR;
   • Z ∩ Φ: INT, DIFF, ZR, EMP, PAIR, UNI.
The formulas S, R and ZR contain x ∈ x and so admit no stratification.
    (F1) Comp(R) gives y with ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈      / x); instantiating x := y gives y ∈ y ↔ y ∈  / y,
hence ⊥.
    (F2) Let {u} be a one-element structure with u ∈ u. Every atomic formula (x = y or x ∈ y)
is true under every assignment, so every positive formula, built from atoms by ∧, ∨, ∀, ∃, is true.
Hence ∀x (x ∈ u ↔ φ) holds for every positive φ and all parameters, and y := u witnesses every
positive comprehension instance. Extensionality holds trivially.
    (F3) The finite and cofinite subsets of N form a countably infinite Boolean algebra FC; let
e : N → FC be a bijection and put x ∈ y : ⇐⇒ x ∈ e(y). For parameters a, b, the extensions of
the stratified menu formulas are N (V), ∅ (EMP), e(a) ∩ e(b) (INT), e(a) ∪ e(b) (UNI), {a, b}
(PAIR), e(a) \ e(b) (DIFF) and N \ e(a) (CMP). All are in FC, hence equal e(y) for some y.
Injectivity of e gives Extensionality.
    (F4) In the hereditarily finite sets with true membership, INT, DIFF and ZR define subsets
of a ∈ HF, which are in HF; EMP, PAIR and UNI define ∅, {a, b} and a ∪ b, which are in HF.
Extensionality and Foundation hold.
    (F5) POS ∪ Z and STRAT ∪ Z contain V and ZR. Comp(V) gives v with ∀x (x ∈ v);
Comp(ZR) with a := v gives y with ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈ v ∧ x ∈        / x), i.e. ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈/ x), and
(F1) applies. POS ∪ STRAT contains S and CMP. Comp(S) gives s with ∀x (x ∈ s ↔ x ∈ x);
Comp(CMP) with a := s gives y with ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈         / s), i.e. ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈ / x), and (F1)
applies.
    (F6) SEP ⊊ Z by the lists. S ∈ POS \ (STRAT ∪ Z), CMP ∈ STRAT \ (POS ∪ Z), V ∈
STRAT \ Z, ZR ∈ Z \ (POS ∪ STRAT), and DIFF ∈ Z \ POS. So the three classes are pairwise
incomparable.

Proof of Theorem 10.28. (i) is Theorem 10.26(a), since NC contains every support and is shortest.
(ii) is (F1); NC is the only incoherent member, so t0 is the size of that refutation. (iii) NC is
incoherent; POS, STRAT and Z are coherent (F2–F4); SEP ⊊ Z is coherent but not maximal;
and POS, STRAT and Z are pairwise incomparable (F6), hence all maximal. They are pairwise
jointly incoherent by (F5).
     (iv) By Theorem 10.26(c), for t ≥ t0 the learner REPt maximizes (cov, −ℓ) over the coherent
classes POS, SEP, STRAT and Z, whose description lengths increase in that order. Let W be
the total weight and supp the support, with all weights in the support positive; cov(c) = W
iff supp ⊆ c. Support ⊆ DC. STRAT and Z contain DC, so both have coverage W , and
STRAT beats Z on ℓ. POS has coverage W iff the support avoids DIFF and EMP; SEP iff
it avoids UNI, PAIR and EMP. The maximal coverage is W , and the shortest class achieving
it is selected: POS if it qualifies, else SEP if it qualifies, else STRAT. So STRAT is selected
iff the support meets both {DIFF, EMP} and {UNI, PAIR, EMP}, as claimed; the full support
DC selects STRAT. ZR ∈ supp ⊆ DC ∪ {ZR}. POS and STRAT miss ZR, so their coverage is
below W . Z has coverage W , and SEP does iff the support avoids UNI, PAIR and EMP. Since
SEP is shorter than Z, SEP is selected in that case and Z otherwise. The full support selects Z.
{ZR, V} ⊆ supp ⊆ DC ∪ {ZR, V}. No class covers everything. Weights outside the support are
0, and

                   cov(STRAT) = W − w(ZR),           cov(Z) = W − w(V),
                      cov(POS) = cov(STRAT) − w(DIFF) − w(EMP),
                      cov(SEP) = cov(Z) − w(UNI) − w(PAIR) − w(EMP).

So POS ties STRAT iff the support avoids DIFF and EMP, and is below it otherwise; SEP
ties Z iff the support avoids UNI, PAIR and EMP, and is below it otherwise. Recall ℓ(POS) <
ℓ(SEP) < ℓ(STRAT) < ℓ(Z). If w(ZR) > w(V), the maximal coverage W − w(V) is reached
by Z, and by SEP exactly when it ties Z; SEP is shorter, so SEP is selected then and Z
otherwise. If w(V) > w(ZR), the maximal coverage W − w(ZR) is reached by STRAT, and by
POS exactly when it ties STRAT, so POS is selected then and STRAT otherwise; for example
{INT, UNI, PAIR, ZR, V} gives POS. If w(ZR) = w(V), STRAT and Z both reach the common
maximum, POS and SEP reach it under their tie conditions, and the shortest class reaching it
wins: POS if the support avoids DIFF and EMP, else SEP if it avoids UNI, PAIR and EMP,
else STRAT. The full support DC ∪ {ZR, V} meets all of DIFF, EMP, UNI and PAIR, so Z is
selected iff w(ZR) > w(V), and ties go to STRAT.

Proof of Proposition 10.31. (a) A step s = (Γ ▷ y) ∈ A0 can be refuted only by a model of T
in which ρ∗ Γ holds and ρ∗ y fails; such a model exists iff s ∈   / |=T . By completeness of monster
presentation, s survives iff s ∈ |=T , so A∞ = A0 ∩ |=T . By Gödel completeness (Gödel, 1930),
each surviving step has a derivation, in any complete calculus C for T , of ρ∗ y from ρ∗ Γ. For an
argument chained from surviving steps, replacing each step by such a derivation and concatenating
yields a C-derivation of the ρ∗ -image of the conclusion from the images of the premises. This is
Lemma 10.6 with the derivations made explicit.
    (b) Here A∞ = {χ ▷ θ : PA ⊢ χ → θ}, which is r.e. but undecidable: with χ the sentence 0 = 0,
membership decides PA-provability of arithmetic sentences. Let C be a complete calculus for
PA satisfying the effectivity assumptions, and suppose A∞ ⊆ StgC for some g. Since StgC ⊆ |=PA
and A0 ∩ |=PA = A∞ , we get A∞ = A0 ∩ StgC , which is decidable because A0 and StgC are.
Contradiction.
                 S
    (c) Let A0 = j≤J inst(Sj ). Under schema-level selection with complete monster presentation,
Sj survives iff none of its instances is refuted, iff all its instances lie in |=T . For each surviving
Sj , the template πj instantiates to a derivation of each instance with at most g rule applications,
and its formulas have size at most |πj | times the size of the instance. Choosing the size bound
of Definition 10.2 to be at least maxj |πj | times the input size, every surviving step is in StgC .
The templates are finitely many derived rules of C, whose instances are the surviving practice.
Pure propositional schemas. Let S have metavariables A1 , . . . , Ak and mention no atoms, with
all instances valid. Its generic instance S[Ai := pi ], for distinct atoms pi , is valid, so it has a
derivation π in a complete propositional calculus with schematic rules. Applying the substitution
pi 7→ φi to every formula of π yields a derivation, with the same number of applications, of
S[Ai := φi ], because schematic rules are closed under uniform substitution. So π is a uniform
template. Failure in PA. Let θ(n) be ¬Prf PA (n, ⌜0 = 1⌝). Each instance θ(n̄) is a true statement
about a numeral, decided by a primitive recursive relation, and is therefore provable in PA (by Σ1 -
completeness, since PA is consistent). Suppose a template with a schematic letter for the numeral
instantiated to a derivation of θ(n̄) for every n. In a standard Hilbert calculus, substituting a
fresh variable x for the schematic letter turns it into a derivation of θ(x), and generalization
gives PA ⊢ ∀x θ(x), i.e. PA ⊢ Con(PA). This contradicts Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.
Calculus relativity. The argument needs rules closed under substituting a fresh variable for a
numeral. A complete calculus whose decidable library contains the zero-premise steps ▷θ(n̄)
for every n (a decidable set of true sentences) makes the schema uniformly 1-step derivable. So
uniform derivability, and hence the bound of (c), is relative to the calculus and its library.

Remark I.9 (Euclid: an analogy). [T4 §6.2] The notes suggest looking at Euclid, who “didn’t have
a full set of axioms”. If a “sharpening” of a diagram is any configuration near it, Manders’s
co-exact properties (Manders, 2008) are the super-determinate ones, his thesis that Euclid reads
off only co-exact properties is the analogue of RCH, and the system E of Avigad et al. (2009),
sound and complete for a class of sequents relative to ruler-and-compass semantics, plays the
role of the robust core of Theorem 10.30(c2). Perturbations are not sharpenings in the sense of
Definition 10.29, so this is an analogy only.




                                                 255
I.6   Language invention: what this section adds to the open problem
The hardest open problem of this section is the first problem of Section 14: affordable soundness
when the learner must invent language. A universal class (all computable (L, R, ρ) with a
                                                                                              ∗
description-length prior) restores realizability: Theorem 10.9 is sound with W ∗ ≥ 2−K(h ) , and,
information-theoretically, objects need at most K(h∗ ) corrections (Theorem 10.19(a), weighted
halving). But corrections are not soundness, since halving is bold; the sound verifier pays
                     ∗
escalations, Θ̃(2K(h ) ) on unstructured parts of the class (Theorem 10.10(c), Section 4), and
paradoxes cannot rescue it (Theorem 10.20). The problem is to find a class that is closed
under the definitional extensions history made (say, predicates defined by formulas of bounded
quantifier rank over the old language) and has escalation dimension, or correction complexity
with objects, polynomial in the target’s description length; or to prove that such closure forces
exponential antichains like the single-culprit class. Definitions are schemas, so the anti-unification
bounds of Section 5 may transfer to definition learning; whether proof-generated concepts can
be learned with O(depth) objects each is the concrete sub-question. Further open problems
from this section are the bag-price conjecture (Conjecture 10.24), misspecified practice (such as
Leibnizian infinitesimals), moving readings, a corpus test of RCH, and identifiability of meaning
without step-expressiveness.

The following results are proved completely in the main text: Propositions 11.4, 11.17, 11.20
and 11.30, Theorems 11.8, 11.14, 11.23 and 11.28, and Lemma 11.18. Proposition J.14

Throughout, w is a world, dom = dom Mw , and δ(F × G) := {λ[D:=µ] : λ ∈ F, µ ∈ G}.

J.1   Preliminaries on the filters of Definition 11.2
Lemma J.1 (Filter bases). (a) For c = DEF(D, λ◦ , G) with parent p, the family Bc = {δ(F ×
G) ∩ dom : F ∈ Fp (w), G ∈ G} is a filter base: X ∈ Fc (w) iff X ⊇ B for some B ∈ Bc , and c is
proper at w iff every member of Bc is nonempty. (b) For c = SUP(A) with parent p, X ∈ Fc (w)
iff X ⊇ F ∩ ∥A∥w for some F ∈ Fp (w). (c) If the parent filter is principal at a point λ, then in
(a) one may take F = {λ}: X ∈ Fc (w) iff X ⊇ {λ[D:=µ] : µ ∈ G} ∩ dom for some G ∈ G.

Proof. (a) δ(F1 × G1 ) ∩ δ(F2 × G2 ) ⊇ δ((F1 ∩ F2 ) × (G1 ∩ G2 )), and F1 ∩ F2 ∈ Fp (w), G1 ∩ G2 ∈ G.
So Bc is directed downward, and the filter it generates consists of the supersets (in dom) of
its members. It contains ∅ iff some member is empty. (b) Likewise {F ∩ ∥A∥ : F ∈ Fp (w)} is
closed under finite intersections. (c) If Fp (w) is principal at λ, every F ∈ Fp (w) contains λ, so
δ({λ} × G) ⊆ δ(F × G), and {λ} ∈ Fp (w).

J.3    Proofs for §11.3: eternalism and realizability
Proof of Proposition 11.9. (a) Take a classical derivation of ⊥ from the designated, classically
inconsistent A, in a Hilbert or sequent-step format. If every step instance in it were in C,
chaining the steps (a consequence relation is monotone and closed under cut) would give A ⊢C ⊥,
contradicting A-coherence. So some step instance is not in C. It is a substitution instance of
the most general instance of its schema, so by structurality that most general instance is not
in C either: the schema is not C-valid, and in particular C ̸⊇ CnCPC . (b) If p, ¬p ⊢C ⊥ for an
atom p, substituting α for p gives α, ¬α ⊢C ⊥, and weakening gives A ⊢C ⊥, again contradicting
coherence.

    The eternalist check summarized after Theorem 11.8 is the following.




                                                 257
Corollary J.2 (Eternalist coherence penalizes correct reasoning). [T3 Cor 2.2, rev.] Call a check
eternalist if it flags a set J of context-indexed judgments (c, Γ, φ) whenever { Γ → φ : (c, Γ, φ) ∈
                                                                                V

J} is unsatisfiable (context indices deleted, suppositions not added). It flags (i) every sound
reductio whose internal judgment (SUP(A), ∅, ⊥) is recorded; (ii) every sound idealization whose
stipulation contradicts a recorded root judgment (Proposition 11.5(a)); (iii) every pair of sound
contexts whose different answers to one query are both recorded (IPhO 2025 Theory Problems 2
and 3). If only the discharged (@, ∅, ¬A) is recorded, nothing is flagged: what is penalized depends
on how much of the reasoning is recorded.

Proof. The stripped sets are unsatisfiable: in (i) the judgment (SUP(A), ∅, ⊥) strips to ⊥; in (ii)
the stipulation and the recorded root judgment contradict each other; in (iii) Q = 1 and Q = 2
do, by standard names. Each judgment is nevertheless sound in its context (Proposition 11.4,
Proposition 11.5(a), and two proper contexts with different declarations). If only (@, ∅, ¬A) is
recorded for a sound reductio and the other recorded judgments are root judgments true at the
actual point, then ¬A also holds there, so the stripped set is satisfiable.

Proof of Corollary 11.15. (a) Let w be a world at which d is proper. The root is proper at

Proposition J.5 (Propagation of ⊥ along informative bridges). [T3 Cor 2.6, propagation clause] Let
c be a DEF context with an informative value-export bridge β cited for c, and suppose c ⊩ ⊥,
πc ⊩ σβ and πc ⊩ ωc are derived. Suppose R̂ contains ex falso (⊥ ▷ ψ) and the kernel of πc
is refutation-complete for finite sets (it derives ⊥ from any finite set of derived sentences that
has no model in K). Then πc ⊩ ⊥ is derivable by adding finitely many synthetic Exp instances.
Iterating along an anchoring chain reaches the root or a certified context. Moreover, fix a world
w at which πc is proper: (i) if c is proper at w, some item of c’s own derivation of ⊥ is unsound
at w; (ii) if c is improper at w, all of c’s own items are sound at w, and some item of the
derivation of πc ⊩ ωc is unsound at w; (iii) without the certificate premise in Exp, in case (ii),
if the derivation of πc ⊩ σβ is sound at w, some synthetic Exp instance is unsound at w: the
bridge applied to an ill-posed context.

Proof. Informativeness gives t1 , . . . , tk with {σβ , εβ (t1 ), . . . , εβ (tk )} unsatisfiable in K. Ex falso
gives c ⊩ Q = t̄i for each i, and k Exp instances give πc ⊩ εβ (ti ). Refutation completeness gives
πc ⊩ ⊥. Iterate for πc along the chain by which c entered Anc.
   (i) is the contrapositive of Theorem 11.14 in c. (ii) If c is improper at w, so is every context
below it (SUP filters refine their parent’s, and a DEF child of an improper context has the empty
generator δ(∅ × G) ∩ dom). Every set lies in an improper filter, so every Ax in c’s subtree is
true at w, and every Step, Imp and Exp instance concluding in that subtree is sound at w. By
Corollary 11.15(c), πc ̸|=w ωc , so by Theorem 11.14 the derivation of πc ⊩ ωc contains an item
unsound at w. (iii) Without ωc , suppose the derivation of σβ is sound at w, so πc |=w σβ . If
every synthetic instance were sound at w, then, as c |=w Q = t̄i trivially, πc |=w εβ (ti ) for all i,
and the finitely many truth sets would have empty intersection in the proper filter Fπc (w).

Proof of Theorem 11.16. (a) Let c′ = SUP(A) be the child of c in which the reductio is carried
out. By Lemma J.1(b), Fc′ (w) ⊇ Fc (w), and ∥A∥ ∈ Fc′ (w). So the premises Kc (true in c) are


                                                     261
true in c′ , A is true in c′ , and every c-sound instance has its truth set in Fc (w) ⊆ Fc′ (w), i.e. is
c′ -sound. By induction along the derivation (filter closure, Proposition 11.3(a)) every line is true
in c′ , so c′ |=w ⊥, and Proposition 11.4 gives c |=w A → ⊥, i.e. c |=w ¬A.
     (b) A derivation of ⊥ from Kc is also a derivation of ⊥ from Kc ∪ {B} for every B, in
particular for B = A and B = ¬A. The set of refuted sentences is then all sentences, whatever
the world.
     (c) From A → q and ¬A → q, case analysis gives q, contradicting ¬q; so K is unsatisfiable.
The valuation A = q = 0 satisfies {A → q, ¬q}, and A = 1, q = 0 satisfies {¬A → q, ¬q}. DA
derives q from A and A → q (modus ponens) and then ⊥ from q, ¬q; D¬A is the same with ¬A.
As a derivation (used premises, steps, conclusion), DA is identical to the reductio of A from the
consistent set K ′ = {A → q, ¬q}, and that reductio is sound because K ′ ∪ {A} is unsatisfiable.
So a test that depends only on the derivation and accepts every sound reductio from a consistent
premise set accepts DA ; likewise D¬A with K ′′ = {¬A → q, ¬q}. The accepted conclusions ¬A
and ¬¬A are jointly unsatisfiable. (hygiene.py checks these facts by truth tables.)
     (d) Suppose N |= A. Every leaf of the reductio is in Kc ∪ {A}, hence true in N ; every step
has true premises and an instance true in N , hence a true conclusion. So N |= ⊥, which is
impossible; thus N |= ¬A. If both A and ¬A were refuted by reductios whose instances N
satisfies, then N |= ¬A and N |= ¬¬A. For the counterexample: if c |= q, the zero-premise
instance ▷ q is c-sound; with Kc = {¬q}, every SUP(B) derives q and ¬q, hence ⊥ by the sound
instance q, ¬q ▷ ⊥, so every B is refuted; a model of ¬q exists but violates the instance ▷ q. For
existence: if c is proper at w, c |=w Kc and the finitely many instances used are c-sound at w,
then the truth sets of the members of Kc and of the instance conditionals φi → ψ all lie in
                                                                                   V

Fc (w); their intersection lies in Fc (w) and is nonempty, and any λ in it gives N = Mw (λ).
     (e) By (b), each A yields both labels; they are jointly unsatisfiable, a fixed function of Kc ,
and the same in every world. If Kc is consistent and R̂ logically sound, a model of Kc satisfies
every instance, so by (d) no A and ¬A are both refuted.

Theorem J.6 (Gronwall finite-horizon export). [T3 Thm 3.6, rev.: (b) new; Gronwall 1919] Let ẋ = f (x)
and ẏ = f (y)+g(t, y) have solutions on [0, T ], L > 0, and B(t) = |x0 −y0 |eLt + Lη (eLt −1). (a) If f
is L-Lipschitz on a set K containing both trajectories and |g(t, y(t))| ≤ η, then |x(t)−y(t)| ≤ B(t).
(b) Checkable form. Let Kr be the closed tube of radius r around x([0, T ]). If f is L-Lipschitz on
Kr , |g| ≤ η on [0, T ] × Kr , and B(T ) < r, then y stays in Kr and the bound of (a) holds.

    Every hypothesis of (b) concerns the computed idealized trajectory and explicit bounds, so
the parent can certify it; those of (a) concern the unknown trajectory. The bound grows with T :
qualitative long-time claims from structurally unstable idealizations do not export, finite-horizon
quantitative ones do.
